<margin>Why the books of Scripture are called canonical.</margin>
These are the books which, according to Divine promises, the infallible Judge—the orthodox Church—most recently proposed to us by decreed sentence in the Council of Trent as divinely inspired, and declared to be Sacred and Canonical. They are called *Canonical* from the "Canon" itself, which is the rule, or catalog, that lists the divine Books and determines them as inviolable. Here, appropriately:

<margin>Which books are proto- and deutero-canonical.</margin>
You may ask: 1. From where did the distinction between *proto-canonical* and *deutero-canonical* books arise?
**Response:** Although the Roman Church, the Mother and Teacher of all others, has always preserved the Apostolic tradition regarding the same catalog of Sacred Books that the Council of Trent proposed, and no Book of Scripture is listed in the Canon today which the sounder part of the ancient Churches did not approve by vote—as is evident from the Third Council of Carthage (attended by St. Augustine under Pope Siricius in the year 397); from the decretal letter of Innocent I to St. Exuperius, Bishop of Toulouse, in 405; from the Sixth Council of Carthage under Boniface in 419; from the Council of Rome under Gelasius in 494; and finally from the Council of Florence under Eugene IV in 1438; by all of whom our catalog of Holy Scriptures, which we have today, is presented in full conformity—nevertheless, because this tradition was not sufficiently known to all the Fathers and specific Churches during the centuries of the early Church shaken by the storm of persecutions, it happened that not everyone held the same opinion regarding the number and authority of the Sacred Books. Hence, those books which were always and everywhere held as written by God's inspiration are usually called *Protocanonical* <note>From the Greek "protos," meaning first.</note>; whereas those which were not immediately received as Divine in all Churches are called *Deuterocanonical* <note>From the Greek "deuteros," meaning second.</note>. Such books from the Old Testament include *Job, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Baruch, and the two books of Maccabees*, along with certain parts of *Esther* and *Daniel*. From the New Testament, they include the *Epistle to the Hebrews, the Epistle of James, the second of Peter, the second and third of John, and Revelation.* From this, it is clear that we must conclude with Augustine:

<column-break/>

<margin>The City of God, Book 15, Chapter 23.</margin>
> ,, The authority of the truthful scriptures has reached us through a most certain and well-known succession. <note>original: "Usque ad nos Auctoritas veracium scripturarum certissima & notissima successione pervehit."</note> For we have no other Canonical Books, whether of the Old or New Testament, than those which the Apostles approved and handed down to the Church.

<margin>1 Timothy 3:15.</margin>
The true Church of Christ makes us most certain of this Tradition; she is the *pillar and foundation of Truth*, and as she is governed by the Holy Spirit, it was impossible for her to have erred in a matter of the greatest importance, according to the clearest testimonies of the Eternal Truth. Truly, if in identifying human books—for example, which ones belong to Homer or Virgil, etc.—the rule is ancient tradition derived from their own times; how much more will the rule for the sacred Books be the testimony of the Church, brought down to us from the times of the Apostles? We do not dwell on the Jewish Canon regarding the deutero-canonical books; for it is not the Canon of the Hebrews, but that of the Church—whose faith is more certain and whose authority is greater—that makes the Scriptures canonical. Furthermore, the <term>synagogue</term> <note>Referring here to the Jewish religious leadership of the early centuries.</note> defined nothing regarding the deutero-canonical books of the Old Testament, nor was it accustomed to add other books to the ancient catalog of Holy Scriptures (which contained only those written in Hebrew), even though by its own confession those books were sacred and approved. The dispute is therefore finished, the case is settled, because the Church of God has pronounced judgment. Certainly, God demands from us this humble and religious subjection: that when we know a matter rests upon the testimony of His Church by divine revelation and the authority of faith, we understand that no reason for doubting remains, but we immediately submit our mind and soul to it. Wretched indeed are those, tossed about by every wind of doctrine, who refuse to receive the Church of Christ—whom the Divine Spirit instructs and moderates alike—as their Mother and Queen!

<margin>Formerly more books of Holy Scripture.</margin>
Question 2. Did more Sacred Books exist in the past?
**Response:** In the affirmative; for several are cited in various places of Scripture, such as the *Book of the Wars of the Lord* (Numbers 21:14), the *Book of the Just* <note>Often referred to as the Book of Jashar.</note> (Joshua 10:13), *Solomon's more than a thousand songs*, etc. (1 Kings 4:32), the *Books of Shemaiah and Iddo the Prophets* (2 Chronicles 12:15), the *Descriptions of Jeremiah* (2 Maccabees 2:1), etc. Since these can no longer be found anywhere, it follows that they perished through the injury of time. From this we ought to learn by what singular benefit of divine Providence the treasure of Sacred Books which is in our hands escaped the common shipwreck.

<margin>Concerning Apocrypha.</margin>
Question 3. Which books are called *apocrypha*?
**Response:** Just as <term>autographs</term> or archetypes are the original manuscripts themselves which the <term>hagiographers</term> <note>Sacred writers, from the Greek "hagios" (holy) and "graphos" (writer).</note> (e.g., Moses, Matthew, etc.) wrote with their own hand, and <term>apographs</term> are the copies themselves which we have today; so *apocrypha* are the opposites of these—namely, hidden books, or those of doubtful and uncertain authority, and therefore excluded from the Canon, such as the *third and fourth books of Ezra, the third and fourth of Maccabees*, etc.

---

### §. III.

->Division of the Sacred Books.<-

**B**esides the division into the Books of the Old and New Testament, which I suggested above, the Sacred Books are usually divided into *legal, doctrinal* (or sapiential), *historical*, and *prophetic*. The <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note> presents the five legal books of the Old Testament, in which, besides the moral laws,

<summary>This page lists the books of the Old and New Testaments in verse and explains the historical development of the biblical Canon, distinguishing between protocanonical, deuterocanonical, and apocryphal works.</summary>
<keywords>Canon of Scripture, Council of Trent, Deuterocanonical, Protocanonical, Apocrypha, Church Tradition, St. Augustine, Pentateuch, lost books of the Bible</keywords>

--- Page 31 ---
<meta>This page continues Ferdinand Kopf’s introduction to the Bible, moving from the list of books to their classification and the nature of divine inspiration.</meta>

->FERDINAND KOPF<-

or the precepts of Natural Law itself proposed more clearly and expressly; they also contain judicial and ceremonial laws. The judicial laws concerned the government and society of the Jews. The ceremonial laws, however, regarded the worship of God. For all the rites and individual ceremonies performed in sacrifices, in the selection of foods, and in the atonement for crimes, were so instituted by the best and wisest God that they might look toward the future Redeemer of the human race—from whose merit they would receive all their power and efficacy—as if they were certain figures and images. At the same time, they were intended to rouse the unrefined and stubborn minds of the Jews to the worship of the true God through the physical and sensory acts of Religion. Those called **Sapiential** <note>Meaning "Wisdom books."</note> are the books that prescribe the lessons of true wisdom and rules of conduct, such as Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Wisdom, and Ecclesiasticus; in the style of the Church, all of these are called the Books of Wisdom. The **Historical** books are those in which the history of events that occurred in the Hebrew Republic from the death of Moses is narrated. There are 16 such books: namely Joshua, Judges, Ruth, Kings, etc. The **Prophetic** books are those in which the future outcomes of events are primarily predicted, such as the Psalter and all the Books of the Prophets. From the New Testament, the **Legal** books are the four Gospels; the **Doctrinal** are the Epistles; the **Historical** is the Acts of the Apostles; and the **Prophetic** is the Book of Revelation. To this pertains another famous division of the Old Testament into the Law and the Prophets. By "the Law," the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note> or the five volumes of Moses are understood; by "the Prophets," however, all the remaining holy writers of the Old Testament are meant, according to that passage in Matthew 22:40: *On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets*; that is, whatever Holy Scripture teaches, commands, or forbids is referred to this double commandment.

### §. IV.
### On the Divine Inspiration of the Sacred Books.

By **F**aith it is certain that all the Canonical Books were divinely inspired, or rather, were written by the light of the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the Prophets; and for that reason, an equal authority and majesty must be granted to all of them. It remains only to discuss very briefly the mode of Inspiration—how the Holy Spirit, as the primary Author of Scripture, related to the Hagiographers <note>The "holy writers" or human authors of the biblical texts.</note> as His instruments.

The writings of the sacred authors can be referred to a two-fold class. In the first are those things which the Sacred Writers knew only by supernatural revelation, such as when they predict the future, or narrate past or present things that were otherwise unknown: for example, Moses in the history of the creation of the world, which he could not have known except divinely. In the other class are those things which they held by natural knowledge, such as when they report things seen with their own eyes, touched with their hands, or received from men

<margin>The Holy Spirit related to the scriptures in two ways.</margin>
worthy of trust: for example, the writer of the second book of Maccabees, and St. Luke in the Gospel and Acts. Hence, a two-fold mode can be conceived by which the Holy Spirit related to the writers: namely, *antecedently* and *concomitantly*. The Holy Spirit acted *antecedently* when He revealed future and other unknown things to the writers, either through an address or a sensory external vision, or through internal inspiration in ecstasy or while awake, so that they,

<column-break/>

understanding themselves to be moved by God through supernatural light and to be speaking the words of God, contributed nothing but the service of writing. He was present *concomitantly* in such a way that, by urging them to write down what they had received through sight or hearing, and by granting them a constant will to report the truth, He directed them by His presence and special assistance so that they would not be subject to forgetfulness or error. From this is gathered the distinction between these two modes; for in this latter one, the sacred Writer had to labor over those things he was writing and consider in what words he should bring them forth. Nor was it necessary for him to know that he was writing with the Holy Spirit assisting, just as in other inspirations of the Holy Spirit it is not always clear to us whether we are moved by the Holy Spirit or by a human spirit. Truly, that saying of St. Augustine also applies here: <margin>City of God, book XII, chapter 25.</margin> *God's hidden power, penetrating all things with an incorruptible presence, causes to be whatever is in any way, to whatever extent it is.* To establish divine authority for writings in this manner, it is sufficient that there be a later revelation, either given by Christ while active on earth, or by the Holy Spirit through the Apostles and handed down to the Church and proposed to us—namely, that such a book was written under the special assistance and direction of the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, that this latter mode of divine inspiration must be acknowledged in certain divine books can be persuaded by the following reasons: I. Where the sacred Writers reported things seen or heard, they did not need a new revelation of the Holy Spirit, but only His special direction. Just as God does not fail in what is necessary, so He does not overflow in what is superfluous. II. Holy Scripture itself places a difference between the Prophets and the sacred Historians. Thus, one frequently finds among the Prophets: *Thus says the Lord: the word of the Lord came to me, saying.* And the royal Prophet <note>King David.</note> testifies: <margin>2 Kings 23:2 <note>In modern Bibles, 2 Samuel 23:2.</note></margin> *The Spirit of the Lord has spoken through me, and his word is on my tongue.* On the contrary, St. Luke in the little preface to his Gospel history promises that he will write everything diligently, just as he had heard it from the mouths of the Apostles, who saw it themselves from the beginning; he does not say: "as I received it from God dictating." III. The writer of the second book of Maccabees uses a kind of excuse, saying that he should be forgiven if perhaps he had not attained all the parts of a good historian. From these points, and from the very diversity of phrasing, it is rightly inferred that the guidance of the Holy Spirit accommodated itself to the talent and skill of the sacred Writers, and many times left the style and mode of writing to them; and thus it happened that one wrote more elegantly than another, but none more truly.

### §. V.
### On the Obscurity and Eloquence of Scripture.

<margin>A two-fold cause of obscurity.</margin>
That Holy Scripture is obscure and difficult to understand in many places is manifest from experience itself, and is proven by so many commentaries published by the Fathers and others to illustrate it. This obscurity arises from two causes: from the things being discussed, and from the way the things are presented. The things are either the sublime mysteries of Faith, at whose light the weak eyes of mortals grow dim; or they are things which indeed fall under the senses...

<meta>catchword: fall</meta>

xxviii

# PROLEGOMENA

<column-break/>

[The previous discussion on the types of laws] fall away; but because we are so far removed in time, and because the customs of the ancients differ so much from our own and are not everywhere sufficiently understood, we are not infrequently shrouded in darkness. Regarding the style, difficulty arises from the very nature of the expression, in which all kinds of **tropes** <note>Figures of speech where words are used in a non-literal way.</note>, **figures**, **idioms**, **symbols**, and various uses of conjunctions and particles occur time and again. God, indeed, wishing to instruct us, deigned to accommodate His thoughts to the weakness of our speech in the Holy Scriptures and to assume a human way of speaking; yet because the Holy Scripture is the word of the Holy Spirit, speaking through both words and events, where often—from a fruitfulness unique to Scripture—the same sentences signify several different things, and where spiritual things are taught through physical ones, and eternal through temporal; it follows that such things, according to the common manner of divine Providence, could not have been delivered otherwise than obscurely. Truly, the Divine Majesty had to be hidden in a certain darkness, so that the brilliance of Divinity, tempered in this way, might shine upon the weak eyes of mortals.

But although Scripture may be obscure here and there, the most good God has provided that most things in the Scriptures are open, historical, easy, pleasant, and so wonderfully suited to us that there is no one who cannot draw from them what is sufficient for himself, provided he approaches the drawing of it with devotion and piety, as true Religion requires. We also have this advantage over the Jews: that now, with the veil of figures torn—under which the sacred volumes had been hidden—we understand Jesus Christ to be the end <note>The ultimate goal or fulfillment.</note> of the Law and the Prophets, and that the oracles were fulfilled in him. However, there is more than one reason why God willed the Scriptures to be partly sealed and closed. 

<margin>Reasons for this same obscurity</margin>
1. So that there might be some in the Church who teach, and others who learn. 2. To avoid boredom; for we tend to despise what is obvious and open, but we desire what is covered and hidden; we seek more ardently what is longed for, and we taste more sweetly what is found. 3. So that Holy Scripture might provide us with a useful and holy occupation. For, as Augustine famously noted in his usual way, just as God placed many things in the divine writings in the clearest light so that we might be fed and hunger might be driven away, so he wrapped many more in most useful obscurities so that we might exercise the skill of our intellect without any satiety. 4. So that the pride of the human mind, having been tamed, might learn to turn itself to the Father of lights, praying with the Psalmist: *open my eyes, etc. give me understanding, etc.* <note>original: "revela oculos meos &c. da mihi intellectum &c."</note> 5. So that the unworthy might be kept away. For just as Holy Scripture holds the attentive by its depth, feeds the great by its truth, and nurtures the little ones by its friendliness; so it mocks the proud by its height. 

<margin>Augustine's preface to Psalm 140. The Eloquence of Holy Scripture.</margin>
I summarize all these points again with the words of the greatest Doctor <note>Referring to St. Augustine.</note> saying: *There are in the Holy Scriptures deep mysteries, which are hidden for this reason, lest they become cheap; they are sought for this reason, that they may exercise the mind; and they are opened for this reason, that they may feed us.* These few words on obscurity shall suffice. Regarding eloquence, we may treat it just as briefly. Even though many things in the Holy Scripture are written in a common and simple style, it is proved to be supremely eloquent in its own kind from the fact that whoever writes or speaks aptly toward the goal he sets for himself—considering the circumstances of place, time, and the persons to whom he writes or speaks—must be judged absolutely eloquent. Hence, the infinite wisdom of God, since He has as His goal in Holy Scripture the moving of human souls

<column-break/>

toward those things which lead more surely to His glory and the attainment of eternal happiness, did not choose that painted and polished speech in which, for the most part, words rather than the things being said tend to tickle and move curious and delicate ears; but He chose a speech that was as simple as it was suitable to its purpose, and holier. He chose, I say, for the most part, the unrefined and rustic words of the law, but they are living, animated, sharp, penetrating to the depth of the spirit, and transforming the whole person with a wonderful power. Light reigns in the Holy Scriptures, by which the mind is illuminated; fire burns, by which hearts are set aflame; it is the Spirit who instructs teachable minds even without the help of art and eloquence. He who is wise is captured not by the glitter of words and the sweetness of speech, but by the excellence of the subject matter, the solidity of the thoughts, and the usefulness of the doctrine: *The word of God is not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the showing of the Spirit and of power.* 
<margin>1 Corinthians 2:4</margin>
Those for whom the diction of Holy Scripture is not sufficiently refined or elegant wish to presume to paint the Wisdom of God with the colors of art, and to adorn her like a girl with the little flowers of Rhetoricians. Yet let no one think that there is a total lack in Scripture of that eloquence which is usually commended not only for its intended purpose, but also for its delivery and elegant diction; for to say nothing of the royal Psalmist <note>King David.</note>, in comparison with whom all the little flowers of the Poets wither; nothing of Hosea, of the Epistle to the Hebrews, of Luke’s Gospel and Acts, etc.; who is there who does not feel in Isaiah alone a divine elegance of speech, a sublimity of thought, and eloquence? He exceeds the force of all Orators and converts hearts. When he rebukes, he does not so much speak as thunder, and he hurls lightnings of words. But when he proclaims the goods of the Church and the New Testament through Christ, nothing is more charming than his words, nothing more delightful. Likewise, in that Song of praise alone, *Let us sing to the Lord, etc.* <note>The Song of Moses from Exodus 15.</note> which Moses offered to God the Savior after the crossing of the Red Sea, the most learned Charles Rollin—who was for many years a Professor of eloquence at the University of Paris—demonstrated that he found such a force and majesty of absolute eloquence in all its parts as is sought in vain, in his judgment, in Homer or Virgil, in Demosthenes or Cicero.

### §. VI.
->Concerning the original language and version of Scripture.<-

It is well agreed among all that the Canonical Books of the Old Testament were first written mostly in **Hebrew**, while the New Testament was mostly written in **Greek**. If, however, the Hebrew language is taken strictly and as distinct from **Chaldaic** <note>A language closely related to Hebrew, often called Aramaic today.</note>, which indeed grew out of it, we must except the Books of Tobit, Judith, and parts of the books of Ezra and Daniel, which had been written in Chaldaic. Conversely, from the New Testament, the Gospel according to Matthew and the Epistle to the Hebrews were composed in Hebrew, or a version of it; for the **Syriac** language, arising from a mixture of Hebrew and Chaldaic after the Babylonian captivity, began to be the common tongue among the Jews. Not a few feel that the Gospel according to Mark and the Epistle to the Romans were written in Latin. However, while this opinion has great probability regarding the Gospel according to Mark, the reasoning regarding the Epistle to the Romans—

### FERDINAND KOPF. XXIX

Scripture

...already has its defenders. Therefore, these three languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—are to be looked upon as sacred, insofar as the word of God was first committed to writing in them. But in this context, the Hebrew language must be understood more broadly, as it also encompasses Chaldean and Syriac, just as the Church Fathers and various writers frequently do, having regard for the three states of the Jewish People: *before, during, and after* the Babylonian captivity. From this distinction of these three states, we also learn which language the Jewish people used in any given age, and how the deposit of the Sacred Books remained with them always, even though it was tossed about once and again by dire fates. For since the Holy Scriptures had suffered no small damage during the time of the captivity, Ezra—that great Reformer of the Jewish State and, as it were, another Moses raised up by God—collected them. He restored them according to the most reliable copies, substituting the Chaldean characters <note>The square-shaped letters used in modern Hebrew today.</note> in place of the ancient ones, which he left to the Samaritans. As for the claim that Ezra dictated all the Holy Books from memory (after they had been lost due to the wickedness of the times) to five scribes, I leave those people to defend it for whom the apocryphal book (specifically the Fourth Book of Ezra) provides a sufficient foundation for such a miracle. Certainly, we are taught by a perpetual series of traditions and authorities that, by the watchful eye of Divine Providence, it happened that no injuries of time could ever snatch away or destroy all the Holy Manuscripts from the hands of the Jews. Thus, even when the soldiers of Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king who persecuted the Jews in the 2nd century BCE.</note> impiously attacked the Sacred Books and burned as many as they could find, many copies were nonetheless withdrawn from their fury and, once the enemies were driven out, were most diligently sought out by Judas Maccabeus and kept in their original integrity. Regarding the various versions of the Holy Books into other languages, they can be reduced to three main types: Greek, Latin, and the vernacular or common tongue. There is no need for me to discuss the latter, since there can be as many versions as there are native languages belonging to each region. Among the translations from Hebrew into Greek, of which nine are counted, by far the most famous is the **version of the seventy** <note>The Septuagint.</note>. Because I am forced to be brief for the sake of this summary, I note the following regarding the history of this version:

1. When Ptolemy Philadelphus, the King of Egypt and a great lover of books, was burning with a great desire to adorn his noble Library at Alexandria with the writings of the Hebrews—which he had heard were divine—he sent ambassadors to Eleazar the High Priest. Having added gifts worthy of royal generosity, he obtained from him seventy-two doctors of the Law, most learned in both languages (Hebrew and Greek), to translate the Holy Books into Greek.

</margin>

Note 2. Although seventy-two men prepared this version (six from each tribe), it is called the *Septuagint* <note>original: "versio septuaginta"</note> because of the common biblical custom of rounding the number.

Note 3. We should prefer the common opinion of the Holy Fathers, by which these seventy-two Elders completed the translation of the Old Testament on the Island of Pharos within a period of seventy-two days. The King, to test their faithfulness, had shut them up individually in cells prepared for that purpose. They completed it

<column-break/>

in such a way that they agreed not only in their meanings but even in their words, as if there were only one translator, with the same Holy Spirit working in them all. Therefore, it is not at all surprising that the authority of this version was so great everywhere that even the Gentiles who were present recognized that the Scriptures had been translated by divine inspiration. Furthermore, Christ Himself and the Apostles frequently used this version when citing testimonies, and the Church of Christ received it as if it were the only one, as Augustine says of his own time.

Note 4. Many critics, along with Saint Jerome, challenge the manner of this version—especially regarding the separate cells—claiming the seventy worked not as Prophets but as translators gathered in one hall comparing their work, and that they did not translate all the books of the Old Testament, but only the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note>. But as the same Augustine remarks: "The Church of Christ judges that no one should be preferred to the authority of so many men chosen for such a great work; even if there had not appeared in them one Spirit, undoubtedly divine, but they had compared the words of their translation among themselves in the human manner, so that what pleased all of them might remain."

<margin>
The City

</margin>

The second Greek version is that of **Aquila of Pontus**, born in the city of Sinope.

The third is that of **Symmachus**, originating from Samaria.

The fourth is that of **Theodotion** of Ephesus. These three versions, which appeared in the second century of the Church, differ in their method of interpreting: Aquila, in his second more corrected edition, expressed it word-for-word; Symmachus expressed it sense-for-sense; while Theodotion walked a middle path between the two. However, all three, as Jerome says, were "Judaizing heretics" who concealed many mysteries of the Savior through deceitful interpretation. Indeed, Aquila, having become a Christian from a Gentile, refused to abandon judicial astrology when warned, was cast out of the Church, and defected to Judaism. Symmachus went from a Samaritan to a Jew, from a Jew to a Christian, and finally became an **Ebionite** <note>A member of an early Jewish-Christian sect that insisted on the necessity of following Jewish law.</note> heretic. Theodotion, after defecting first from the Church and then from the Tatian and Marcionite heretics, followed Aquila and likewise went over to the Jews. Nevertheless, his version—except for those parts he changed in the manner of heretics to defend his apostasy—was approved and preferred over the others.

<margin>
Preface
to Job.
</margin>

The fifth and sixth versions are by unknown authors; one was found at Jericho, the other at Nicopolis. From these places, each took its name.

The seventh is by **Saint Lucian the Martyr**, and the eighth is by the monk **Hesychius**. The former was most widely accepted in Greece, the latter in Egypt.

Finally, the ninth is by **Origen**, who, around the middle of the third century, through "adamantine labor" <note>An unshakeable or indomitable effort.</note>, produced the *Tetrapla*, *Hexapla*, and *Octapla*—that is, he displayed the four, six, and eight versions mentioned so far in as many columns as the page was divided into. Let these things said about the Greek versions suffice.

### §. VII.

#### Concerning our Vulgate.

<margin>Among the Latin versions, only two are truly famous: the *Itala* and the *Vulgate*.</margin>
Of the Latin editions—which according to St. Augustine were almost innumerable—I only need to note two. The first is that very ancient version called the *Itala*. Its author is unknown, but it was translated from the text of the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> for the Old Testament. It held the first place because it was more faithful to the original words while maintaining clarity of meaning. For this reason, it was accepted for common use in the Church until the time of Gregory the Great, around AD 590.

The second is our present-day *Vulgate*, which the Church of God has used for over a thousand years and will continue to use until the end of the age. Here is its origin and progress in brief: around the end of the fourth century, there was a great multitude of conflicting Latin versions. Furthermore, those among the faithful who were of Jewish origin <note>original: "Judaizque fidelibus"</note> were insulting Christians because they did not have the Scriptures drawn directly from the Hebrew source. Divine Providence deigned to provide the Church with a Doctor who, equipped with holiness of life, erudition, and skill in languages, was uniquely suited for such a great work.

<margin>Jerome, the Author of the Vulgate.</margin>
This was Jerome. Broken neither by labor nor by the jealousy of others, he translated most of the books of the Old Testament from the still-clear Hebrew sources with the highest level of faithfulness—a task no one before him had attempted. Furthermore, at the urging of Pope Damasus, he corrected the New Testament, which had been marred by errors creeping in through sleepy scribes, and restored it to the purity of the Greek text. I said *most* of the Old Testament, for Jerome did not translate the books of Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus <note>Sirach</note>, Baruch, or the two books of Maccabees, either because they no longer existed in Hebrew or because he was prevented by death. Therefore, these books were retained in our Vulgate from the old *Itala* version. Similarly, the Psalter we use today was kept from the edition of St. Lucian as amended by Jerome; this was done to avoid confusion, since all the churches were already accustomed to it in the Divine Office and in chant.

Furthermore, a second success followed St. Jerome's version, which even the Hebrew teachers admitted was truthful. After it had been used for some time alongside the old *Itala*, shortly after Gregory the Great, it was accepted by the silent consensus of all the Fathers and Doctors. By the middle of the 7th century, as Isidore of Seville testifies, all churches everywhere were using it. This was because it was truer in its meaning and clearer in its words, responding more properly and faithfully to the Hebrew source from which it was derived. Finally, it received the height of authority when the Church of God, 

<margin>Session IV. AD 1546</margin>
gathered in the Holy Spirit at the Council of Trent, declared this version to be *Authentic* by a public and solemn judgment. By a broad decree, the Council commanded that it be printed in as corrected a form as possible. This was happily achieved through the pastoral care of two Popes, Sixtus V and Clement VIII. Thus, through the Vulgate, the variety of Latin interpreters—and the doubt that had arisen from it—was removed.

<margin>Possevino in the *Bibliotheca*, Book II, chapter 22.</margin>
The Vulgate stands as a column of truth and a harbor where we ought to dock from the waves of disagreeing versions. For since it is "Authentic"—that is, of full and infallible authority in matters pertaining to Faith and good morals—it successfully expresses the meaning intended by the Holy Spirit in conformity with the originals. It is therefore rightly defended by the most serious and 

<column-break/>

<margin>The Authority of the Vulgate.</margin>
highly skilled linguists. As things now stand, in questions of faith and morals, one should not appeal from the Vulgate to the Hebrew or Greek manuscripts; rather, the Vulgate should not be corrected by the Hebrew and Greek codices if they happen to disagree, but those codices should be corrected by the Vulgate. 

Indeed, even if it must be granted that the Vulgate was not preferred over the Hebrew and Greek sources in the Decree of Trent (since no mention was made of them, and sources, as long as they are pure, are always to be preferred to or at least equaled with the streams, because all the purity of the streams flows from the purity of the sources), it is nonetheless the sounder advice, as 

<margin>Melchior Cano, *On the Places of Theology*, Book II, chapter 14.</margin>
Cano and others warn, to drink clear water from purified pools than from a muddied spring. A pure stream can and should be preferred to muddied sources by a right and prudent judgment. In the age of St. Jerome, there was a necessity to return to the sources because they were not yet so muddied, and because of the great discord among Latin manuscripts at that time, which could not be resolved unless the Latin copies were compared to the Greek and Hebrew. But that variety has now ceased, and there is a single agreement among all Latin copies. 

However, no one will easily deny that the reliability of the Hebrew and Greek manuscripts wavers here and there today,

<margin>Concerning the reliability of the Hebrew and Greek manuscripts.</margin>
if they look closely and without bias at the circumstances, the changes over time, the neglect and ignorance of scribes, and even the characters themselves. I will remain silent about the Jewish Masoretes or Grammarians, who first added vowel points to the text in AD 476 (or according to others, AD 512) during a great assembly held at Tiberias. Certainly, Bonfrère, among others, strives to show with examples that in said assembly—where the Babylonian Talmud was also produced—certain passages regarding the Christian religion were maliciously corrupted. Among others, in Psalm 21 <note>Psalm 22 in modern numbering</note>, instead of "they pierced my hands," they erased a letter and substituted "like a lion" <note>original: "foderunt manus meas" vs "sicut leo". This refers to the debate over the Hebrew word *Ka’ari* vs *Ka’aru*.</note>. Likewise, commentators on John chapter 8 note that many Greek New Testament manuscripts have been corrupted. 

Therefore, the Hebrew and Greek text circulated today is not as certain as the Vulgate. We are taught by the infallible authority of the Church that the Vulgate's manuscripts—drawn from sources that were still pure, and preserved with such consensus by so many churches and through so many centuries of common care—have not had, and could not have, any corruption introduced regarding faith and morals. From this, however, it does not follow that inspecting the sources is rejected; for no prudent person would deny that this has great power to illuminate what the translator sometimes rendered less clearly. Nor does the "Authenticity" of the Vulgate require that there be nothing in it that could have been expressed more clearly or distinctly. It is also freely granted that the translator was more concerned with the faithfulness of the version than with elegance of style or the minutiae of grammarians. But the degree of the Vulgate’s faith and authority above all others is one thing; the degree of utility that arises from inspecting the sources to understand the Vulgate is quite another.

<summary>This page discusses the history of the Latin Bible, tracing the transition from the Old Latin (Itala) to Jerome's Vulgate, and defends the Vulgate's supreme doctrinal authority as established by the Council of Trent. It argues that while original Hebrew and Greek sources are theoretically superior, the Vulgate is a more reliable "pure stream" than the "muddled" manuscripts currently available in those languages.</summary>

FERDINANDUS KOPF.

# LECTURE II.

## CONCERNING THE USE OF HOLY SCRIPTURE.

->§. I.<-
->What the fourfold sense of Scripture is.<-

<margin>The multiple senses of Holy Scripture.</margin>
**F**irst, regarding the proper use of Scripture, the most important point is its "sense" or meaning; the entire matter hinges on this. For we must not think that the Gospel consists merely in the words of the Scriptures, but in their sense; not on the surface, but in the marrow <note>original: "non in superficie, sed in medulla"</note>; not in the leaves of the words, but in the root of reason. Generally speaking, the "sense" of Scripture is that which the words signify by the intention of the Holy Spirit. It is divided into the *literal* and the *mystical*. The literal sense—also called the *historical* sense, because it primarily prevails in the historical books—is that which the words themselves, whether taken literally or metaphorically, present directly and immediately to the reader. Indeed, common human usage dictates that words are not always used in their primary, original meaning, but are often used figuratively or through metaphor. Therefore, for the sake of clarity, the literal sense is correctly divided into two types: the *proper* literal sense, when words are taken in their basic meaning, and the *figurative* literal sense, when words are taken improperly or through metaphor (understanding metaphor here to include any figure of speech). Some also call this the *parabolic* sense, because it is found everywhere in parables, the use of which was familiar to the inhabitants of Palestine. For example, in Matthew 3: *Christ will clear his threshing floor: and he will gather his wheat into the granary, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.* In this passage, through similarity and figure of speech, the "threshing floor" signifies the Church, the "wheat" the elect, the "granary" heaven, and the "chaff" the reprobate. Likewise, in the same chapter: *He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.* Here again, "fire" is taken metaphorically for grace, charity, and other gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which the soul is purified, inflamed, and drawn toward heavenly things as if by fire; and so it is in countless places. For whenever words taken literally would produce something absurd—that is, something contrary to Faith or good morals—they must be understood in the figurative or metaphorical literal sense, such as when Christ is called a *Lamb, a Lion, a door, a rock, a vine*, etc. Whenever Scripture speaks of God in human terms, otherwise "the letter would kill." <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6: "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life."</note> From this, it is easily concluded that no place or text can be found in Scripture that does not have some literal sense, whether proper or figurative.

<margin>When the figurative sense is to be preferred.</margin>
The *mystical sense* is that which is indicated by the Holy Spirit through the actual things signified by the words. It is called "mystical" or "spiritual" because, like a spirit, it is hidden and lies within the things themselves, like a kernel within a shell. It differs from the literal sense because, as stated, it is not gathered directly from the words, but from the things themselves; nor can it exist without the literal sense being presupposed as its foundation and root. On the other hand, the literal sense very often exists without a mystical one; there are also many passages of Scripture that do not even admit a mystical sense, such as: *You shall love the Lord your God* or *I and the Father are one*, etc. The mystical sense has three types,

<column-break/>

corresponding to the three theological virtues <note>Faith, Hope, and Charity</note>. If it pertains to Faith or things to be believed, it is *allegorical*; if it pertains to Charity or things to be done, it is *tropological* or *moral*; if it pertains to Hope or things to be hoped for, it is *anagogical*. This is captured in the well-known verses:
> The Letter teaches what happened; Allegory what you believe;
> The Moral what you do; Anagogy where you are going.
<note>This famous medieval mnemonic rhyme helped students remember the four senses of Scripture.</note>

<margin>John 3.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 12.</margin>
For example: *The bronze serpent raised up by Moses* and *Jonah saved for three days in the belly of the whale*, besides their literal or historical sense, also provide a mystical allegorical sense; for the former signified Christ hanging on the cross for the salvation of the world, and the latter signified the Lord’s burial and Resurrection. *Ishmael and Isaac*, the sons of Abraham, allegorically designated the two testaments. *Ishmael*, expelled from his father’s house with his mother Hagar the bondwoman, prefigured the Synagogue, finally rejected for its crimes; while *Sarah* and *Isaac* prefigured the Church and the elect children of the New Testament. *You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain* means, in the mystical tropological sense, that he who serves the altar should live from the altar. The *Promised Land* or Palestine, flowing with milk and honey, *anagogically* denoted the eternal dwelling place of the living. From these points:

<margin>Galatians 4.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 9.</margin>
<margin>Hebrews 11.</margin>
You may conclude 1: That the mystical sense is most clearly founded upon Scripture itself, and it is unique to Scripture alone to have both "letter" and "spirit" simultaneously; for it belongs to the Divinity alone to ordain and establish actual historical events to signify other things.

You may conclude 2: That there are texts, though rare, in which all three types of the mystical sense can be found; others admit two, or only one. For example: *Jerusalem* represents the Church militant allegorically; the Church triumphant *anagogically*; and the faithful soul *tropologically*. The *Sabbath* allegorically signifies Christ’s rest in heaven; tropologically, it signifies rest and cessation from sins. Things frequently said in Scripture about the earthly *Sion* pertain to the allegorical and anagogical senses; things handed down concerning legal impurities and purifications pertain to the tropological sense. And thus one must reason proportionately about other Old Testament types and figures foreshadowing the New, such as *Noah’s Ark, the Egyptian bondage and the passage through the Red Sea, the Manna, the Paschal Lamb, and various sacrifices*, the Kingdom of David and Solomon, etc., the mystical sense of which I believe is hidden from no one.

Note: The Holy Fathers and some interpreters do not always accurately distinguish these aforementioned senses; instead, they sometimes call the literal sense (which we call figurative or metaphorical) "mystical" due to a certain similarity with the strictly mystical sense. Likewise, they may simply call the strictly mystical sense "figurative," and refer to every mystical meaning as an *allegory*.

---

->§. II.<-
->Several questions concerning the sense.<-

<margin>Are there sometimes multiple literal senses?</margin>
**Y**ou may ask 1: Are there sometimes multiple literal senses even in one and the same passage of Scripture? Answer: The common opinion of interpreters, following Augustine and Thomas Aquinas, holds that there are. For such a great abundance of truth befits the Majesty of God, so that many different things may be comprehended in a few words. The Hebrew language was particularly suited for this, as it is easy for the same word to often have multiple meanings...

<summary>This page explains the fourfold method of biblical interpretation, distinguishing between the literal sense (proper and figurative) and the mystical sense (allegorical, tropological, and anagogical). It provides classical examples, such as Jerusalem and the bronze serpent, to illustrate how one text can contain multiple layers of meaning.</summary>
<keywords>hermeneutics, literal sense, mystical sense, allegory, tropology, anagogy, biblical interpretation, fourfold sense, figurative language, types and figures</keywords>

--- Page 36 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the historical background of the biblical text to the methodology of its interpretation. It specifically examines the "plurality of senses"—the idea that a single passage of the Bible can have multiple layers of meaning intended by God.</meta>

<page-num>xxxii</page-num>
->PROLEGOMENA<-

...can also mean several things, and could, whether the writer understands all these things or not.

<margin>Regarding Hebrews 1:5.</margin>
Those words of the eternal Father to the Son, *I have begotten you today (Psalm 2)*, signify the day of eternity and eternal generation; the day of the incarnation; and the day of the Resurrection. <margin>Hebrews 5:5.</margin> <margin>Acts 13:33</margin> *Psalm 8: You have put all things under his feet* is indeed said with excellence regarding Christ in *Hebrews 2*, but also regarding mankind in general, as is clear from the context. That passage from *Isaiah 52: Who shall declare his generation?* <note>original: "Isa. LII." This is usually cited as Isaiah 53:8 in modern Bibles.</note> is commonly accepted as referring to both his divine and human nature, for both are inexpressible. A few things said literally about Solomon and Cyrus also apply literally and primarily to Christ; what is said of Antiochus applies to the Antichrist; and no one is ignorant that what is said of the destruction of Jerusalem pertains to the end of the world. Finally, in those words of the Lord’s Prayer, *our bread* etc., besides the sustenance of the body, one can also rightly understand the food of the soul—the Eucharist, grace, and the Word of God. Likewise, in the words *I am with you* etc., who would deny that this can be understood to mean simultaneously through the Eucharist, through grace, through Doctrine, and through protection? From this, however, it should not be inferred that such multiple meanings occur everywhere in Scripture; rather, no text should be asserted as having them without sufficient reason, such as: 1. Scripture itself, when it clearly presents the same words in another sense in a different passage; 2. The common interpretation of the Church or the Fathers. For multiple senses of the same passage, which some interpreters occasionally offer, are indeed good and not to be despised if they do not deviate from the proposed literal meaning, yet they are not certain, but only probable.

*Note:* This plurality of senses is not opposed to one another, nor does it bring about ambiguity or the danger of deception, because it should be accepted cumulatively, so that each sense is true. The truth of one does not destroy the truth of the other.

<margin>The sacred writers did not always intend a double sense.</margin>
**Q. 2.** Did the Sacred Writers <term>Hagiographi; literally 'holy writers,' referring to the human authors of the Bible</term> know all such senses regarding the same passage? **R.** Although there is no sufficient reason to deny it, it was not necessary for them to understand every sense. For it was enough that the Sacred Writer conceived one sense in his mind and intended to express it; the Holy Spirit could reserve the other senses to be revealed in His own time. This is evident because it is not contradictory for the Holy Spirit to dictate something to a writer such that the writer either does not understand what he is writing, or intends something far different from the intention of the Holy Spirit. In spoken prophecy, there is a very clear example of this in *John 11:50*, where Caiaphas is said to have prophesied without understanding his own words prophetically. If this is the case in spoken prophecy, there seems to be no reason why it could not happen in written prophecy. Since the entire infallibility of Scripture, as well as its legitimate sense, proceeds not from the secondary author and instrument (who is the writer), but from the primary Author, the Holy Spirit, who can simultaneously intend and signify several things with the same words or objects...

<column-break/>

...in this fruitfulness of senses consists, in part, the wondrous and never-exhausted depth of Scripture. Furthermore, if several things can be signified by the same objects (as was demonstrated in the preceding section regarding the mystical sense), why not also by words? For objects are no more suited to signify multiple things than words are. But to remove all doubt, let Scripture itself be heard.

<margin>When the mystical sense has the power of proof.</margin>
**Q. 3.** Does the mystical sense also have the power to prove a point? **R.** If it is established that a sense is truly mystical, and consequently intended by the Holy Spirit, it is just as valid for proof as the literal sense. However, this must be established for us in the way I mentioned regarding the plurality of senses in the same passage: namely, either from Scripture itself or from the declaration of the Church. Because this happens more rarely, it is safer to adhere primarily to the literal sense. For this sense, as the solid foundation of the other senses, is more open and obvious, as it is the one to which the very meaning of the words and the entire context lead. Therefore, the boldness of those who, being ignorant of the literal sense or wishing to ignore it, daringly offer mystical senses as if from an oracle <note>original: "quasi ex tripode" – a reference to the tripod of the Delphic Oracle</note> is not to be tolerated. They devise I-know-not-what allegories in almost every passage of Scripture and do not fear to thrust them forward as the hidden Sacraments of the Church. I said *primarily*; for those things which we do not see fulfilled literally must certainly be taken according to the spirit. Truly, here too one must walk a middle path; the mystical sense should not be rejected when sufficient authority suggests it. To do so would be to delight in the husk and throw away the kernel; because sometimes the spiritual sense, although it is always founded upon the literal and presupposes it, is the chief sense and the one primarily intended, as is clear in *Exodus 12:46*: <margin>John 19:36. 1 Corinthians 9.</margin> *You shall not break a bone of it* and *Deuteronomy 25:4: You shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain on your floor.*

*Note:* Scripture is also fulfilled in the mystical sense, as is clear from the words of Christ in *Luke 24:44 [cited as 25 in text]: All things must be fulfilled which were written in the law of Moses, and the Prophets, and the Psalms concerning me.* In these, many things were predicted about Christ in the spiritual sense.

<margin>The New Testament allows for mystical exposition.</margin>
**Q. 4.** Is there also a mystical sense in the New Testament? **R.** Yes. Because even the New Law is a figure of the future glory that will be revealed in us. Thus, Christ’s Resurrection allegorically figured our own; for where the glory of the Head has gone before, there the hope of the body is called. Tropologically <term>The tropological sense is the moral or ethical application of a text to the life of the believer</term>, however, it signifies our spiritual resurrection to the life of grace, just as Christ’s Ascension signifies our way of life in heaven and the elevation of our minds to heavenly things. Likewise, through the blood and water from Christ’s side, the Sacraments of the New Law are taught; <margin>Matthew 14.</margin> through the little boat tossed by the waves, the winds of temptation, and the storms of persecution (by which Peter’s boat, the Church, was to be shaken but not submerged); <margin>John 13.</margin> through the washing of feet, the purity of heart with which one must approach the table of the Lord, as well as the duties of humility and mutual charity are taught. Finally, the interpretation <note>original: "exegesis"</note> or exposition of the Holy Fathers warns us that every action of Christ is our instruction, and the very deed of the Word is a word for us. However, as I noted above, it is permitted for no one to allegorize without a sufficient foundation, and this must be observed most strictly in the New Testament, where it occurs much more rarely than in the Old Testament. For the Old Testament abounded in allegories, figures, and symbols representing the things of the New Testament precisely because its goal was to lead the people of God to Christ, like a schoolmaster <note>original: "Pædagogus"</note>. But what the Old Testament announced, the New exhibits. *Truth puts the shadow to flight; light eliminates the night.*

<summary>This page explores the multi-layered "senses" of Scripture, arguing that the Holy Spirit can intend multiple meanings (literal and mystical) within a single text. It cautions that while the literal sense is the primary foundation for doctrine, the mystical sense is valid when supported by Scripture or Church tradition, particularly in how the Old Testament foreshadows the New.</summary>

This page continues the methodology of interpretation, defining the "accommodated sense" and providing rules for determining the "literal sense."</meta>

<page-num>XXXIII</page-num>
->FERDINAND KOPF<-

<column-1>

<margin>
The meaning of the accommodated sense.
</margin>
**Q. 5. What is the <term>accommodated sense</term>?** <note>Also known as "accommodation," this is the practice of applying a biblical verse to a situation or person the original author did not have in mind.</note> Answer: It is when the words of the sacred text, beyond the author’s original intent, are transferred and adapted to signify something else. Therefore, it is not strictly a "sense" of Scripture because it was not intended by the Holy Spirit; rather, it is a mere application and imitation of the words of Scripture to signify something else conceived and intended by a human being. From this it follows that this sense is not valid for proving doctrine, and therefore, where matters of Faith are concerned, it should by no means be employed.

<margin>
It can, however, be useful,
</margin>
However, its use can be beneficial when—following the example of the Church—it nourishes the well-founded devotion of the faithful, such as in contemplating the Passion of the Redeemer or in praising the merits of the Saints. Thus, things said in the Scriptures regarding Wisdom, or the sanctity and glory of the Church, are deservedly attributed to the glorious Virgin Mary; for she is the Mother of God, the Seat of Wisdom, full of grace, and by far the most excellent among all members of the Church.

<margin>
but it must be used with caution.
</margin>
The use of accommodation must therefore be circumspect. This is achieved if the application is fitting to the subject and if regard is given to gravity and decorum, so that nothing from the divine words is brought forward that is not heard seriously, piously, and usefully. For this reason, the Holy Council of Trent <note>An ecumenical council of the Catholic Church held between 1545 and 1563.</note> sought to restrain the rashness of those who, contrary to all reverence due to the divine Scriptures, do not shrink from twisting and sacrilegiously profaning sacred texts for the sake of witticisms and jokes, etc., through a very grave decree.

*Note:* The Sacred Writers of the New Testament do not use words brought from the Old Testament in an accommodated sense; rather, they produce them in the sense intended by the Holy Spirit, proving that the oracles of the Prophets which they cite have been fulfilled. For what was not predicted and intended by the Holy Spirit through the Prophets cannot be said to have been "fulfilled."

### § III. Three Rules for the Literal Sense.

Rule 1. The words of Scripture are to be taken properly and literally, nor should one resort to a metaphorical sense unless something absurd—that is, something repugnant to Faith or good morals—would follow from the words if taken literally. Thus, because Scripture teaches and sound reason dictates that it is a sin to mutilate oneself, it follows that the passage in *Matthew 18: If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off, etc.* and the other in *Chapter 19: There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven*, are figurative expressions. In the latter case, the discourse concerns a purpose or vow of chastity; in the former, it signifies that everything which would be a cause or occasion of spiritual ruin must be fled and cast away, even if it is joined to us by blood or friendship, or is most useful or precious. And so it is in countless places. For the figurative or metaphorical literal sense occurs very frequently in Holy Scripture, as I have already noted above.

Rule 2. Careful attention must be paid to who is speaking in the Scriptures, and to whom; likewise at what time, in what place, and for what purpose something was written. Thus, in the Psalms, several speaking personas are often introduced without this being openly indicated. The Prophets, prophesying about the State or the Church, say things that do not pertain to all its members, but some to this part and some to that. They are also frequently accustomed to digress from temporal things to spiritual things, from a <term>type</term> <note>A "type" is a person, event, or thing in the Old Testament seen as a foreshadowing of something in the New Testament.</note> to the
</column-1>

<column-break/>

<column-2>
reality overshadowed by that type, so that the words are to be understood not of the type, but of the reality figured through it. For example, when they deal with the people of Israel, being filled with a certain greater light, they secretly turn their speech to the spiritual Israel, or the Christian people. And while they rail against the crimes of their own time and predict punishments, they suddenly begin a discourse about the Christ who is to come, mixing in joyful things and offering comfort. Likewise, they have a habit of designating the plagues of the world, regions, and cities according to the position they hold with respect to Palestine or Jerusalem. Hence, "the sea" denotes the West, because the Mediterranean Sea is to the West of Palestine. "The right hand" signifies the South, and "the left hand" the North, because such is the orientation of parts for a person turning their face toward the East. To this also belongs that passage in *Jeremiah 1:14: From the North evil shall break forth, etc.*, that is, from Babylon. Thus, if all things are restored to their proper places, causes, and times, things that seemed obscure become plain.

Rule 3. The text whose meaning is being sought must be carefully compared with what precedes and follows it. For the genuine literal sense is that with which the preceding and following parts rightly agree. Thus, the connection and context teach that in those words of *Psalm 17 <note>original: "Psalm. XVII." In modern Bibles using the Masoretic numbering, this is Psalm 18:25-26.</note>: With the holy you will be holy, etc.*, the subject is not good or bad company, but David speaking to God in this sense: "With a holy, pious man of an upright and sincere heart, O God, you act likewise piously and mercifully, by granting good things and removing harmful ones; but with the perverse, wicked, and deceitful, you will conduct yourself otherwise and vice-versa, and you will maintain a manner foreign to your kindness, namely by deserting and severely punishing them." Similarly, in *Psalm 38 <note>Psalm 39:3 in modern numbering.</note>: In my meditation a fire shall flame out*, the discourse is not about the fervor of devotion and the fire of charity, but of religious indignation against sinners. Likewise, *Isaiah 1:6: From the sole of the foot even to the top of the head, there is no soundness in it.* This does not concern the Passion of the Lord (which the Prophet describes elsewhere like an Evangelist), but the Synagogue as a political body corrupted from the lowest to the highest. Brevity forbids bringing forward more examples. Indeed, this rule cautions lest the words of Scripture be cited many times in a sense not their own.

### § IV. Canons for Interpretation Itself.

Canon 1. Scripture must be interpreted according to that sense which the Holy Mother Church has held and holds, to whom the possession of Holy Scripture is so proper that adversaries put their sickle into another's harvest whenever they handle the Scriptures. For because the legitimate sense of Scripture pertains most of all to Religion, God—willing to provide sufficiently for the salvation of men—constituted His Church as the visible and supreme Judge of controversies of Faith. Therefore, whoever fears being deceived by the obscurity of some question (for example, whether real and natural water is required for baptism) should consult the Church, which Holy Scripture demonstrates without any ambiguity. *As in Matthew 16: I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, etc.; likewise 17: But if he will not hear the Church, etc.; likewise Matthew 23: Whatever they tell you, observe and do; Luke 22:32; Acts 2 and 15; 1 Corinthians 12:28; 2 Peter 1:20.*
</column-2>

It concludes by asserting that the ultimate authority for biblical interpretation rests with the Catholic Church.</summary>

<page-num>XXXIV</page-num>
# PROLEGOMENA

**Canon 2.** The consensus of the Holy Fathers is to be held as the faithful interpreter of Scripture. The Church itself appeals to this. Hence that shout so often repeated in the Councils: *This is the faith of the Fathers!*

<margin>Book II on Christian Doctrine, chapter 6.</margin>
**Canon 3.** The primary interpreter of Scripture is Scripture itself: the clear interprets the obscure, and the certain interprets the doubtful. For almost nothing (according to Augustine) is drawn out from those obscurities that is not found most plainly stated elsewhere. Indeed, frequent and attentive reading, meditation, and comparison of the Scriptures—where light is shed on obscure texts by comparing them with clearer ones, and ambiguous words are defined by other certain ones—is the supreme rule for understanding Scripture. For if the phrasing and the spirit itself become familiar, then understanding becomes clear from accustomed speech. From this flows:

**Canon 4.** One must not act against clear passages of Scripture based on obscure and doubtful ones; on the contrary, a doubtful text must be explained by a more certain one.

**Canon 5.** Knowledge of the New and Eternal Testament is the best method for understanding the Old and temporary one. For the New exactly corresponds to the Old. The Prophets bear witness to the Gospel and inspire faith; the Gospel, in turn, gives authority and understanding to the prophets. Hence the Savior said in *John 5*: "If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also; for he wrote about me." <note>original: "Si crederetis Moysi, crederetis forsan & mihi; de me enim ille scripsit."</note> And Paul in *Romans 1*: "The Justice of God is revealed from faith to faith," <note>original: "Revelatur Iustitia Dei ex fide in fidem"</note> that is, from the faith of the Old Testament into the Evangelical faith of the New Testament. *From the faith of the Law into the faith of the Gospel.*

**Canon 6.** Just as the mutual comparison of both Testaments leads to the understanding of Scripture, so it also helps to know the difference between the two. St. John expressed this excellently in a few words in *Chapter 1:17*, saying: *"The Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ."* Truly, Moses, the servant of God, instituted the Synagogue; the Son of God founded the Church. The Old Law, given only to the Jews, was a law of fear: it nourished servants and did not confer grace of itself; it was like a temporary scaffold <note>original: "machina" — refers to a temporary structure used during construction.</note> for a building being constructed, which is removed once the work is finished and the goal reached, because it has no reason to remain longer. But the New Law, proposed to all Nations, is a law of love; it forms children and provides strength, being perennial and immutable. *"Of his kingdom there shall be no end"* (Luke 1:33).

<margin>The City of God, Book XVII, chapter 6. God speaks in human phrasing.</margin>
**Canon 7.** The sense of words depends on the usage of those speaking, and most of all on the intention of the one uttering them. Therefore, nothing else is to be sought than what the speaker intends. Hence, because in the Scriptures God speaks through humans in the manner of humans, and the common mode of speaking does not always care for <term>scholastic rigor</term> <note>Scholasticism was a method of critical thought in medieval universities that emphasized extremely precise logical and linguistic distinctions.</note> and its minutiae, the words of Scripture are very often to be taken not in scholastic rigor, but according to common custom. Just as a King, deigning to speak with a soldier, craftsman, or farmer, uses their technical terms and phrases so that he may be more easily understood by them; so God lowers Himself to our capacity, nor does He think it foreign to His Majesty to use those phrases by which He may be better understood. This rule of the greatest importance, which has the widest use everywhere, must be explained further. Therefore, while we read of *anger, fury, eyes, ears, and hands* concerning God, and while He is said to *descend, repent, etc.*, it is forbidden to suspect anything human. For Scripture accommodates itself to the weakness of the listeners, so that humans, especially the more unrefined, might perceive the various operations of God more easily—

<margin>Cyril of Alexandria, On the Holy Trinity, chapter 12.</margin>

<column-break/>

—and at least in a human way. Since Scripture, Faith, and reason demonstrate that God is the simplest and purest Spirit, lacking all bodily affection and human passion. Thus God is said to "speak" when, without any sound of voice, He manifests His will either through inspiration or through an angel. He is said to "descend" when He does something on earth that is wonderfully done outside the usual course of nature, showing His presence in a certain way. To be "angry"— <margin>Augustine, The City of God, Book XVI, chapter 5.</margin> while He exercises justice and does what a judge, indignant at a crime, usually does among men. To "forget" or "sleep" while He withdraws help by a just judgment. To "not know" while He does not love, but reproves. "He does not remember our iniquities" when, by sparing us, He does not show a practical knowledge of sins. To "repent" when a change of affairs is signified, while Divine Foreknowledge remains immutable. These things concern divine matters; I move on to others: for example, in Scripture one is called "naked" who is not dressed in the way they usually are or should be, as with Saul or David. No one from Job's friends is said to have spoken a word to him for seven days and nights, because due to the man's intense grief, they spoke rarely and little. *Matthew 11:* John came "neither eating nor drinking," namely in the manner of other men, but sparingly, and using the cheapest food.

*Psalm 13:* we read: *"All have turned aside together, etc."* and *John 1:* "His own did not receive him," likewise *Luke 2:* regarding Anna the Prophetess: "She did not depart from the temple." The reason for these and similar things is that in common speech, a designation is usually taken from the majority or the more prominent part, and what applies to most or the primary ones is attributed to everyone.

In *Galatians 4:6*, it is written: *"The Lord sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts crying out,"* that is, making us cry out. We, certainly, are the ones who cry out, ask, and groan; but He is said to cry out because He brings it about that we cry out. Because, you see, what is proper to a physical cause is commonly attributed to a moral cause: or what someone said or did through another is asserted to have been said or done by themselves. Thus it is said of Pharaoh: *"He hanged the other on the gallows."* <note>Referring to the chief baker in Genesis 40; the executioner did the physical act, but it is attributed to Pharaoh as the authority.</note> And to David: *"You have struck Uriah the Hittite with the sword."* <margin>Genesis 40:12. 2 Samuel 12:9.</margin>

*Genesis 25:23:* It was predicted of Esau and Jacob: *"The elder shall serve the younger."* Which, however, was first fulfilled under David among the Edomites, the descendants of Esau. This is because frequently something is said of those to whom it does not personally apply, but rather to their ancestors or fellow citizens; just as it is accepted in common speech that the honors and disgraces of parents are attributed to their children and grandchildren.

*Matthew 1:* Joseph is called the "husband" of Mary, because Scripture follows the mode of speaking familiar to the Jews, who called betrothed men husbands and betrothed women wives. For the same reason, the words *Father, Son, Brother, and Sister* often have a broad meaning.

*John 11:4:* Christ said of Lazarus: *"This sickness is not unto death."* Because he was not going to remain dead; and *Chapter 17:11:* of himself: *"Now I am no longer in the world."* Because things about to happen very soon are spoken of as already done, according to that trite saying: "one about to be girded is considered already girded." In this way, the common mode of speaking, which Scripture follows, does not overflow with as many scruples as the scholastic mode, and therefore does not care for those...
