<meta>This page continues the "Prolegomena" (Introduction) by Ferdinand Kopf, specifically detailing the "Canons" or rules for interpreting the literal sense of the Bible. The previous page (XXXIV) established that the Church Fathers and the internal consistency of Scripture are the primary guides. This page picks up with Canon 8 and moves through nuances of biblical language, such as hyperbole, metaphors, and the distinction between God's active command and His permission.</meta>

<page-num>XXXV</page-num>

->**FERDINAND KOPF**<-

...which in their own way are minor and light, are related as a caution. Thus, regarding lies [concerning] duration, distance, and number. Hence, the Egyptian midwives seem to be commended <note>original: "obstetrices Ægyptiæ"</note> — 
<margin>Exodus 1:20</margin>
why a fixed number is so often put for an indefinite one, and a round number for an uneven one, not caring about the small amount that exceeds or falls short. But there would be no end if I wished to bring forward everything that belongs to this rule. From what follows, it will be clear that many other rules which greatly aid interpretation can be reduced to this one.

**Canon 8.** The appearances and speeches attributed to God in the Old Testament were performed through the ministry of Angels representing the infinite Majesty of God. *Acts 7; Galatians 3:19.*

<margin>St. Jerome on Jeremiah, ch. 28.</margin>
**Canon 9.** Many things in the Scriptures are said according to the opinion of the time in which the events are related, and not according to what the truth of the matter contained. Thus, St. Joseph is called the "Father of the Lord" in *Matthew 11:25* <note>The author likely refers to the common perception of Joseph, though the citation may be an error for Matthew 1:16 or Luke 2:48.</note>; and it is said of the Scribes and Pharisees: *You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent,* because they were commonly held to be such. John 5:31: *If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true* <note>original: "testimonium meum non est verum"</note>—namely, in your judgment. In Jeremiah 28, Hananiah is called a "Prophet," though he was actually a false prophet.

**Canon 10.** Sometimes Scripture speaks in such a way as to allude precisely to the human manner of speaking, as in Genesis 18:10, where the Angel said to Abraham: *I will return to you at this time next year, life accompanying* <note>original: "vita comite," a phrase indicating the passage of a year or the presence of life/health</note>. For this is how men are accustomed to speak about their future affairs.

**Canon 11.** Scripture is sometimes accustomed to use hyperbolic expressions <term>hyperbole: an intentional exaggeration for emphasis</term>, as in 3 Kings 10 <note>1 Kings 10 in modern Bibles</note>, where in the time of Solomon there is said to have been as great an abundance of silver in Jerusalem as there were stones. Matthew 19: *It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, etc.* and Chapter 24: *Not one stone shall be left upon another.* Nor is this foreign to the truth and majesty of Scripture, because such expressions are proverbial formulas of speech, signifying a matter most worthy of note due to its greatness, rarity, or special difficulty. The sense, therefore, is not to be sought so much from the words themselves as from the usage of speech attributed to these formulas and from the circumstances.

**Canon 12.** In the manner of Scripture, a person is said to *do* something when they certainly announce that something *is* or *will be*. Thus in Leviticus 13, the Priest is said to *defile* <note>original: "contaminare"</note> the one whom he declares to be defiled. And the Prophets are said to *blind, uproot, and build, etc.* when they predict that such things will happen.

**Canon 13.** Just as threatening words are to be understood hypothetically and as things currently stand (for example, Jonah 3: *Yet forty days...*), so sometimes words that seem to be uttered absolutely are to be taken restrictively, as in Isaiah 38:1: *Set your house in order, for you shall die*—that is, considering the nature of the disease and the present circumstances.

**Canon 14.** Something is said to *be* or *happen* then, when it is manifested, although it already existed before; for example, *Hallowed be thy name* <note>original: "Sanctificetur nomen tuum"</note>: that is, let it be known everywhere as holy, and be held holy by all. In Luke 2, Jesus is said to have *increased in wisdom and grace*, that is, not by acquiring them, but by manifesting them through new external signs. Again in 1 Corinthians 15:28: *Then the Son himself will be subjected to him*, that is, then it will be manifest that he is subject to God the Father—namely, in regard to his human nature.

**Canon 15.** There are some things in the Scriptures not to be judged solely from the narrative, such as examples of evil deeds, which are not approved but are related for...

<column-break/>

...warning. Thus, in the case of the Egyptian midwives, it is not the lie concerning their duties that is approved, but their piety of soul, fear of the Lord, and mercy.

**Canon 16.** The past tense is very often used for the future, especially among the Prophets; for example, Isaiah 9:6: *A child is born to us* <note>original: "Parvulus natus est nobis"</note>. Augustine gives the reason: in the usual manner, things are narrated as past which were prophesied as future, because things that were to come were already as if done in the predestination and foreknowledge of God, since they were certain. Conversely, it is not rare to find the future for the past, as in the Song of Habakkuk: *God will come from the South, etc.*

<margin>The City of God, Book 17, ch. 18.</margin>
**Canon 17.** Many things which seem to indicate God’s active operation or command are to be understood as His permission alone. For example, *And lead us not into temptation*, that is, do not permit us to be overcome by temptation. This rule especially applies where the discourse is about the wicked, whom God punishes by withdrawing grace, not by imparting malice <note>original: "non impertiendo malitiam," meaning God does not inject evil into them</note>. As when He is said to *blind* or *harden*. In 3 Kings 22, it is said to the lying spirit: *Go out and do so.* Similarly in Ezekiel 20:25: *I gave them precepts that were not good*, that is, I permitted them, as a punishment for despising my law, to follow the ruinous institutions of neighboring nations. In Romans 1:24: *God gave them up to the desires of their heart, etc.*, that is, He permitted those left to themselves to fall into crimes. John 2: *Destroy this temple*; that is, destroy me without my resistance. For it is a familiar expression in Scripture where the imperative mood is used for the future, especially in curses; for example, Psalm 107: *Let his days be few, etc.*, that is, they *shall be*. For such things are not said by wishing for them, but are predicted by prophesying under the appearance of a wish: not so that they may happen, but because they will happen. To this also belongs that saying in John 13 to the betrayer: *What you do, do quickly.* This voice is not one of commanding, but of permitting; not of one trembling, but of one prepared, says St. Leo in Sermon 7 on the Passion. That the passive mandatory future is used everywhere for the imperative is known of itself, and is clear from the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> itself.

**Canon 18.** The right of God, the supreme Lord of all, which He sometimes exercises through men, must be accurately distinguished from the right of men among themselves. Observing this, it is easily understood that the Hebrews despoiling the Egyptians by God’s command did not commit theft. The same applies to homicide and other matters.

**Canon 19.** Because the Hebrews greatly loved tropes <term>trope: a figurative use of a word</term> and comparisons, all kinds of tropes and figures occur frequently in the Scriptures, especially metaphors. Thus, joy and happiness are designated by light; sorrow and distress by darkness. The expressions of the Prophets are especially vivid and sharp. They address the earth, mountains, and cities as if they were endowed with life and sense. Moses himself, at the very beginning of Genesis, relates the history of the Fall of our first parents—a matter of the greatest importance—using metaphorical phrases. Yet he handles the matter with such caution that he sufficiently suggests to the Hebrews (who were accustomed to the metaphorical style and knew the whole history very well) that he has in view a serpent quite different from the one that spoke with Eve—namely, *that* ancient one, by which name Scripture calls the devil.

**Canon 20.** In parables, not all parts are to be scrupulously urged; for some serve as support or ornament; only those things are to be taken which belong to the argument and the speaker's purpose...

<sig>C 2</sig>
<meta>The catchword "polito" at the bottom suggests the next page begins with a word like "polito" (polished/refined) or a related grammatical form.</meta>

<summary>This page lists several interpretive "canons" (Rules 8-20) for reading the Bible, explaining that Scripture often uses human figures of speech like hyperbole, metaphors, and the "past tense for the future" in prophecy. It also clarifies that when God is said to "harden hearts" or "lead into temptation," it refers to His permission or the withdrawal of grace rather than an active command to do evil.</summary>

<header>INTRODUCTION</header>

...agree with the position. As in *Judges* 9:8. Moreover, parables are used where examples are set down, but names are kept silent.

**Rule 21.** One should not cling too anxiously to the order of the narrative. For the Sacred Writers sometimes anticipate things that happen later through anticipation, sometimes repeat things for emphasis through recapitulation, or recall things omitted by others. This is especially important to note regarding the Evangelists <note>The authors of the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.</note>, whose intention was not to report all of Christ’s words and deeds, but only a few out of many that lead especially to our faith and morals. *John, last chapter.*

**Rule 22.** The Canonical Writers of the New Testament often forge one testimony out of the words of different Prophets and from their various passages, attributing it to the more famous Prophet. Examples are in *Matthew* 21:5, likewise 27:9, *Mark* 1:2, etc. This is because there is such harmony and unity among the Prophets through the one Spirit speaking through them that what belongs to one can also be attributed to another. <note>original: "Aug. L. III. de concord. Evang." — St. Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, Book 3.</note>

**Rule 23.** In controversial matters and in moral commands, one should not look for allegories <note>Symbolic or spiritual interpretations.</note>, but must stick to the literal sense itself. For whatever pertains to Faith or morals that is proposed in Scripture through a mystical sense is usually taught openly in other places through the literal sense. Therefore, clear prophecies about the future should not be weakened by uncertain allegories. For the Apostle does not say in *1 Corinthians* 10 that simply "all things" happened to the Jews as a figure <note>A symbolic foreshadowing.</note>, but "all these things" of which he speaks. And when the Holy Fathers say that the very syllables and accents are full of meaning, they should be understood to mean that this is often the case.

**Rule 24.** Careful attention must be paid to punctuation, so that one can see what should be joined together, what should be separated, or what should be read as a question.

**Rule 25 and last.** Since the Author of Holy Scripture, the Holy Spirit, is necessarily consistent with Himself in all things, a marvelous consensus shines forth from such a great multitude and variety of divine speeches—one that exceeds all human thought. Therefore, there can be no real <term>antilogies</term> <note>From the Greek *antilogia*, meaning a contradiction or conflicting statement.</note>, but only apparent ones. These arise partly from the loss of many ancient records, and partly from the nature of the Hebrew language, in which there are many <term>polysemous</term> words <note>Words that have multiple meanings.</note> corresponding to several Latin ones. Added to these are similar events that happened at different times, or the same man or place having several names, and the like. Despite these things, the labor of learned Interpreters has long since ensured that whatever appeared to conflict on the surface has been quite suitably and clearly reconciled. Certainly, if the genuine sense is assigned to any passage by attending to these rules of exposition, every apparent contradiction must vanish. For example, in *Jeremiah* 22:30, one reads concerning King Jechoniah: *Write this man down as childless.* Yet in *Matthew* 1, Jechoniah fathered Salathiel. But if one attends to the goal of the communication—that Jeremiah is speaking of a son as an heir to the Kingdom who would sit upon the throne of David (which neither Salathiel nor Zerubbabel did)—the whole difficulty is removed. Another example is *Matthew* 18:3, where the Savior says: *Unless you are converted and become like little children, you will not enter the Kingdom of heaven.* Yet the Apostle in *1 Corinthians* 14:20 seems to teach the opposite by saying: *Brothers, do not become children in your thinking. But if, according*

<column-break/>

*to the given rules, the context, the goal of both teachings, and the circumstances are weighed,* it will be clearly seen that in the first passage we are called to the humble and gentle spirit of children, which is without ambition and deceit; while in the second, we are called away from the shallow nature of children and their inconsistency in conducting affairs. Thus, the herald of truth <note>St. Paul</note> in no way contradicts the Supreme Truth <note>Christ</note>.

### § V.

### Which guides should be followed.

There are two things above all that open the surest way into the Holy of Holies of Scripture: purity of mind and an education in secular literature. Because the Holy Fathers—such as Irenaeus, Hilary, Athanasius, Basil, Cyril of Jerusalem, Nazianzen, Ambrose, Chrysostom, Jerome, Augustine, Leo the Great, Gregory the Great, etc.—were miraculously equipped with these gifts and had so consecrated themselves entirely to the study of the Sacred Letters that they agreed in them until they died; it follows indeed that the ancient Fathers of the Church, both Greek and Latin, should be employed for the exposition of Scripture above all others. For God placed the Fathers in the Church as Doctors, and through them, as legitimate interpreters worthy of His majesty and that of the Scriptures, He revealed so many hidden Mysteries to us. However, because few can afford the precious volumes of the Fathers, it will suffice to point out just a few from the new and innumerable writers who have followed in the footsteps of the Fathers and performed outstanding work in publishing commentaries—those who can be more easily acquired and who can abundantly assist students.

1. **The work of Calmet**, comprised of eight volumes and most recently reprinted in Augsburg and Venice, is such that nothing more excellent or better in this genre should be expected from a man. <note>Antoine Augustin Calmet (1672–1757), a French Benedictine monk famous for his massive Bible dictionary and commentaries.</note>

2. **Jacobus Tirinus** stands out among those who provide a learned and solid explanation of the entire Scripture in a compendium. <note>Jacques Tirin (1580–1636), a Jesuit whose "Bible Commentary" was a standard reference for centuries.</note>

3. I have not yet been able to inspect **James Gordon’s** commentary. But in Calmet’s judgment, the work is very similar to Tirinus, though more detailed and pleasantly composed. It was published in Paris in 1632.

4. **John Stephen Menochius** likewise gave a brief and well-founded explanation of the whole Holy Scripture. The edition with supplements, such as the one from Venice in the year 1722, is to be preferred. <note>Giovanni Stefano Menochio (1575–1655), an Italian Jesuit scholar.</note>

5. **Emmanuel Sa’s** brief annotations on the whole Scripture are most useful for beginners and those whose other labors steal away much of their leisure. <note>A Portuguese Jesuit (1530–1596) known for his concise, practical notes.</note>

But those who are kept away by the expense of the larger books should turn their minds to the **Biblical Lexicon**, which was published a few years ago by a man of all-around learning and a singular credit to our Academy, Father Ignatius Weitenauer. Indeed, this can be acquired for a small price and, if kept as a manual, will take the place of more than one interpreter. <note>Ignatius Weitenauer (1709–1783) was a Jesuit professor of Oriental languages and a colleague of the author.</note>

### § VI.

### On Citation.

For the use of Scripture, it is also necessary to know the method of citing it. The matter is easy and is performed thus: where there are several books of the same name...

<page-num>XXXVII</page-num>
<header>FERDINAND KOPE.</header>
<columns>2</columns>

...of the name or Title, three numbers are used. The first is placed before the name and indicates which book it is, expressed in its initial letters; the second, placed after the book, indicates the chapter; and the third, the verse. For example, if you wish to cite from the third book of Kings <note>original: "III. Reg." — In older Catholic Bibles, 1 & 2 Samuel were called 1 & 2 Kings, and 1 & 2 Kings were called 3 & 4 Kings.</note> in the fourth chapter, verse 32, you proceed in this way: III. Kings IV. or 3 Kings 4, 32. If you desire to cite from the second Epistle to the Corinthians in the first chapter, verse 22, you would set it up thus: II. to Cor. I. or 2 Cor. 1, 22. However, the particle "to" can be omitted because it is understood; likewise, if the text is very well known, the third number is often left silent. For citing books with a single or unique title, as most are, only two numbers are needed, which, placed after the book, signify its chapter and verse: for example, Gen. 1, 26. I add this one thing: the book of Ecclesiastes is not to be confused with the book of Ecclesiasticus <note>Ecclesiasticus is also known as the Wisdom of Sirach.</note>; for the former is usually cited as *Eccle.*, while the latter is cited as *Eccli.*

# LECTURE III.

## AIDS FOR THE EASIER USE OF SCRIPTURE.

### §. I.

->Spiritual Aids.<-

I have already noted above with what aids we should approach the handling of the Sacred Letters, where I briefly explained the qualities of the "Guides" whom we ought to imitate. For, as the Mellifluous Doctor <note>A title for St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), known for his eloquent writing.</note> warns: with the same spirit in which the Scriptures were made, in that spirit they must be read and understood. Because to seek to know the secrets of the Spirit without the Spirit would be the same as wanting to see without light. Above all, it is necessary that with a pure and humble mind we earnestly ask for this divine knowledge from the Father of Lights and the Lord of Sciences. <margin>Proverbs 1, etc.</margin> For indeed, *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.* And where there is humility, there is wisdom. *But God resists the proud, nor will wisdom enter into a malevolent soul*; and as Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher.</note> says excellently <margin>On the Consolation of Philosophy, book III.</margin>: that splendor by which the heavens are ruled and flourish avoids the dark ruins of the soul and follows the shining mind. Hence:

**Question.** What should be thought regarding reading in the common language? **Answer.** It would indeed be desirable that everyone might receive an increase in faith and piety from reading the Sacred Scripture, which was established for the salvation of all. But because sad experience has very often taught that reading in the vernacular language <note>The native language of the people, such as German or English, rather than Latin.</note>, if permitted to everyone everywhere and without any distinction, brings more harm than benefit; the provident Mother Church has ordered the Pastors of souls to be watchful, so that Sacred Bibles—specifically those faithfully translated, such as those by Eck, Dietenberger, etc., for our Germany <note>Johann Eck and Johannes Dietenberger were Catholic scholars who produced German translations to counter Martin Luther's version.</note>—are granted only to those who can be presumed to read them prudently and humbly.

<column-break/>

### §. II.

->Natural Aids.<-

Just as wanting a harvest without sowing is to tempt God, so wanting knowledge without the study of learning is to want a miracle. If labor and diligence are required even in the smallest arts, certainly for acquiring knowledge of the Sacred Letters there is a need for sharp study and constant reading. The Holy Spirit himself recommends this to us: <margin>Joshua 1:8.</margin> *Let not the volume of this law depart from your mouth: but you shall meditate on it day and night.* St. Jerome <note>The 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> insists on the same, saying: Let sleep steal upon you while holding the Holy Book, and let the sacred page receive your falling face. However, so that the labor may be easier and the reading rendered more ready, the Scriptures must be loved before they are learned; for he who loves the Scripture honors even what he does not understand in it. Then, support should be sought from the more elegant studies and sciences. Indeed, literary skills and all human disciplines contribute greatly to the understanding of Sacred Scripture. Therefore, whoever intends to keep a correct method and progress in the most useful study of the Sacred Letters should not approach unless previously instructed in the natural sciences, and:

1. He should take care to know the sacred and profane Commonwealth of the Hebrews, their laws, customs, and government. For history is the light and teacher of almost all sciences. Therefore, the Sacred historical books are to be diligently unfolded.

2. He should by no means neglect Chronology and Geography. For both bring a great defense to all histories, and especially to the divine ones.

3. He should know that among the primary aids, and providing many advantages, is the knowledge of languages, especially Hebrew and Greek. This indeed helps greatly in explaining those expressions which, due to an almost innate property, the Latin speech does not fully express. it also helps in drawing out multiple good senses from the same passage; in refuting errors, in settling controversies, and finally and especially, in the understanding of idioms <term>idiotismorum: linguistic constructions unique to a specific language</term> and phrases, the knowledge of which is entirely necessary. For every language has certain proper types of speech which, when they are transferred into another language, seem either obscure or absurd; but they become clear and pleasing through knowledge of the type of speech. Armed with these defenses, everyone should begin this most sacred study with the New Testament. For this, as I said recently, levels the path and holds out a torch for understanding the Old Testament. As for the aids from profane history and geography—the plan of this compendium does not allow them to be treated here—they can be conveniently sought from the dissertations of Calmet <note>Dom Augustin Calmet (1672–1757), a famous French Benedictine Bible scholar.</note>, which are both inserted in his commentary and published separately, from the supplements of Menochius <note>Giovanni Stefano Menochio (1575–1655), an Italian Jesuit scholar.</note>, and others. The remaining matters, which ought not to be absent from the Prolegomena <note>Introductory remarks.</note>, I will indicate immediately:

<page-num>XXXVIII</page-num>
<header>PRELIMINARY REMARKS</header>
<columns>2</columns>

...relates, while keeping silent about its own epoch, through six ages, it is divided in this manner:

*The first age, from the creation of the world to the flood, encompasses* 1656 *years.*
*The second, from the flood to the calling of Abraham,* 426 *years.*
*The third, from the calling of Abraham to the departure from Egypt, or to the law brought by Moses,* 430 *years.*
*The fourth, from the giving of the law to the founding of the temple by Solomon,* 480 *years.*
*The fifth, from the founding of the temple to the end of the Babylonian captivity,* 474 *years.*
*The sixth, from the end of the captivity by Cyrus to the birth of Christ the Lord,* 534 *years.*
Thus, from the beginning of the world until the birth of Christ, approximately 4000 years have flowed.

There are approximately two millennia from Adam to Abraham: from Abraham to Solomon is the third, and from Solomon to Christ is the fourth. At the end of the fourth millennium, according to the opinion of Ussher <note>James Ussher (1581–1656) was an Archbishop who famously calculated the date of creation to be 4004 BC.</note>, to whom almost all more recent scholars subscribe, the Nativity of the Lord is established, and from there is derived the Christian Era, which is also called the "common" or "vulgar" era, and the "Dionysian" era after Dionysius Exiguus <note>original: "Dionysio exiguo" — A 6th-century monk who invented the AD/BC dating system.</note>. I set aside the variety of authors on this matter. For those who follow the Hebrew chronology come more or less close to the aforementioned sum, although they conflict among themselves regarding the exact year of the Lord’s Nativity, which most critics establish four full years prior to the common Era itself. I only note that the Greeks, who follow the codices of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in the calculation of years, differ so much that they count approximately 5500 years from the beginning of the world to the Incarnation of the Lord.

<margin>City of God, Book XV, ch. 14.</margin>
But as Augustine notes, that diversity in numbers among the Greeks can be attributed to the error of the scribe who first received the codex to be copied from the library of King Ptolemy. Indeed, because the Hebrew codices mark the years with whole countable words, while the Greeks use the tips of letters and arithmetic marks, a mistake could more easily creep into the latter than into the accurate Hebrew extension.

The year of the Hebrews always consisted of twelve months. In the age of Moses, it was solar and 30 days for each month, except for the twelfth month, which encompassed 35 days. This is gathered from the calculation of the flood in Genesis VII. After the completion of the Jerusalem Talmud, around the year 300 of the common era, they began to use only lunar years, assigning 29 and 30 days alternately to each month. However, so that the period of the years may remain consistent with the course of the sun, after the third year they add one lunation, or a thirteenth month, which they call *Ve Adar* or the second Adar.

The sacred or Ecclesiastical year destined for religion began among the Jews in the spring; the civil year began in autumn.

The Sabbatical year, in which the land rested from cultivation, recurred every seventh year; and the Jubilee year, in which slaves became their own masters and lands returned to their former owners, recurred in the fiftieth year.

The months among the ancient Hebrews did not have specific names but were called first, second, third, etc. But after the Babylonian captivity, they were granted these names:

<column-break/>

**Nisan**, the beginning of the sacred year, corresponding roughly to our March.
**Iiar** corresponding to April; and so for the rest.
**Sivan**.
**Thammuz**.
**Ab**.
**Elul**.
**Tisri**, or **Tishri**, the beginning of the civil year.
**Marcheshvan**.
**Kislev**.
**Tebeth**.
**Shevat**.
**Adar**.
**Ve Adar** or the second Adar, intercalary after the third year.

<margin>Leviticus XXV.</margin>
The week among the Hebrews was of two kinds: one of days, the other of years. The former, drawn from one Sabbath to another, comprised seven days; the latter, encompassing as many years, gave the count for the Sabbatical and Jubilee years.

<margin>Leviticus XXIII.</margin>
The day, simply and without distinction, was bounded from evening to evening according to that saying: *From evening unto evening shall you celebrate your Sabbaths* (Leviticus 23). For the Hebrews insisted on the creation of things, in which darkness preceded light, and hence it is said: *And the evening and the morning were the first day.* But after Judea was subdued by the Romans, while the old custom was preserved for feast days, in other matters they imitated the Romans and extended the civil day from morning to morning (according to other writers, from midnight to the following midnight). Therefore, for the books of the New Testament, one must carefully attend to the distinction between the legal or sacred day and the civil day; for according to John 13, Christ is said to have instituted the Last Supper before the feast day of the Passover, while by the other Evangelists it is noted at the same time in reality as the first day of unleavened bread, namely, the 14th day of the month Nisan at evening. For John records the civil day, and the other Evangelists the legal day. The legal, or Ecclesiastical and sacred day, is that according to which feasts and matters pertaining to religion are ordered. The civil day is that which any nation defines by its own judgment for handling civil business.

Night in the books of the Old Testament is read as being in three distinct parts: evening, midnight, and the morning watch. In the books of the New Testament, however, following the custom of the Romans, a distinction into four watches is observed, each of which consisted of three unequal hours according to the different times of the year.

Properly called hours did not formerly exist for the Jews, but they divided the natural day, or the course of the sun from its rising to its setting, into four parts: morning, midday, the first evening, and the second evening. The first evening denoted the sun already declining, the second its setting. But at the time of the Lord’s Advent, they counted twelve unequal hours of the natural day according to the change of the days—longer in summer, shorter in winter. They took the first hour from the rising of the sun, which (speaking of the equinox) corresponds to our six in the morning: the Third agrees with our nine in the morning; the Sixth with noon, and so for each, e.g., one reads in Acts 3: *Now Peter and John went up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer*, that is, around three in the afternoon for us. And because the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours were better known than the others, being destined for sacrifices and prayers, the entire daytime...

time used to be indicated such that the first hour was counted through to the third, the third through to the sixth or noon, and so each span was considered to encompass a space equivalent to three distinct hours. The same is to be understood regarding the sixth and ninth hours. When this is well observed, that contradiction <note>original: "antilogia"</note> vanishes wherein we read in Mark 15:25 that Christ was fixed to the cross at the third hour, and in John 19:14 at roughly the sixth hour. Namely, they speak of the "hour of prayer" used in an extensive sense, or of the middle time between the third and sixth hour which was not yet finished—Mark speaking of the third hour as it ended, and John of the sixth as it was already approaching. It had become the custom that the time flowing between the hours of prayer was named either from the preceding or the following hour.

## § IV.
-> Concerning Coins and Measures <-

**S**ince in ancient times commerce was established partly by bartering goods and partly by weighing out gold or silver worked into rods or crude plates, both of these methods caused no small inconvenience. Eventually, the use of minted and stamped money <note>original: "monetæ"</note> was introduced, to which the name "pecunia" <note>This Latin word for money is derived from "pecus," meaning cattle, reflecting a time when wealth was measured in livestock.</note> stuck, because of the image of a flock—specifically sheep or cattle—impressed upon it. Following the Rabbis in this matter, most interpreters teach that this custom was already held by the Hebrews in the age of Abraham, or at least Jacob, based on that passage in *Genesis 33:19* where Jacob is said to have bought a part of a field for one hundred lambs. They wish this to be understood <margin>Last chapter of Job</margin> not as one hundred sheep, but as many coins marked with the figure of a lamb. They feel the same regarding the "one sheep" which is read to have been given by friends to Job when his better fortune returned. For unless this gift were considered a precious coin, it would have to be judged too trivial and unworthy. Furthermore, the coins of which mention occurs more frequently in Scripture, with their prices reduced approximately to the value of our own currency, are the following:
The **As** <note>original: "Asis"</note>, as a small coin, concerning which Matthew 10 says: *Are not two sparrows sold for an as?* It corresponds roughly to our **Kreuzer** <note>original: "crucigero" — a common small coin in the author's time.</note>.
The **Obolus**, the twentieth part of a shekel, corresponds roughly to our one-and-a-half **Kreuzers**.
The **Dipondium** <note>A Roman bronze coin</note> corresponds to two *ases*.
The Hebrew **Drachma** corresponds to 16 **Kreuzers**. However, the Hebrew drachma is twice as large as the Greek or Attic one, which is also to be understood regarding the Hebrew **Mina** and **Talent**.
The **Didrachma**, or double drachma, equivalent to the Attic tetradrachm, corresponds to 32 **Kreuzers**.
The silver **Shekel** <note>original: "Siclus"</note> or **Stater** likewise corresponds to 32 **Kreuzers**. Whenever "piece of silver" is read in Scripture without anything added, "Shekel" is understood.
The **Half-shekel**, the head-tax imposed on the Israelites by Moses, corresponds to 16 **Kreuzers**.
The **Mina** (or *Mna*), consisting of 60 shekels, corresponds to 32 **Florins** <note>original: "florenis" — a gold or silver guilder.</note>.
The **Talent of Silver** corresponds to 1,600 **Florins**.
The **Talent of Gold** corresponds to 19,200 **Florins**, for according to writers, the value of gold exceeded the value of silver twelvefold.

<column-break/>

-> Dry measures for the Hebrews were: <-

The **Corus** or **Chomer** was the greatest of all, containing 30 *modii* <note>bushels</note>. It also served for liquids, for we read that Solomon gave twenty *Cors* of oil to King Hiram. <margin>1 Kings 5:11</margin>
The **Ephi** or **Epha**: this was the tenth part of a Cor, thus having three *modii*, or three *Sata*.
The **Gomor** or **Affaron**: this was the tenth part of an Epha.
The **Cab** or **Cabus**: this was the sixth part of one *modius*.
The **Artaba** was a Babylonian measure of five *modii*.

---

-> Liquid measures: <-

The **Bath** <note>original: "Bathus"</note> contained, according to Calmet, about 30 Parisian measures (*pints*). However, one Parisian pint is said to be equivalent to nearly two of our short **Innsbruck measures** <note>original: "Cenipontanis"</note>.
The **Metreta** of the Greeks roughly corresponds to the Bath; so too the **Amphora** of the Romans.
The **Hin** was the sixth part of a Bath.
The **Log** or **Logus** was the fourth part of a Cab.

---

-> Measures of distances: <-

From four barley grains joined crosswise is composed the 
**Roman Digit** <note>finger-breadth</note>, but the Hebrews commonly attribute six grains to the Hebrew digit. From this measure all others arise: thus,
The **Tophach**, or minor palm, has 4 digits.
The **Zereth**, or major palm, has 12 digits.
The **Foot** has four minor palms.
The **Pace** has five feet.
The **Cubit**—six minor or ordinary palms. The cubit is that length from the bend of the arm to the extremity of the middle finger, and is considered the fourth part of the stature of a well-formed man.
The **Reed** <note>original: "Calamus"</note>—six cubits.
The **Stadium** has 125 paces.
The **Mile**—eight stadia or 1,000 paces.
A **Sabbath's Journey** was that space which the Hebrews were permitted to complete by walking on the Sabbath. Some define this space as one thousand paces, others as two thousand.
*Note:* For the ancient Hebrews, in place of paces, stadia, and miles, there were cubits, cords, and poles.

## § V.
-> Concerning Idioms. <-

**T**here are two principal sources of **Idioms** <note>original: "Idiotismorum" — here meaning cultural linguistic peculiarities or figures of speech.</note>. 1. Innumerable phrases and expressions are taken from the fields and vineyards. The reason is that at the time when God, speaking through men, established the Holy Scripture, agriculture and the pastoral life were held in the highest esteem even among the Great and the Leaders of the people; it is natural for the greater part of expressions to refer to those things which thrive most among everyone. 2. For the same reason, many idioms have their origin in the customs of the Hebrews, such as from their clothing, marriages, banquets, etc. For example, that phrase in Luke 12:35, *Let your loins be girt* etc., in the literal sense means: [be] prompt and ready.

--- Page 44 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient customs necessary for understanding Biblical metaphors, specifically focusing on idioms related to clothing, social rituals, and the "Forest of Hebrew Idioms"—a guide to the unique linguistic structures of the Hebrew language as they appear in the Latin Vulgate.</meta>

[be] ready <note>original: "estote"</note>. This is a clothing-related idiom; for the Hebrews wore long garments reaching to their ankles, which they would gird up <note>tie with a belt or sash</note> so they could be unhindered for a journey or other business. The "cup," or a portion of a cup, is frequently used to signify someone's lot and condition—whether good or bad—because at banquets, a specific portion of wine was usually assigned according to each person’s age. Likewise, because the use of thorns to kindle a fire was very common in Palestine, it is said proverbially in Psalm 57: *Before your thorns can feel the buckthorn* etc., which means: before the thorns can grow to the size of a buckthorn bush, divine wrath will suddenly seize and destroy my enemies, however well they seem to be doing. Psalm 2:12 signifies the same thing: *kiss the son*, meaning to adore him, and *embrace discipline*, or to subject oneself to his law and power; this is because, in ancient times, homage was paid to new Kings by a kiss. To understand the parable of the ten virgins, one must know and pay attention to wedding rituals. And so it is for countless other passages. Indeed, the Sacred Pages are full of these examples.

### § VI.

->A Little Forest of Hebrew Idioms.<-

<margin>Calmet on Isaiah chapter 46.</margin>
The Hebrews are accustomed to repeat the same thing in the same part of a sentence using different words that mean the same thing. This is most notable in the Psalms, where the sacred Prophets express the same thought in various words so that the speech, progressing as if by certain steps, is finally completed with an emphatic rhythm. For example, the rule in these cases is: *if the beginning of a verse is obscure, light arises from the half-line* <note>original: "hemistichio," the second half of a verse in poetic structure</note>. 
<margin>Psalm 75</margin>
However, there is no fault of "battology" <term>idle repetition of words</term> or redundancy in such repetitions; rather, the same thing emphasized through different phrases in Scripture possesses energy and wit. At the same time, it signifies that the matter is not just any way, but is fully, solidly, and most certainly past, present, or future, as in Jeremiah 17:14: *Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved.* Similarly, when it is said of John the Baptist in John 1:20: *And he confessed, and did not deny; and he confessed* etc., it marks how great and unusual was the modesty of the Precursor <note>John the Baptist</note>, by which he constantly rejected the honor of being the Messiah, which was offered to him by the messengers sent from the Sanhedrin. Doubled words have a similar emphasis, such as *doing he shall do*, which means he will most certainly do it. *Weeping she wept*, meaning she wept vehemently. *Waiting I waited*, meaning with the greatest desire, yet constantly and relying on hope.

Through ellipsis <note>the omission of words</note>, something is often understood but left out, to be supplied or repeated from the context. For example, Psalm 117: *It is time to act, O Lord*: namely, to show us mercy and take vengeance on your enemies, because they have scattered your law. In Psalm 132: *Like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion*. The words "like the dew" must be repeated in this way: like the dew of Hermon, and like the dew which descends upon Mount Zion. The same must be observed where a negation has preceded, for this is sometimes also understood in the following part. As in Psalm 43:19: *And our heart has not turned back, and [not] turned aside* etc., meaning: you have not permitted our paths to turn aside from the way of your law. And in Matthew 10: *Neither tunics, nor shoes, nor a staff*, meaning: neither double shoes (or sandals), nor a double staff (or multiple 

<column-break/>

sticks), as seen in Mark 6:8. Also, when a preposition is doubled, for example, Psalm 77: *From behind the ewes* <note>original: "fœtantes," sheep giving birth or nursing</note> *he took him*, meaning that God took David from the field from behind the nursing sheep and established him as King. Matthew 4:25: *From across the Jordan*, meaning from the region across the Jordan. Luke 17:24: *Lightning flashing from under heaven*, meaning from or out of the clouds which are under the sky. Scripture tends to state negatively that which is far less in respect to something else; for example, Luke 14: *If anyone comes to me, and does not hate his father* etc., meaning he does not love him much less than me and my law. Malachi 1: *I have loved Jacob, but Esau I have hated*, meaning I have loved him less. Hosea 6: *I desired mercy and not sacrifice*, meaning I prefer mercy over sacrifice. 1 Corinthians 3:7: *Not I, but the grace of God*, meaning not so much I, as the grace of God: the Grace of God with me. Matthew 15:24: *I am not sent except to the sheep* etc., meaning primarily and for that specific purpose.

For the sake of allusion or emphasis, the meaning of a name is sometimes put in place of the proper name of persons and places. For example, Genesis 46:1: *He came to the well of the oath*, meaning to the city of Beer-sheba. 2 Samuel 21:19: *The son of the forest*, meaning the Son of Jair. Psalm 75:3: *His place was made in peace*, meaning in Salem, commonly known as Jerusalem. Proverbs 30: *The words of the gatherer, the son of the vomiter*, meaning the words of Agur, son of Jakeh. For the same reason, there is no lack of paronomasia or "wordplay"; for example, Zephaniah 2:4: *Ekron shall be uprooted.* "Ekron" <note>original: "Accaron"</note> the city sounds like "uprooting" or "tearing out" <note>In Hebrew, 'Ekron' and 'te'aker' (shall be uprooted) share the same root sounds</note>.
<margin>See 1 Chronicles 4:22 and also chapter 7:18.</margin>
Verbs are not infrequently placed in the position of adverbs, such as Psalm 125: *The Lord has magnified to do with us*, meaning he has done magnificently. Psalm 77: *They were turned, and they tempted God*, meaning they tempted God again.

Neutral verbs must sometimes be explained actively, for example, Psalm 51:7: *He will emigrate you*: he will make you emigrate; he will expel you from your home.

The *Conjunctive* <note>the 'and' or connecting mood</note> is frequently expressed through *Gerunds*, for example, Psalm 115: *In the Lord turning the captivity*, meaning when the Lord turned or released the captivity; and Psalm 142:4: *In my spirit failing from me*: when my spirit was failing.

Scripture often uses *Abstract* nouns (or quasi-abstracts) in place of *Concrete* ones. Thus, *circumcision* is put for the circumcised person, *uncircumcision* <note>original: "præputium," literally foreskin</note> for a Gentile, and *redemption* for a redeemer.

*Power* or the *act* of power is used for the object itself: *understanding* for the thing understood; *vision* for the thing seen; *hearing* for the thing heard. The same applies to hope, fear, patience, custody, etc. Likewise, one sense or its action is put for another; for example, Exodus 20:18: *The people saw the voices*, meaning they heard them.

Scripture calls *Sons* or *Daughters* whatever is drawn out from something else, as if born from it. Thus, the "sons of the threshing floor" are the grains of corn threshed on the floor. "Daughter of the quiver" refers to arrows. Likewise, whatever has a special relation to another thing, or imitates its offspring. Such as *son of death*, *son of pride*, *offspring of vipers*.

The *doubling of a word* in the same case denotes an abundance of the thing, such as *man and man*, meaning very many men. *The tribes, the tribes of the Lord*: all the tribes. *Generation and generation*: all generations. However, sometimes this doubling merely signifies a duality or diversity. This is easily gathered from the subject matter: for example, in...

<keywords>Hebraisms, biblical idioms, paronomasia, ellipsis, parallelism, biblical metaphors, Hebrew grammar, philology</keywords>

--- Page 45 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Forest of Hebrew Idioms," moving from general conceptual metaphors to specific grammatical structures and figures of speech used in the Latin translation of the Bible to reflect the original Hebrew style.</meta>

<page-num>xli</page-num>
<header>FERDINAND KOPF.</header>

*They spoke with a heart and a heart* <note>original: *corde & corde locuti sunt*</note>, that is, with a double heart or deceitfully—honey in the mouth, but gall in the heart. Likewise, *a weight and a weight* <note>original: *pondus & pondus*</note>, meaning double and differing weights used to deceive buyers.

The **comparative** degree is expressed through the particle *above* <note>original: *prae*</note>; for example: *beautiful in form above the sons of men* (Psalm 44), meaning more beautiful than the sons. *I will place him high above the Kings of the earth* (Psalm 88), meaning higher than the Kings. Often, however, the **positive** degree is used in place of the comparative; for example, Psalm 117: *It is good to trust in the Lord, than to trust in man*, meaning it is *better* to trust, etc.

A word doubled in such a way that it is placed once in the genitive case has the force of a **superlative** and implies excellence; for example, *the song of songs* <note>original: *canticum canticorum*</note>, meaning the most excellent song. *Vanitas vanitatum*: the vainest thing. *The heaven of heaven*: the highest heaven. *Daughter of women*, meaning the most beautiful. Similarly, the names of God added to words take the place of the superlative. Thus, *Lebanon, Bashan, Carmel, Gilead, Salmon, Hermon* are called *mountains of God*, meaning the highest mountains; likewise the *Cedar of God*, *Prince of God*, etc. Nouns used instead of adjectives also carry energy, such as a *Tower of strength*, meaning the strongest tower. *Mammon of iniquity*: ill-gotten wealth. *A man of bloods*: a cruel man. *A vessel of election*: a chosen instrument.

Through **syllepsis** <term>syllepsis: a grammatical figure where a word agrees with only one of two or more words it should logically modify</term>, the plural number is sometimes used for the singular, and vice versa; as in Jeremiah 2:12: *be astonished, O heaven, and its gates*, etc. Examples of the plural for the singular are found in Joshua 7:1: *But the sons of Israel committed a trespass.* This refers to a single man, *Achan*. In Hebrews 11:33, regarding Daniel: *They shut the mouths of lions.* In Matthew 27: *And the thieves reviled him*: yet only one of them blasphemed him. Likewise, the use of the plural number is frequent to signify magnitude, excellence, or dignity.

Scripture sometimes uses *many* for *all*. So it was said to Abraham in Genesis 17: *I have made you a father of many nations*, which means: of all nations. *In your seed all nations shall be blessed* (Genesis 22). The same occurs in the following: *He bore the sins of many. Many are called. Poured out for many. Many were made sinners*, namely through Adam, in whom *all have sinned* (Romans 5).

<margin>Malachi 3.</margin>
The proper name of a **figure** <term>figure: a symbolic representation or "type" of something to come later</term> is often attributed to the things being figured. Thus, the Priests of the New Testament are called *sons of Levi*: *He shall purify the sons of Levi*. Similarly, because the Priesthood according to the order of Aaron was a figure of the future eternal Priesthood, when eternity was promised to it, it was promised not to the shadow and figure itself,
<margin>Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 17, chapter 6.</margin>
but to that which was foreshadowed and figured by it.

**Change of person** is a frequent figure in Scripture, such that it speaks of the same thing in the same discourse now in the first, now in the second, and now in the third person.

A **noun** is often used in place of a **pronoun**; for example, when in Numbers 12:8 God says of Moses: *He sees the Lord openly*, that is: he sees *me*. Similarly,

The pronouns *to me, to you, to himself, his*, etc., are used through **pleonasm** <term>pleonasm: the use of more words than are necessary to convey meaning, often for emphasis</term>, for the sake of elegance alone; they are redundant when compared to Latin custom. For example: *The Lord in heaven, his seat*, meaning the Lord’s seat is in heaven. *His right hand has saved for himself*, meaning the power of God has saved us. *Blessed is he, whose helper is the God of Jacob*: it is the same as the proposition in, for example, *I have spoken in my tongue.*

<column-break/>

The **masculine** or **feminine** is substituted for the **neuter**, which the Hebrew language lacks. For example: *one thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek* <note>original feminine: *unam... hanc*</note>, meaning *one thing, this* <note>neuter: *unum, hoc*</note> in Psalm 26. Likewise: *this thing was done for me* <note>original feminine: *haec*</note>, meaning *this was done for me* <note>neuter: *hoc*</note> in Psalm 118.

I have noted more than once that **tropes** <term>tropes: figurative uses of words</term> and figures of every kind are familiar to the Hebrew language and consequently to the Scriptures. Therefore, it is appropriate here to subjoin some examples.

Through **metaphor**, the most frequent of all, *wolves, bears, and dragons* are fierce and untamable men.

Through **synecdoche** <term>synecdoche: a figure of speech in which a part is made to represent the whole or vice versa</term>, *Lebanon* is taken for the temple built from the cedars of Lebanon, and *flesh* for man: *The Word was made flesh* (John 1). It is also used for brothers and relatives: *You shall not despise your own flesh* (Isaiah 58).

Through **metonymy** <term>metonymy: the substitution of the name of an attribute or adjunct for that of the thing meant</term>, *sin* is understood as the punishment for sin, or for the sacrificial victim offered for sin. Thus in Hosea 4:8, the Priests are said to *eat the sins of the people*, meaning the offerings made for sins. And in 2 Corinthians 5:21, *Christ, who knew no sin, was made sin for us*, meaning a sacrificial victim for sins. But it is right to assume that the varied use of these tropes is well-known from classical studies.

**Irony** is found in Genesis 3: *Behold, Adam has become as one of us.*

**Antiphrasis** <term>antiphrasis: the use of a word in a sense opposite to its proper meaning</term> is found in 1 Kings 21:10: *He blessed God and the king*, meaning he cursed them. Likewise in Job 1.

**Hypallage** <term>hypallage: a transposition of the natural relations of two elements in a proposition</term> is in Psalm 17:6: *He set his tabernacle in the sun*, meaning he set the sun in his tabernacle, or in the heavens.

It is clear in itself how frequent **enallage** <term>enallage: the substitution of one grammatical form for another</term> is, or the change of gender, person, number, or tense.

Many **proverbial** <note>original: *adagiales*</note> formulas of speaking familiar to the Hebrews are given in the Scriptures: for example, Ezekiel 18:2: *The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the children are set on edge*, meaning the children pay the penalties for the crimes of their fathers. Luke 10:4: *Salute no one by the way*, meaning proceed in haste, neglecting empty duties of urbanity and conversations with those you meet.

Nor are **hieroglyphics and symbols** <note>symbolic imagery used by the prophets</note> lacking, especially among the Prophets. Examples are obvious in Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and Revelation: where through *wrath* or a *sword*, the *Dove of the Chaldeans* <note>referring to the standards or symbols of the Babylonians</note> carrying a dove on a rim; through a *razor* shaving the hair and beard is meant the hostile sword slaughtering the common people and the Princes; through a *four-part statue and four beasts* are meant the four Monarchies; and by the *he-goat* Alexander the Macedonian is designated.

### §. VII.

->Hebrew Idioms of Various Particles.<-

The particle **"And"** <note>original: *Et*</note> is very friendly to the Hebrews and Greeks; it is very often repeated and begins several Sacred Books. Sometimes it has the same value as *because* or *or*; for example, Isaiah 64:5: *Behold, you are angry, and we have sinned*, meaning *because* we have sinned. Acts 3:6: *Silver and gold have I none*: meaning silver *or* gold, for either one would suffice for alms. Likewise 1 Corinthians 11:29: *For he who eats and drinks*, meaning *or* drinks, as the Apostle himself had already declared in the preceding verse 27.

**"If"** and **"unless"** <note>original: *Si* and *nisi*</note> are often the signs of one swearing an oath, and these or similar words must be understood: *May I not*...

# PROLEGOMENA BY FERDINAND KOPF.

<columns>2</columns>

is held as true: for example, Psalm 94 <note>Psalm 95 in English Bibles; original: *Si introibunt in requiem meam*</note>: *If they shall enter into my rest*, likewise:

If at the beginning of a proposition, the word <term>if</term> <note>original: *si*</note> <term>often</term> sounds like a question. 
For example, Matthew 22: *Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar?* <note>original: *Si licet censum dare Casari?*</note>

The little word <term>as if</term> <note>original: *quasi*</note> does not signify a mere similarity, but the thing itself and the truth of it, as in John 1: *as if of the only begotten* <note>original: *quasi unigeniti*</note>, that is, truly; and James 2:9: *as if transgressors* <note>original: *quasi transgressores*</note>.

The words <term>since</term> <note>original: *quoniam*</note> and <term>because</term> <note>original: *eo quod*</note> are also accepted to mean <term>although</term> <note>original: *quamvis*</note>. Isaiah 12:1: *I will confess to you, Lord, since you were angry with me*. Jeremiah 7:10: *We are delivered, because we have done all these abominations*, which means: although you were angry... although we have done...

In the common phrase, <term>unto the ages of ages</term> signifies absolute eternity, but the words *not beyond*, *age*, and *eternal* <note>original: *non ultra, saeculum, aeternum*</note> often denote only a long or very long time.

The particles <term>perhaps</term> <note>original: *forte*</note> and <term>perchance</term> <note>original: *forsitan*</note> do not imply doubt, but instead note free will, or the small number of those who are going to do the thing being discussed.

Comparative particles like <term>as</term> <note>original: *sicut*</note>, <term>just as</term> <note>original: *veluti*</note>, and <term>like</term> <note>original: *instar*</note> must more often be understood implicitly: for example, Psalm 67:31 <note>Psalm 68 in English Bibles</note>: *Rebuke the wild beasts of the reeds* etc. This means: restrain, O God, our enemies, who are like wild beasts fed among the reeds, and like a gathering of bulls who rage among the herds, and who try to exclude from their promised inheritance those who were chosen by you and tested like silver <note>original: *instar argenti*</note>. In this way, that otherwise most obscure passage in 1 Kings 13 <note>1 Samuel 13:1 in modern Bibles</note> is also commonly explained: *Saul was a son of one year* etc. meaning that Saul was innocent like a one-year-old boy when he began to reign; but he reigned in this way over Israel for only two years, and quickly degenerated from that sanctity of life. Furthermore, when the aforementioned particles imply equality, property, or merely similarity, it must be gathered from the subject matter.

The particles <term>before</term> <note>original: *antequam*</note>, <term>until</term> <note>original: *donec*</note>, and <term>up to the time when</term> <note>original: *usquedum*</note> do not always indicate the cessation of the thing being discussed, but often indicate its continuation: for example, Genesis 8: *The raven is said to have not returned* (namely into the interior of the Ark, even if it flew back to the roof, as it is in the Hebrew) *until the waters were dried up*. Here the sense is certainly that the raven did not return even after the waters were dried. In Psalm 109 <note>Psalm 110</note>, it is read that *Christ shall reign until all his enemies are placed under his feet*. But he certainly will not stop reigning once those enemies are subdued. Psalm 106: *The just man shall not be moved, until he looks down upon his enemies*. And again in Psalm 122:

<column-break/>

*Our eyes are toward the Lord, until he has mercy on us*. The same Hebraism occurs in the books of the New Testament. Matthew 1: *Before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit*. And *he did not know her until she brought forth her firstborn son* <note>The author uses these examples to argue that "until" describes the state leading up to an event without implying the state changed afterward, a common point in historical theology regarding the Virgin Mary</note>.

The particle <term>that</term> <note>original: *ut*</note> in the prophets signifies not the cause of the event, but the event itself: for example, where in John 12:37 it is said of the blindness of the Jews: *They did not believe in him: that the word of the Prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled* etc. Matthew, following the sense rather than the words of the prophecy according to his custom, explains it thus: *The prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled in them, saying: in hearing you shall hear, and you shall not understand* etc. Surely the prophecy of Isaiah was neither the cause nor the occasion for the stubbornness of the Jews; rather, they turned their eyes away from the light and blocked their ears by their own choice and out of mere malice. They were not able to believe because they did not want to; indeed, God foresaw their evil will and foretold it through the Prophet.

The use of prepositions is also varied: as follows.

<term>A</term> or <term>ab</term> <note>from/by</note> sounds at times like <term>before</term>, <term>more than</term>, and <term>on account of</term>: for example, *I have not acted impiously from my God*, that is, before God. *The publican went down justified from that Pharisee*, that is, more than him. *Woe to the world from scandals*, on account of scandals.

<term>Ad</term> <note>to/at</note> is equivalent to <term>about</term> or <term>because of</term>: for example, Hebrews 1: *To the angels indeed he says* etc., that is, about the angels. Mark 10:5: *At the hardness of your heart*, that is, because of the hardness.

<term>Apud</term> <note>among/at the house of</note> also is equivalent to *in*: for example, John 1: *The Word was with God*, that is, in God.

<term>Contra</term> <note>against</note> also is equivalent to <term>before</term>: for example, Psalm 50: *My sin is against me always*, that is, before me.

<term>De</term> <note>from/of</note> sounds like <term>for</term> or <term>in</term>: for example, *I will ask the Father from you*, that is, for you. *Praise the Lord from the heavens*, that is, in the heavens.

<term>Propter</term> <note>on account of</note> is also used for <term>through</term>: John 6:58: *I live on account of the Father: and he who eats me, he shall live on account of me*.

The preposition <term>In</term> acts in place of almost all others: for sometimes it is equivalent to <term>with</term>, <term>of</term>, <term>against</term>, or <term>for</term>. The same is to be noted regarding the preposition <term>Super</term> <note>over/above</note>; for this is sometimes used for <term>to</term>, <term>against</term>, <term>toward</term>, <term>in</term>, <term>near</term>, or <term>after</term>. This must be determined from the subject matter and the context. From these things, however, the studious reader will observe and infer that Holy Scripture attends not so much to the rules of grammarians as to the weight and sense of its own words.

# LECTURE I.

->ON THE BOOKS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT.<-

->§. I.<-

->Concerning the Pentateuch.<-

<margin>
The
Penta-
teuch
</margin>
That Moses, a man of the highest talent and outstanding holiness, is the author of the Pentateuch—the "Five Books" <note>from the Greek *penta* (five) and *teuchos* (volume)</note> which are the first in the Canon <note>the official list of books in the Bible</note> and older than any Greek works that have reached us—must be placed beyond all controversy. Indeed, an unbroken tradition of both the Synagogue <note>the Jewish community</note> and the Church demonstrates this, a fact which Christ himself made invincible and inviolable by his own endorsement. Certain minor additions, such as the account of Moses' death and so on, added by Joshua or some other sacred writer, do not stand in the way of this; otherwise, even after the passing of a single century, no one would be considered the owner of their own writing.

When Moses composed the Pentateuch during the time of wandering in the deserts of Arabia, all nations throughout the world, with the exception of the Hebrew nation, were shrouded in gathering darkness regarding true religion. The Jews themselves were still a rough and unrefined people, and due to their long stay in Egypt, they were highly inclined toward idolatry. To oppose this evil like a bulwark and establish the ancestral religion, the most wise writer [Moses] focused entirely on depicting the infinite perfections of the one God, Creator of heaven and earth, in vivid colors—yet in a style suited to the understanding of an uneducated people. At the same time, he recalled those great promises made by God to their fathers concerning the sending of a future Deliverer, toward whom indeed all prayers, the Law itself, and the entire religion were aimed, as if toward a single goal and fulfillment. Furthermore, although Moses was able to learn many of the things he narrated through tradition received from the Fathers (for Abraham lived for a long time with Shem, son of Noah; Noah lived with Methu-

<column-break/>

selah, and he with Adam himself), nevertheless, the reliability of these books is by no means to be sought from that source, but rather from the Divine Spirit, who reveals hidden things to the sacred writers and grants infallible authority to things known through the reports of others.

<margin>
The Book
of Genesis
contains
50
chapters.
</margin>
Therefore, the BOOK OF GENESIS (called *Bereschit* <note>meaning "In the beginning"</note> by the Hebrews, because they name the books of Moses after the first word appearing at the start of the work) draws its name partly from the creation of heaven and earth and partly from the genealogy of the Patriarchs traced therein. It relates the first origins of things, the flood, the confusion of languages, the division of nations, and the lives of the Patriarchs. According to the calculation of the Vulgate <note>the standard Latin Bible translation</note> following the Hebrew text, it encompasses a history of 2,369 years from the creation of the world until Joseph, with whose death it ends.

<margin>
Exodus
has 40
chapters.
</margin>
EXODUS, so named from the departure of the Israelites from Egypt, continues the sacred history for 154 years from the death of Joseph to the erection of the tabernacle at Mount Sinai. It describes the harsh slavery, the liberation marked by astounding plagues and wonders, and the proclamation of the divine law. What should especially hold the reader's attention in this work is the covenant entered into by God with the Israelites; for God, in the Commonwealth of the Hebrews established by Him—which you might correctly call a Theocracy or divine polity—wished to claim for Himself the role of supreme Lawgiver, King, and Father. He showed this primarily by bringing the Hebrews, through the ministry of Moses, laws that were moral, judicial, and ceremonial. These emphasize that the happiness of the Commonwealth and the strength of the entire kingdom consist in these things, and that if these [laws] in which they were instructed are kept, all things are safe. Nor did that fearsome array of ceremonial laws aim at anything else than that the inward holiness of a pure mind be commended through external signs, and that the people, imbued with this discipline and placed before their God as if in the court of their Prince, would fear to offend the eyes of so great a King and would not dare to commit [transgressions]. Because the Mosaic Law <note>the Law of Moses</note> had as its goal leading them to Jesus Christ—who was to give a stable and perfectly complete law—much like a Pedagogue <note>in antiquity, a tutor or guardian who led a child to school; a reference to Galatians 3:24</note>, especially the judicial laws provided all discretion for a weak people...

<summary>This page introduces the Pentateuch, defending Moses as its author and explaining the purpose of Genesis and Exodus. It frames the Mosaic Law as a pedagogical tool designed to curb idolatry and lead the Israelites toward a future Deliverer.</summary>

provisions should be viewed severely, and that they contain several things—such as usury against foreigners, polygamy, and divorce—which God, acting as the Prince and King of the Hebrews, merely tolerated, must be carefully noted.

<margin>
Leviticus has 27 Chapters.
</margin>

## LEVITICUS
takes its name from the "Laws of the Priests," as it pertains to the laws and duties of the Priests, the Levites, and the sacrifices. It treats at length the sacrificial victims and the persons to be chosen for the sacred ministry; it determines the feast days throughout the year and the offerings; it provides the distinction between clean and unclean animals, the signs of leprosy in humans, and the laws for marriage. All these were prescribed in the first month of the second year after the Departure <note>the Exodus from Egypt</note>, while the people remained at Mount Horeb. Furthermore, the reader of this book should be advised to consider the ceremonial laws according to their spirit, looking beneath the outer shell <note>original: "detracto cortice," literally "having pulled back the bark"</note>. For these laws were not enacted merely to keep the people occupied with a multitude of sacrifices, nor just to steady the flighty minds of the Hebrews with the weight of rituals—lest, being prone to superstition, they might slaughter victims to demons—but rather so that they might foreshadow through these sacrifices how great Jesus the Savior and Messiah would be, and to prepare them for the spiritual sacrifices of a pure heart. Since most of the Jews paid too little attention to this, relying only on external ceremonies and clinging only to the figures and shadows while neglecting the greatest precepts of the law—namely, the love of God and neighbor—the Prophets, as interpreters of the law, never ceased to cry out with one voice most sharply against such a great abuse.

<margin>
The Book of Numbers has 36 Chapters.
</margin>

## THE BOOK OF NUMBERS
taking its name from the census <note>the numbering or counting</note> of the people and the Levites, presents the history of the deeds performed during the journey through the desert over a span of nearly 39 years. It describes the seditions and murmurings of an ungrateful people, which were soon repressed either by a fire sent from heaven or by serpents suddenly let loose into the camp. Other events most worthy of the reader's attention include Korah <note>original: "Core"</note> and his companions being swallowed up by the gaping earth, the miraculously flowering Rod of Aaron, the victories won over Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, and the most famous sorcerer Balaam, who, instead of the curses he had prepared, pronounced—even against his will—all manner of blessings upon Israel.

<margin>
Deuteronomy has 34 Chapters.
</margin>

## DEUTERONOMIUM
or the "Second Law" <note>from the Greek *deuteros* (second) and *nomos* (law)</note> is so called not because it is a new law, but because it is a summary, repetition, and explanation of the law previously given in Exodus and the other books. There was a twofold reason for this repetition: first, the elders who had received the law promulgated at Mount Sinai had already met their death in the desert due to their disobedience and murmuring; thus, almost everyone among the present people was either not yet born at that time or, by reason of age, not yet capable of understanding the matters then being handled. Second, Moses, certain of his approaching death, wished to speak these final words to the people so they might cling more firmly and vividly to the minds of the children, as the last words spoken by a most loving father about to say farewell. When the man of God had performed this, and after pronouncing the blessing and specific oracles for the future events of each individual tribe, he ascended the peak of Mount Nebo at God's command. There, having laid down a mortal life of 120 years, he departed to the Bosom of Abraham <note>a phrase referring to the place of rest for the righteous dead before the time of Christ</note>, while the people migrated into Canaan under the leadership of Joshua.

<column-break/>

### §. II.

<margin>
The Book of Joshua has 24 Chapters.
</margin>

## THE BOOK OF JOSHUA
is clearly shown to have the author whose name it bears by those words in the final chapter: *And Joshua wrote all these words, etc.* For there is no reason why this testimony should be accepted as referring only to the final chapter, since all the characteristics of this work—containing the deeds performed by Joshua himself during the 17-year span in which he led the people—suit no one else. Certain names of places and other matters of minor importance inserted here do not strip the author of the book, just as we said regarding the Pentateuch. Specifically, the Prophets who came after Moses and Joshua, while reviewing the sacred books, judged that something should be added here and there for the sake of clarifying the work. We therefore receive such additions with the same veneration as the rest of the text, as things received from the same fountain of the Holy Spirit and derived through the channel of most holy men. How great a Savior Joshua was, given by God, and how he was—no less than in his name <note>the name Joshua/Jeshua is the same as "Jesus," meaning "The Lord Saves"</note>—a "type" of Christ the Lord <note>a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a prophetic symbol of someone or something in the New Testament</note>; with what happy success of arms he fought, and with what great force of miracles he entered upon the journey: the army crossing safely through the shallows of the Jordan, the walls of Jericho collapsing at the sound of the trumpets, enemies routed everywhere, and thirty-one kings defeated. The Sun and Moon halting their course so that the day might be extended for the convenient slaughter of the enemies declare these things more than sufficiently.

<margin>
The Book of Judges has 21 Chapters. 21 Chapters.
</margin>

## THE BOOK OF JUDGES
gained its name from the thirteen Judges whose deeds it encompasses over 317 years, from Joshua until the death of Samson. A "Judge" in this context is not understood as a man who held only a judicial office, but as one who acted in God's place in the administration of the Republic with supreme power, both in time of peace and war. For since the Hebrews at that time frequently departed from the divine law, they were handed over to their enemies for a period of scourging by God, the avenger of crimes. But when, pressed by the yoke of slavery, they began to return to their senses and obedience and to perform penance, God raised up and gave to them a man distinguished by strength of body and greatness of soul, who, aided by supreme protection and inspiration, might snatch them from the hands of the enemies. Among these, Ehud <note>original: "Aod"</note>, Shamgar, Barak with Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson excel with singular glory for their deeds. Furthermore, the more accepted opinion is that this book was collected by Samuel from the diaries which each Judge had written.

<margin>
The Book of Ruth has 4 Chapters.
</margin>

The same judgment applies regarding the author of the **BOOK OF RUTH**, which serves as an appendix to the preceding book and a kind of preface to the books of Kings. It presents a singular example of Divine Providence in Ruth the Moabitess, who, being joined in a second marriage to the very wealthy man Boaz during the time of Samson <note>the author's chronological placement of Ruth</note>, gave birth to Obed, the grandfather of David, and thus obtained an illustrious place among the ancestors of Christ himself.

<margin>
The First Book of Kings <note>now known as 1 Samuel</note> has 31 Chapters. Samuel born in the Year of the World 2849.
</margin>
