<margin>Book II has 24 chapters.</margin>
...tical order, having broken the Philistines in war, he governs the people with singular piety and prudence for 20 years. Saul, while seeking his father's lost donkeys, finds a kingdom; but later, on account of his contempt for divine commands, he is rejected. David is substituted in his place, who—due to the glory he reported from the prostrate Goliath—was for a long time harassed by the envy of Saul in wondrous ways, yet was always protected by the shield of Divine Providence. Finally, Saul, having in vain summoned the spirit of Samuel and being conquered by the Philistines in battle, laid violent hands upon himself in the mountains of Gilboa and perished.

<term>THE SECOND BOOK</term> <note>Known today as 2 Samuel</note> presents the Davidic kingdom through 40 years, most renowned for victories and most flourishing in peace, until—after the crime committed against Bathsheba and Uriah—a sad change of affairs was introduced by the slaughter of Amnon, the conspiracy of Absalom, and a cruel raging plague. When the penitent Prince piously submitted himself to these scourges, he spent his final years of life again in peace and rested in a holy end.

<margin>Book III has 22 Chapters.</margin>
<term>THE THIRD</term> <note>Known today as 1 Kings</note>, spanning 126 years, describes the Kingdom of Solomon and the division made under his son Rehoboam into the kingdoms of Judah and Israel: also the history of 4 Kings of Judah and 8 Kings of Israel up to Ahab, under whom lived the Prophet Elijah, no less famous for the holiness of his life than for the glory of his miracles.

<margin>Book IV has 25 Chapters.</margin>
<term>THE FOURTH</term> <note>Known today as 2 Kings</note> contains the deeds of 16 Kings of Judah and 12 of Israel through 308 years; moreover, it contains the life and wonders of the Prophet Elisha, who, like Elijah, stood like a wall against the impious to protect Religion; but as impiety finally prevailed, the avenging sword of the Lord could no longer be restrained. Thus, in the 254th year after the secession from Judah, under King Hoshea, Samaria—the capital of the kingdom—was captured by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, and the ten tribes were led away into the cities of the Medes. After the kingdom of Israel was overturned, the kingdom of Judah still remained for 134 years; once these had elapsed, having stood for about 500 years, it likewise fell, and Judah was carried away from its land into the Babylonian captivity <margin>Last [chapter] of 4 Kings.</margin>. Regarding the authors of the Books of Kings: the first two, which among the Hebrews are called the Books of Samuel, are commonly ascribed for the most part to the Prophets Nathan and Gad, who flourished under David; the latter two are ascribed partly to Isaiah and Jeremiah, and partly to Ezra, who collected them from their authentic annals.

<margin>Chronicles</margin>
The following two books the Hebrews call "The Words of the Days" or annals, and the Latins call them by the Greek name <term>Paralipomena</term> <note>meaning "things passed over" or "omitted"</note>, as if they were a supplement added to the Books of Kings, containing many things omitted in them. However, it appears the primary intention of the Holy Writer was to describe accurately what the status of the families was before and after the release from captivity: likewise the duties, genealogies, and orders of the priests and Levites—in a word: those things which pertain to the worship of the Lord and the temple.

<margin>Book I has 29 Chapters.</margin>
<term>BOOK THE FIRST</term> <note>1 Chronicles</note> sets forth the Summary of Holy History from the beginning of the world until the death of David, spanning 2990 years.

<margin>Book II has 36 chapters.</margin>
<term>THE SECOND</term> <note>2 Chronicles</note> describes the History of the Kings of Judah, and in part also the Kings of Israel, from the beginning of Solomon until the end of the captivity, through 478 years. The common opinion holds that both Books—in which, according to Saint Jerome <margin>St. Jerome in the Letter to Domnio.</margin>, all the learning of the Scriptures is contained—were arranged by Ezra from the left-behind records of the Prophets.

<column-break/>

<margin>The Book of Ezra has 10 Chapters.</margin>
<term>THE FIRST BOOK OF EZRA</term>, reporting the liberty granted by Cyrus to return from Babylon, the restoration of the sacred objects and the temple, and the efforts of enemies to the contrary, encompasses a history of 82 years. The author is Ezra himself, of priestly lineage, called in Scripture a "swift scribe," that is, one most skilled in the law. He was indeed a man full of the Spirit of God, having served most excellently in the reformation of the Jewish Republic and in the collection and ordering of the sacred books; he was himself the greatest part and an eyewitness of the history he committed to writing.

<margin>Book II has 13 Chapters.</margin>
<term>THE SECOND BOOK OF EZRA</term> <note>commonly called the Book of Nehemiah</note> is so titled not because Ezra is the author, but because in the Hebrew text it was formerly joined in one series with the preceding one, and it contains those things which were performed by Ezra and Nehemiah together. For according to the common opinion, the author is Nehemiah, also of the priestly order. Although some contend that he descended from the royal line of the tribe of Judah. Whatever the case may be, he was certainly a great man in all things; while he served Artaxerxes, King of the Persians, in the most noble office of *atherfara* <note>a Persian title</note> or Cupbearer, he came to the aid of his people's afflicted affairs, eluded the traps of enemies, restored and dedicated the city, and turned all his care to uprooting the abuses that had crept into the Republic. It is a history of about 30 years.

<margin>The Book of Tobit has 14 Chapters.</margin>
<term>THE BOOK OF TOBIT</term> had both Tobits <note>the father and the son, Tobias</note> as authors, though the last two verses were added by a collector. We owe the most clear translation of this miraculous history to Saint Jerome, who prepared it from a work written in Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldaice"</note>, which he accepted as the original manuscript. Moreover, because this book presents outstanding examples of exceptional piety, patience, and Divine Providence (whose ministers are the Holy Angels), it must be diligently attended to by all who desire to imbue the youth with the most wholesome precepts of life and morals, so that they may drink from this divine fountain to instill these things in tender souls. Also—

<margin>The Book of Judith has 16 Chapters.</margin>
<term>THE BOOK OF JUDITH</term>, translated from Aramaic by St. Jerome, reports a history most worthy of being "preserved in eternal cedar" <note>an idiom for a work of timeless value</note> concerning Judith, the widow of Manasseh and a woman of proven virtue, who struck down Holofernes, the fierce Assyrian General, having captured him by a stratagem. She liberated the city of Bethulia from siege and all of Judea from a great crisis. The certain author of this book is indeed hidden; however, since it was the duty of the Priests to reduce the more famous deeds of their nation into commentaries, it is likely attributed to the High Priest Joachim, or Eliakim, who is mentioned therein. There is greater controversy regarding the timing of the history: but the opinion more accepted among the best chronologists, and supported by better reasons, is the one that teaches it happened before the Babylonian captivity under King Manasseh. This was when he, having learned to be wise amid adversity and being restored to liberty, devoted himself entirely to penance; therefore, he no longer involved himself in the affairs of the Republic, but according to the prophecy of <margin>Isaiah 22.</margin> Isaiah, committed all things to be managed by the High Priest Eliakim. This is not the place to refute the inept quibbles of dissenting writers <note>original: "heterodoxorum"</note> against this book; Bellarmine, Serarius, Huet, Montfaucon, Calmet, and other most excellent writers have long since unraveled them.

<margin>The Book of Esther has 16 Chapters.</margin>
<term>THE BOOK OF ESTHER</term> provides a singular proof of the Providence of God, who humbles the proud and exalts the humble, in Esther (or Hadassah), who <meta>catchword: in place of</meta>

In the place of Queen Vashti, who was repudiated because she proudly refused the King's command to enter before the guests, Esther was taken into the royal bed. She so fortunately averted the extermination of her entire nation—which Haman, elated by the King's friendship, had decreed by public edict because Mordecai refused him divine honors—that Haman, after being forced to serve as a groom for the highly honored Mordecai, perished by hanging from the same beam he had prepared for the Queen’s uncle. It is much more probable that the history of this book took place under Darius, son of Hystaspes; the Jews have religiously preserved the memory of it by establishing the annual solemn feast of Purim <note>original: "Phurim"</note>, that is, the feast of lots. That the writers were Mordecai and Ezra <note>original: "Elisam"; likely referring to Ezra the scribe</note> is gathered clearly enough from the Sacred Text itself in Chapter IX.

<margin>The Book of Job has 42 Chapters.</margin>
The Book of Job presents an illustrious proof of justice and patience in a man who, composing his life according to the norm of <term>natural law</term> <note>Universal moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature, accessible even without divine revelation</note> among pagans, became an extraordinary image of the most harsh and laborious life of Christ the Lord. By his example, he taught what constant virtue can achieve, both amidst the allurements of misfortune and the storms of calamity. Stripped of all his goods, bereaved of his children, mocked by his wife, and burdened by the slanders of his friends, he nevertheless obeyed the will of his Creator with the most perfect submission of soul; he venerated the hand that struck him, celebrated His Majesty, and adored His Judgments. And when he noticed anything expressed too sharply by the force of pain, he revoked it, mourning dressed in sackcloth and sprinkled with ashes. Furthermore, it is rightly believed that this Job is the same

<margin>Genesis 36:32.</margin>
as Jobab, descended from the line of Esau, who reigned in Dinhabah <note>original: "Denaba"</note>, the capital of Eastern Idumea or desert Arabia, at the time when the Hebrews were making their journey through the desert. Among the learned, there is a controversy regarding the author of the Book, which is composed partly in prose and partly in verse. Some contend it was written in Arabic by Job himself and gifted to the Hebrews in their tongue by Moses. Others, because of the agreement of the logic of its sentences and its majesty with those found in the books of Solomon, attribute it to Solomon. But since it is certain and well-ascertained that the Author was one whose mind was illuminated by divine light and whose hand was directed by God so that he might religiously and holily narrate the deeds and speeches of this holy man, nothing further needs to be laboriously sought. More correctly, for the easier understanding of the reader, the theme of the entire book is proposed, which turns on this question of greatest importance: Whether God punishes only the impious with the evils of this life, or whether He also sometimes exercises the just with these same evils to test their constancy and increase their perfection and merit? Job's three friends—Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar, joined by a fourth, Elihu—falsely defended the former view. From this, they constantly asserted that Job, who, secure in the testimony of his conscience, sharply defended the truth of the latter view, had provoked such a whirlwind of evils upon himself by his own impiety and hypocrisy. Finally, God, speaking from the cloud and adjudging the dispute to Job, imposed an end to the lengthy debate.

<column-break/>

### §. III.

<margin>There are 150 Psalms.</margin>
The Book of Psalms, which is divided into five parts among the Hebrews, is a single volume among the Latins, with the number defined in both cases as 150 Psalms. These are believed to have been collected by Ezra <note>original: "Esdra"</note> without regard for the order of subject matter or time. Whether the sole Author of all of them is to be considered David, the most holy of Kings, is a famous controversy. Those who attribute the primary role to the Royal Psalmist in this most divine work, yet without excluding other authors, bring forward arguments that are by no means to be despised, following the authority of Saints Jerome, Hilary, and others. Among others, there is this argument: the Psalms that bear the name of David on their front are ascribed to David; therefore, those which have the name of Asaph or others prefixed to them must be attributed to those same men by equal right. If you say that the name Asaph only signifies a most skilled singer, you do not solve the argument; for in <term>2 Chronicles</term> <note>original: "II. Paralip."</note> 29:30, King Hezekiah commanded the Levites to praise the Lord with the words of David and of Asaph the <term>seer</term> <note>original: "videntis"; a term for a prophet or visionary</note>. Therefore Asaph, just like David, is proclaimed as a seer, that is, one inspired by the Divine Spirit and foreknowing the future. A no less effective argument is sought from the marks of time and the subject matter of the Psalms; for there are several which show the Jews as if living in the midst of the Babylonians, pleading with God for the pardon of their crimes and a return from captivity: they describe the most corrupt customs of Babylon: and finally, they resonate with sad lamentations over the destruction of the temple and unjust oppression. Others, on the contrary, offer congratulations for the liberty granted by Cyrus, the repair of the temple, and its solemn dedication. I confess, indeed, that even Psalms of this kind could be claimed for the Royal Prophet by the same spirit through which he foretold many things regarding Christ and the Church; but those who assert this introduce great marvels without necessity. Furthermore, there is a significant disparity between prophecies pertaining to the law of grace and those pertaining to the Babylonian captivity; for it is evidently clear from elsewhere that all the Prophets aimed at Christ as their target. But indeed, it is nowhere read that the Prophets predicted some singular vengeance to be taken upon the people before they were stained with the crimes that uniquely provoked it. When Isaiah began to announce the Babylonian captivity and the ruin of the city and temple to the Jews, the people had already fallen into a depth of evils; from the sole of the foot even to the 
<margin>Isaiah 1</margin>
crown of the head, there was no soundness in them; idolatry and other crimes of both Kings and people had already so overflowed that they extorted some notable vengeance from the Lord. This is manifest from the Books of Kings. But there was nothing of the sort in the age of David. Hence we learn from Scripture that neither the fall of his son Solomon nor the defection of the ten tribes from his house—which were nevertheless to happen shortly after—were openly foretold by him. As for the Psalms marked with no name, according to the rule of Saint Jerome, they are referred to the author named most recently, unless sacred authority or evident reason suggests otherwise. Six, therefore, beyond a hundred <note>106</note> are to be said to belong to the Royal Psalmist. But enough of this: for although the labor by which the writers of the Books are sought out can serve for instruction and edification alongside commendable erudition, it is nevertheless a contentious...

<margin>The sentiments of the Holy Fathers regarding the Psalter.</margin>
...that the study of virtue and wisdom might be more easily and certainly advanced, rather than pulling the rope of contention in similar controversies. I judge it unnecessary to argue over the "pen" <note>This refers to the human scribe or author (such as David) vs. the divine inspiration.</note>, lest, although we all faithfully hold the Holy Spirit to be the Author, we nevertheless seem to want to fight over the instrument. It will be more worthwhile to repeatedly urge students of Holy Scripture to always hold this most noble part of the Divine Code especially dear, and to look up to it as a compendium of both Testaments; for the Psalter supplies testimonies even for the Law of Grace <note>The New Testament/Gospel era</note>, so that if one wished to cite every instance, almost the entire book would have to be transcribed. And if you listen to the Holy Fathers, the Book of Psalms is a most fertile fountain of Truths: the sum of all moral discipline; a common and inexhaustible treasure of life; a medicine seasoned by heaven with the flavor of sweet eloquence and poetry, and most ready to heal any evils of the soul. It is a Book in which doctrine competes with grace, the reading of which is none more pleasant, none more useful to all: whether you desire to praise God’s Majesty, Power, Wisdom, and Providence, etc.; or to implore the Mercy of the Supreme Judge; or to seek help from God in war, in disease, or in calamities of every kind; or to return thanks for benefits received; or finally, if you desire to instruct or correct your neighbor and lead them back to the duties of piety and justice—the one book of Psalms alone suffices for all these great needs at once. However, because the Psalms are a very ancient form of Poetry, as far removed from common speech by the greatness and variety of their subjects as by the sublimity of their style, the verses are not to be run through in a haphazard manner to understand them; rather, beyond attentive reading, the occasion of the writing, the theme, the mind of the Author, and other circumstances must be diligently kept before one's eyes. I note this one thing further: no one should be moved by those passages where the sacred Prophet seems to call down the gravest evils upon the enemies of God; for through a <term>Hebraism</term> <note>A characteristic Hebrew idiom or grammatical structure translated literally</note>, the imperative mood is frequently expressed in place of the future indicative tense: for example, *let the devil stand at his right hand* instead of *he will stand.* Hence, such things are to be received not as the wish of one's soul, but as an oracle foretelling things to come. See Part one, Lecture II, Canon 17.

<margin>The Book of Proverbs has 31 Chapters.</margin>
# THE BOOK OF PROVERBS 
contains the entire treasure of that Wisdom with which we know the wisest of Kings was adorned by God. Indeed, it delivers a norm of living fit for the condition of all men, as well as rules of moral, political, and economic Discipline with such variety that it allows no reader to depart empty-handed. The name "Proverbs" here denotes any illustrious maxims, parables, likenesses, apothegms, and enigmas written in a grave and concise style. All these are designated by the name *Misle* <note>original: "Misle"; the Hebrew "Mishlei," meaning Proverbs</note>, by which the Hebrews call the book. Maxims joined together by no internal connection of subject matter are proposed through antitheses and comparisons—which are mostly derived from natural and well-known things—in such a way that they make a complete sense, clearly separated from the rest. Moreover, this Book is a most choice part of those 
<margin>1 Kings 4:31. <note>In modern Bibles, 1 Kings 4:32.</note></margin>
three thousand parables which it is established that Solomon wrote; the first nine Chapters are like a preface to the whole Book, and aim toward this: that the son or disciple, whom Solomon intends to instruct, being fortified against the allurements of pleasures and the snares of loose women, might be led...

<column-break/>

...toward his goal.
<margin>Ecclesiastes has 12 Chapters.</margin>
# ECCLESIASTES 
or "The Preacher" is called *Coheleth* by the Hebrews, the meaning of the name being the same, as it likewise indicates one convening an assembly and speaking before a congregation. For in this Book, Solomon, as if teaching the people in an assembly—and especially men of mature age—brings forward and refutes the cavils of the impious, so that at the same time he might undertake to demonstrate that, on the one hand, all things of this life possess a great deal of vanity and trouble; but on the other hand, only one solid and perpetual thing remains, which we ought to pursue with all effort: namely, the fear of God, piety, and faithful obedience to divine laws. To prove this, he runs through all conditions of life in a long sequence, weighs all vices, reviews the foolish thoughts and actions of men, and shows the vanity of wealth and pleasures by his own proposed example and experience. Finally, suddenly drawing together the scattered discourse as if into one, he grips the reader and forces him to confess that there is nothing stable in this world, nothing that deserves all our love and effort, except the fear of God, virtue, and a profound reverence for the Judgments of the eternal Divinity. The Author aims at this goal while he concludes his speech thus: *Let us all hear the end of the matter together: Fear God, and keep his commandments. For this is the whole man.* <note>Ecclesiastes 12:13</note> This, indeed, is the total perfection of man;
<margin>City of God, Book 20, chapter 3.</margin>
this is the sum of human duties. For whoever, as Augustine says, is not a keeper of God's commandments, is nothing. Therefore, the attentive Reader ought to distinguish between those things which the Author speaks for himself, and those which he speaks from the persona of the impious. If he does this, he will avoid the rocks, reconcile maxims that seem to fight against each other, and become accustomed to the mind of the sacred Writer, who vividly depicts the vanity of things, 
<margin>Ibid. <note>Augustine, same location</note></margin>
*certainly not for any other reason, except that we might desire that life which has no vanity under this sun, but truth under Him who made this sun.* Furthermore, from this very argument of the work which the Author treats, and from its goal, the more common opinion of Interpreters is not a little strengthened, which contends that the Book was written by Solomon in his repentance as a perpetual monument of his return to his senses. However, this is not certain; otherwise, doubt about the eternal salvation of Solomon would cease; but concerning this, the question remains, to be decided only by divine Authority.
<margin>The Song of Songs has 8 Chapters.</margin>
# THE SONG OF SONGS 
or "The Canticle," the most excellent of all among the many written by Solomon, is conveniently distributed into as many dialogues as it has Chapters. In these, the speaking persons introduced are the Bridegroom and the Bride, and the companions and attendants of both. For under the figure of a marriage—alluding to the ceremonies and solemnity of weddings which, according to the custom of the Jews, lasted for seven days—is celebrated the spiritual and divine marriage of Jesus Christ with human nature, with the Church, and with the soul of every individual just person; or rather, an intimate union through incomprehensible charity. This is like the key with which the mystery of this most Holy Book is opened. The Bridegroom, who speaks now as a King, now as a Shepherd, is God himself, Christ the Lord himself. The Bride represents now the devoted and chaste soul, now the whole Church; and under the name of "Bride" or "Vineyard" in Holy Scripture...

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the wisdom books of the Bible, transitioning from the Song of Songs to the Book of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus (Sirach), before beginning a new section on the nature and purpose of the Prophets.</meta>

...is designated many times in Scripture. In the Song itself, a perpetual allegory reigns: nothing occurs more frequently than ointments, spices, fruits, wine, gardens, and fountains—the delights of the Holy Land. The Jews loved this metaphorical style of speech so much that they sometimes used even more remote and intense figures of speech. Therefore, because of the nature of the work, the mind must be raised higher, and the mystical sense hidden under the "bark of the letter" <note>The literal or surface meaning of the text.</note> must be extracted with the eyes of a pure mind. Here the torches of love burn, but they are lit by that celestial fire which Christ came to send upon the earth. For this reason, anyone who is unequal to allegorical and mystical things, or who tastes only of "flesh and blood" <note>Meaning someone who thinks only in physical or worldly terms.</note>, should abstain from reading it; otherwise, instead of the "life-giving spirit," they will stumble over the "killing letter" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6: "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life."</note>. The Synagogue <note>The Jewish religious community.</note>, although it always held this Song as a divinely inspired work, called it by the name "Holy of Holies," and likewise explained it as the covenant of the Lord with His people as a spiritual marriage; nevertheless, it judged that the weaker or profane should be kept away. Hence, it provided by law that no one should presume to read it before their thirtieth year of age.

<margin>The Book of Wisdom has 19 Chapters.</margin>
THE BOOK OF WISDOM is so called among the other Wisdom books by *Antonomasia* <term>Antonomasia: the use of a title or epithet in place of a proper name to show excellence</term>, or by a certain privilege of excellence; because it treats most sublimely of Wisdom, both uncreated [Divine] and created. It is divided into three parts: the *first* up to Chapter 7 is an exhortation to the love and study of Wisdom. The *second* up to Chapter 10 explains its origin. The *third* displays the effects and fruits of Wisdom. However, the name "Wisdom" here is not taken merely as a bare knowledge of general truths, but for Religion, piety, the fear of God, and justice. Kings, Princes, and all Magistrates are urged again and again, both by words and by the examples set before them, to devote themselves entirely to the study of this Wisdom. This is the sole aim of this Book, in which the Greek Text is held as the archetype <note>The original or primary version used for this edition.</note>, because the Hebrew original or copy (if any ever existed) had already disappeared by the time of Jerome <note>The 4th-century scholar who translated the Latin Vulgate.</note>. Who the writer was is actually uncertain. Neither the opinion that attributes this work to Solomon, nor the other that attributes it to Philo—not the famous Philo of Alexandria, but one of the Seventy [translators] of the same name—rises beyond the level of a probable opinion. This much is certain: we may remain ignorant of which instrument the Holy Spirit used without any loss to our faith.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus has 51 Chapters.</margin>
ECCLESIASTICUS, that is, *The Preacher*, this Book is titled both to distinguish it from and to imitate Ecclesiastes, with which it shares the same goal: namely, to pave the way to Wisdom. Therefore, it proposes not only all moral philosophy—and indeed more abundantly than the <margin>Book of Proverbs.</margin>—but also rules of instruction for governing the state well. This book was published in Hebrew by a certain Jesus, son of Sirach, during the time of the Seventy [Translators], or (as others believe) during the persecution stirred up by Antiochus Epiphanes; his grandson of the same name translated it into Greek. This is clear from the Prologue, to which, however, we are not forced to assert divine authority, since it flowed from the pen of the Translator alone, not from the sacred Writer.

<column-break/>

### §. IV.

-> *Before I review the prophetic books in order, I think it will not be out of place to briefly provide some general remarks about the Prophets.* <-

<margin>Prophets were called Seers.</margin>
The Prophets, formerly called *Seers* <note>original: "Videntes"</note> by the Hebrews, as if seeing divine things, were men who spoke driven by divine instinct, and who instructed, rebuked, and comforted the people with promises while foretelling the future. The Holy Spirit—which is one by nature but manifold in its effects—communicated itself to them in many ways: through the quiet of the night, through visions, in ecstasy, but most often through a secret inspiration of the soul, which illuminated their minds with an inner light and stirred their wills so that they might open up in words and commit to writing the things they perceived were suggested by the Holy Spirit.

Prophecy, the gift of which was usually granted by God through the ordinary way only to holy men pursuing a humble way of life, was a most clear argument for true Religion; the Prophets themselves were placed by God in the midst of the people as living proofs of His Presence and Will. Hence, whenever they spoke to either Princes or the people, they followed the gentle guidance of the Holy Spirit and spoke with the gravity that befits the ambassadors of the Supreme God.

<margin>To what the oracles of the Prophets looked.</margin>
All the Oracles of the Prophets, by the counsel of the Holy Spirit, were aimed primarily at providing clear evidence of the coming of the Messiah, His Passion, Resurrection, the calling of the Gentiles, the rejection of the Jews, and the establishment of the Church. Even those oracles that seemed of lesser importance served to confirm the truth of these, such as those concerning the political state of the Jews, Nineveh, Babylon, Tyre, etc.; for the truth of those things, fulfilled before the eyes of the whole world, demonstrated the reliability of the oracles regarding the kingdom of the Messiah in the same way. Thus, while Isaiah predicted the liberation of King Ahaz, <margin>Chapter VII.</margin> and the destruction of the Kings of Samaria and Damascus, the observed truth of these events provided a most certain proof for the birth of the Messiah from a Virgin Mother, which he foretold at the same time and toward which he primarily looked. Therefore, the histories that the Prophets describe must be understood so that, besides the literal sense, the mystical sense is properly noted. For instance, where the magnificence of Solomon’s Kingdom is praised, or where the victories of Cyrus and the liberty he granted to the captive Jews are proclaimed, one must rise from the historical sense concerning Solomon and Cyrus to the spiritual sense; for the goal and finish line of all such oracles was placed in Jesus Christ, whom they presented as the Principal One under the names and figures of those men. See *Part I, Lecture II, Section 3, Rule 3.*

Furthermore, the prophecies displayed both clarity and obscurity, depending on their focus. Those which pertained to the political state of the Jews and other nations were open to everyone in the era of the Prophets themselves. Those which concerned the Messiah and the Church, however, were wrapped in a certain sacred darkness; for although the coming Liberator was announced repeatedly and indeed in the clearest words, his qualities and the entire history of his coming into the world were mostly covered by a veil of figures. In turn, these Prophecies sometimes present us with a cross <note>Metaphor for a difficulty or a burden to understand.</note> which <meta>catchword: con-</meta>

# THE WORKS OF FERDINAND KOPF

However, whatever concerns the Messiah and the Church came into open light after the Advent of Jesus Christ, whose role it was to remove the appropriate seals <note>A reference to the "Seven Seals" in Revelation, which only the Lamb/Christ can open to reveal divine mysteries.</note>. This light is unseen only by the treacherous blindness of the Jews, who have a veil before their eyes <note>A common historical theological trope based on 2 Corinthians 3:14, suggesting that those who do not accept the Christian interpretation of the Old Testament are "blinded."</note>. This very blindness was predicted more than once by

<margin>
Isaiah
has
66
Chapters.
</margin>

ISAIAH, the first among the four Major Prophets, so called because of the more extensive works of his that have reached us. He performed his prophetic office for approximately 60 years, distinguished no less by the splendor of his birth—as he was the grandson of King Amaziah of Judah through his brother—and the majesty of his royal eloquence, than by the sanctity of his life and the glory of his wonders. His ministry is calculated from immediately after the death of Uzziah and the beginning of the reign of Jotham until the first or second year of Manasseh. According to the constant tradition of the Hebrews and Christians, he died a glorious martyr, sawn in two <note>According to tradition, Isaiah was executed by King Manasseh by being placed inside a hollow log and sawn in half.</note>, because the King could not endure his bolder warnings. His prophecies, which are much more easily understood when joined and considered together than when inspected only in parts, can be distributed such that the first six chapters pertain to the time of King Jotham, the following six to Ahaz, and the remainder to the times of Hezekiah. In this prophecy of his, which according to Jerome is a "compendium of the most beautiful things," the man of God always kept before his eyes the goal of foretelling the Babylonian captivity and the happy return from it; for under this image, he describes the human race fallen into sin and the future Redemption through Jesus Christ. In the final part of the prophecy, he is entirely occupied with the Advent of the Messiah, the calling of the Gentiles, and the rejection of the Jews; and he treats the Kingdom of Christ, His Passion, and His death so openly that he seems not so much to prophesy about the future as to weave a history of the past. Therefore, he deservedly ought to be called an Evangelist rather than a Prophet.

<margin>
Jeremiah
has
52
Chapters.
</margin>

JEREMIAH, born of a priestly line in the village of Anathoth in the Tribe of Benjamin, was consecrated a Prophet from his mother's womb. He pursued his office, which he was commanded by God to undertake from the fifteenth year of his age, for 45 years until the capture of Jerusalem. He is almost entirely occupied with announcing the punishments soon to be inflicted by God, the avenger of crimes. From this, he inveighs against the crimes of the Jews with sharp oratory and exhorts them to avert the imminent whirlwind of evils from the Chaldeans through serious repentance. He also acts as a Prophet to the Nations, predicting that the cup of divine fury would be passed to them in equal measure. Nevertheless, here and there among these sad oracles, after the manner of all Prophets, he mixes joyful promises about the return from the 70-year Babylonian captivity and flies toward the Redeemer of the world and the calling of the Gentiles. He never allowed himself to be deterred from preaching these truths freely; though burdened with lashes and chains, he stood like a bronze wall and an iron pillar against all the injuries of the princes and the people. When he witnessed the evils he had announced, he wrote the *Threni* <note>original: "Threnos" — The Book of Lamentations.</note>, in which he deplores the sad turns of the overturned Jerusalem and the mournful state of the captive people. This doleful poem is constructed with such artifice that each verse begins with the letters of the alphabet in order <note>This refers to the acrostic structure of Lamentations, where each verse or stanza begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet.</note>. How much the Lamenting Prophet excelled in this genre of writing is 

<column-break/>

more than sufficiently declared by his elegant style, which is most suitable for moving the soul. Ignatius, Jerome, and others testify that he lived as a perpetual virgin, a claim founded on Chapter XVI:2 <note>Jeremiah 16:2 states: "You shall not take a wife, nor shall you have sons or daughters in this place."</note>. It is the opinion of many that he was overwhelmed by stones <note>i.e., stoned to death.</note> by an ungrateful and obstinate people in the city of Tahpanhes in Egypt.

<margin>
Baruch
has
6
Chapters.
</margin>

BARUCH, although born of an illustrious lineage and the brother of Prince Seraiah in the tribe of Judah, did not blush to act as the scribe <note>original: "Amanuensem"</note> for Jeremiah. He received the prophecies from him as he dictated them, as if reading from a book, and adhering to him most constantly, he was a most faithful companion and sharer in all his labors and afflictions. It is for this reason that Baruch's prophecy is more frequently praised by the Church Fathers under Jeremiah’s name, and no open mention is made of it in the ancient catalogs of the Sacred Books. After Jeremiah departed from this life, Baruch went from Egypt to Babylon, and there he wrote this volume, in which he consoles his captive brothers and teaches them to appease God through the flight from idolatry and a sincere conversion of the heart. Speaking of the future as if it were the past, in the manner of the Prophets, he predicted the Mystery of the Divine Incarnation with these words: *Afterward he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men.* <note>Baruch 3:38. This verse was historically cited by Christians as a prophecy of Christ's earthly life.</note>

<margin>

Ezekiel
has
48
Chapters.
</margin>

EZEKIEL, sprung from a noble stock of priests, was among the very first who were transported to Babylon along with King Jeconiah. In the fifth year after the deportation, he was raised up by God to refute the false prophets who were preaching peace and all prosperity, and to confirm the prophecies of Jeremiah, who was still prophesying in Jerusalem at that time. Hence, the subject matter of both is the same; however, Ezekiel treats it in such a way that, after the manner of the Chaldeans among whom he lived, he more frequently uses metaphors and figures. The Roman Martyrology holds that he likewise died a martyr, killed by a leader of the Jews against whom he had more vehemently inveighed on account of their idolatry. It is well established that he prophesied for 20 years, most famous for his sanctity as well as his erudition and eloquence.

<margin>
Daniel
has
14
Chapters.
</margin>

DANIEL, descended from the blood of the Kings of Judah, was deported to Babylon in the first flower of his youth, in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim. There, selected for the excellence of his body and character along with three other companions to serve in the royal court, he lived in such a way that he shone forth wonderfully both in the sanctity of his morals and in his wisdom—the first specimen of which he exhibited in vindicating the innocence of Susanna <note>Referring to the story in Daniel 13 (Deuterocanon) where Daniel saves Susanna from false accusations.</note>. Since he was additionally gifted by God with a prophetic spirit and the power of interpreting dreams, he obtained the highest honors in the most splendid Palace of the whole world, being appointed governor of the province of Babylon and chief of all the Wise Men among the Chaldeans. To promote the affairs of his people, he remained in Persia until his death, always occupied with the most ample duties of the kingdom; he was prodigiously delivered time and again from the most present danger of death prepared by the envy of malevolent men, when the mouths of the lions were shut. However, in what year and whether he closed his final day in Babylon or Susa is uncertain. Yet he holds this distinction among the other Prophets: not only did he predict the coming of Christ in that terrible statue representing the succession of kingdoms, in the goat representing the victory of Alexander the Great, etc., and in the stone cut from the mountain without hands that subverts all kingdoms; but he also clearly indicated the time of the coming itself in the mystery of the seventy weeks <note>Daniel 9:24-27, often interpreted in Christian tradition as a precise chronological countdown to the arrival and death of the Messiah.</note>. # INTRODUCTION

The Prayer of Azariah, the Hymn of the Three Youths, and the stories of Susanna and of Bel and the Dragon had already disappeared from the Hebrew texts by the time of Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was the scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate; he noted that these sections were only found in the Greek Septuagint.</note>, remaining only in the Greek version. For this reason, there was some doubt as to whether they were Canonical <note>Meaning officially accepted as part of the divinely inspired Bible.</note>, until the tradition and authority of the Church finally settled the hesitating minds of some.

<margin>
XII.
The Minor Prophets.
</margin>
The twelve Minor Prophets—to whom we owe many precious monuments of history in addition to the prophecies regarding Christ and the Church—are so called not because of their age or their level of authority, but because of the smaller size of their writings. Among these, the first is:

<margin>
Hosea
has
14
Chapters.
</margin>
HOSEA lived in the kingdom of Samaria, also known as the Ten Tribes, to whom his prophecies primarily look. That "prostitute woman" whom the Prophet was commanded to convert to modesty and take as a wife represented those tribes; they were betrothed to God through faith, but became unfaithful and "adulterous" through their worship of idols. Through this symbolic figure and the appearance of the actual Prophet, he predicts the rejection of the Synagogue <note>In this historical context, "Synagogue" refers to the ancient Jewish religious community that did not accept Jesus.</note>, whose crimes he sharply attacks, and the calling of the Gentiles, while simultaneously promising mercy and glory to those who repent. The time and duration of his prophesying are found at the beginning of the work.

<margin>
Joel has 3 Chapters.
</margin>
JOEL, a contemporary of Hosea or, according to others, Jeremiah, issued his prophecies to the Kingdom of Judah. Using a comparison drawn from a cloud of locusts, he threatens the invasions of the Chaldeans—or rather, the devastation and famine to be brought by locusts, which he describes most elegantly under the appearance of a hostile army. However, he soon promises to those who do penance a singular abundance of crops, and especially the greatest blessings of the Law of Grace: namely, the sending of the Teacher of Justice, the pouring out of the Holy Spirit upon all flesh, and the salvation that will come to all who call upon the name of God. Finally, looking toward the end of the world, he announces the Last Judgment to be held in the Valley of Jehoshaphat.

<margin>
Amos
has
9
Chapters.
</margin>
AMOS was not the father of Isaiah <note>A common clarification in biblical studies to distinguish between Amos the prophet and Amoz, the father of the prophet Isaiah.</note>, but a shepherd from the village of Tekoa in the Tribe of Judah. Called to the prophetic office by a special nod from God, he prophesied under Jeroboam II, King of Israel, two years before a terrifying earthquake shook Jerusalem; this is commonly said to have happened in the 23rd year of King Uzziah of Judah. His prophecies primarily strike the Kingdom of Israel, whose luxury, pride, and injustice he rebukes, threatening them with the gravest evils and even destruction unless they repent. First, however, he deals with the neighboring nations of Palestine, predicting they will most certainly be punished for "three and four" crimes—that is, for the full measure of many sins.

<margin>
Obadiah
has
one
Chapter.
</margin>
OBADIAH, about whose homeland and deeds nothing certain is known, threatens the Edomites with final destruction because they acted proudly and cruelly toward the Jews, joining the Chaldeans when they captured Jerusalem. From this, it is inferred that he prophesied after the city’s destruction and was a contemporary of Jeremiah. Under the figure of Zion being restored and making its enemies subject to it, he foreshadows the greatness of the glorious Church of Christ.

<margin>
Jonah
has
4
Chapters.
</margin>
JONAH, a Galilean by birth from the city of Gath-hepher in the Tribe of Zebulun, and a contemporary of the Prophet Amos, was a great marvel of his age. By God—who can do all things and disposes all things by His eternal counsel—he alone among the Prophets was sent to the Gentiles. Just as he provided a sure pledge of the Church to be gathered from the unbelievers through the conversion of the Ninevites, so too,

<column-break/>

miraculously preserved for three days in the belly of the whale, he expressed in himself a living image of the Burial and Resurrection of Jesus Christ. Thus, indeed, not only the oracles of the Prophets but even their very deeds speak of the Messiah and represent the divine Prototype everywhere: Jonah is committed to the sea so that he might free his shipmates from shipwreck; Christ is handed over to be crucified so that He might save the entire human race from destruction. Jonah emerges unharmed from the fish; Christ rises glorious from the tomb, the victor over death and hell. Even the shading ivy (or "Palm of Christ") <note>The Latin text uses "hedera" (ivy) and "palma Christi" (castor oil plant) to describe the plant that shaded Jonah, which is famously translated differently in various Bible versions.</note>, which later withered when struck and exposed the Prophet to the burning heat of the sun, is not without mystery. For it was a figure of the Law of the Jews; they were covered by its shadow for a time, but are now entirely deprived of it, wandering among the nations and miserably sweltering amidst hardships, sorrows, and afflictions.

<margin>
Hosea 9:17.
</margin>

<margin>

has
7

Chapter 5.
</margin>
MICAH, arising from the village of Moresheth in the Tribe of Judah, was a contemporary of Isaiah and similar to him in spirit and style. He poured out oracles against the two kingdoms of Judah and Israel, threatening the punishments due for the unrestrained crimes reigning in both places. However, he also added many things that pertain uniquely to the Church of Christ. He clearly indicated the very Divinity of the Messiah, whom he predicted would come out of Bethlehem, with these words: *His going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.* <note>original: "Egressus Ejus ab initio, a diebus aeternitatis."</note>

<margin>
Nahum
has
3
Chapters.
Year of the World
3378.
</margin>
NAHUM, from the village of Elkosh in Galilee, flourished in the time of King Hezekiah of Judah. He prophesies against Nineveh, painting its destruction with such a marvelous force of eloquence and vivid colors that he seems not so much to describe it as to place it before one's very eyes. This prophecy is to be understood as concerning the final destruction, when the Assyrian Monarchy—of which Nineveh was the royal seat and metropolis—was so overturned by Astyages and Nabopolassar (the father of Nebuchadnezzar the Great) that it never rose again.

<margin>
Habakkuk has 3 Chapters.
</margin>
HABAKKUK, born in the city of Beth-zachar in the Tribe of Simeon and a contemporary of Jeremiah, complains with sharp and vivid speech about the happiness of the wicked. But when he soon understands through God’s revelation that a terrible vengeance hangs over the kingdom of Judah via the Chaldeans, and that these men themselves will pay the penalty for their crimes after they have punished the Jews as ministers of divine justice, his troubled mind is calmed. He admires the loftiness and wisdom of God's judgments and celebrates in a most noble song the ancient benefits bestowed upon Israel: the liberation from captivity in Egypt and Babylon, and, under this figure, the Redemption of the human race through the Messiah. Finally, he adds that he hopes, with God's help, to escape like a deer to the mountains, fleeing the hands of the Chaldeans who lay waste to Judea, and to enjoy tranquil peace. Having attained things greater than he hoped, Habakkuk—while occupied with farming after the departure of the Chaldeans—merited to be transported to Babylon by a great miracle to feed Daniel with the meal he had prepared for the reapers, and was soon restored to his homeland by the Angel of the Lord <note>This refers to a story found in the deuterocanonical portion of the Book of Daniel (Bel and the Dragon), where Habakkuk is miraculously transported to the lions' den.</note>. There, he peacefully finished the remaining course of his life and crowned it with a holy end.

<margin>
Zepha-
niah
has
3
Chapters.
</margin>
ZEPHANIAH, whose oracles are to be set at the beginning of the reign of Josiah, is said to have been born of an illustrious lineage in the Tribe of Simeon. He exhorts the Jews and other peoples to penance, warning that they will be punished most severely if they do not comply. Nevertheless, as Prophets are accustomed to do, he promises happier things in the midst of the gravest threats, and intersperses several points whose full truth was not fulfilled until after the Advent of Jesus Christ.

HAGGAI was born in Babylon during the time of the captivity and is believed to have returned with Zerubbabel. He commanded the leaders of the people to return to the construction of the Temple, which had been interrupted for several years. He demonstrated that this negligence was the source of the evils of infertility and famine with which they had been afflicted since their return. The princes and the people obeyed the Prophet's words and began to push the work forward with a single shoulder <note>A metaphor for working together with a common purpose.</note>. For this reason, the messenger of the Lord promised not only the fertility of the earth, but also offered a memorable prophecy about the coming of the Messiah. He announced that this new Temple would far surpass the glory of the old one—not through the glitter of gold or silver, but by the presence of the one "Desired by all Nations."

ZECHARIAH, son of Berechiah, was a supporter and promoter of the restoration of the Temple alongside Haggai. Through likenesses and enigmas, he predicted the various changes for the Synagogue and the kingdoms. However, he has very clear prophecies concerning the harvest of grace: he presents the Messiah not only under the figure of Zerubbabel, but he discusses His life, His solemn entry into the city, His passion and death, the persecutions that would be stirred up against the Church, and the vengeance upon its enemies so distinctly that—just as Isaiah is called the Evangelical Prophet among the Major Prophets—he himself has every right to be called the Evangelical Prophet among the Minor Prophets.

Furthermore—and this is most worthy of note—he proposes through such a clear prophecy the abolition of the old sacrifices and the pure sacrifice of the New Law <note>In this context, referring to the Eucharist.</note>, to be offered in all places within the Church chosen from the Gentiles, so that its brilliance cannot be obscured by any darkness. The succession of Prophets mentioned so far, which easily extends through 400 years, ended with Malachi in such a way that it is not at all certain that any other Prophet shone in Israel from his time until John the Baptist, whom he preceded by about 400 years.

## LECTURE II.
### ON THE BOOKS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT.
### §. I.

<margin>
Romans
10:3.
</margin>
The New Testament succeeded the Old: light followed shadow, truth followed the figure, and the goal and fulfillment followed the ancient Law. "Christ is the end of the Law, for righteousness to everyone who believes." Among the Books of the New Testament—which the Christian Church preserves with singular care and veneration as the Book of Life, of the miracles and doctrine of Christ the Lord their God, and as the rule of their faith and morals—the first place is held by

<margin>
Matthew
has
28
Chapters.
</margin>
THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. "Gospel" means the good news of liberty and salvation obtained for all mortals by Jesus Christ. Moved by the prayers of the faithful in Palestine, Matthew was the first of all to write a Gospel. He is called by another name, Levi; he was a Galilean by birth, and before he was called by the Lord, he was a tax collector or gatherer of tolls by profession. All the oldest Greek manuscripts testify that the Evangelist committed this divine work to writing in the eighth year after the Lord's Resurrection. The original <note>original: "Autographum"</note> was written in the Hebrew or Syriac language, which was native to the Jews at that time. However, because the Church noticed it had been corrupted by the Ebionites <note>A group of early Jewish-Christian heretics who denied the full divinity of Christ.</note> (heretics of the first century), she set it aside and rejected it. Instead, she began to treat the Greek version—which had been very faithfully expressed from the archetype during the age of the Apostles themselves while it was still pure—as the original. Furthermore, the goal that St. Matthew had in view when writing the Gospel was none other than to benefit both the faithful and the Jews: to give rules of Christian life to the former, and to demonstrate to the latter the divinity of Jesus Christ, the true Messiah born of a Virgin Mother, showing that He came not to overturn the Law, but to perfect and fulfill it. He performed this so accurately that he holds the same place among the writers of the New Covenant that Moses holds among the writers of the Old.

<margin>

has
16
Chapters.
John 6.
Around
A.D.
43.
</margin>
MARK is not to be confused with the John Mark known in the Acts of the Apostles; according to the opinion of the Fathers, he was one of the seventy-two disciples. He had initially left the Lord, having been offended along with the people of Capernaum by those words of Christ: "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man," etc. Afterward, however, he was led back to the faith by St. Peter and remained most faithful to him while Peter was founding the Roman Church. At the request of the brothers in Rome, he wrote his Gospel just as he had heard it from his teacher, Peter. The Apostle approved the writing and, by his own authority, delivered it to the Church to be read. To St. Augustine, Mark is the "abridger of Matthew"; and indeed, it is easily understood from a comparison of both that his Gospel can be considered an epitome of Matthew's. Whether Mark wrote his Gospel in Latin or Greek is a significant question among scholars. Weighty authors stand in favor of the Latin language, supported by the Syriac and Arabic texts, and several...

for when, in our age, Bernard de Montfaucon was given the opportunity to inspect it, he testified that he detected Latin letters on Egyptian papyrus, even though the book was already almost ruined by age and the dampness of the place where it is kept.

<margin>
Luke has 24 Chapters.
Around 53 A.D.
</margin>
**LUKE, a disciple of St. Paul and companion on his journeys**, was a native of Antioch, the metropolis of Syria. He was celebrated for his medical skill and, according to Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus, a 14th-century church historian who recorded the tradition that Luke was an artist.</note> and others, also for the science of painting; but he became far more illustrious through his Apostolic labors and the Gospel he wrote. He committed this to writing in Greek in Achaia, where he lived many years after the death of his master and laid down his mortal life as an old man of 84. This is the more commonly accepted opinion.

<margin>
John has 21 Chapters.
Around 98 A.D.
</margin>
**THE GOSPEL OF JOHN** is the most choice portion of the entire New Testament, serving as the seal by which the other Gospels are authenticated. This beloved disciple of Christ was born in Bethsaida in Galilee, the son of Zebedee and Salome. When he was asked by the Bishops of the Churches of Asia—which he himself had founded—to write a Gospel, he would only set himself to the work after public prayers and a fast had been declared. His purpose was to refute the heresies of Cerinthus and Ebion <note>Early heretics who denied the divinity of Christ.</note> then arising against the Divinity of Christ, and to supply what had been omitted by the other Evangelists. According to most, he completed this in Ephesus as an old man, after his exile was ended, and there he died full of days, being over 90 years old. That John differs from the other Evangelists in his style of writing should be no surprise, for speech follows the nature of the subject: John reveals the most sublime mysteries of our Religion. Therefore, among the Church Fathers, he is known as "The Divine" <note>original: "Theologus"</note> par excellence, and is compared to an Eagle, because from the very beginning he raises himself higher than the others and flies all the way to the throne of God.

<margin>
Acts of the Apostles has 28 Chapters.
Around 63 A.D.
</margin>
**THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES**, written by Luke, provides the history of the nascent Church for 30 years and offers as many medicines for healing souls as it does sentences. It was not the Sacred Writer’s only plan or scope to oppose the counterfeit "apostolic acts" fashioned by the fraud of evil men with a genuine history of the deeds of the Apostles Peter and Paul, explored with his own eyes; rather, by placing the life and discipline of the first believers and their illustrious examples of virtue before our eyes, he intended to draw the reader to follow in their footsteps. Regarding the time the work was written, the more common opinion is that it was handed down in writing while Luke was staying with the Apostle in Rome during his two-year house arrest.

<column-break/>

->§. II.<-

### XIV. The Epistles of St. Paul.

**Paul, formerly Saul**, of the Tribe of Benjamin and born in Tarsus in Cilicia, was changed from a persecutor of the Church into a "vessel of election" and the Apostle to the Gentiles. He learned everything pertaining to the formation of morals and the mysteries of the Christian Religion from Christ the Lord himself, and expressed it in his Epistles, which overflow with heavenly wisdom. Among these, both because of its own excellence and because of the dignity and preeminence of the Roman Church, the first is

<margin>
Epistle to the Romans has 16 Chapters.
Around 58 A.D.
</margin>
**THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS**, in which the very weighty question of the works of the law and of grace is treated. For a contention had arisen in Rome between the Jews and Gentiles converted to the faith of Christ concerning justification: the former ascribed the grace of the Gospel to the works of the Mosaic law, and the latter to the works of the law of nature—both, essentially, to their own merits. Because St. Peter happened to be absent at that time for the purpose of spreading the faith, this disagreement grew so strong that it reached the ears of Paul in Corinth. Therefore, to settle these domestic dissensions, in this Epistle sent from Corinth, he undertook to demonstrate that both Jews and Gentiles, before they were called to the faith of Christ, were subject to sin and unworthy of the Redeemer; and that neither the works of the Mosaic nor the natural law had any power to merit the grace of faith. Consequently, justification is a free gift of God, and it is obtained through faith in Jesus Christ, animated by charity and adorned with the good works that proceed from faith.

<margin>
1st to the Corinthians has 16 Chapters.
56 A.D.
</margin>
**THE FIRST TO THE CORINTHIANS** was sent from Ephesus primarily to suppress the abuses that had crept into the assemblies of the faithful. They were being split into sects, naming themselves after the teacher by whom they were converted and baptized, some saying they were "of Paul" and others "of Apollos." Then he deals with the Holy Eucharist, Virginity, things sacrificed to idols <note>original: "idolothytis"</note>, etc., and (which is the general theme of the Pauline Epistles) he inculcates the true doctrine of faith and morals and the pursuit of charitable peace. He teaches that the Mosaic rites have been abolished by the new law of Christ; he extinguishes spreading heresies and fortifies the faithful of the Church of Corinth against those yet to be born. Corinth was the most celebrated and wealthy metropolis of Achaia in Greece.

<margin>
2nd to the Corinthians has 13 Chapters.
57 A.D.
</margin>
**THE SECOND TO THE CORINTHIANS** was written in Macedonia, though whether at Philippi or another city of that region is not certain. The occasion for writing was this: the Apostle had learned from Titus how much success the previous Epistle had achieved among most of them; however, in the meantime, certain false apostles and detractors had slipped in, who were forcing the observation of the Mosaic law upon the faithful. Therefore, lest these deceitful workers destroy what he himself had built, Paul set out to expose their wickedness and refute their error in such a way that, out of charity and for the edification of the faithful, he showed he was forced to commend his own ministry and to glory in the Lord.

<margin>
Epistle to the Galatians has 6 Chapters.
55 A.D.
</margin>
**THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS**, inhabitants of a province of Asia Minor who traced their origin to Gaul <note>The Galatians were descendants of Celtic groups who migrated to central Asia Minor in the 3rd century B.C.</note>, is believed according to common opinion to have been written in Ephesus. In this, Paul again defends the Apostleship committed to him by Christ himself, and maintains that justification does not come from circumcision...

<meta>This page continues the "Prolegomena" or introduction to the New Testament. The previous page discussed the Gospels of Luke and John, the Acts of the Apostles, and the early Epistles of St. Paul (Romans, Corinthians, and Galatians).</meta>

# FERDINAND KOPF. 53

<margin>Epistle to the Ephesians, 6 chapters.</margin>
...but must be sought from faith working through charity; for some converts from Judaism had come who, by disturbing the most flourishing Church of the Galatians—which had been established chiefly by the work and preaching of Paul—belittled the authority of the Holy Doctor <note>A traditional title for St. Paul, the "Doctor of the Gentiles."</note> and preached that the Legal observances <note>original: "Legalia," referring to the ceremonial laws and rituals of the Old Testament Jewish law.</note> must be joined with the Gospel.
**THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS**, more sublime than the others, treats the great mysteries of our Faith: of Redemption through Christ, of the calling of the Gentiles to the Faith, and of predestination. It then provides most healthy moral precepts for various states of human life. Furthermore, Ephesus—to which this Epistle was sent by the Apostle from Rome during his first imprisonment via Tychicus—was the metropolis of Asia Minor, famous throughout the whole world for its celebrated temple of Diana and its dense population.

<margin>Epistle to the Philippians, 4 chapters.</margin>
**THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS**, a Roman colony in Macedonia, was likewise written from prison and around the same time as the previous one; it is a great testament to the virtue of the Philippians. Indeed, he addresses them most sweetly and does not rebuke them, but only encourages them again and again to continue in the well-begun purpose of the Christian life and to beware of the "evil workers" who promote Jewish legalism.

<margin>Epistle to the Colossians, 4 chapters.</margin>
**THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS** (Colossae was a city of Phrygia in Asia Minor), given in the same year and place as the two preceding ones, defends the orthodox faith of the Colossians against false apostles who, introducing a superstitious worship of Angels alongside legal observances, taught that they [the angels] alone were the mediators through whom access to God is open.

<margin>1 Thessalonians, 5 chapters.</margin>
**THE FIRST TO THE THESSALONICANS**, preceding all others in the order of writing and sent from Corinth, commends the citizens of Thessalonica (the metropolis of Macedonia) for their remarkable progress in the holy Religion, confirms them in the profession of faith, and instructs them regarding the mystery of the Resurrection.

<margin>2 Thessalonians, 3 chapters.</margin>
**THE SECOND TO THE THESSALONICANS**, which differs from the former in neither place nor time, aims chiefly at removing the empty fear that certain false interpreters of the first epistle had struck into the faithful by asserting that, according to the Apostle's mind, the *Day of the Lord* was already at hand; it also strengthens them in both present and imminent adversities.

<margin>1 & 2 Timothy and Titus, 4 chapters <note>The note 'cap. IV' likely refers to a specific grouping in this edition's layout.</note></margin>
I join together the **TWO TO TIMOTHY**, Bishop of the Ephesian Church, **AND ONE TO TITUS**, Bishop of the Cretan Church, because they were not only given around the same time—specifically the first to Timothy and that to Titus while the Apostle was staying in Macedonia with the Philippians, and the second to Timothy from Rome during his second imprisonment, shortly before he completed his course with a glorious martyrdom—but they are also similar in subject matter. They aim to extensively instruct all Overseers <term>Bishops: from the Greek 'episkopos', meaning overseer</term> of the Churches, in the persons of Timothy and Titus, regarding the duties of rightly administering their office. Therefore, the Doctor of the Gentiles repeatedly warns and commands that the Leaders and Teachers of the Christian people should diligently apply themselves to the study of the Sacred Scriptures, because of the most abundant fruits that will redound both to themselves and to others from that study; nor should they show themselves too easy in ordaining and promoting ministers of the Church.

<margin>Epistle to Philemon, 1 chapter.</margin>
**THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON**, a citizen of Colossae conspicuous for his power and wealth as much as for his Piety and liberality, is a letter of recommendation

<column-break/>

for Onesimus. He, guilty of domestic theft and a fugitive from his Master, came to Rome; but soon, led by repentance, he betook himself to the captive Paul, whom he knew to be a very close friend of his master, and devoted himself to his service. Once he was imbued with the Faith and sufficiently confirmed in piety, Paul sent him back with this Epistle, in which, with wonderful skill and the energy of eloquence, he acts to reconcile Onesimus to his Master—not now as a useless slave, but as a most beloved son. Once received back into favor, Onesimus turned out to be an exceptional man; indeed, according to certain Martyrologies, he was the Bishop of Ephesus after Timothy and a glorious Martyr under Trajan. Certainly, he is the clearest proof to us that one should never despair of the salvation of any man, however lost he may be.
<margin>62 A.D.</margin>

<margin>Epistle to the Hebrews has 13 chapters.</margin>
**THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS**, which both the magnitude of its sublime matters and the elegance of its speech wonderfully commend, is proved to be by St. Paul, written by him to the Jews of Palestine after he had been released from his two-year Roman imprisonment, by the unanimous consensus of the Latin and Greek Churches, the Fathers, and the Interpreters; this is sufficiently proven from the final Chapter, verse 23 alone, among other arguments of the greatest weight. It has a twofold argument: for in part, it succinctly shows the new Priesthood of the Son of God once the Aaronic <note>original: "Aaronico," referring to the Levitical priesthood descended from Aaron.</note> priesthood was abolished, according to the prophecies of the Prophets; and in part, it consoles the faithful Hebrews who were unjustly harassed by the unbelieving Jews, and exhorts them to patience and the expectation of the divine Judge. Why it does not bear the name of Paul in the title of the epistle is explained among other reasons as follows: namely, the Apostle knew that [his name] was hated as an adversary of the ancient law, not only among the Jews who were still unbelievers but even among certain faithful who were addicted to legal observances; lest, therefore, they be deterred from reading what he had written for their salvation by the placement of a less pleasing name in the inscription, he judged it better to remain silent about it. But in what language was it written—Hebrew or Greek? The Fathers and Interpreters more commonly hold the first, because it was written by Paul the Hebrew to the Hebrews, therefore in Hebrew; they add, however, that it was soon translated into Greek by Luke or Clement of Rome. Some more recent Critics defend the second [Greek origin] and prove it from the epistle itself, which savors of a Greek origin; they are not moved by the fact that it was given to the Hebrews, asserting that at that time the use of the Greek language was just as common as Hebrew even in Palestine.
<margin>63 A.D.</margin>

->§. III.<-

->VII. Catholic or Universal Epistles.<-

<margin>Seven Epistles in the Canon.</margin>
**THEY ARE CALLED SO** because they were written not just to one Church, but directed to all the faithful. They are also called Canonical because, being received into the Canon, they prescribe rules of Faith and morals. Of these, the first in the usual order is placed:

<margin>Epistle of James, 5 chapters.</margin>
**OF THE APOSTLE JAMES**, commonly called THE LESS, the first Bishop of the Church of Jerusalem. The chief argument of the epistle is to fortify the faithful against the heresies of Simon [Magus], Nicolaus, and the like, who, abusing certain passages of Paul to the Romans, preached that faith without works was sufficient for salvation. From this, it is rightly inferred that it was written around 62 A.D.

<margin>1 Peter has 5 chapters.</margin>
**THE FIRST OF PETER**, the Prince of the Apostles

# PROLEGOMENA

...few in words, but weighty in meaning, and full of Apostolic majesty, it delivers precepts of Christian life to all, and rouses them to patience, obedience, and the zeal for other good works <note>This opening fragment concludes the introduction to the First Epistle of Peter.</note>. It is established that it was written in Rome; but as to what time, Interpreters vary so much that nothing certain can be determined.

<margin>The second indeed has 3 Chapters. 66 A.D.</margin>
**THE SECOND EPISTLE OF PETER** exhorts the faithful to constancy in the faith, and warns them that they should diligently beware of the lying and deceptive teachers to come in the last days. The Apostle himself indicates clearly enough in Chapter 1:14 that he also wrote this in Rome as his last will and testament, as it was shortly before his death.

<margin>1 John has 5 Chapters.</margin>
**THE FIRST EPISTLE OF JOHN** the Apostle—which, according to the tradition of the ancients, was sent to the Parthians <note>A historic empire in what is now Iran; some early traditions suggest John preached there.</note>, whose empire was then vast and name famous—teaches and defends the Divinity of Christ against heretics. Regarding the time in which this and the following two were written, there is no agreement among the commentators.

<margin>The second has a single Chapter.</margin>
**THE SECOND** follows the theme of the first, especially against Basilides <note>An early Gnostic teacher in Alexandria who denied the physical reality of Christ's body.</note> and his followers who deny the true humanity of Christ; against this impiety he fortifies the *Elect Lady* and her children. The more common opinion holds her to be a faithful Matron near Ephesus; however, there are those who wish to understand a certain Church under this figurative expression.

<margin>The third again has a single Chapter.</margin>
**THE THIRD** praises a certain Gaius, whom most confuse with the Gaius who was St. Paul's host in Corinth, for his piety and hospitality, and encourages him to continue in what he has well begun.

<margin>The Epistle of Jude has a single Chapter.</margin>
**THE EPISTLE OF JUDE** the Apostle (he was the brother of James the Less, named Thaddaeus, or Lebbaeus and "the Zealot") treats the same theme as the Second Epistle of Peter; for he likewise acts against the Nicolaitans <note>An early sect mentioned in the Book of Revelation, often associated with moral laxity.</note> and men of a similar cloth, who were later divided into many sects and became known under the common name of Gnostics. It seems to have been written around 67 A.D.

<margin>The Apocalypse has 22 Chapters.</margin>
**THE APOCALYPSE**, or Revelation, in the judgment of the most excellent Interpreters, is a Book superior to all praise, incomparable in the artistry and magnificence of its style, and venerable even for its very obscurity—an obscurity which is not so much to be referred to the words as to the things themselves.

<column-break/>

<margin>95 A.D.</margin>
That it was written by John the Apostle on the Island of Patmos is a certain opinion. Regarding the subject matter, the business is straightforward concerning the first three and the last three chapters; for it is admitted by all that those [first three] deal with the seven Churches of Asia, while these [last three] look toward the coming of the Antichrist, the end of the world, the final judgment, and the happiness of the righteous. Therefore, all difficulty remains regarding the sixteen intermediate chapters. Most of the ancients, and those who follow them, interpret these as concerning the time of the Antichrist and the end of the world. On the other hand, many Moderns, seeking the key from Ecclesiastical history and the Roman Empire, explain them as being about the Church driven by persecutions in the first four centuries and finally victorious—concerning the vengeance upon the persecutors and the destruction of idolatry. This path, which those greatest of men, Bossuet <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704), a French bishop and theologian.</note> and Calmet <note>Antoine Augustin Calmet (1672–1757), a French Benedictine monk known for his massive biblical commentaries.</note> etc., have smoothed over, can rightly be seen not only as easier, but even as approaching closer to the truth. Indeed, it is very hard—and something the mind shrinks from even conceiving in thought—that Rome, which by divine favor was made from the Mistress of errors and superstitions into the center of true Religion and holiness, would fall back into such impiety as to become an idolatrous city and a seducer of the Nations; yet this must be admitted by those who accept the aforementioned Chapters, especially XVII and XVIII, not as already fulfilled, but as yet to be fulfilled. Truly, John himself at the very beginning of his prophecy sends forward, and at the end repeats, that *God here shows to his servants through his Angel the things which must happen soon.* He also adds that it was said to him: *do not seal the words of the prophecy of this Book: for the time is near.* But the Spirit of the Prophets is not accustomed to speak thus when dealing with the secrets of a very remote time; <margin>Daniel 8:26</margin> thus Daniel received the command: *You, therefore, seal up the vision, because it shall be after many days.* Since, therefore, the plainly contrary is repeatedly hinted at in the Apocalypse, it is gathered clearly enough that the faithful are warned in it about events to be fulfilled not long after, so that they might have strength and solace in their persecutions. Let these things be said sufficiently regarding the subjects of the Sacred Books for a easier understanding.
