### CHAPTER II.

*Holofernes is sent by Nebuchadnezzar to devastate all kingdoms and peoples: the power of his army is described; after many places were conquered by him, a terrible fear seized everyone.*

**1** In the thirteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonosor". While historically a Babylonian king, the Book of Judith identifies him as King of the Assyrians ruling from Nineveh.</note>, on the twenty-second day of the first month, the word was given in the house of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, that he should avenge himself.
**2** And he called all the elders, and all the leaders, and his warriors, and shared with them the secret of his plan:
**3** And he said that his intention was to bring the whole earth under his empire.
**4** When this saying had pleased them all, Nebuchadnezzar called Holofernes, the commander-in-chief of his military,
**5** And said to him: "Go out against every kingdom of the west, and especially against those who despised my command.
**6** Your eye shall not spare any kingdom, and you shall subjugate every fortified city to me."
**7** Then Holofernes called the leaders and magistrates of the power of the Assyrians: and he mustered men for the expedition, as the king commanded him, one hundred and twenty thousand foot soldiers, and twelve thousand horsemen and archers.
**8** And he made his entire expedition go before him with a multitude of countless camels, with all that would suffice the armies in abundance, as well as herds of oxen and flocks of sheep, which were without number.
**9** He ordered grain from all of Syria to be prepared for the passage.
**10** He also took a great deal of gold and silver from the king’s house.
**11** And he himself set out, and all the army, with chariots, and horsemen, and archers, who covered the face of the earth like locusts.
**12** And when he had passed the borders of the Assyrians, he came to the great mountains of Ange, which are to the left of Cilicia <note>An ancient region on the south coastal road of modern-day Turkey.</note>: and he ascended all their castles and seized every fortification.
**13** He also broke the most noble city of Melothi, and plundered all the children of Tarshish, and the children of Ishmael, who were opposite the desert, and to the south of the land of Cellon.
**14** And he crossed the Euphrates and came into Mesopotamia: and he broke all the high cities that were there, from the torrent of Mambre until one reaches the sea:
**15** And he occupied its borders, from Cilicia to the edges of Japheth, which are toward the south.
**16** And he led away all the children of Midian <note>original: "Madian".</note>, and plundered all their wealth, and killed all who resisted him with the edge of the sword.
**17** And after these things, he descended into the plain of Damascus in the days of the harvest, and set fire to all the crops, and had all the trees and vineyards cut down:
**18** And the fear of him fell upon all the inhabitants of the land.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER III.

*Terrified by such great forces, the leaders of all the cities and provinces voluntarily surrender themselves to Holofernes, from whom he takes auxiliary troops for himself: and yet he destroys their cities and gods, so that Nebuchadnezzar alone might be considered a god.*

**1** Then the kings and princes of all the cities and provinces sent their ambassadors, namely of Syria of Mesopotamia, and Syria Zobah <note>original: "Syriæ Sobal".</note>, and Libya, and Cilicia; who, coming to Holofernes, said:
**2** "Let your indignation toward us cease: for it is better that we serve Nebuchadnezzar the great king while living, and be subject to you, than that we die and suffer the loss of our liberty along with our destruction.
**3** All our cities, and all our possessions, all the mountains, and hills, and fields, and herds of oxen, and flocks of sheep, and goats, and horses, and camels, and all our resources, and our families, are in your sight:
**4** Let all that is ours be under your law.
**5** We, and our children, are your servants.
**6** Come to us as a peaceful master, and use our service just as it shall please you."
**7** Then he descended from the mountains with horsemen in great power, and occupied every city, and every inhabitant of the land.
**8** And from all the cities he took for himself auxiliary men who were strong and chosen for war.
**9** And such great fear lay upon those provinces, that the inhabitants of all the cities—the princes and honorable men along with the common people—went out to meet him as he came,
**10** Welcoming him with crowns and torches, leading dances with tambourines and flutes.
**11** Yet even by doing these things, they could not soften the ferocity of his heart:
**12** For he both destroyed their cities and cut down their sacred groves.
**13** For King Nebuchadnezzar had commanded him to exterminate all the gods of the earth, specifically so that he himself alone might be called god by those nations which could be subjugated by the power of Holofernes.
**14** Then, passing through Syria Zobah, and all Apamea, and all Mesopotamia, he came to the Idumeans in the land of Geba <note>original: "Gabaa".</note>,
**15** And he took their cities, and stayed there for thirty days, during which days he ordered the entire army of his power to be gathered together.

## CHAPTER VI.

*An angry Holofernes orders Achior to be led to Bethulia, so that once it is conquered, he may be punished at the same time; but the servants, driven back by the slingers, tie him to a tree: having been released, the children of Israel learn the cause and kindly comfort him, humbly imploring God.*

**1** And it happened when they had finished speaking, Holofernes, being greatly incensed, said to Achior:
**2** "Since you have prophesied to us, saying that the nation of Israel is defended by its God, I will show you that there is no God but Nebuchadnezzar:"
**3** "When we have struck them all down as one man, then you yourself shall perish with them by the sword of the Assyrians, and all Israel shall be destroyed with you:"
**4** "And you will prove that Nebuchadnezzar is the lord of the whole earth: then the sword of my soldiers shall pass through your sides, and you shall fall pierced among the wounded of Israel, and you shall breathe no more until you are exterminated with them."
**5** "Furthermore, if you think your prophecy is true, let not your face fall, and let the paleness that has taken hold of your face depart from you, if you think these words of mine cannot be fulfilled."
**6** "But so that you may know that you will experience these things along with them, behold, from this hour you shall be joined to their people, so that when they receive the rightful punishments of my sword, you yourself shall be subjected to the same vengeance."
**7** Then Holofernes commanded his servants to seize Achior, and lead him to Bethulia <note>original: "Bethuliam." The exact historical location of Bethulia is debated; it serves as the strategic gateway to Jerusalem in this account.</note>, and deliver him into the hands of the children of Israel.
**8** And taking him, the servants of Holofernes set out through the plains: but when they approached the mountains, the slingers <term>slingers: soldiers who used a strap or cord to hurl stones with great force and accuracy</term> came out against them.
**9** But they, turning aside from the mountain slope, tied Achior to a tree by his hands and feet, and thus left him bound with ropes, and returned to their master.
**10** Then the children of Israel, descending from Bethulia, came to him: whom they untied and led <column-break/> to Bethulia, and placing him in the midst of the people, they asked what the matter was, that the Assyrians had left him bound.
**11** In those days the leaders there were Uzziah <note>original: "Ozias."</note> son of Micah, of the tribe of Simeon, and Charmi, who is also called Gothoniel.
**12** Therefore, in the midst of the elders, and in the sight of everyone, Achior told all that he had spoken when questioned by Holofernes: and how the people of Holofernes had wanted to kill him because of this word,
**13** And how Holofernes himself, being angry, had commanded him to be delivered to the Israelites for this reason: so that when he conquered the children of Israel, he might then order Achior himself to die by various torments, because he had said: "The God of heaven is their defender."
<margin>Above 5. 6.</margin>
**14** And when Achior had explained all these things, all the people fell on their faces, worshipping the Lord, and with a common lamentation and weeping, they poured out their prayers to the Lord with one accord,
**15** Saying: "Lord God of heaven and earth, behold their pride, and look upon our lowliness, and regard the face of your holy ones, and show that you do not abandon those who trust in you: and those who trust in themselves, and boast in their own strength, you bring low."
**16** And so, when the weeping was finished, and the prayer of the people throughout the whole day was completed, they comforted Achior,
**17** Saying: "The God of our fathers, whose power you have proclaimed, will himself give you this reward: that you may rather see their destruction."
**18** "And when the Lord our God has given this freedom to his servants, may God be with you also in our midst: so that, as it shall please you, you may live with us with all your people."
**19** Then Uzziah, when the council was finished, received him into his house, and made a great feast for him.
**20** And having called all the elders, they refreshed themselves together once the fast was over.
**21** But afterward, all the people were called together, and throughout the whole night they prayed within the assembly <note>original: "ecclesiam," here meaning the gathering or congregation of the people.</note>, seeking help from the God of Israel.

## CHAPTER VII.

*Holofernes besieges Bethulia; and having cut the aqueduct, he orders all the springs to be guarded: therefore the citizens, tortured by thirst, desire to surrender the city; however, Uzziah, the leader of the people, persuades them to delay this for five days.*

**1** On the next day, Holofernes commanded his armies to march up against Bethulia.
**2** There were one hundred twenty thousand foot soldiers and twenty-two thousand horsemen, besides the preparations of those men who had been taken captive, and who had been brought away from the provinces and cities of all the youth.
**3** All prepared themselves together for the fight against the children of Israel, and they came along the edge of the mountain even to the summit, which looks over Dothain, from the place called Belma, unto Chelmon, which is opposite Esdraelon <note>original: "Esdrelon."</note>.
**4** But the children of Israel, when they saw their multitude, prostrated themselves upon the earth, putting ashes upon their heads, praying with one accord that the God of Israel would show his mercy upon his people.

**5** And taking up their weapons of war, they took their positions in places that lead toward the narrow mountain paths between the highlands, and they guarded them all day and night.
**6** Furthermore, while Holofernes was making his rounds, he discovered that the spring which flowed into their aqueduct from the southern side outside the city was accessible; and he ordered their aqueduct to be cut.
**7** However, there were springs not far from the walls from which they were seen to draw water in secret, more for a brief refreshment than for a full drink.
**8** But the sons of Ammon and Moab approached Holofernes, saying: "The children of Israel do not trust in spear or arrow, but the mountains defend them, and the hills set in steep places fortify them."
**9** "Therefore, so that you may overcome them without a clash of battle, station guards at the springs so they cannot draw water from them; thus you will kill them without a sword, or certainly, exhausted, they will surrender their city, which they believe cannot be conquered because of its mountain position."
**10** And these words pleased Holofernes and his attendants, and he appointed commanders of a hundred men over every single spring.
**11** And when this watch had been maintained for twenty days, the cisterns and water reservoirs failed for all the inhabitants of Bethulia, so that there was not enough within the city to satisfy them for even a single day, because water was given to the people daily by measure.
**12** Then all the men, women, youths, and children gathered to Ozias <note>Ozias is the prince or chief magistrate of the city of Bethulia.</note>, all together with one voice

**13** They said: "† Let God judge between us and you, because you have done evil against us by refusing to speak peaceably with the Assyrians, and because of this, God has sold us into their hands."
**14** "And so there is no one to help us, as we are being cast down before their eyes in thirst and great destruction."
**15** "And now gather everyone who is in the city, so that we may voluntarily surrender ourselves to the people of Holofernes."
**16** "For it is better for us to bless the Lord as living captives than to die and be a disgrace to all flesh, when we have seen our wives and our infants die before our eyes."
**17** "We call heaven and earth to witness today, and the God of our fathers, who punishes us according to our sins, that you should now surrender the city into the hand of Holofernes' army, so that our end may be swift by the edge of the sword, which is otherwise being prolonged by the dryness of thirst."

**21** "So that they do not say among the nations: 'Where is their God?'"
**22** And when they had fallen silent, exhausted by these cries and weary from weeping,

### CHAPTER VIII.

> *Judith, whose lineage and praise are described, rebukes the wavering elders who, out of distress, are considering surrender on the fifth day, because they have prescribed a time for the Lord’s mercy; she encourages them to inspire the people to patience by the example of their fathers, and to pray to God on her behalf, without scrutinizing her own action.*

**1** AND it happened, when the widow Judith had heard these words—she was the daughter of Merari, son of Idox, son of Joseph, son of Ozias, son of Elai, son of Jamnor, son of Gideon, son of Raphaim, son of Achitob, son of Melchias, son of Enan, son of Nathanias, son of Salathiel, son of Simeon, son of Reuben <note>The genealogy traces Judith back through the tribe of Simeon, though the last name "Ruben" suggests a link to the tribe of Reuben.</note>:
**2** And her husband was Manasses, who died during the days of the barley harvest:
**3** For he was supervising those binding sheaves in the field, and the heat came upon his head, and he died in his city of Bethulia, and was buried there with his fathers.
**4** Now Judith had been left as his widow for three years and six months.
**5** And in the upper parts of her house, she made a private chamber for herself, in which she remained secluded with her maids,
**6** And wearing sackcloth upon her loins, she fasted every day of her life, except for the Sabbaths, the New Moons, and the festivals of the house of Israel.
**7** Moreover, she was of an exceedingly elegant appearance, and her husband had left her great wealth, many servants, and lands full of herds of oxen and flocks of sheep.
**8** And she was most famous among all, because she feared the Lord greatly, and there was no one who spoke an ill word about her.
**9** Therefore, when she had heard that Ozias had promised to surrender the city after the fifth day had passed, she sent for the elders Chabri and Charmi.
**10** And they came to her, and she said to them: "What is this word that Ozias has agreed to, to surrender the city to the Assyrians if help does not come to you within five days?"
**11** "And who are you, that you should tempt the Lord?"
**12** "This is not a word that provokes mercy, but rather one that excites anger and kindles fury."
**13** "You have set a time for the Lord's mercy, and according to your own judgment, you have appointed a day for Him."
**14** "But because the Lord is patient, let us repent for this very thing and ask for His forgiveness with flowing tears:"
**15** "For God will not threaten like a man, nor will He be inflamed to anger like a son of man." <note>original: "filius hominis." This phrase emphasizes that God does not share human emotional volatility or limitations.</note>
**16** "And therefore, let us humble our souls before Him, and having been established in a humble spirit, serving Him,"
**17** "Let us say to the Lord with weeping that He should show His mercy to us according to His will; so that just as our heart was troubled by their pride, so also we may glory in our humility:"
**18** "Because we have not followed the sins of our fathers..."

### CHAPTER IX.

->*Judith, afflicting and humbling herself, prays prostrate for the liberation of the people, asking that she be given the strength to overthrow Holofernes.*<-

When they had left, Judith entered her oratory; and putting on sackcloth, she put ashes upon her head. Prostrating herself before the Lord, she cried out to the Lord, saying:

<margin>† Genesis 34:26</margin>
2 O Lord God of my father Simeon, † who gave him a sword to defend against the foreigners, who were violators in their defilement, and who stripped the thigh of a virgin to her shame;

<column-break/>

3 And You gave their women as prey, and their daughters into captivity, and all their spoils to be divided among Your servants who were fired with zeal for You; help me, I beseech You, O Lord my God, a widow.

4 For You performed the deeds of old, and planned the things that followed them; and that which You willed has come to pass.

5 For all Your ways are prepared, and You have placed Your judgments in Your providence.

<margin>† Exodus 14:9</margin>
6 † Look upon the camp of the Assyrians now, just as You deigned to see the camp of the Egyptians then, when they ran armed after Your servants, trusting in their chariots, and in their cavalry, and in the multitude of their warriors.

7 But You looked upon their camp, and darkness exhausted them.

8 The abyss held their feet, and the waters covered them.

9 So let it be with these also, Lord, who trust in their great numbers, and in their chariots, and in their pikes, and in their shields, and who glory in their arrows and spears.

10 And they do not know that You are our God, who crushes wars from the beginning, and the Lord is Your name.

11 Lift up Your arm as in the beginning, and crush their power by Your power; let their strength fall by Your wrath, they who promise to violate Your sanctuary, and to pollute the tabernacle of Your name, and to cast down the horn of Your altar <note>The 'horns' were projections at the four corners of the altar, symbolizing strength and sanctuary.</note> with their sword.

12 Bring it to pass, Lord, that his pride may be cut off by his own sword.

13 May he be caught in the snare of his own eyes upon me, and strike him down by the words of my lips. <note>Judith asks for the power of persuasion and charm to defeat the general.</note>

14 Give me constancy in my soul that I may despise him, and strength that I may overthrow him.

<margin>† Judith 13:21 & 15:26</margin>
15 † For this will be a memorial to Your name, when the hand of a woman casts him down.

16 For Your power, Lord, is not in numbers, nor does Your will rest in the strength of horses, nor have the proud pleased You from the beginning; but the prayer of the humble and the meek has always pleased You.

17 O God of the heavens, Creator of the waters, and Lord of every creature, hear me, a wretched woman, praying and trusting in Your mercy.

18 Remember, Lord, Your covenant, and put the right words in my mouth, and strengthen the plan in my heart, so that Your house may remain in Your holiness;

19 And all nations may acknowledge that You are God, and there is no other besides You.

"If your God does this for me, He shall also be my God; and you shall be great in the house of Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonosor"</note>, and your name shall be renowned throughout the whole earth."

### CHAPTER XII.

*Judith, having been introduced into the place of Holofernes' treasures, obtains the freedom to eat her own food and to go out at night for prayer; on the fourth day, she is brought to a banquet, eats and drinks in the presence of Holofernes, who, burning with lust for her, becomes exceedingly drunk.*

1 Then he ordered her to enter where his treasures were stored, and commanded her to remain there, and he decided what should be given to her from his own banquet.
2 Judith answered him and said: "Now I will not be able to eat from these things which you command to be given to me, lest an offense <note>original: "offensio" — a religious transgression or stumbling block regarding dietary laws</note> should come upon me; but I will eat from the things which I have brought with me."
3 Holofernes said to her: "If these things which you brought with you should fail, what shall we do for you?"
4 And Judith said: "As your soul lives, my lord, your handmaid shall not spend all these things before God performs by my hand the things I have planned." And his servants led her into the tent <note>original: "tabernaculum"</note> he had ordered.
5 And she asked that, when she entered, she might be granted the power to go out at night and before daybreak to pray and to entreat the Lord.
6 And he commanded his chamberlains <note>original: "cubiculariis"</note> that she should be allowed to go out and come in as she pleased, to adore her God for three days.
7 And she went out in the nights into the valley of Bethulia, and washed <note>original: "baptizabat se" — ritually purified herself</note> herself in a fountain of water.
8 And as she came up, she prayed to the Lord God of Israel that He would direct her way for the deliverance of His people.
9 And entering, she remained pure in the tent until she took her food in the evening.
10 And it happened on the fourth day, Holofernes made a supper for his servants, and said to Bagoas <note>original: "Vagao"</note> his eunuch: "Go, and persuade that Hebrew woman to consent of her own accord to dwell with me.
11 For it is considered a disgrace among the Assyrians if a woman mocks a man by acting so that she passes from him untouched."
12 Then Bagoas entered to Judith and said: "Let not this good maiden fear to enter to my lord, that she may be honored before his face, and eat with him, and drink wine with joy."
13 Judith answered him: "Who am I, that I should contradict my lord?
14 Everything that is good and best before his eyes, I will do. And whatever pleases him, that shall be best for me all the days of my life."
15 And she rose and adorned herself with her garments, and entering, she stood before his face.
16 And the heart of Holofernes was moved, for he was burning with lust for her.
17 And Holofernes said to her: "Drink now, and sit down in joy, for you have found favor before me."
18 And Judith said: "I will drink, my lord, for my soul is magnified this day above all the days of my life."
19 And she took, and ate, and drank before him those things which her maidservant had prepared for her.

<column-break/>

20 And Holofernes became joyful because of her, and he drank very much wine, more than he had ever drunk in his life.

### CHAPTER XIII.

*Judith, having made a prayer to God, cuts off the head of the drunken Holofernes with a scimitar; carrying it to her fellow citizens in Bethulia, she exhorts them to give thanks, while she herself is blessed by all, and Achior is struck with awe upon seeing Holofernes' head.*

1 And when it was late, his servants hurried to their lodgings, and Bagoas closed the chamber doors and went away.
2 And they were all weary with wine.
3 And Judith was alone in the chamber.
4 Now Holofernes lay upon the bed, overcome by a deep sleep from too much wine.
5 And Judith told her maid to stand outside before the chamber and to keep watch.
6 And Judith stood before the bed, praying with tears and the movement of her lips in silence,
7 Saying: "Strengthen me, O Lord God of Israel, and look in this hour upon the works of my hands, that, as You promised, You may raise up Your city Jerusalem: and that I may perform this thing which I have planned, believing it could be done through You."
8 And when she had said this, she went to the pillar that was at the head of his bed, and she unfastened his dagger <note>original: "pugionem" — elsewhere referred to as an "acinace" or scimitar</note> which hung tied to it.

10 And she struck twice upon his neck and cut off his head; and she took his canopy <note>original: "conopeum" — a mosquito net or decorative bed-curtain</note> from the pillars and rolled away his headless body.
11 And after a little while she went out and gave the head of Holofernes to her maidservant, and ordered her to put it into her bag.

13 And Judith said from afar to the watchmen of the walls: "Open the gates, for God is with us, who has performed great power in Israel."
14 And it happened, when the men had heard her voice, they called the elders of the city.
15 And they all ran to her, from the least to the greatest, because they had hoped she would no longer return.
16 And lighting lamps, they all gathered around her; and she, ascending to a higher place, commanded silence. When all were silent,
17 Judith said: "Praise the Lord our God, who has not forsaken those who hope in Him.
18 And in me, His handmaid, He has fulfilled His mercy which He promised to the house of Israel: and He has slain the enemy of His people by my hand this night."
19 And bringing the head of Holofernes out of the bag, she showed it to them, saying: "Behold the head of Holofernes, the general of the Assyrian army; and behold his canopy, in which he lay in his drunkenness, where the Lord our God struck him by the hand of a woman."

### CHAPTER XIV.

->*The head of Holofernes is hung from the wall of Bethulia, and after Achior is circumcised, the Jews rush upon the Assyrians; those who try to wake Holofernes, finding him dead, are struck by a powerful fear.*<-

**1** Then Judith said to all the people: "Listen to me, brothers; hang this head upon our walls:

**2** And it shall be that when the sun rises, let every man take up his arms and go out with an assault, not as if you were descending to the valley, but as if making an attack.

**3** Then it will be necessary for the scouts to flee to their prince to wake him for the battle.

**4** And when their leaders have run to the tent of Holofernes and find him a headless corpse rolled in his own blood, fear will fall upon them.

**5** And when you know they are fleeing, go after them safely, for the Lord will crush them under your feet."

**6** Then Achior, seeing the power that the God of Israel had displayed, abandoned his pagan rituals <note>original: "relicto gentilitatis ritu"</note> and believed in God; he circumcised the flesh of his foreskin and was joined to the people of Israel, as is all the succession of his lineage to this day.

**9** Furthermore, those who were in the tent came and made a noise before the entrance of the bedchamber, making a disturbance on purpose to wake him, so that Holofernes might wake up from the noise rather than from those trying to rouse him.

**15** And entering the tent of Judith, he did not find her, and he leaped outside to the people,

**18** And an incomparable outcry arose in the midst of their camp.

### CHAPTER XVI.

*The song of Judith for the victory: the people come to Jerusalem to offer burnt offerings with thanksgiving: finally, Judith dies full of days; and the day of this victory is perpetually celebrated among the Jews in the number of holy days.*

**1** Then Judith sang this song to the Lord, saying:
**2** Begin unto the Lord with timbrels, sing to the Lord with cymbals, tune a new psalm to Him, exalt Him, and call upon His name.
**3** The Lord puts an end to wars; the Lord is His name.
**4** He has set His camp in the midst of His people, to deliver us from the hand of all our enemies.
**5** The Assyrian came from the mountains out of the North in the multitude of his strength: his multitude blocked up the torrents, and their horses covered the valleys.
**6** He said he would set fire to my borders, and kill my young men with the sword, give my infants as prey, and my virgins into captivity.
**7** But the almighty Lord has struck him, and delivered him into the hands of a woman, and pierced him through.
**8** For their mighty one did not fall by the young men, nor did the sons of the Titans <note>The Latin translator uses "Titan" to refer to the Rephaim or giants of old</note> strike him, nor did the tall giants set themselves against him; but Judith, the daughter of Merari, undone him by the beauty of her face.

put on the garment of joy in the exultation of the children of Israel.

**11** Her sandals ravished his eyes, her beauty made his soul a captive, and she cut off his neck with a dagger.
**12** The Persians shuddered at her constancy, and the Medes at her boldness.
**13** Then the camp of the Assyrians howled, when my lowly ones appeared, parched with thirst.
**14** The sons of the handmaids <note>Likely referring to the Israelite soldiers who were looked down upon as slaves by the Assyrians</note> have pierced them through, and they killed them like fleeing boys: they perished in the battle before the face of the Lord my God.

**30** And in all the time of her life there was no one who troubled Israel, nor for many years after her death.
**31** But the day of this victory is accepted by the Hebrews in the number of holy days, and is honored by the Jews from that time until the present day.

# THE BOOK OF ESTHER.

## CHAPTER ONE.

*While Ahasuerus celebrates a splendid feast lasting a full half-year to display his power and glory, Queen Vashti, being summoned, refuses to come, and is therefore repudiated: and by the counsel of the wise men, a decree is published that wives should show honor to their husbands.*

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'I' depicting a king (likely Ahasuerus/Assuerus) seated on a throne, wearing a crown and holding a scepter, surrounded by advisors or attendants in a palace setting.</image-desc>
**1** IN the days of Ahasuerus <note>Also known as Xerxes I, who ruled the Persian Empire from 486 to 465 BCE</note>, who reigned from India even unto Ethiopia, over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces:
**2** When he sat upon the throne of his kingdom, the city of Susa was the capital <note>original: "exordium," meaning the principal seat or origin</note> of his kingdom.
**3** Therefore, in the third year of his reign, he made a great feast for all his princes and his servants, the most valiant men of the Persians and the Medes, the nobles and the governors of the provinces before him,
**4** That he might show the riches of the glory of his kingdom, and the greatness and boastfulness of his power, for a long time, namely, one hundred and eighty days.
**5** And when the days of the feast were accomplished, he invited all the people who were found in Susa, from the greatest even to the least: and he commanded a feast to be prepared for seven days in the entrance of the garden and the grove, which had been planted by royal care and hand.
**6** And there hung on every side hangings of sky-blue color, and of fine linen and violet, supported by cords of fine linen and purple, which were threaded through ivory rings, and were supported by marble columns. There were also couches of gold and silver, placed upon a pavement of emerald and Parian stone <note>A fine white marble from the Greek island of Paros</note>, laid in order: which a painting of wonderful variety decorated.
**7** Moreover, those who were invited drank from golden cups, and food was brought in various different vessels. Also wine, as was worthy of royal magnificence, was provided in abundance and of the finest quality.
**8** Nor was there anyone who compelled those who were unwilling to drink, but as the king had appointed, placing over the tables each of his princes, so that every man might take what he wished.
**9** Queen Vashti also made a feast for the women in the palace where King Ahasuerus was accustomed to dwell.
**10** Therefore, on the seventh day, when the king was more cheerful, and had become warm after too much drinking, he commanded Mehuman, and Biztha, and Harbona, and Bigtha, and Abagtha, and Zethar, and Carcas, the seven eunuchs who served in his presence,
**11** That they should bring in Queen Vashti before the king, with the crown set upon her head, to show all the people and the princes her beauty: for she was exceedingly beautiful.
**12** But she refused, and scorned to come at the king's command, which he had sent by the eunuchs. Whereupon the king was angry, and being kindled with exceeding fury,
**13** He questioned the wise men, who according to royal custom were always with him, and he did all things by their counsel, as they knew the laws and rights of their ancestors:

<column-break/>

**14** (Now the first and nearest to him were Carshena, and Shethar, and Admatha, and Tarshish, and Meres, and Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of the Persians and the Medes, who saw the face of the king, and were accustomed to sit first after him)
**15** To what sentence Queen Vashti should be subject, who had refused to do the command of King Ahasuerus, which he had sent by the eunuchs.
**16** And Memucan answered, in the hearing of the king and the princes: "Queen Vashti has not only wronged the king, but also all the peoples and the princes who are in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus.
**17** For the news of the queen will go out to all women, so that they will despise their husbands, and say: 'King Ahasuerus commanded that Queen Vashti should come in to him, and she would not.'
**18** And by this example, all the wives of the princes of the Persians and the Medes will little regard the commands of their husbands: wherefore the king's indignation is just.
**19** If it please you, let an edict go out from your presence, and let it be written according to the law of the Persians and the Medes, which it is unlawful to transgress, that Vashti shall no more come in to the king, but another who is better than she shall receive her kingdom.
**20** And let this be proclaimed throughout all the empire of your provinces (which is very wide), and let all wives, both of the greater and the lesser, show honor to their husbands."
**21** His counsel pleased the king and the princes: and the king did according to the counsel of Memucan;
**22** And he sent letters to all the provinces of his kingdom, so that every nation could hear and read, in different languages and characters, that husbands should be the princes and masters in their own houses: and that this should be proclaimed among all the peoples.

## CHAPTER TWO.

*Esther, the hidden niece of Mordecai the Jew, being pleasing above all other virgins sought for Ahasuerus, is made queen in the place of Vashti, with a magnificent wedding feast celebrated and gifts bestowed. Furthermore, Mordecai, remaining at the palace gate, betrays the eunuchs who were plotting against the king, which deed of Mordecai is inscribed in the annals.*

**1** After these things were done, when the indignation of King Ahasuerus had cooled, he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what she had suffered:
**2** And the king's servants and his ministers said: "Let there be sought for the king young virgins and beautiful,
**3** And let men be sent to look through all the provinces for beautiful young virgins: and let them bring them to the city of Susa, and deliver them into the house of the women under the hand of Hegai the eunuch, who is the overseer and keeper of the royal women: and let them receive feminine ornaments <note>original: "mundum muliebrem," referring to the cosmetics, oils, and clothing required for their preparation</note>, and other things necessary for use.
**4** And whichever among them all shall please the king's eyes, let her reign instead of Vashti." The word pleased the king: and he commanded it to be done as they had suggested.

**7** And he was the foster-father of his brother’s daughter Hadassah <note>original: "Edissa"</note>, who by another name was called Esther. She had no power to return to the king unless the king desired it and commanded her to come by name.
**15** As the time moved through the order, the day arrived when Esther, the daughter of Abihail the brother of Mordecai—whom he had adopted as his daughter—was due to go in to the king. She did not seek any extra feminine finery, but took only what Hegai the eunuch, the guardian of the virgins, chose to give her for her adornment. For she was exceedingly shapely and of incredible beauty, appearing gracious and lovely in the eyes of all.
**16** So she was led to the bedchamber of King Ahasuerus in the tenth month, which is called Tebeth <note>Corresponding to December/January</note>, in the seventh year of his reign.
**17** And the king loved her more than all the other women; she found grace and mercy before him above all women, and he placed the royal diadem upon her head and made her queen in the place of Vashti.
**18** And he commanded a most magnificent feast to be prepared for all his princes and servants because of his union and marriage to Esther. He also granted rest <note>likely a tax exemption or holiday</note> to all the provinces and bestowed gifts according to his princely magnificence.
**19** And when young women were being sought and gathered a second time, Mordecai remained at the king’s gate.
**20** Esther had not yet revealed her country or her people, according to his command. For whatever Mordecai commanded, Esther observed;

<column-break/>

and she did everything just as she was accustomed to at the time when he was raising her as a small child.
**21** At that time, therefore, while Mordecai stayed at the king's gate, Bigthan <note>original: "Bagathan"</note> and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs who were doorkeepers and presided over the first threshold of the palace, became angry and wanted to rise up against the king and kill him.
**22** This did not escape Mordecai’s notice, and he immediately reported it to Queen Esther; she in turn told the king in the name of Mordecai, who had brought the matter to her.
**23** The matter was investigated and discovered to be true, and both of them were hanged on a gallows <note>original: "patibulo"</note>. This was commanded to be written in the histories and handed down in the annals before the king.

### C H A P T E R III.

*Haman is elevated by the king above all the princes of the Medes and Persians; he is indignant that Mordecai the Jew alone does not bow to him. For this reason, he obtains from Ahasuerus the destruction of all the Jews and sends letters to all the provinces, sealed with the king's ring, so that on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month all Jews everywhere may be killed.*

**1** After these things, King Ahasuerus exalted Haman, the son of Hammedatha <note>original: "Amadathi"</note>, who was of the lineage of Agag. He placed his throne above all the princes that he had.
**2** And all the king's servants who were at the palace gates bowed their knees and honored Haman, for so the emperor had commanded them. Only Mordecai did not bow his knee nor honor him.
**3** The king’s attendants who presided at the palace gates said to him: "Why do you not observe the king’s command unlike all the others?"
**4** When they said this to him frequently and he refused to listen, they reported it to Haman, desiring to know whether he would persist in his resolution; for he had told them that he was a Jew.
**5** When Haman heard this and proved by experience that Mordecai did not bow his knee to him nor honor him, he was very angry.
**6** And he considered it a small thing to lay his hands on Mordecai alone—for he had heard that he was of the Jewish race—but he preferred instead to destroy the entire nation of the Jews who were in the kingdom of Ahasuerus.
**7** In the first month (which is called Nisan) in the twelfth year of the reign of Ahasuerus, the lot—which in Hebrew is called *Pur* <note>original: "phur"</note>—was cast into an urn before Haman to determine on which day and in which month the Jewish people should be killed; and the lot fell on the twelfth month, which is called Adar <note>Corresponding to February/March</note>.
**8** And Haman said to King Ahasuerus: "There is a people dispersed through all the provinces of your kingdom and separated from one another, using new laws and ceremonies, and moreover despising the king’s decrees. And you know very well that it is not expedient for your kingdom that they should grow insolent through such license."
**9** "If it please you, decree that they perish, and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver to the keepers of your treasury."
**10** Then the king took the ring which he used from his hand and gave it to Haman, the son of Hammedatha of the race of Agag, the enemy of the Jews.
**11** And he said to him: "The silver which you promise, let it be yours; as for the people, do with them what pleases you."

12 Then the king’s scribes were summoned in the first month, Nisan <note>The first month of the Hebrew calendar, occurring in March-April.</note>, on the thirteenth day of the same month. As Haman had commanded, a decree was written to all the king’s satraps <note>term: Satraps (local governors in the Persian Empire)</note>, to the judges of the provinces, and to the various nations, so that every people could read and hear it in their own language. It was issued in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with his own ring.
13 These letters were sent by the king’s couriers to all the provinces, ordering them to kill and destroy all the Jews, from the young to the old, including little children and women, on a single day—that is, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is called Adar <note>The twelfth month, occurring in February-March.</note>—and to plunder their goods.

### CHAPTER IV.

*Mordecai and the rest of the Jews mourn because of the destruction prepared for them. Esther, however, at Mordecai's command, meets the threat of the Jews' slaughter; though not summoned, she approaches the king, ordering a three-day fast to be observed for her, doing the same herself with her maidservants.*

When Mordecai had heard these things, he tore his clothes and put on sackcloth <note>term: Sackcloth (a coarse garment worn as a sign of extreme grief or repentance)</note>, sprinkling ashes on his head. In the middle of the city square, he cried out with a loud voice, showing the bitterness of his soul.
2 He walked with this wailing even to the gates of the palace; for it was not permitted for anyone clothed in sackcloth to enter the king’s court.
3 In all the provinces, towns, and places where the king’s cruel decree had reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting, wailing, and weeping; many used sackcloth and ashes as their bed.
4 Then Esther’s maids and eunuchs <note>term: Eunuch (a high-ranking court official often overseeing the royal household)</note> came in and told her. Hearing this, she was overcome with grief. She sent garments for Mordecai to put on, so that he might take off the sackcloth, but he would not accept them.
5 Having called for Hathach, the eunuch whom the king had given her as an attendant, she commanded him to go to Mordecai and learn from him why he was doing this.
6 Hathach went out and found Mordecai standing in the city square before the palace gate.
7 Mordecai told him everything that had happened: how Haman had promised to pay a sum of silver into the king’s treasuries for the slaughter of the Jews.
8 He also gave him a copy of the edict that was posted in Susa, so that he might show it to the queen and advise her to go in to the king and plead with him for her people.
9 Hathach returned and told Esther everything Mordecai had said.
10 She answered him and commanded him to say to Mordecai:
11 "All the king’s servants and all the provinces under his rule know that if any man or woman enters the king’s inner court without being called, they are to be put to death immediately and without delay—unless the king happens to extend the golden scepter <note>The scepter was a staff held by the king as a symbol of his absolute authority.</note> to them as a sign of mercy, so they may live. How then can I enter to the king, when I have not been called to him for thirty days now?"

<column-break/>

12 When Mordecai heard this,
13 he sent word back to Esther, saying: "Do not think that you alone will save your life just because you are in the king’s house, above all other Jews.
14 For if you remain silent now, relief for the Jews will arise from another place; but you and your father’s house will perish. And who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"
15 In turn, Esther sent these words back to Mordecai:
16 "Go and gather all the Jews you find in Susa, and pray for me. Do not eat or drink for three days and three nights. I, along with my handmaidens, will fast in the same way. Then I will go in to the king, acting against the law, even though I have not been called, handing myself over to death and danger."
17 So Mordecai went and did everything Esther had commanded him.

### CHAPTER V.

*Esther, disregarding the danger to her life, goes to the king and requests that he come with Haman to her banquet. There, when the king, cheered by the feast, asks about her petition, she invites both of them again to a banquet the following day. Meanwhile, Haman, indignant that he is not honored by Mordecai, prepares a gallows for him.*

On the third day, Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the king’s house, opposite the king’s hall. The king was sitting on his throne in the council chamber of the palace, facing the entrance of the house.
2 And when he saw Queen Esther standing there, she found favor in his eyes, and he extended toward her the golden scepter he held in his hand. She approached and kissed the top of his scepter.
3 The king said to her: "What do you wish, Queen Esther? What is your request? Even if you ask for half the kingdom, it shall be given to you."
4 She answered: "If it pleases the king, I beseech you to come to me today, and Haman with you, to a banquet I have prepared."
5 The king said immediately, "Call Haman quickly, so that Esther’s wish may be fulfilled." So the king and Haman came to the banquet the queen had prepared for them.
6 After he had drunk wine abundantly, the king said to her: "What do you ask to be given to you? For what do you petition? Even if you ask for half of my kingdom, you shall obtain it."
7 Esther replied: "My petition and my prayers are these:
8 If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it pleases the king to grant what I ask and fulfill my petition, let the king and Haman come to the banquet I have prepared for them, and tomorrow I will open my will to the king."
9 So Haman went out that day happy and cheerful. But when he saw Mordecai sitting before the palace gates—who not only did not rise for him, but did not even move from his seat—he was greatly incensed.
10 Yet hiding his anger, he returned to his house and called together his friends and his wife, Zeresh.
11 He described to them the greatness of his riches, his many sons, and the great glory with which the king had elevated him above all his princes and servants.

### CHAPTER VI.

*The king, finding in the annals read to him at night the faithfulness of Mordecai in uncovering the eunuchs' plot against the king, orders him to be honored as second to the king by Haman, his chief enemy.*

1 That night the king spent sleepless, and he ordered the histories and annals of former times to be brought to him. As they were being read in his presence, 
2 they came to the place where it was written how Mordecai had reported the plot of Bigthan and Teresh <note>original: "Bagathan & Thares"</note>, the eunuchs who wanted to kill King Ahasuerus. 
3 When the king heard this, he said: "What honor or reward has Mordecai received for this loyalty?" His servants and ministers said to him: "He has received no reward at all."
4 Immediately the king said: "Who is in the court?" For Haman had entered the inner court of the king’s house to suggest to the king that he should order Mordecai to be fixed to the gallows <note>term: Patibulo (a gallows or wooden frame for execution)</note> which had been prepared for him. 
5 The servants answered: "Haman is standing in the court." And the king said: "Let him enter." 
6 When he had entered, the king said to him: "What ought to be done for the man whom the king desires to honor?" But Haman, thinking in his heart and imagining that the king would want to honor no one else but himself, 
7 answered: "The man whom the king desires to honor 
8 should be clothed in royal robes, and placed upon the horse that the king himself rides, and receive the royal crown <note>original: "diadema"</note> upon his head; 
9 and let the first of the king's princes and lords <note>original: "tyrannis," used here in the classical sense of 'rulers' or 'nobles'</note> hold his horse, and as he goes through the street of the city, let him cry out and say: 'Thus shall he be honored, whomsoever the king wishes to honor!'" 
10 And the king said to him: "Hurry! Take the robe and the horse, and do just as you have spoken to Mordecai the Jew, who sits before the gates of the palace. Take care that you do not omit any of those things which you have spoken." 
11 So Haman took the robe and the horse, and clothing Mordecai in the street of the city and placing him on the horse, he went before him crying out: "He is worthy of this honor, whomsoever the king has willed to honor." 
12 And Mordecai returned to the palace gate; but Haman hurried to go to his house, mourning and with his head covered. 
13 And he told Zeresh his wife and his friends everything that had happened to him. The wise men whom he had in his counsel and his wife answered him: "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of the seed of the Jews, you will not be able to resist him, but you will surely fall in his sight."

<column-break/>

14 While they were still speaking, the king’s eunuchs arrived and quickly compelled him to go to the banquet which the queen had prepared.

### CHAPTER VII.

*Esther, at the banquet, with the king now cheered by wine, prays for her life and the life of her people, and accuses Haman, the adversary of the Jews; the king orders him to be hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai.*

1 So the king and Haman entered to drink with the queen. 
2 And the king said to her again on the second day, after he was warmed with wine: "What is your petition, Esther, that it may be given to you? And what do you wish to be done? Even if you ask for half of my kingdom, you shall obtain it." 
3 To him she answered: "If I have found favor in your eyes, O king, and if it pleases you, give me my life, for which I ask, and my people, for whom I entreat. 
4 For we have been handed over, I and my people, to be crushed, to be slaughtered, and to perish. And if only we were being sold as male and female slaves, it would be a bearable evil, and I would have mourned in silence; but now our enemy is one whose cruelty flows back upon the king." 
5 And King Ahasuerus answering said: "Who is this, and of what power, that he should dare to do such things?" 
6 And Esther said: "Our enemy and most wicked foe is this Haman!" Hearing this, he was immediately struck dumb, unable to bear the look of the king and the queen. 
7 But the king, being angry, rose up and left the place of the banquet and entered the garden planted with trees. Haman also rose to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he understood that evil was prepared for him by the king. 
8 When the king had returned from the garden of trees and entered the place of the banquet, he found Haman had fallen upon the couch where Esther lay, and he said: "Does he even wish to assault the queen in my presence, in my own house?" The word had not yet left the king’s mouth when they immediately covered Haman's face. 
9 And Harbona, one of the eunuchs who stood in the king's service, said: "Behold the beam <note>original: "lignum," referring to the gallows</note> which he had prepared for Mordecai, who spoke for the king, stands in Haman’s house, being fifty cubits high." The king said to him: "Hang him upon it." 
10 So Haman was hanged on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai; and the king's anger subsided.

### CHAPTER VIII.

*With Mordecai appointed to Haman's place, Esther obtains from the king that he should cancel Haman's fatal and old letters with new ones, providing security for the Jews and allowing them to avenge themselves on their enemies, from which great joy arises everywhere.*

1 On that day, King Ahasuerus gave the house of Haman, the adversary of the Jews, to Queen Esther; and Mordecai came before the king. For Esther had confessed to him that he was her uncle <note>original: "patruus," a father's brother. In some traditions, Mordecai is identified as Esther's cousin.</note>. 
2 And the king took the ring which he had ordered to be taken back from Haman, and handed it to Mordecai. And Esther appointed Mordecai over her house.

3 Not content with this, she fell at the feet of the king, and wept, and speaking to him she pleaded that the malice of Haman the Agagite <note>A descendant of Agag, the king of the Amalekites, who were traditional enemies of Israel.</note>, and his wicked schemes which he had devised against the Jews, might be ordered to be made void.
4 But he, according to custom, extended the golden scepter with his hand, which was shown as a sign of mercy; and she, rising up, stood before him,
5 And said: "If it pleases the king, and if I have found favor in his eyes, and my petition does not seem contrary to him, I beseech you, that by new letters, the old letters of Haman—the plotter and enemy of the Jews, by which he had commanded them to perish in all the king’s provinces—might be corrected."
6 "For how can I endure the death and slaughter of my people?"
7 And King Ahasuerus answered Queen Esther and Mordecai the Jew: "I have granted the house of Haman to Esther, and I have ordered him to be fixed to a cross <note>original: "affigi cruci" — while this term literally means 'crucified,' in this context it refers to the ancient Persian practice of impaling or hanging an enemy on a high wooden stake.</note>, because he dared to lay his hand upon the Jews."
8 "Write therefore to the Jews, as it pleases you, in the king's name, sealing the letters with my ring." For it was the custom that letters which were sent in the king’s name and were sealed with his ring, no one would dare to contradict.
9 And the king’s scribes and secretaries were called (it was then the time of the third month, which is called Sivan <note>A month corresponding to late May or June.</note>) on the twenty-third day of it; letters were written, as Mordecai wished, to the Jews, and to the princes, and the governors, and the judges, who presided over the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India even to Ethiopia: to province and province, to people and people, according to their languages and scripts, and to the Jews, as they were able to read and hear.
10 And these letters, which were sent in the king’s name, were sealed with his ring, and sent by couriers: who, running through all the provinces, would overtake the old letters with the new messages.
11 To whom the king commanded that they should gather the Jews in every city, and order them to be assembled together, that they might stand for their lives, and kill and destroy all their enemies, with their wives and children and all their households, and seize their spoils.
12 And one day of vengeance was appointed through all the provinces, that is, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar <note>A month corresponding to February or March.</note>.
13 And the summary of the letter was this: that in all the lands and peoples who were subject to the empire of King Ahasuerus, it should be made known that the Jews were ready to take vengeance on their enemies.
14 And the swift couriers went out carrying the news, and the king's edict hung in Susa <note>original: "Susan," the winter capital of the Persian Empire.</note>.
15 But Mordecai, going out from the palace and from the presence of the king, shone in royal garments, namely, of hyacinth-blue and sky-blue <note>original: "hyacinthinis... & aereis"</note>, wearing a golden crown on his head, and wrapped in a silk and purple cloak. And the whole city rejoiced and was glad.
16 But to the Jews, a new light seemed to rise: joy, honor, and jubilation.
17 Among all peoples, cities, and provinces, wherever the king's commands came, there was wonderful exultation, feasts, and banquets, and a holiday: so much so that many of other nations and sects joined themselves to their religion and ceremonies. For a great terror of the Jewish name had fallen upon them all.

## CHAPTER IX.

> *The Jews everywhere slaughter their enemies on the same day that had been appointed for the slaughter of the Jews; and with the ten sons of Haman having been hanged, Mordecai established the day of Purim, that is, the Day of Lots, as a perpetual holiday.*

1 Therefore, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which we have already said is called Adar, when the slaughter was being prepared for all the Jews, and their enemies were thirsting for their blood, the situation was reversed, and the Jews began to be superior and to avenge themselves on their adversaries.
2 And they were gathered together in every city, town, and place, to stretch out their hand against their enemies and persecutors. And no one dared to resist, because the fear of their greatness had penetrated all peoples.
3 For even the judges of the provinces, and the leaders, and the governors, and every dignitary who presided over each place and task, extolled the Jews for fear of Mordecai:
4 For they had learned that he was the prince of the palace, and was very powerful: the fame of his name also grew daily, and flew through the mouths of everyone.
5 And so the Jews struck their enemies with a great slaughter, and killed them, rendering to them what they had prepared to do to themselves:
6 Inasmuch as even in Susa they killed five hundred men, besides the ten sons of Haman the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews: whose names are these:
7 Parshandatha, and Dalphon, and Aspatha,
8 And Poratha, and Adalia, and Aridatha,
9 And Parmashta, and Arisai, and Aridai, and Vaizatha.
10 When they had killed them, they would not touch the plunder from their goods <note>The Jews intentionally avoided taking the property of those they killed to show that their actions were purely for self-defense, not for profit.</note>.
11 And immediately the number of those who had been killed in Susa was reported to the king.
12 Who said to the queen: "In the city of Susa the Jews have killed five hundred men, and the other ten sons of Haman: how great a slaughter do you think they have carried out in all the provinces? What more do you ask, and what do you wish that I should order to be done?"
13 To whom she answered: "If it pleases the king, let power be given to the Jews, that as they have done today in Susa, so they may do tomorrow, and that the ten sons of Haman may be hanged on gallows."
14 And the king commanded that it should be so done. And immediately the edict hung in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged.
15 When the Jews were gathered on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar, three hundred men were killed in Susa: nor was their property plundered by them.
16 But also through all the provinces, which were subject to the king's dominion, the Jews stood for their lives, their enemies and persecutors having been killed: so much so that seventy-five thousand of those killed were counted, and no one touched anything of their goods.
17 Now the thirteenth day of the month of Adar was the first day of the slaughter among all, and on the fourteenth day they ceased to kill. This they established to be a holiday, so that in it from then on they might devote themselves to feasts, joy, and banquets.
18 But those who had carried out the slaughter in the city of Susa—

30 And they sent to all the Jews who were in the hundred and twenty-seven provinces of King Ahasuerus, that they might have peace, and receive truth,

31 Observing the days of lots <note>original: "fortium" — likely a transcription variant for "sortium" (lots) in the Latin tradition.</note>, and celebrating them with joy in their own time, just as Mordecai and Esther had ordained; and they took upon themselves and their offspring the obligation to observe fasts, and cries <note>Lamentations or prayers.</note>, and the days of lots,

# CHAPTER X.

->Explanation of Mordecai's dream, concerning the restoration of the Jewish people to liberty.<-

1 Indeed, King Ahasuerus made all the land and all the islands of the sea tributary:

2 His strength and empire, and the dignity and high rank with which he exalted Mordecai, are written in the books of the Medes and the Persians:

3 And how Mordecai of the Jewish race was second after King Ahasuerus: and great among the Jews, and acceptable to the people of his brothers, seeking good for his people, and speaking those things which pertained to the peace of his offspring.

*Those things which are held in the Hebrew [manuscripts] are expressed with full faith. However, these things which follow, I found written in the common edition, which are contained in the Greek language and letters: and meanwhile, after the end of the book, this chapter was being circulated: which according to our custom we have pre-marked with an obelo, that is, a spit-mark.* <note>The translator, likely St. Jerome, is noting that the following verses are "Apocryphal" additions found in Greek versions of Esther but not in the original Hebrew. An "obelo" or "obelus" is a mark used by ancient scholars to indicate suspected or non-canonical text.</note>

4 And Mordecai said: "These things were done by God.
5 I remembered the dream I had seen, which signified these very things: nor was any of them in vain.
6 A small spring, which grew into a river, and turned into light and sun, and overflowed into many waters: this is Esther, whom the king took as his wife, and willed to be queen.
7 Moreover, the two dragons: I am one, and Haman is the other.
8 The nations that had gathered: these are those who attempted to destroy the name of the Jews.
9 But my nation: is Israel, who cried to the Lord, and the Lord saved his people: and he delivered us from all evils, and performed great signs and wonders among the nations:
10 And he commanded that there be two lots, one for the people of God, and another for all the nations.
11 And both lots came into the day appointed from that time forward before God for all nations:
12 And the Lord remembered his people, and had mercy on his inheritance.
13 And these days shall be observed in the month of Adar, on the fourteenth and fifteenth day of the same month, with all zeal and joy in one assembly of the people gathered together, through all the generations of the people of Israel hereafter."

# CHAPTER XI.

->The Dream of Mordecai.<-

1 In the fourth year, during the reign of Ptolemy and Cleopatra, Dositheus (who said he was a priest and of the Levite race) and Ptolemy his son brought this letter of *Purim*, which they said Lysimachus, son of Ptolemy, had translated in Jerusalem.

*This also was the beginning in the common edition, which is found neither in the Hebrew, nor among any of the [other] translators.*

2 In the second year, during the reign of Artaxerxes the Great <note>In the Greek additions to Esther, the king is referred to as Artaxerxes rather than Ahasuerus.</note>, on the first day of the month of Nisan <note>The first month of the Hebrew year, occurring in March or April.</note>, Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, saw a dream:

# THE BOOK OF ESTHER.

3 A Jewish man, who lived in the city of Susa, a great man and among the first of the royal court.
<margin>
† 2 Kings 24:15.
Above, 2:6.
</margin>
4 † He was of the number of captives whom Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon, had transported from Jerusalem with Jeconiah, the King of Judah.
5 And this was his dream: There appeared voices, and tumults, and thunders, and earthquakes, and a disturbance upon the earth.
6 And behold, two great dragons appeared, ready to fight against each other.
7 At their cry, all nations were stirred up to fight against the nation of the just.
8 And that day was one of darkness and danger, of tribulation and distress, and there was a massive dread upon the earth.
9 And the nation of the just was troubled, fearing their own evils, and they were prepared for death.
10 They cried out to God; and as they were shouting, a small spring grew into a very great river, and overflowed into many waters.
11 Light and the sun rose up, and the humble were exalted, and they devoured the illustrious.
12 When Mordecai <note>original: "Mardochæus"</note> had seen this and had risen from his bed, he wondered what God willed to do: and he kept it fixed in his mind, desiring to know what the dream signified.

## C H A P T E R XII.

### *The revelation of the eunuchs' plot against the king by Mordecai, as found in the second chapter.*

<margin>
Above, 2:21 and 6:2.
</margin>
At that time, he was staying in the king's court with Bigthan <note>original: "Bagatha"</note> and Teresh <note>original: "Thara"</note>, the king’s eunuchs, who were the gatekeepers of the palace.
2 And when he understood their thoughts and looked into their concerns more diligently, he learned that they were attempting to lay hands on King Artaxerxes <note>The name used in the Greek and Latin traditions for the king often identified as Ahasuerus.</note>, and he reported this to the king.
3 After an inquiry was held regarding both of them, the king ordered those who confessed to be led to their death.
4 Moreover, the king wrote what had happened in the chronicles; but Mordecai also committed the memory of the event to writing.
5 And the king commanded him to stay in the court of the palace, giving him gifts for the information provided.
6 But Haman <note>original: "Aman"</note>, the son of Hammedatha, a Bugaean <note>original: "bugæus" — likely a variation of "Agagite," referring to the ancestral enemies of Israel.</note>, was most glorious in the sight of the king; and he wished to harm Mordecai and his people because of the two eunuchs of the king who had been put to death.

## C H A P T E R XIII.

### *A copy of the royal letter which Haman sent to the governors of the provinces concerning the slaughter of the Jews, and Mordecai’s prayer for their deliverance.*

Artaxerxes, the great king, to the princes and governors of the one hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia, who are subject to his empire: Greetings.
2 Although I rule over many nations, and have

<column-break/>

subjugated the entire world to my authority, I have no wish to abuse the greatness of my power, but rather to govern my subjects with clemency and mildness, so that, passing their lives in quietness without any terror, they might enjoy the peace desired by all mortals.
3 But when I asked my counselors how this might be fulfilled, one who excelled the others in wisdom and loyalty, and was second only to the king, named Haman,
4 Pointed out to me that there is a people scattered throughout the whole world that uses strange laws, and acting against the customs of all nations, despises the commands of kings, and violates the harmony of all nations by its own discord.
5 When we learned this, seeing one rebellious nation against the whole human race using perverse laws, and going against our commands, and disturbing the peace and harmony of the provinces subject to us,
6 We commanded that whomever Haman—who is set over all the provinces, and is second to the king, and whom we cherish as a father—shall point out, they shall be destroyed by their enemies with their wives and children, and that no one shall have mercy on them, on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month of Adar of the present year;
7 So that these wicked men, descending to the underworld in a single day, may restore to our empire the peace which they had disturbed.

->*Thus far the copy of the letter.*<-
->*What follows, I found written after that place where it is read:*<-

And Mordecai, departing, did all things that Esther had commanded him.

->*Yet these things are not held in the Hebrew, and are recorded by absolutely none of the translators.*<-

8 But Mordecai prayed to the Lord, mindful of all his works,
9 And said: "Lord, Lord, almighty King, for all things are placed within your authority, and there is no one who can resist your will, if you have decreed to save Israel.
10 You made heaven and earth, and whatever is contained within the compass of heaven.
11 You are the Lord of all, and there is no one who may resist your majesty.
12 You know all things, and you know that it was not out of pride or contempt, or any desire for glory, that I did this—refusing to adore the most arrogant Haman,
13 (For I would have been ready to kiss even the soles of his feet gladly for the salvation of Israel.)
14 But I feared lest I should transfer the honor of my God to a man, and lest I should adore anyone except my God.
15 And now, O Lord King, God of Abraham, have mercy on your people, because our enemies wish to destroy us and blot out your inheritance.
16 Do not despise your portion, which you redeemed for yourself from Egypt.
17 Hear my prayer, and be merciful to your lot and your heritage <note>original: "sorti & funiculo tuo" — literally "your lot and your measuring cord," referring to Israel as God's allotted portion.</note>, and turn our mourning into joy, so that while living we may praise your name, O Lord, and do not close the mouths of those who sing to you."
18 All Israel also, with like mind and supplication, cried out to the Lord, because certain death hung over them.

### CHAPTER XIV.

*Esther mourns, beseeching God in a spirit of humility.*

1 **Q**ueen Esther also fled to the Lord, fearing the danger that was imminent.
2 And when she had laid aside her royal garments, she took up clothing fit for weeping and mourning; instead of various ointments, she filled her head with ashes and filth, and humbled her body with fasting: and every place where she had previously been accustomed to rejoice, she filled with the tearing of her hair.
3 And she prayed to the Lord God of Israel, saying:
> My Lord, who alone are our King, help me, a solitary woman, who has no other helper besides You.
> 4 My danger is in my hands <note>original: "Periculum meum in manibus meis est" — a Hebrew idiom meaning she is risking her life.</note>.
<margin>† Deuteronomy 4:20, 34 and 32:9.</margin>
> 5 † I have heard from my father that You, Lord, took Israel from among all nations, and our fathers from all their predecessors, so that You might possess an eternal inheritance, and You did for them as You spoke.
> 6 We have sinned in Your sight, and therefore You have delivered us into the hands of our enemies:
> 7 For we worshipped their gods. You are just, O Lord.
> 8 And now it is not enough for them that they oppress us with the harshest servitude, but attributing the strength of their hands to the power of idols,
> 9 They wish to change Your promises, and to blot out Your inheritance, and to shut the mouths of those praising You, and to extinguish the glory of Your temple and altar,
> 10 So that they might open the mouths of the nations, and praise the strength of idols, and preach of a fleshly king forever.
> 11 Do not hand over Your scepter, O Lord, to those who are nothing <note>Meaning the idols or the pagan nations.</note>, lest they laugh at our ruin: but turn their counsel against them, and destroy him <note>Referring to Haman (Aman).</note> who began to rage against us.
> 12 Remember us, O Lord, and show Yourself to us in the time of our tribulation, and give me confidence, O Lord, King of gods and of all power.
> 13 Grant a well-ordered speech in my mouth in the presence of the lion <note>A metaphorical reference to the King.</note>, and turn his heart to hatred of our enemy, so that both he and the others who agree with him may perish.
> 14 But deliver us by Your hand, and help me, who have no other helper but You, Lord, who have knowledge of all things,
> 15 And You know that I hate the glory of the wicked, and detest the bed of the uncircumcised and of every foreigner.
> 16 You know my necessity: that I loathe the sign of my pride and glory <note>Her royal crown or diadem.</note> which is upon my head in the days of my public appearance, and I detest it like a menstrual cloth, and I do not wear it in the days of my silence.
> 17 And that I have not eaten at Haman's table, nor has the king's feast pleased me, nor have I drunk the wine of drink-offerings.
> 18 And Your handmaid has never rejoiced from the time I was brought here until the present day, except in You, O Lord God of Abraham.
> 19 O God, powerful above all, hear the voice of those who have no other hope, and deliver us from the hand of the wicked, and rescue me from my fear.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER XV.

*By Mordecai's command, Esther enters to the king, terrified by his countenance.*

---

->*These things also I found added in the Vulgate edition.*<-

1 **A**nd he commanded her (there is no doubt that Mordecai commanded Esther) to enter to the king, and to plead for her people and for her country.
2 "Remember," he said, "the days of your lowliness, how you were raised by my hand; for Haman, the second after the king, has spoken against us unto death.
3 And you, call upon the Lord, and speak to the king for us, and deliver us from death."

---

->*And also these things which follow.*<-

4 On the third day she laid aside her garments of finery and was clothed in her glory.
5 And when she shone in royal attire, and had called upon God, the ruler and savior of all, she took two handmaids,
6 And she leaned upon one, as if unable to carry her own body due to delicacy and extreme tenderness.
7 But the other of the handmaids followed her mistress, holding up the garments trailing on the ground.
8 Her face was flushed with a rosy color, and with graceful and shining eyes she hid her sad mind, which was gripped by extreme fear.
9 Having therefore passed through all the doors in order, she stood before the king, where he sat upon the throne of his kingdom, clothed in royal robes, glittering with gold and precious stones, and he was terrible to behold.
10 And when he had raised his face, and with burning eyes indicated the fury of his heart, the queen collapsed; and her color changing to paleness, she rested her weary head upon her little maid.
11 And God turned the spirit of the king into mildness, and in haste and fear he leaped from the throne, and supporting her in his arms until she returned to herself, he coaxed her with these words:
12 "What is the matter, Esther? I am your brother <note>A term of endearment and royal equality used by the King to comfort her.</note>; do not fear.
13 You shall not die: for this law was not established for you, but for all others.
14 Come near, then, and touch the scepter."
15 And when she remained silent, he took the golden rod and placed it upon her neck, and kissed her, and said: "Why do you not speak to me?"
16 She answered: "I saw you, my lord, as an angel of God, and my heart was troubled for fear of your glory.
17 For you are truly wonderful, my lord, and your face is full of graces."
18 And while she was speaking, she collapsed again and almost fainted.
19 But the king was troubled, and all his servants comforted her.
