31 And behold, nettles had filled it all, and thorns had covered its surface, and the stone wall was destroyed.
32 When I had seen this, I took it to heart, and by the example I learned a lesson.
33 You will sleep a little, I said, you will slumber a moment, you will fold your hands a little while to rest:
34 And poverty shall come upon you like a runner, and beggary like an armed man.

### CHAPTER XXV.

> *The glory of God and of kings: the heart of the king: dross and wickedness: do not exalt yourself: do not detract: keep your secrets: golden apples and a golden earring: cold in the harvest: clouds without rain: a soft tongue: honey found: a sharp arrow: a decayed tooth: vinegar: a moth: do good to your enemy: the corner of a roof: cold water: a troubled fountain: too much honey eaten: a city without a wall.*

1 **These** are also the proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah, transcribed.
2 It is the glory of God to conceal a word, and the glory of kings to search out a matter.
3 The heaven above, and the earth below, and the heart of kings are unsearchable.
4 Remove the dross from silver, and a most pure vessel shall come forth.
5 Take away wickedness from the face of the king, and his throne shall be established in justice.
6 Do not appear glorious before the king, and do not stand in the place of great men.
7 For it is better that it be said to you: "Come up here," than that you should be humbled before the prince.
8 The things which your eyes have seen, do not bring out quickly in a quarrel: lest later you cannot make amends, when you have dishonored your friend.
9 Treat your cause with your friend, and do not reveal a secret to a stranger:
10 Lest perhaps he insult you when he hears it, and never cease to reproach you.
-> Grace and friendship deliver: keep these for yourself, lest you become a reproach. <-
11 Like golden apples in silver settings is he who speaks a word in its proper time.
12 As a golden earring, and a shining pearl, so is he who rebukes a wise man, and an obedient ear.

<column-break/>

13 Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to him who sent him, for he refreshes his soul.
14 Like clouds, and wind, and rain that does not follow, is a boastful man who does not fulfill his promises.
<margin>† Above 15:1.</margin>
15 † By patience a prince shall be appeased, and a soft tongue shall break hardness. <note>original: *duritiam*—literally "hardness," often translated as "bone" in this proverb to show the power of gentle speech.</note>
16 Have you found honey? Eat what is enough for you, lest perhaps being filled you vomit it up.
17 Withdraw your foot from the house of your neighbor, lest at any time being weary of you, he hate you.
18 A dart, and a sword, and a sharp arrow, is a man who speaks false witness against his neighbor.
19 A decayed tooth, and a weary foot, is he who hopes in an unfaithful man in the day of trouble,
20 And who loses his cloak in the day of cold.
As vinegar on soda, so is he who sings songs to a very evil heart. <note>original: *nitro*—natron or soda. The reaction creates a useless fizz, much like singing cheerful songs to someone in deep distress.</note>
As a moth to a garment, and a worm to wood: so the sadness of a man hurts the heart.
<margin>† Rom. 12:20.</margin>
21 † If your enemy is hungry, feed him: if he is thirsty, give him water to drink.
22 For you shall heap coals of fire upon his head, and the Lord will reward you. <note>This "heaping of coals" is often interpreted as causing a burning sense of shame that leads to repentance.</note>
23 The north wind drives away rain, and a sad face drives away a backbiting tongue.
<margin>† Above 21:9.</margin>
24 † It is better to sit in a corner of the roof, than with a brawling woman, and in a shared house.
25 As cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.
26 A fountain troubled with the foot, and a corrupted spring, is a righteous man falling before the wicked.
27 As it is not good for a man to eat much honey: † so he who is a searcher of majesty, shall be overwhelmed by glory. <note>A warning against trying to over-analyze the mysteries of God's divine nature.</note>
<margin>† Sirach 3:22.</margin>
28 As a city that lies open and without the circuit of walls, so is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking.

### CHAPTER XXVI.

> *Glory in a fool: a flying bird: a whip for a horse: answering a fool: a foolish messenger: the proverb of a fool: the honor of a fool: imposing silence on a fool: a dog to its vomit: wise in his own judgment: meddling in a quarrel: hurting a friend: a whisperer: the passionate: swelling lips: an enemy: covering hatred: digging a pit: a deceitful tongue.*

1 **As** snow in summer, and rain in harvest: so glory is unseemly for a fool.
2 As a bird flying to other places, and a sparrow going where it will: so a curse uttered without cause shall come upon someone.
3 A whip for the horse, and a bit for the donkey, and a rod for the back of the imprudent.
4 Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you be made like him.
5 Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself. <note>These two verses are a famous paradox: the first warns against stooping to a fool's level, while the second advises correcting them so they don't remain arrogant.</note>
6 He is lame in his feet, and drinks iniquity, who sends words by a foolish messenger.
7 As a lame man has beautiful legs in vain: so a proverb is unseemly in the mouth of fools.
8 As he who casts a stone into the heap of Mercury: so is he who gives honor to a fool. <note>original: *acervum Mercurii*—referring to the Greek/Roman custom of throwing stones onto a roadside pile (cairn) dedicated to the god Hermes/Mercury.</note>
9 As if a thorn should grow in the hand of a drunkard: so is a proverb in the mouth of fools.

### C H A P T E R XXVII.

> *Not to boast of tomorrow; do not praise yourself; how heavy is the anger of a fool; open correction; the wounds of one who loves; a satisfied soul; a neighbor nearby; pledging for a stranger; a quarrelsome woman; hell is insatiable; a man is proven by the mouth of the one praising; a crushed fool; recognize the face of the flock; goats' milk for food.*

1 Do not boast of tomorrow, for you do not know what the coming day may bring forth.
2 Let a stranger praise you, and not your own mouth: a foreigner, and not your own lips.
<margin>Sirach 22:18.</margin>
3 † Heavy is a stone, and burdensome is sand: but the anger of a fool is heavier than both.
4 Anger has no mercy, nor breaking fury: and who can withstand the onset of one who is provoked?
5 Open correction is better than hidden love.
6 Better are the wounds of one who loves than the deceitful kisses of one who hates.
<margin>Job 7.</margin>
7 A satisfied soul will tread upon a honeycomb: and a hungry soul will take even the bitter for sweet.
8 Like a bird wandering from its nest, so is a man who leaves his place.

<column-break/>

9 The heart is delighted by ointment and various perfumes: and the soul is sweetened by the good counsels of a friend.
10 Do not forsake your friend, and your father's friend: and do not enter your brother's house in the day of your affliction.
A neighbor nearby is better than a brother far off.
11 Study wisdom, my son, and gladden my heart: so that you may answer a word to one who reproaches you.
12 The clever man, seeing evil, is hidden: the little ones passing by have suffered losses.
<margin>† Above 20:16.</margin>
13 † Take his garment who has stood surety for a stranger: and for foreigners, take a pledge from him.
14 He who blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the night, shall be like one who curses. <note>The suggestion here is that excessive or ill-timed flattery is suspicious and annoying.</note>
<margin>† Above 19:13.</margin>
15 † Leaking roofs on a cold day and a quarrelsome woman are compared:
16 He who restrains her is as one who would hold the wind, and he shall call upon the oil of his right hand. <note>original: "oleũ dexteræ suæ vocabit" — Meaning she is as difficult to hold as the wind or as slippery as oil.</note>
17 Iron is sharpened by iron, and a man sharpens the face of his friend.
18 He who tends the fig tree shall eat its fruit: and he who is the guardian of his master shall be glorified.
19 As faces shine back in the water to those looking in, so the hearts of men are manifest to the prudent.
<margin>† Sirach 14:9. † Above 17:3.</margin>
20 Hell and destruction are never filled: likewise the † eyes of men are insatiable.
21 † As silver is tried in the refinery, and gold in the furnace: so is a man tried by the mouth of the one praising.
The heart of the wicked seeks evils, but the upright heart seeks knowledge.
22 Though you should crush a fool in a mortar with a pestle hitting from above, as if striking groats, his folly will not be taken away from him.
23 Diligently know the face of your cattle, and consider your flocks:
24 For you shall not have power forever: but a crown shall be given from generation to generation.
25 The meadows are open, and the green herbs have appeared, and hay is gathered from the mountains.
<margin>† 1 Timothy 6:8.</margin>
26 † Lambs for your clothing: and kids for the price of the field.
27 Let goats' milk suffice you for your food, and for the necessities of your house, and for the living of your handmaids.

### C H A P T E R XXVIII.

> *Of the flight of the wicked and the security of the just; many are the princes of a land because of its sins; a poor man calumniating the poor; a poor suppliant and a crooked rich man; unwilling to hear the law; the exultation of the just; hiding his crimes; blessed is the one always fearful; a wicked prince like a lion; a leader lacking prudence; working his land; taking away from a father.*

1 The wicked man flees when no one pursues: but the just man, like a confident lion, shall be without fear.
2 Because of the sins of a land, its princes are many: and because of the wisdom of a man, and the knowledge of those things which are said, the life of the leader shall be longer.
3 A poor man who slanders the poor is like a violent rain in which famine is prepared.
4 Those who forsake the law praise the wicked: those who keep it are kindled against him.

### C H A P T E R XXIX.

->*Not listening to one rebuking: the multiplication of the just: the love of wisdom: a just king: a flattering friend: pestilent men: contending with a fool: men of blood: bringing forth the whole spirit: words of lying: the poor man and the creditor: a just king: correction: the multiplication of the impious: instruct your son: prophecy: swift to speak: delicately nourishing a servant: the angry man: the proud: participating with a thief: fearing man: the just abominate the impious, and vice versa.*<-

1 For a man who with a stiff neck despises one who rebukes him, sudden destruction shall come upon him: and health shall not follow him.
2 In the multiplication of the just, the common people shall rejoice: when the impious take leadership, the people groan.
<margin>† Luke 15:13.</margin>
3 A man who loves wisdom makes his father glad: † but he who nourishes harlots loses his substance.
4 A just king raises up the land; a greedy man will destroy it.
5 A man who speaks to his friend with flattering and feigned words spreads a net for his steps.
6 A snare shall involve an unjust man when he sins: and the just shall praise and rejoice.
7 The just man knows the cause of the poor: the impious man is ignorant of such knowledge.
8 Pestilent men <note>original: *pestilentes*; meaning those who are socially or morally infectious/harmful to the community</note> destroy a city: but wise men turn away fury.
9 If a wise man contends with a fool, whether he be angry or laugh, he shall find no rest.
10 Men of blood <note>original: *viri sanguinum*; a Hebrew idiom for murderers or violent men</note> hate the simple: but the just seek his soul.
11 A fool brings forth his whole spirit <note>meaning he blurts out everything he thinks or feels immediately without restraint</note>: a wise man puts it off and reserves it for later.
12 A prince who willingly hears words of lying has all his ministers impious.
13 The poor man and the creditor have met each other: the Lord is the enlightener of both.
14 A king who judges the poor in truth, his throne shall be established forever.
15 The rod and rebuke bestow wisdom: but a child who is left to his own will shames his mother.
16 In the multiplication of the impious, crimes shall be multiplied: and the just shall see their ruins.
17 Instruct your son, and he shall refresh you, and give delights to your soul.
18 When prophecy fails, the people shall be scattered: but he who keeps the law is blessed.
19 A servant cannot be instructed by words: because he understands what you say, but despises to answer.
20 Have you seen a man swift to speak? Folly is more to be hoped for than his correction.
21 He who delicately nourishes his servant from childhood shall afterward find him stubborn.
22 An angry man provokes brawls: and he who is easy to be indignant shall be more prone to sin.
<margin>† Job 22:29.</margin>
23 † Humility follows the proud: and glory shall receive the humble in spirit.
24 He who shares with a thief hates his own soul: he hears one taking an oath <note>refers to a formal judicial oath to testify against a crime</note> and does not reveal it.

### CHAPTER XXX.

*A man close to God judges himself foolish, and the works of God incomprehensible; the word of God is refined by fire, to which nothing should be added; he prays against vanity, lying words, poverty, and riches; a servant should not be accused before his master; several detestable generations; two leeches; three insatiable things; three things by which the earth is moved; four smallest things of the earth; three things that walk well; the one who wipes [the nose] violently.*

The words of the Gatherer <note>original: *Congregantis*; a literal Latin translation of the Hebrew name *Agur*</note>, son of the Vomiter <note>original: *Vomentis*; a literal Latin translation of the Hebrew name *Jakeh*</note>. The vision which the man spoke, with whom God is, and who, being strengthened by God dwelling with him, said:
2 I am the most foolish of men, and the wisdom of men is not with me.
3 I have not learned wisdom, and I do not know the knowledge of the saints.
4 Who has ascended into heaven and descended? Who has gathered the wind in his hands? Who has bound the waters as if in a garment? Who has raised up all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is the name of his son, if you know?
<margin>Psalm 11:7 <note>The marginal reference likely refers to the purity of God's word.</note></margin>
5 Every word of God is refined by fire; he is a shield to those who hope in him.
<margin>Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32.</margin>
6 Do not add anything to his words, lest you be rebuked and found to be a liar.
7 Two things I have asked of you; do not deny them to me before I die:
8 Remove vanity and lying words far from me. Give me neither beggary nor riches; grant me only the necessities for my livelihood,
9 Lest perhaps being full, I be enticed to deny you and say: "Who is the Lord?" Or compelled by poverty, I might steal and commit perjury against the name of my God.
10 Do not accuse a servant to his master, lest he curse you and you fall.
11 There is a generation that curses its father, and does not bless its mother.
12 There is a generation that seems pure to itself, and yet is not washed from its filthiness.
13 There is a generation whose eyes are lofty, and whose eyelids are raised on high.
14 There is a generation that has swords for teeth and devours with its molars, so that it may eat the needy from the earth and the poor from among men.
15 The horseleech <note>original: *Sanguisugæ*; literally "blood-sucker"</note> has two daughters who say: "Bring, bring."
There are three things that are insatiable, and a fourth that never says: "It is enough."
16 The grave, and the mouth of the womb, and the land that is not satisfied with water; but fire never says: "It is enough."
17 The eye that mocks his father and despises the labor of his mother, let the ravens of the brooks pick it out, and the young of the eagle eat it.

<column-break/>

18 Three things are difficult for me, and a fourth I am entirely ignorant of:
19 The way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent upon a rock, the way of a ship in the middle of the sea, and the way of a man in his youth.
20 Such also is the way of an adulterous woman, who eats and, wiping her mouth, says: "I have done no evil."
21 By three things the earth is moved, and a fourth it cannot sustain:
22 By a servant when he reigns; by a fool when he is filled with food;
23 By a hateful woman when she is taken in marriage; and by a handmaid when she is the heir to her mistress.
24 There are four smallest things of the earth, and they are wiser than the wise:
25 The ant, a weak people, who prepares its food in the harvest;
26 The rock-badger <note>original: *Lepusculus*; literally "little hare," but referring to the hyrax or coney</note>, a people without strength, who places its lair in the rock;
27 The locust has no king, and yet they all go forth by their bands;
28 The lizard <note>original: *Stellio*; a gecko or spotted lizard</note> climbs with its hands and stays in the palaces of kings.
29 There are three things that walk well, and a fourth that marches happily:
30 A lion, the strongest of beasts, who will fear the onset of no one;
31 A cock with girded loins <note>original: *Gallus succinctus lumbos*; likely referring to a strutting rooster</note>; and a ram; and there is no king who can resist him.
32 And he who has appeared a fool after he was lifted up on high; for if he had understood, he would have laid his hand upon his mouth.
33 But he who strongly squeezes the teats to bring out milk, presses out butter; and he who violently blows his nose, brings forth blood; and he who provokes anger, brings forth strife.

### CHAPTER XXXI.

*He is exhorted not to give his substance to women, nor wine to kings, but rather to those in mourning; open your mouth for the mute; defend the needy; the praise and rarity of a valiant woman; beauty is a vain grace.*

The words of King Lemuel. The vision by which his mother instructed him.
2 What, my beloved? What, O beloved of my womb? What, O beloved of my vows?
3 Do not give your substance to women, nor your riches to the destruction of kings.
4 Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel, do not give wine to kings; because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns.
5 Lest perhaps they drink and forget judgments, and change the cause of the children of the poor.
6 Give strong drink <note>original: *siceram*; fermented liquor other than wine</note> to those in mourning, and wine to those who are of a bitter heart:
7 Let them drink and forget their poverty, and let them remember their sorrow no more.
8 Open your mouth for the mute, and for the causes of all the children who pass by.
9 Open your mouth, decree what is just, and judge the needy and the poor.
10 Who shall find a valiant woman? <note>original: *Mulierem fortem*; often translated as "virtuous woman" or "woman of valor"</note> Her price is from afar and from the furthest ends.
11 The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he shall have no need of spoils.
12 She will render him good and not evil all the days of her life.

# ECCLESIASTES,
### WHICH BY THE HEBREWS
## IS CALLED COHELETH. <note>A Hebrew title meaning "The Gatherer" or "The Preacher," referring to one who speaks to an assembly.</note>

### CHAPTER ONE.

> *All things are vain, and there is nothing new under the sun; also that the investigation of all things is difficult, vain, and an affliction of the spirit.*

<image-desc>Historiated initial 'V' containing a seated king (David) holding a harp.</image-desc>
1 The words of Ecclesiastes, the son of David, king of Jerusalem.
2 Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes; vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.
3 What more does a man have from all his labor, by which he labors under the sun?
4 A generation passes away, and a generation comes, but the earth stands forever.
5 The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; and there being born again,
6 It circles through the south, and turns toward the North; the spirit <note>original: *spiritus*; can refer to the wind or a life-force</note> goes traversing all things in a circuit, and returns into its circles.
7 All rivers enter into the sea, and the sea does not overflow; to the place from which the rivers come out, they return so that they may flow again.
8 All things are difficult; man cannot explain them in speech. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing.
9 What is it that was? The same thing that shall be. What is it that was done? The same thing that is to be done.
10 Nothing under the sun is new, nor can anyone say: Behold, this is recent; for it has already gone before in the ages which were before us.
11 There is no memory of former things; but neither of those things which shall be hereafter will there be a remembrance among those who shall be in the end.
12 I, Ecclesiastes, was king over Israel in Jerusalem,
13 And I proposed in my mind to seek and investigate wisely concerning all things which are done under

<column-break/>

the sun. This worst occupation God gave to the sons of men, that they might be occupied in it.
14 I have seen all things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit.
15 The perverse are corrected with difficulty, and the number of fools is infinite.
16 I spoke in my heart, saying: Behold, I have become great, and I have surpassed all in wisdom who were before me in Jerusalem; and my mind has contemplated many things wisely, and I have learned.
17 And I gave my heart to know prudence and doctrine, and errors and foolishness; and I recognized that in these things also there was labor and affliction of spirit:
18 Because in much wisdom there is much indignation; and he who adds knowledge, adds also labor.

### CHAPTER II.

> *In the abundance of delights, riches, and buildings, and in the labor of these, there is vanity and affliction of spirit; he also says how great a vanity it is to gather for a future heir, for whom it is unknown what kind of person he will be.*

1 I said in my heart: I will go and abound in delights, and enjoy good things. And I saw that this also was vanity.
2 Laughter I counted as error, and to joy I said: Why are you deceived in vain?
3 I thought in my heart to withdraw my flesh from wine, so that I might transfer my mind to wisdom and avoid foolishness, until I might see what would be useful for the sons of men; which deed must be done under the sun for the number of the days of their life.
4 I magnified my works, I built houses for myself, and planted vineyards.

5 I made gardens and orchards, and I planted them with trees of every kind.
6 I constructed pools of water to irrigate my forest of growing trees.
7 I possessed servants and handmaids, and had a great family; I also had herds and large flocks of sheep, more than all who were before me in Jerusalem.
8 I heaped up for myself silver and gold, and the wealth of kings and provinces. I provided myself with male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men: cups and pitchers <note>original: *scyphos, & urceos*; these refer to fine vessels used for serving wine in a royal court</note> to serve wine.
9 and I surpassed in riches all who were before me in Jerusalem; wisdom also remained with me.
10 And everything my eyes desired, I did not deny them; nor did I restrain my heart from enjoying every pleasure, and delighting itself in the things I had prepared. And I considered this my portion: to enjoy the fruit of my labor.
11 But when I turned myself toward all the works my hands had made, and the labors in which I had sweated in vain, I saw in all things vanity <note>original: *vanitatem*; in this context, it suggests breath, vapor, or something fleeting and empty</note> and affliction of the soul, and that nothing remains under the sun.
12 I passed on to contemplate wisdom, and errors, and folly (for what is man, I said, that he should be able to follow the King, his Maker?)
13 And I saw that wisdom surpassed folly as much as light differs from darkness.
<margin>† Proverbs 17:24; below 8:1</margin>
14 The eyes of a wise man are in his head; the fool walks in darkness. And I learned that the death of both was the same.
15 And I said in my heart: If the end of the fool and of myself shall be one, what does it profit me that I have given myself to greater wisdom? And speaking with my own mind, I perceived that this also was vanity.
16 For there shall be no lasting memory of the wise man, just as there is none for the fool, and future times shall cover all things alike with oblivion; the learned man dies just as the unlearned.
17 And therefore I was weary of my life, seeing that all things under the sun are evil, and all is vanity and affliction of spirit.
18 Again, I detested all my industry, by which I labored most studiously under the sun, for I am to have an heir after me,
19 Whom I do not know, whether he shall be wise or a fool; yet he shall rule over my labors, for which I have sweated and been anxious. Is anything so vain?
20 Wherefore I ceased, and my heart renounced laboring any further under the sun.
21 For when one man labors in wisdom, and doctrine, and care, he leaves what he has gained to an idle man; and this therefore is vanity, and a great evil.
22 For what shall it profit a man from all his labor, and the affliction of spirit, with which he is tormented under the sun?
23 All his days are full of sorrows and hardships, nor does his mind rest even at night. And is this not vanity?
24 Is it not better to eat and drink, and to show his soul the good things of his labors? And this is from the hand of God.
25 Who shall feast and overflow with delights as much as I have?

<column-break/>

26 To the man who is good in His sight, God has given wisdom, and knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner He has given affliction and needless care, to add, and to gather, and to hand over to him who has pleased God. But this also is vanity, and a hollow anxiety of the mind.

### CHAPTER III

->*That all things happen in their own time and pass away; and that in these fleeting things there is no rest for the mind; also that the death of man and of beasts is the same.*<-

1 All things have their time, and all things under heaven pass away through their own spaces.
2 A time to be born, and a time to die.
A time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted.
3 A time to kill, and a time to heal.
A time to destroy, and a time to build.
4 A time to weep, and a time to laugh.
A time to mourn, and a time to dance.
5 A time to scatter stones, and a time to gather them.
A time to embrace, and a time to be far from embraces.
6 A time to get, and a time to lose.
A time to keep, and a time to cast away.
7 A time to rend, and a time to sew.
A time to keep silence, and a time to speak.
8 A time of love, and a time of hatred.
A time of war, and a time of peace.
9 What more does a man have from his labor?
10 I have seen the affliction which God has given to the sons of men, that they may be exercised in it.
11 He has made all things good in their time, and has delivered the world to their consideration <note>original: *disputationi*; implying that God has given humans the world to study and debate, even if they cannot fully grasp His work</note>, so that man cannot find out the work which God has wrought from the beginning even to the end.
12 And I have known that there is nothing better than to rejoice, and to do well in one's life.
13 For every man who eats and drinks, and sees good from his labor, this is the gift of God.
14 I have learned that all the works which God has made continue forever; we cannot add anything to them, nor take away from those things which God has made so that He may be feared.
15 That which has been made remains; the things that are to come have already been; and God restores that which has passed away.
16 I saw under the sun, in the place of judgment, impiety; and in the place of justice, iniquity.
17 And I said in my heart: God shall judge both the just and the impious, and then shall be the time of every thing.
18 I said in my heart concerning the sons of men, that God would prove them, and show them to be like the beasts.
19 Therefore the death of man and of beasts is one, and the condition of them both is equal: as man dies, so they also die. All things breathe alike, and man has nothing more than the beast; all things are subject to vanity.
20 And all things go to one place: of earth they were made, and into earth they return together.
21 Who knows if the spirit of the sons of Adam ascends upward, and if the spirit of the beasts descends downward?
22 And I perceived that there is nothing better than for a man to rejoice—

that a man should rejoice in his own work, and that this is his portion. For who can bring him to know what will happen after him?

# C H A P T E R IV.

*The wise man proves the vanity of this life by the oppression of the innocent, and shows that human industry is subject to envy: likewise, how the fool lives securely in idleness, while another without an heir toils to store up treasures: he explains the advantages of companionship, the vanity of kings and kingdoms, and prefers obedience over the sacrifices of fools.*

1 I turned to other things, and I saw the oppressions <note>original: *calumnias*; in this context, it refers to legal harassment or being crushed by the false accusations of the powerful</note> that are carried out under the sun, and the tears of the innocent, and that no one comforted them: nor could they resist the violence of those who oppressed them, being destitute of help from all.
2 And I praised the dead more than the living:
3 And I judged him to be happier than both who has not yet been born, nor seen the evils that are done under the sun.
4 Again, I contemplated all the labors of men, and I observed that their industries are exposed to the envy of their neighbors: and in this, therefore, is vanity <note>original: *vanitas*; the Hebrew word *hevel* literally means breath or vapor, suggesting something fleeting or hollow</note> and superfluous care.
5 The fool folds his hands together and eats his own flesh, saying:
6 Better is a handful with rest than both hands full with labor and affliction of the mind.
7 Considering this, I found also another vanity under the sun:
8 There is one who is alone, and has no second—no son, no brother—and yet he does not cease to labor, nor are his eyes satisfied with riches: nor does he stop to think, saying: "For whom do I labor and deprive my soul of good things?" In this also is vanity and a most wretched affliction.
9 It is better, therefore, that two should be together than one: for they have the reward of their companionship.
10 If one falls, he shall be supported by the other. Woe to him who is alone: for when he falls, he has no one to lift him up.
11 And if two sleep together, they shall warm each other: how shall one be warmed alone?
12 And if anyone prevails against one, two shall resist him: a threefold cord is not easily broken.
13 Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who does not know how to look forward to the future.
14 For sometimes a man comes out of prison and chains to a kingdom: and another, born into royalty, is consumed by poverty.
15 I saw all the living who walk under the sun with the "second youth" <note>this likely refers to a successor or a new favorite who rises to replace the old king</note> who shall rise up in his place.
16 There is no end to the number of all the people who were before him: and those who come after shall not rejoice in him: but this also is vanity and affliction of spirit.
<margin>† 1 Kings 15:22; Hosea 6:6</margin>
17 Guard your step when you enter the house of God, and draw near to listen. † For obedience is much better than the sacrifices of fools, who do not know what evil they do.

<column-break/>

# C H A P T E R V.

*Nothing should be spoken rashly concerning God and His providence: vows must be paid: one should not wonder at the oppression of the poor, since the wicked have a judge: likewise, how wretched is the condition of the greedy who are never satisfied, and of the rich man who keeps his wealth to his own harm.*

1 Do not speak anything rashly, nor let your heart be quick to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven, and you are upon the earth: therefore, let your words be few.
2 Dreams follow many cares, and folly is found in many words.
3 If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay to pay it: for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases Him: but whatever you have vowed, pay it.
4 And it is much better not to vow than, after a vow, not to perform what was promised.
5 Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin: nor should you say before the angel <note>likely referring to a priest or a messenger of God at the temple</note>: "There is no providence" <note>original: *non est providentia*; the speaker warns against denying God's oversight of the world</note>: lest perhaps God, being angry at your words, should destroy all the works of your hands.
6 Where there are many dreams, there are many vanities and innumerable words: but you, fear God.
7 If you see the oppressions of the poor, and violent judgments, and justice subverted in a province, do not wonder at this matter: for another is higher than the high, and there are others still more eminent over them.
8 And moreover, the king of the whole earth commands his servant.
9 The greedy man is not filled with money: and he who loves riches shall take no fruit from them: and this, therefore, is vanity.
10 Where there are many riches, there are also many who eat them. And what does it profit the owner, except that he sees the riches with his eyes?
11 Sleep is sweet to the laborer, whether he eats little or much: but the satiety of the rich man will not let him sleep.
<margin>† Job 20:20</margin>
12 † There is also another most wretched sickness which I have seen under the sun: riches kept to the harm of their owner.
13 For they perish in the worst affliction: he has fathered a son who shall be in the greatest poverty.
<margin>† Job 1:21; 1 Timothy 6:7</margin>
14 † As he came out naked from his mother's womb, so shall he return, and he shall take nothing with him from his labor.
15 A truly miserable sickness: as he came, so shall he return. What then does it profit him that he has labored for the wind?
16 All the days of his life he eats in darkness, and in many cares, and in misery and sadness.
17 And so, this has seemed good to me: that a man should eat and drink, and enjoy the happiness of his labor in which he toils under the sun, for the number of the days of his life which God has given him: and this is his portion.
18 And to every man to whom God has given riches and substance, and has granted him the power to eat from them, and to enjoy his portion, and to rejoice in his labor: this is the gift of God.
19 For he shall not much remember the days of his life, because God occupies his heart with delights.

# CHAPTER VI.

*The vanity of the miser is wretched, for he does not even dare to use the things he has acquired even for his own needs.*

1 There is also another evil that I have seen under the sun, and indeed it is frequent among men:
2 A man to whom God has given riches, and substance, and honor, and nothing is lacking to his soul of all that he desires: yet God does not give him the power to eat from it, but a stranger shall devour it: this is vanity, and a great misery.
3 If a man should father a hundred children, and live many years, and have many days of life, yet his soul does not make use of the goods of his substance, and he lacks a burial: of this man I pronounce that a stillborn child is better than he.
4 For it comes in vain, and goes into darkness, and its name shall be blotted out by oblivion.
5 It has not seen the sun, nor known the distance between good and evil:
6 Even if he should live two thousand years, and has not enjoyed good things: do not all things hasten to one place?
7 All the labor of man is for his mouth: but his soul shall not be satisfied.
8 What more has the wise man than the fool? And what has the poor man, except to go where there is life?
9 It is better to see what you desire, than to long for what you do not know: but this also is vanity, and a presumption of spirit <note>original: *praesumptio spiritus*; a phrase suggesting a "striving after wind" or a futile grasping of the mind</note>.
10 He who is to be, his name has already been called, and it is known that he is a man, and that he cannot contend in judgment against one stronger than himself.
11 There are many words, which have much vanity in disputing.

# CHAPTER VII.

*It is vain to seek things higher than oneself; and among many things which are to be chosen above others, wisdom is more useful when joined with riches: a bad day must be guarded against: do not be more wise or just than is necessary: how bitter and dangerous is the company of a woman: and that man was created upright by God.*

1 What need is there for a man to seek things greater than himself, when he is ignorant of what is useful for him in his life, in the number of the days of his pilgrimage, and in the time that passes like a shadow? Or who can tell him what shall be after him under the sun?
<margin>Proverbs 22:1</margin> 2 A good name is better than precious ointments; and the day of death better than the day of birth.
3 It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to the house of feasting: for in the former, the end of all men is brought to mind, and the living reflects on what is to come.
4 Anger is better than laughter <note>original: *ira*; here implying a serious or somber disposition that leads to reflection</note>: because through the sadness of the face, the mind of the offender is corrected.
5 The heart of the wise is where there is sadness, and the heart of fools is where there is mirth.
6 It is better to be rebuked by a wise man, than to be deceived by the flattery of fools.
7 For as the sound of thorns burning under a pot, so is the laughter of a fool: but this also is vanity.
8 Oppression <note>original: *calumnia*; here referring to the weight of social injustice or false accusation</note> disturbs the wise man, and shall destroy the strength of his heart.
9 The end of a speech is better than the beginning. The patient man is better than the arrogant.

<column-break/>

10 Do not be quick to anger: for anger rests in the bosom of a fool.
11 Do not say: "Why do you think the cause is that former times were better than they are now?" For such an inquiry is foolish.
12 Wisdom is more useful with riches, and is more profitable to those who see the sun.
13 For as wisdom protects, so money protects: but this also has learning and wisdom, that it grants life to its possessor.
14 Consider the works of God, that no one can correct whom He has despised.
15 In a good day enjoy good things, and guard against a bad day: for God has made both the one and the other, so that man may find no just complaints against Him.
16 These things also I have seen in the days of my vanity: the just man perishes in his justice, and the wicked man lives a long time in his malice.
17 Do not be excessively just: nor be wiser than is necessary, lest you become stupid.
18 Do not act too wickedly: and do not be a fool, lest you die before your time.
19 It is good for you to support the just man, but also do not withdraw your hand from him: for he who fears God neglects nothing.
20 Wisdom has strengthened the wise man more than ten princes of the city.
<margin>1 Kings 8:46, 2 Chronicles 6:36, Proverbs 20:9, 1 John 1:8</margin> 21 For there is no just man on earth who does good and does not sin.
22 But do not apply your heart to all words that are spoken: lest perhaps you hear your servant speaking ill of you.
23 For your own conscience knows that you also have frequently spoken ill of others.
24 All things I have tried in wisdom. I said: "I will become wise": and wisdom itself retreated further from me
25 Much more than it was before: and it is a deep depth, who can find it?
26 I surveyed everything in my mind, that I might know, and consider, and seek out wisdom and reason: and that I might know the wickedness of the fool, and the error of the imprudent.
27 And I found a woman more bitter than death, who is the snare of hunters, and her heart is a net, and her hands are chains: he who pleases God shall escape her: but he who is a sinner shall be caught by her.
28 Behold, this I have found, said the Preacher <note>original: *Ecclesiastes*; the Greek title for the "Speaker" or "Convener" of the assembly</note>, examining one thing after another to find the reason,
29 Which my soul still seeks, and I have not found. One man among a thousand I have found, but a woman among all these I have not found.
30 Only this I have found: that God made man upright, and he has entangled himself in infinite questions. Who is like the wise man? And who has known the solution of a matter?

### CHAPTER IX.

> *No one knows whether they are worthy of God's hatred or love: because all things happen the same to everyone here: and since after this brief and uncertain life no time for work remains, he advises that one must now insistently apply oneself to works: and although wisdom excels over strength, in a poor man it is nonetheless undervalued.*

1 All these things I have turned over in my heart, so that I might understand them carefully: the righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God: and yet a man does not know whether he is worthy of love or of hatred:
2 But all things are kept uncertain for the future, because all things happen equally to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the evil, to the clean and the unclean, to him who offers victims and to him who despises sacrifices:

<column-break/>

as with the good man, so also with the sinner; as with the perjurer, so also with the one who swears a true oath.
3 This is the worst among all things that are done under the sun: that the same things happen to all. From this, the hearts of the sons of men are filled with malice and contempt during their lives, and after these things they are led down to the underworld <note>original: *inferos*; in this context, the place of the dead or the grave.</note>.
4 There is no one who lives forever, or who has confidence in this matter: a living dog is better than a dead lion.
5 For the living know that they are going to die, but the dead know nothing more, nor do they have any further reward: for the memory of them is given over to oblivion.
6 Their love, as well as their hatred and their envy, have perished together; nor do they have a part in this world, or in the work that is performed under the sun.
7 Go, therefore, and eat your bread in joy, and drink your wine with gladness: because your works please God.
8 Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil not be lacking from your head <note>A reference to ancient festive customs where white clothing and scented oils signified joy and celebration.</note>.
9 Enjoy life with the wife you love all the days of your unstable life, which are given to you under the sun all the time of your vanity: for this is your portion in life, and in your labor by which you toil under the sun.
10 Whatever your hand is able to do, work at it instantly: because neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge will exist in the underworld, toward which you are hastening.
11 I turned to another thing, and I saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the learned, nor favor to the skillful; but time and chance happen in all things.
12 Man does not know his own end, but just as fish are caught with a hook, and as birds are captured in a snare, so are men caught in an evil time, when it suddenly comes upon them.
13 This wisdom also I have seen under the sun, and I have proved it to be very great:
14 There was a small city, and few men in it; a great king came against it, and besieged it, and built fortifications all around, and the siege was complete.
15 And there was found in it a man, poor and wise, and he delivered the city through his wisdom; and yet no one afterward remembered that poor man.
16 And I said that wisdom is better than strength: how then is the wisdom of the poor man despised, and his words not heard?
17 The words of the wise are heard in silence, more than the cry of a prince among fools.
18 Wisdom is better than weapons of war: and he who fails <note>original: *peccaverit*; literally "to sin" or "to miss the mark," here implying a single error or moral failure.</note> in one thing shall lose many good things.

### CHAPTER X.

> *The difference between a wise man and a fool: the spirit of a powerful man must be resisted in temptations: concerning the fool and the servant who are elevated, and the rich man and the prince who are humbled: the hidden slanderer is compared to a serpent; concerning the child king, and the princes who eat in the morning; and that one must disparage neither the king nor the rich man.*

1 Dying flies ruin the sweetness of the ointment. Wisdom and glory are more precious than a small and temporary folly.
2 The heart of the wise man is at his right hand, and the heart of the fool is at his left.

<sig>Ee 2</sig>

3 Moreover, when a fool walks along the way, since he himself is senseless, he considers everyone else to be a fool.
4 If the spirit of one in power rises against you, do not leave your place, for healing <note>In this context, "healing" or "composure" suggests a calm spirit that can soothe great offenses.</note> will cause the greatest sins to cease.
5 There is an evil I have seen under the sun, appearing as an error proceeding from the face of a prince:
6 A fool set in high dignity, and the rich sitting in a low place.
7 I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking upon the ground like servants.
<margin>† Proverbs 26:27; Ecclesiasticus 27:29</margin>
8 † He who digs a pit shall fall into it, and he who breaks down a hedge, a serpent shall bite him.
9 He who moves stones shall be hurt by them, and he who cuts wood shall be wounded by it.
10 If the iron be blunt, and it is not as it was before, but has become dull, it shall be sharpened with much labor; and wisdom shall follow after industry.
11 If a serpent bites in silence, he who slanders in secret is no better.
12 The words of a wise man’s mouth are grace, but the lips of a fool shall throw him down headlong.
13 The beginning of his words is folly, and the end of his talk is a most evil error.
14 A fool multiplies words. A man does not know what has been before him, and who can tell him what shall be after him?
15 The labor of fools shall afflict those who do not even know how to go into the city. <note>An ancient idiom suggesting that a fool lacks even the most basic common sense or direction.</note>
16 Woe to you, O land, whose king is a child, and whose princes eat in the morning.
17 Blessed is the land whose king is noble, and whose princes eat in due season, for refreshment and not for luxury.
18 Through slothfulness the roof-beam shall be brought low, and through weakness of hands the house shall leak.
19 They make bread for laughter, and wine to cheer the living; and all things obey money.
20 Do not disparage the king even in your thought, nor curse the rich in the secret of your bedroom; for even the birds of the air will carry your voice, and those with wings will announce your words.

## CHAPTER XI.

> *He advises us to share with others and always to work well: because man's judgment after death is unchangeable; we must also keep in mind the future judgment in which we are all to be judged: anger and malice should be removed from the heart.*

Cast your bread upon the running waters, for after many days you shall find it again.
2 Give a portion to seven, and even to eight, for you do not know what evil may come upon the earth.
3 If the clouds are full, they will pour out rain upon the earth. If a tree falls to the south or to the north, in whatever place it falls, there it shall lie.
4 He who observes the wind shall not sow, and he who considers the clouds shall never reap.
5 Just as you do not know the way of the spirit, nor how the bones are joined together in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the works of God, who is the maker of all things.
6 In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand cease; for you do not know which shall grow better,

<column-break/>

this or that, and if both grow together, it shall be even better.
7 The light is sweet, and it is a delightful thing for the eyes to see the sun.
8 If a man lives many years and is happy in them all, he must remember the dark time and the many days; when they come, the past shall be accused of vanity. <note>original: "vanitas" — referring to the transient, breath-like nature of human existence.</note>
9 Rejoice therefore, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart be in what is good during the days of your youth; walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, but know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.
10 Remove anger from your heart and put away malice from your flesh. For youth and pleasure are vain.

## CHAPTER XII.

> *Keep God before your eyes in youth, before troublesome old age and finally death succeed; and since all things are vanity, observe God's commandments, for an account must be given for everything.*

Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the time of affliction comes and the years draw near of which you shall say: "They do not please me."
2 Before the sun, and the light, and the moon, and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain;
3 When the keepers of the house <note>An allegory for the hands.</note> shall tremble, and the strongest men <note>The legs.</note> shall stagger, and the grinders <note>The teeth.</note> shall be idle because they are few, and those looking through the holes <note>The eyes/vision.</note> shall grow dark.
4 And they shall shut the doors in the street, with a low voice of the one grinding, and they shall rise up at the voice of a bird, and all the daughters of music shall grow deaf.
5 They shall also fear high places and be afraid in the way; the almond tree shall flourish, the locust shall be made fat, and the caper-berry shall be scattered; because man shall go into the house of his eternity, and the mourners shall go about in the street.
6 Before the silver cord is broken, and the golden fillet shrinks back, and the pitcher is crushed at the fountain, and the wheel is broken upon the cistern,
7 And the dust returns into its earth from whence it was, and the spirit returns to God, who gave it.
8 Vanity of vanities, said the Preacher, <note>original: "Ecclesiastes"</note> and all is vanity.
9 And whereas the Preacher was most wise, he taught the people and declared what he had done; and searching diligently, he composed many parables.
10 He sought useful words and wrote down most upright discourses, full of truth.
11 The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails deeply fastened, which by the counsel of masters are given from one shepherd.
12 Beyond these, my son, require no more. Of making many books there is no end, and much study is an affliction of the flesh.
13 Let us all hear the conclusion of the discourse together: Fear God and keep His commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.
14 And all things that are done, God will bring into judgment for every error, whether it be good or evil.

## SHIR HASHIRIM.

### CHAPTER ONE.

*This entire song is mystical, most full of the incomprehensible love of Christ toward his bride, and in turn of the bride toward Christ the bridegroom.* <note>original: "Hoc canticum totum est mysticum..." This introductory note reflects the common Medieval and Early Modern view that the book is not merely love poetry, but a profound spiritual allegory.</note>

<margin>1</margin> Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth: for your breasts <note>The Latin 'ubera' literally means breasts, though in the original Hebrew and many modern versions, this is translated as 'love'.</note> are better than wine,
<margin>2</margin> Smelling of the best ointments. Your name is as oil poured out: therefore the young maidens have loved you.
<margin>3</margin> Draw me: we will run after you in the fragrance of your ointments. The king has brought me into his storerooms: we will exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts more than wine: the righteous love you.
<margin>4</margin> I am black but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar <note>Kedar (Cedar) refers to a nomadic tribe known for dark-colored tents made of goat hair.</note>, like the curtains of Solomon.
<margin>5</margin> Do not look at me because I am dark, for the sun has discolored me: my mother's sons fought against me, they made me a keeper in the vineyards: my own vineyard I have not kept.
<margin>6</margin> Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture your flock, where you rest at noon, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.
<margin>7</margin> If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go forth and follow after the tracks of the flocks, and feed your young goats beside the tents of the shepherds.
<margin>8</margin> I have compared you, my love, to my team of horses among Pharaoh's chariots.
<margin>9</margin> Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove: your neck like necklaces.
<margin>10</margin> We will make you small chains of gold, inlaid with silver.
<margin>11</margin> While the king was on his couch, my nard <term>Spikenard, a costly aromatic ointment made from a Himalayan plant</term> gave forth its scent.
<margin>12</margin> A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me, he shall abide between my breasts.
<margin>13</margin> A cluster of cypress <note>original: "cypri" – likely referring to henna blossoms common in the region</note> is my beloved to me, in the vineyards of En-Gedi.
<margin>14</margin> Behold, you are beautiful, my love, behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are those of doves.
<margin>15</margin> Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and handsome. Our little bed is flowery.
<margin>16</margin> The beams of our houses are of cedar, our rafters are of cypress.

whom I had desired, I sat: and his fruit was sweet to my taste.

<margin>9</margin> My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, looking through the lattices.
<margin>10</margin> Behold, my beloved speaks to me: Arise, make haste, my love, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.
<margin>11</margin> For now the winter has passed, the rain is over and gone.

<margin>17</margin> Until the day breathes, and the shadows incline. Return; be like, my beloved, a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Bether.

1 How beautiful you are, my love, how beautiful you are! # CHAPTER V.

1 Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat the fruit of his orchard. I have come into my garden, my sister, my spouse,

<column-break/>

I have gathered my myrrh with my spices: I have eaten the honeycomb with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk: eat, O friends, and drink, and be inebriated <note>In a spiritual context, this "drunkenness" refers to being overwhelmed by divine love.</note>, my dearly beloved.
2 I sleep, but my heart watches: the voice of my beloved knocking: Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled: for my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the nights.

4 My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly <note>In ancient thought, the 'venter' (belly or bowels) was considered the seat of deep emotion and compassion.</note> trembled at his touch.
5 I rose up to open to my beloved: my hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of the choicest myrrh.

7 The watchmen who go about the city found me: they struck me and wounded me: the keepers of the walls took away my cloak from me.
8 I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you tell him I languish with love.
9 What kind of beloved is your beloved, O most beautiful of women? What kind of beloved is your beloved, that you have so adjured us?
10 My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands.
11 His head is the finest gold: His hair is like the flowering branches of palms, black as a raven.
12 His eyes are like doves over the brooks of waters, which are washed with milk and sit beside the fullest streams.
13 His cheeks are like beds of spices, planted by the perfumers. His lips are lilies, dripping with the finest myrrh.
14 His hands are turned gold, full of hyacinths <note>original: "hyacinthis" - likely referring to blue gemstones like sapphires or zircons rather than the flower.</note>. His belly is of ivory, set with sapphires.
15 His legs are pillars of marble, which are founded upon bases of gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars.
16 His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable: such is my beloved, and he is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.
17 Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful of women? Where has your beloved turned aside? and we will seek him with you.

<meta>This page transitions from the Song of Songs to the beginning of the Book of Wisdom. While the previous page concluded the poetic descriptions of the bride and groom in the Song of Solomon, this page introduces a new work of "Wisdom Literature," traditionally attributed to King Solomon, focusing on the necessity of justice, the nature of the soul, and the origins of death.</meta>

-># THE BOOK OF WISDOM.<-

*Let judges be just: the Lord is found if he is sought with a simple heart and faith, but he flees from sinners and unstable thoughts: since he fills all things, nothing can be hidden from him. Grumbling, detraction, and lying are to be detested: God made all things for life, not intending death, which sinners have summoned to themselves.*

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>† 1 Kings 3:9. Isaiah 56:1.</margin>
**L**ove † justice, you who judge the earth. Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart.

<margin>† 2 Chronicles 15:2.</margin>
2 † For he is found by those who do not tempt him: and he reveals himself to those who have faith in him.

3 For perverse thoughts separate one from God: and when his power is put to the test, it rebukes the foolish.

4 For wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sin.

5 For the holy spirit of discipline <note>original: "spiritus sanctus disciplinæ" - This refers to the instructional or guiding aspect of God's spirit.</note> will flee from the deceitful, and will withdraw itself from thoughts that are without understanding, and will be rebuked when iniquity rushes in.

<margin>† Galatians 5:22. † Jeremiah 17:10.</margin>
6 † For the spirit of wisdom is benevolent, and will not acquit the speaker of evil from the consequences of his lips: † for God is the witness of his innermost being <note>original: "renum" - literally "kidneys," which in biblical Hebrew and Latin thought were considered the seat of emotions and hidden intentions.</note>, and the true searcher of his heart, and the hearer of his tongue.

<margin>† Isaiah 6:3.</margin>
7 † For the spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world: and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice.

8 Therefore, he who speaks unjust things cannot remain hidden, nor shall the chastising judgment pass him by.

9 For there shall be an inquiry into the thoughts of the wicked: and the sound of his words shall reach God, for the punishment of his iniquities.

10 For the ear of jealousy hears all things, and the noise of grumbling shall not be hidden.

11 Keep yourselves, therefore, from grumbling, which is of no use, and refrain your tongue from detraction, for a secret word <note>original: "sermo obscurus" - literally "dark speech," referring to whispers or gossip intended to be hidden.</note> shall not go for nothing: and the mouth that lies kills the soul.

12 Do not seek death in the error of your life, nor bring destruction upon yourselves by the works of your hands.

<margin>† Ezekiel 18:3. & 33:11.</margin>
13 † For God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living.

14 For he created all things so that they might exist: and he made the nations of the earth healthy: and there is no poison of destruction in them, nor is the kingdom of hell upon the earth.

15 For justice is perpetual and immortal.

16 But the wicked, with their hands and words, have summoned death: and thinking it a friend, they have pined away, and made a pact with it: because they are worthy to belong to its side.

<column-break/>

*The entire future life of the wicked who have no hope is focused on enjoying the pleasures of this life, and therefore they cannot bear the just man, who looks toward a different end, but they persecute him even unto death: just as by the envy of the Devil, man—created immortal by God—was made mortal.*

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>† Job 7:1. & 14:1.</margin>
For they said, reasoning with themselves not rightly: † The time of our life is short and tedious, and there is no relief at the end of a man's life, and no one is known to have returned from the underworld:

2 For we were born from nothing, and after this we shall be as if we had never been: for the breath in our nostrils is smoke: and our speech is a spark to move our heart:

3 When this is extinguished, our body shall become ashes, and our spirit shall be scattered like thin air, and our life shall pass away like the trace of a cloud, and shall be dissolved like a mist that is driven away by the rays of the sun, and weighed down by its heat:

4 And our name shall be forgotten in time, and no one shall have a memory of our works.

<margin>† 1 Chronicles 29:15.</margin>

<margin>† Isaiah 22:13. & 56:12. 1 Corinthians 15:32.</margin>
6 † Come, therefore, and let us enjoy the good things that exist, and let us use the creation quickly, as in youth.

8 Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither: let there be no meadow that our luxury does not pass through.

9 Let none of us be without a share in our decadence: let us leave signs of joy everywhere: for this is our portion, and this is our lot.

11 But let our strength be the law of justice: for that which is weak is found to be useless.

12 Let us, therefore, lie in wait for the just man, because he is useless to us, and he is contrary to our works, and reproaches us for transgressions of the law, and spreads abroad the sins of our way of life.

<margin>† Matthew 27:43. † John 7:7.</margin>

15 He is grievous for us even to behold, for his life is unlike others, and his ways are changed.

17 Let us see, then, if his words be true, and let us test what will happen to him, and we shall know what his end shall be.

### CHAPTER III.

->Concerning the happiness of the righteous, who in this life were despised by the wicked and tested by God through trials: and concerning the unhappiness of the wicked: likewise concerning the reward of chastity and good works, and the misery of the children of adulterers.<-

<margin>Deuteronomy 33:3. Below 5:4.</margin>
But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment of death shall touch them.
2 In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to die: and their departure was considered an affliction:
3 And their journey away from us, utter destruction: but they are in peace.
4 And though in the sight of men they suffered torments, their hope is full of immortality.
5 Afflicted in a few things, they shall be well rewarded in many: because God tested them, and found them worthy of himself.
6 As gold in the furnace he proved them, and as a whole burnt offering <term>holocaustum: a sacrifice entirely consumed by fire</term> he accepted them, and in the time of their visitation they shall be cared for.
<margin>Matthew 13:43. 1 Corinthians 6:2.</margin>

10 But the wicked shall be punished according to their own imaginings: they who neglected the righteous man, and withdrew from the Lord.
11 For he who rejects wisdom and discipline is miserable: and their hope is empty, and their labors without fruit, and their works useless.
12 Their wives are foolish, and their children are most wicked.
13 Their offspring is cursed, because the barren woman is happy: and she who is undefiled, who has not known a sinful bed, shall have fruit in the visitation of holy souls.
<margin>Isaiah 56:3.</margin>

15 For the fruit of good labors is glorious, and the root of wisdom never withers.
16 But the children of adulterers shall not come to maturity, and the seed of an unlawful bed shall be rooted out.

### CHAPTER IV.

->The chaste generation differs in many ways from the adulterous one: concerning the rest of the righteous man overtaken by death: what constitutes a venerable old age, and that the righteous are often taken from the world by God so they are not led astray by the wicked, and how great the difference is between the ends of both.<-

O how beautiful is the chaste generation with brilliance! For the memory of it is immortal: because it is known both by God and by men.
2 While it is present, they imitate it: and they long for it when it has withdrawn itself, and it triumphs forever, crowned, winning the prize of undefiled struggles.
3 But the prolific multitude of the wicked shall not be profitable, and spurious seedlings <term>vitulamina: shoots or suckers of a plant</term> shall not strike deep roots, nor establish a stable foundation.
<margin>Jeremiah 17:6. Matthew 7:27.</margin>
4 † And though they may sprout branches for a time, being weakly placed, they shall be shaken by the wind, and by the violence of the winds they shall be uprooted.
5 For the unfinished branches shall be broken, and their fruits useless, and too bitter to eat, and fit for nothing.
6 For children born from unlawful sleep are witnesses of wickedness against their parents when they are examined.
7 But the righteous man, if he is overtaken by death, shall be at rest.
8 For a venerable old age is not defined by length of time, nor measured by the number of years: but a man's understanding is his gray hair,
9 And a spotless life is the peak of old age.
<margin>Hebrews 11:5.</margin>
10 † Being pleasing to God, he was loved, and living among sinners, he was translated <note>original: "translatus" — taken up to God, much like the biblical figure Enoch.</note>.
11 He was snatched away lest malice should change his understanding, or lest deceit should beguile his soul.
12 For the fascination of vanity <note>original: "nugacitatis" — worthlessness or trifling things</note> obscures what is good, and the fickleness of desire undermines a mind that is without malice.
13 Having been perfected in a short time, he fulfilled many years:
14 For his soul was pleasing to God: therefore he hastened to bring him out of the midst of iniquities. But the people saw, and did not understand, nor did they take such things to heart:
15 That the grace of God and mercy is with his saints, and his care is for his elect.
16 But the righteous man who is dead condemns the living wicked, and youth quickly perfected condemns the long life of the unjust.
17 For they shall see the end of the wise man, and shall not understand what God has planned for him, and why the Lord has kept him safe.
18 They shall see and despise him: but the Lord shall laugh them to scorn.
19 And after this they shall fall without honor, and be a reproach among the dead forever: for he shall burst them asunder, puffed up and speechless, and shall shake them from their foundations, and they shall be utterly laid waste: and they shall be in sorrow, and the memory of them shall perish.

### CHAPTER V.

> *The wicked, in the judgment, marvel at the glory of the righteous whom they had despised here; they lament their own misery, seeing that all their happiness was but momentary, while that of the righteous shall be perpetual. Furthermore, God arms Himself, both through His creatures and by His own power, to punish the wicked.*

1 Then shall the righteous stand with great constancy against those who afflicted them and who took away the fruits of their labors.
2 Seeing this, the wicked shall be troubled with terrible fear, and shall marvel at the suddenness of their unexpected salvation,
3 Saying within themselves, repenting and groaning for anguish of spirit: "These are they whom we once held in derision, and as a proverb of reproach.
<margin>Above, 2.</margin>
4 † We fools esteemed their life as madness, and their end to be without honor:
5 Behold how they are numbered among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints!
6 Therefore, we have erred from the way of truth; the light of justice has not shined for us, and the Sun of understanding <note>original: "Sol intelligentiæ" — a metaphor for divine wisdom or clarity of mind.</note> did not rise for us.
7 We wearied ourselves in the way of iniquity and perdition; we have walked through difficult paths, but the way of the Lord we have not known.
8 What has pride profited us? Or what has the boasting of riches brought us?
<margin>1 Chronicles 29:15; Above, 2; Proverbs ch. 19.</margin>
9 † All those things have passed away like a shadow, and like a messenger running by,
10 † And like a ship that passes through the surging waters: which, when it is gone by, its trace cannot be found, nor the path of its keel in the waves.
11 Or like a bird that flies through the air, of whose passage no mark can be found, but only the sound of its wings beating the light wind, and parting the air by the force of its flight; moving its wings, it flies away, and after that, no sign of its path is found.
12 Or like an arrow shot at a target: the divided air immediately closes in upon itself again, so that its passage is unknown.
13 So we also, as soon as we were born, ceased to be: and were able to show no sign of virtue, but were consumed in our own wickedness."
14 Such things did those who sinned say in hell:
<margin>Psalm 1:4; v. 28; 11:7.</margin>
15 † For the hope of the wicked is like thistledown <note>original: "lanugo" — the fine, soft hair or fluff of a plant, easily blown away.</note> that is carried away by the wind; and like a thin froth that is dispersed by the storm; and like smoke that is scattered by the wind; and like the memory of a guest of a single day who passes by.
16 But the righteous shall live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and the care for them is with the Most High.
17 Therefore, they shall receive a kingdom of glory <note>original: "decoris" — meaning beauty, honor, or splendor.</note> and a crown of beauty from the hand of the Lord: for with His right hand He shall cover them, and with His holy arm He shall defend them.
<margin>Isaiah 59:17.</margin>
18 † His zeal shall take up armor, and He shall arm His creature <note>original: "creaturam" — here referring to the physical world or creation itself, which fights alongside God.</note> to take revenge on His enemies.
19 He shall put on justice as a breastplate, and shall take true judgment instead of a helmet.
20 He shall take equity as an invincible shield.

<column-break/>

21 He shall sharpen His stern wrath into a spear, and the whole world shall fight with Him against the senseless.
22 Then the shafts of lightning shall go directly, and as from a well-drawn bow of clouds, they shall be fly out and leap to the designated mark.
23 And hailstones full of wrath shall be cast as from a stone-bow; the water of the sea shall rage against them, and the rivers shall crash together cruelly.
24 A spirit of power shall stand against them, and like a whirlwind shall scatter them: and their iniquity shall bring all the earth to a desert, and wickedness shall overturn the seats of the mighty.

### CHAPTER VI.

> *He exhorts kings and judges to pursue wisdom and justice, showing how severe a punishment awaits unjust rulers; likewise, how wisdom is readily found by those who seek her, and that the acquisition of her is profitable, though the envious man is not capable of it.*

<margin>Ecclesiastes 9:18.</margin>
1 Wisdom is better than strength, and a prudent man is better than a strong one.
2 Hear therefore, O kings, and understand; learn, O you judges of the ends of the earth.
3 Give ear, you who rule the multitudes, and who take pleasure in the crowds of nations:
<margin>† Romans 13:1.</margin>
4 † For power is given to you by the Lord, and strength by the Most High, who shall examine your works and search out your thoughts.
5 For though you were ministers of His kingdom, you have not judged rightly, nor kept the law of justice, nor walked according to the will of God.
6 Horribly and speedily shall He appear to you: for a most severe judgment shall be for those who are in authority.
7 For mercy is granted to the lowly, but the mighty shall suffer torments mightily.
<margin>† Deuteronomy 10:17; 2 Chronicles 19:7; Ecclesiasticus 35:15; Acts 10:34; Romans 2:11; Galatians 2:6; Ephesians 6:9; Colossians 3:25; 1 Peter 1:17.</margin>
8 † For God will not exempt any person, nor will He stand in awe of anyone's greatness: for He made both the small and the great, and He has equal care for all.
9 But a stronger trial is reserved for the strong.
10 To you, therefore, O kings, are these my words, that you may learn wisdom and not fall away.
11 For they who have kept just things justly shall be justified: and they who have learned these things shall find what to answer.
12 Covet therefore my words, love them, and you shall have instruction.
13 Wisdom is bright, and never fades: she is easily seen by those who love her, and found by those who seek her.
14 She anticipates those who desire her, so that she may first show herself to them.
15 He who watches for her from the break of day shall have no labor: for he shall find her sitting at his doors.
16 To think therefore upon her is perfect understanding: and he who watches for her sake shall quickly be secure.
17 For she goes about seeking such as are worthy of her, and she shows herself cheerfully to them in the ways, and meets them with all providence.
18 For the true beginning of her is the desire for instruction.
19 The care for instruction is love: and love is the keeping of her laws: and the keeping of the laws is the assurance of incorruption.
20 And incorruption <note>original: "incorruptio" — meaning immortality or freedom from decay.</note> brings one near to God.
