9 † Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion, shout for joy, O daughter of Jerusalem: BEHOLD YOUR KING comes to you, the Just One and the Savior: He is poor, and riding upon a donkey, and upon a colt, the foal of a donkey.
10 And I will destroy the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war shall be broken: and He shall speak peace to the Nations, and His power shall be from sea to sea, and from the rivers even to the ends of the earth.
11 You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit in which there is no water.
12 Turn to the stronghold, O prisoners of hope, today I also announce that I will render to you double.
13 For I have stretched out Judah for myself like a bow, I have filled Ephraim <note>as an arrow</note>: and I will raise up your sons, O Zion, over your sons, O Greece: and I will set you like the sword of the mighty.
14 And the Lord God shall be seen over them; and His arrow shall go forth like lightning: and the Lord God shall sound with the trumpet, and He shall go in the whirlwind of the South.
15 The Lord of hosts shall protect them: and they shall devour, and subdue with sling-stones: and drinking they shall be inebriated as with wine, and they shall be filled like bowls, and like the horns of the altar.
16 And the Lord their God shall save them in that day, as the flock of His people: for holy stones shall be lifted up over His land.
17 For what is His good thing, and what is His beautiful thing, but the grain of the elect, and wine that brings forth virgins? <note>This verse poetically describes the abundance and purity of the messianic age</note>

### CHAPTER X.

*Only the Lord can grant rain, who will strengthen the Jews: and having had mercy on them, He will gather them from various places of captivity into their original land, their enemies having been humbled.*

1 Ask of the Lord rain in the latter time, and the Lord will make the snows, and will give them showers of rain: to every man, grass in the field.
2 For the idols have spoken useless things, and the diviners have seen a lie, and the dreamers have spoken in vain: they comforted fruitlessly: therefore they were led away like a flock: they shall be afflicted, because they have no shepherd.
3 My wrath is kindled against the shepherds, and I will visit upon the male-goats: for the Lord of hosts has visited His flock, the house of Judah, and has made them like the horse of His glory in battle.
4 From him is the cornerstone, from him the peg, from him the bow of battle, from him every oppressor shall come forth together.
5 And they shall be like mighty men treading down the mud of the streets in battle: and they shall fight, because the Lord is with them: and the riders of horses shall be confounded.
6 And I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph: and I will bring them back, because I will have mercy on them: and they shall be as they were when I had not cast them off: for I am the Lord their God, and I will hear them.
7 And they shall be like the mighty men of Ephraim, and their heart shall rejoice as if from wine: and their children shall see, and shall rejoice, and their heart shall exult in the Lord.
8 I will whistle for them <note>original: "sibilabo"—a shepherd’s signal</note>, and I will gather them, because I have redeemed them: and I will multiply them as they had been multiplied before.
9 And I will sow them among the peoples, and from afar they shall remember me: and they shall live with their children, and shall return.
10 And I will lead them back from the land of Egypt, and I will gather them from the Assyrians, and I will bring them to the land of Gilead and Lebanon, and a place shall not be found for them <note>meaning the land will be so crowded with people</note>.
11 And He shall pass through the strait of the sea, and shall strike the waves in the sea, and all the depths of the river shall be confounded, and the pride of Assyria shall be humbled, and the scepter of Egypt shall depart.
12 I will strengthen them in the Lord, and in His name they shall walk, says the Lord.

### CHAPTER XIV.

*After Jerusalem has suffered captivity and her other afflictions from the Gentiles, there will be a day known to the Lord when living waters shall flow out from Jerusalem. Then the people of Israel shall return to dwell securely in Jerusalem. The Lord shall strike with a plague the Nations that fought against Jerusalem; their remnants shall go up to worship the Lord in Jerusalem, and even the bells on the horses' bridles shall be holy.*

1 Behold, the days of the Lord are coming, and your spoils shall be divided in your midst.
2 And I will gather all the Nations to Jerusalem for battle, and the city shall be taken, the houses plundered, and the women violated; half of the city shall go forth into captivity, and the rest of the people shall not be taken away from the city.
3 Then the Lord shall go forth and fight against those Nations, just as he fought in the day of battle.
4 And his feet shall stand in that day upon the Mount of Olives, which is opposite Jerusalem to the east; and the Mount of Olives shall be split in half from the east to the west by a very great valley, and half of the mountain shall move toward the North and half toward the South.
<margin>Amos 1:1.</margin> 5 And you shall flee to the valley of those mountains, for the valley of the mountains shall be joined even to the next; and you shall flee just as you fled from the face of the earthquake in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah. And the Lord my God shall come, and all the saints with him.
6 And it shall be in that day: there shall be no light, but cold and frost.
7 And it shall be one day, which is known to the Lord—not day nor night—and at evening time there shall be light.
8 And it shall be in that day: living waters shall go out from Jerusalem; half of them to the eastern sea,

<column-break/>

and half of them to the farthest sea; they shall flow in summer and in winter alike.
9 And the Lord shall be king over all the earth; in that day there shall be one Lord, and his name shall be one.
10 And all the land shall return to a desert-like plain, from the hill of Rimmon to the South of Jerusalem; and the city shall be exalted and shall dwell in her place, from the Benjamin gate to the place of the former gate, and to the corner gate; and from the tower of Hananeel to the king's winepresses.
11 And they shall dwell in it, and there shall be no more anathema <note>original: "anathema"; referring to a divine curse or a decree of total destruction.</note>; but Jerusalem shall sit secure.
12 And this shall be the plague with which the Lord shall strike all the Nations that fought against Jerusalem: the flesh of every man shall waste away while he stands upon his feet, and his eyes shall waste away in their sockets, and their tongue shall waste away in their mouth.
13 In that day there shall be a great tumult from the Lord among them; and a man shall seize the hand of his neighbor, and his hand shall be raised against the hand of his neighbor.
14 But even Judah shall fight against Jerusalem; and the riches of all the Nations round about shall be gathered: gold, silver, and very many garments.
15 And such shall be the destruction of the horse, the mule, the camel, the donkey, and all the beasts that shall be in those camps, even as this destruction.
16 And all who remain of all the Nations that came against Jerusalem shall go up from year to year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, and to celebrate the feast of tabernacles <note>A Jewish harvest festival (Sukkot) commemorating the sheltering of the Israelites in the wilderness.</note>.
17 And it shall be: if any of the families of the earth do not go up to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, no rain shall fall upon them.
18 And if the family of Egypt does not go up and does not come, the rain shall not be upon them; but there shall be the destruction with which the Lord shall strike all the Nations that do not go up to celebrate the feast of tabernacles.
19 This shall be the sin of Egypt, and this the sin of all Nations that do not go up to celebrate the feast of tabernacles.
20 In that day, even what is upon the horse's bridle shall be "Holy to the Lord"; and the cooking pots in the house of the Lord shall be like the sacrificial bowls before the altar.
21 And every pot in Jerusalem and Judah shall be sanctified to the Lord of hosts; and all who sacrifice shall come and take them, and cook in them; and there shall be no merchant <note>original: "mercator"; in some contexts, this is translated as 'Canaanite,' symbolizing someone who treats the temple as a place of business.</note> anymore in the house of the Lord of hosts in that day.

# THE PROPHECY OF MALACHI.

## CHAPTER ONE.

> *The prophecy of Malachi to Israel, whom the Lord rebukes for ingratitude, because they did not recognize that they were loved in Jacob, from whom they descended, while Esau and his people were rejected: therefore He complains that He is not honored or feared by Israel, and that the priests despise the name of the Lord, whose sacrifices He rejects, favoring the pure offering that is offered to Him in every place.*

1 The burden of the word of the Lord to Israel by the hand of Malachi.
2 <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial O depicting a figure in a landscape</image-desc> I have loved you, says the Lord, and you have said: "In what way have you loved us?" Was not Esau the brother of Jacob? says the Lord, and † I loved Jacob,

7 You offer polluted bread upon my altar, and you say: "In what way have we polluted you?" In that you say: "The table of the Lord is contemptible."
8 If you offer the blind for sacrifice, is it not evil? and if you offer the lame and the sick, is it not evil? Offer it to your governor <note>original: "duci tuo"</note>, if it will please him, or if he will accept your person, says the Lord of hosts.
9 And now beseech the face of God that he may have mercy on you (for this has been done by your hand), if in any way he may accept your faces, says the Lord of hosts.

FIRST BOOK OF MACCABEES.

## CHAPTER ONE.

*After the death of Alexander the Great, who had defeated Darius, Antiochus the Illustrious eventually succeeded him in Greece: under whom certain wicked men from the sons of Israel profaned Jerusalem: Antiochus, however, having defeated Ptolemy the king of Egypt, invaded Jerusalem; and having taken away all the vessels of the temple and the treasures, he committed a great slaughter, from which arose a massive mourning: a chief collector of tribute sent by him did similarly, burning Jerusalem and leading many into captivity: Antiochus established laws of idolatry for the Jews, taking away all the ceremonies of divine worship and building an idol of desolation, miserably butchering those who resisted: many impious men followed his edicts, but the pious rejected them, being prepared to undergo death instead.*

1 <image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' featuring a figure in biblical or classical dress seated in a landscape with a tree.</image-desc> And it came to pass, after Alexander the Macedonian, son of Philip <note>original: "Alexander Philippi Macedo"</note>, who first reigned in Greece, having come out of the land of Chittim <note>original: "Cethim"; a term used in the Bible to refer to the islands and coastlands of the Mediterranean, here specifically Greece or Macedonia</note>, had struck down Darius, king of the Persians and Medes:
2 He waged many wars, and gained hold of all their fortresses, and killed the kings of the earth:
3 And he traveled even to the ends of the earth, and took the spoils of a multitude of nations: and the earth was silent in his presence.
4 And he gathered power, and a very strong army: and his heart was exalted and lifted up:
5 And he held the regions of the nations, and their rulers <note>original: "tyrannos"; used here in the classical sense of absolute monarchs or local lords</note>: and they became tributaries to him.
6 And after these things he fell into his bed, and knew that he was about to die.
7 And he called his noble servants, who had been raised with him from his youth: and he divided his kingdom among them while he was still living.
8 And Alexander reigned twelve years, and then died.
9 And his servants took over the kingdom, each in his own place.
10 And they all put on crowns <note>original: "diademata"</note> after his death, as did their sons after them for many years, and evils were multiplied on the earth.
11 And there came out of them a wicked root, Antiochus the Illustrious <note>original: "Antiochus illustris"; also known as Antiochus IV Epiphanes</note>, son of King Antiochus, who had been a hostage at Rome: and he began to reign in the one hundred and thirty-seventh year of the kingdom of the Greeks <note>The Seleucid era, approximately 175 BCE</note>.
12 In those days, certain wicked sons came out of Israel, and they persuaded many, saying: "Let us go, and make a covenant with the nations that are around us: because since the time we withdrew from them, many evils have found us."
13 And the proposal seemed good in their eyes.
14 And some of the people determined to go, and they went to the king: and he gave them authority to practice the customs of the Gentiles <note>original: "justitiam Gentium"; the "justice" or "ways" of the Greeks</note>.
15 And they built a gymnasium in Jerusalem according to the laws of the nations.
16 And they undid their circumcision <note>original: "fecerunt sibi praeputia"; a physical procedure to hide their Jewish identity in the Greek gymnasium</note>, and withdrew from the holy covenant, and were joined to the nations, and were sold to do evil.

<column-break/>

17 And the kingdom was established before Antiochus, and he began to reign in the land of Egypt, so that he might reign over two kingdoms.
18 And he entered into Egypt with a heavy multitude, with chariots, and elephants, and horsemen, and a vast number of ships.
19 And he engaged in war against Ptolemy, the king of Egypt, and Ptolemy was terrified by his presence and fled, and many fell wounded.
20 And he captured the fortified cities in the land of Egypt: and he took the spoils of the land of Egypt.
21 And Antiochus returned, after he had struck Egypt in the one hundred and forty-third year: and he went up against Israel.
22 And he went up to Jerusalem with a heavy multitude.
23 And he entered into the sanctuary with pride, and took the golden altar, and the lampstand of light, and all its vessels, and the table of showbread <note>original: "mensam propositionis"</note>, and the bowls, and the vials, and the golden mortars, and the veil, and the crowns, and the golden ornament that was on the face of the temple: and he broke everything in pieces.
24 And he took the silver, and gold, and the precious vessels: and he took the hidden treasures which he found: and having taken everything, he departed to his own land.
25 And he committed a slaughter of men, and spoke with great pride.
26 And there was great mourning in Israel, and in every place of theirs:
27 And the leaders and the elders groaned: the virgins and the young men were weakened: and the beauty of the women was changed.
28 Every bridegroom took up a lamentation: and she who sat in the marriage bed mourned:
29 And the earth was moved for those inhabiting it, and the whole house of Jacob was clothed with confusion.
30 And after two full years, the king sent a chief collector of tribute <note>original: "principem tributorum"</note> into the cities of Judah, and he came to Jerusalem with a great crowd.
31 And he spoke peaceful words to them in deceit: and they believed him.
32 And he fell upon the city suddenly, and struck it with a great blow, and destroyed much people from Israel.
33 And he took the spoils of the city: and he set it on fire, and destroyed its houses and its walls in a circuit:
34 And they led the women captive: and the children and the cattle they took as their own.
35 And they built the City of David <note>The old fortress area of Jerusalem</note> with a great and strong wall, and with strong towers, and it became a citadel <note>original: "arcem"; known as the Acra</note> for them.
36 And they placed there a sinful nation, wicked men, and they grew strong in it: and they stored weapons and food, and gathered the spoils of Jerusalem:
37 And they stored them there: and they became a great snare.
38 And this became an ambush for the sanctuary, and an evil adversary <note>original: "diabolum malum"; literally an "evil devil" or "slanderous enemy"</note> in Israel:
39 And they shed innocent blood all around the sanctuary, and they defiled the sanctuary.

### CHAPTER II.

->*Mattathias with his sons mourns the affliction of the city and the profanation of the holy things; and having shown signs of sorrow, he responds to those sent by the king, that neither he nor his kin will obey this decree: he kills an idolatrous Jew and a minister of the king, and flees with his sons into the mountains: many wishing to obey are butchered, since they would not resist their enemies on the sabbath: Mattathias, having gathered an army of the pious, restores the worship of God, having destroyed idolatry and slain the garrison of Antiochus: and as he is about to die, he exhorts his sons to always protect the law of the Lord after the example of their fathers, giving his son Simon as a counselor, and Judas as the leader in the military.*<-

1 IN those days rose up Mattathias <note>original: "Mathathias"</note> son of John, son of Simeon, a priest of the sons of Joarib from Jerusalem, and he settled on the mountain of Modin:

2 And he had five sons: John, who was surnamed Gaddis:

3 And Simon, who was surnamed Thasi:

7 And Mattathias said: Woe is me, why was I born to see the destruction of my people, and the destruction of the holy city, and to sit there, while it is given into the hands of enemies?

8 The holy things have fallen into the hand of strangers: her temple has become like a man without honor <note>original: "ignobilis"</note>.

9 The vessels of her glory have been carried away captive: her old men have been butchered in the streets, and her young men have fallen by the sword of the enemies.

10 What nation has not inherited her kingdom, and has not obtained her spoils?

11 All her ornaments have been taken away. She who was free has become a slave.

12 And behold, our sanctuary, and our beauty, and our glory is laid waste, and the Nations have defiled them.

13 To what end then should we live any longer?

14 And Mattathias and his sons rent their garments: and they covered themselves with sackcloth, and mourned greatly.

15 And those who were sent by King Antiochus came there, to compel those who had fled into the city of Modin to sacrifice, and to burn incense, and to depart from the law of God.

16 And many of the people of Israel, consenting, approached them: but Mattathias and his sons stood firm.

17 And those who were sent by Antiochus, responding, said to Mattathias: You are a prince, and most illustrious and great in this city, and adorned with sons and brothers:

18 Therefore approach first, and perform the king's command, as all the Nations have done, and the men of Judah, and those who remained in Jerusalem: and you and [your]

# THE FIRST BOOK OF MACCABEES

### CHAPTER III.

*Judas Maccabeus is proclaimed an exceptional leader; traveling through the cities of Judah, he slew all the impious. After killing the leader Apollonius and dispersing his army, he defeated the most powerful Syrian army along with their leader Seron using only a few men. King Antiochus, enraged by this, departed for Persia and appointed Lysias as viceroy, providing him with the equipment for war against the Jews. Lysias sent Gorgias with an army against the land of Judah; however, Judas and his followers prepared themselves for war, chiefly through works of penance and prayer to God.*

And Judas, who was called Maccabeus, his son, rose up in his place.
2 And all his brothers helped him, as did all those who had joined themselves to his father, and they fought the battle of Israel with gladness.
3 And he broadened the glory of his people, and put on his breastplate <note>original: "loricam"</note> like a giant, and girded himself with his weapons of war in battle, and protected the camp with his sword.
4 He became like a lion in his deeds, and like a lion's cub roaring in the hunt.
5 And he pursued the wicked, searching them out; and those who troubled his people, he burned with flames.
6 And his enemies were repulsed for fear of him, and all the workers of iniquity were confounded; and deliverance was directed by his hand.
7 And he grieved many kings, and gladdened Jacob <note>The name Jacob is used here poetically to represent the whole nation of Israel</note> by his works, and his memory is blessed forever.
8 And he traveled through the cities of Judah, and destroyed the impious out of them, and turned away wrath from Israel.
9 And he was renowned even to the utmost part of the earth, and he gathered together those who were perishing.
10 Then Apollonius gathered the Gentiles together, and a great and mighty force from Samaria, to fight against Israel.
11 And Judas knew of it, and went out to meet him; and he struck him and killed him. Many fell wounded, and the rest fled.
12 And he took their spoils; and Judas took the sword of Apollonius, and he fought with it all his days.
13 And Seron, the commander of the army of Syria, heard that Judas had gathered a gathering of the faithful and the assembly with him,
14 And he said: "I will make a name for myself, and I will be glorified in the kingdom, and I will defeat Judas and those who are with him, who have despised the king's word."
15 And he prepared himself; and there went up with him the camp of the impious, strong helpers, to take vengeance upon the children of Israel.
16 And they approached as far as Bethoron; and Judas went out to meet him with a few men.
17 But when they saw the army coming to meet them, they said to Judas: "How shall we, being so few, be able to fight against so great and so strong a multitude, especially as we are faint from fasting today?"
18 And Judas said: "It is an easy matter for many to be shut up in the hands of a few; and there is no difference in the sight of the God of heaven to deliver by many or by few.
19 For the victory of battle is not in the multitude of the army, but strength is from heaven.
20 They come against us in a rebellious multitude and in pride, to destroy us, and

<column-break/>

our wives, and our children, and to despoil us.
21 But we will fight for our lives and our laws.
22 And the Lord himself will crush them before our face; but as for you, do not fear them."
23 And as soon as he had ceased speaking, he leaped upon them suddenly; and Seron and his army were crushed in his sight.
24 And he pursued him down the descent of Bethoron even into the plain, and eight hundred men of them fell; and the rest fled into the land of the Philistines <note>original: "Philisthiim"</note>.
25 And the fear of Judas and his brothers, and a dread, fell upon all the nations round about them.
26 And his name reached the king, and all the nations spoke of the battles of Judas.
27 But when King Antiochus heard these words, he was angry in his mind; and he sent and gathered the army of his whole kingdom, a very strong camp.
28 And he opened his treasury and gave pay to the army for a year, and commanded them to be ready for all things.
29 And he saw that the money failed from his treasures, and the tributes of the region were small because of the dissension and the plague which he had brought upon the land, to take away the laws which had been from the first days.
30 And he feared that he would not have enough, as he had once and twice, for the charges and the gifts which he had given before with a liberal hand; for he had abounded more than the kings who had been before him.
31 And he was greatly dismayed in his mind, and thought to go into Persia, and to take the tributes of the regions, and to gather much silver.
32 And he left Lysias, a nobleman of the royal lineage, over the king's affairs, from the river Euphrates even to the river of Egypt;
33 And to nourish Antiochus his son, until he should return.
34 And he delivered to him half the army and the elephants, and gave him orders concerning all that he would have done, and concerning the inhabitants of Judea and Jerusalem:
35 And that he should send an army against them, to crush and root out the strength of Israel and the remnant of Jerusalem, and to take away the memory of them from the place;
36 And that he should settle the children of foreigners in all their borders, and distribute their land by lot.
37 And the king took the remaining part of the army, and departed from Antioch, the city of his kingdom, in the one hundred and forty-seventh year <note>Approximately 165 BCE in the Seleucid calendar</note>; and he crossed the river Euphrates and traveled through the upper regions.
38 Then Lysias chose Ptolemy the son of Dorymenes, and Nicanor, and Gorgias, mighty men among the king's friends.
39 And he sent with them forty thousand men and seven thousand horsemen, to come into the land of Judah and to destroy it according to the king's word.
40 And they went forth with all their power, and came and camped near Emmaus in the plain country.
41 And the merchants of the regions heard their fame, and took silver and gold in great abundance, and servants, and came into the camp to take the children of Israel as slaves; and there were added to them the forces of Syria and of the land of the foreigners.

57 Then they moved the camp and pitched it to the south of Emmaus.

### CHAPTER IV.

->Gorgias seeks out Judas; but Judas, having encouraged his men, routs the enemies, and again after Gorgias's army is dispersed, he collects the spoils. After prayers are offered again to God, he defeats the army of Lysias; and afterward, having purified the temple, he erects a new altar. Once all things required for the worship of God were prepared and sacrifices offered, they celebrated its dedication with great joy for eight days; an annual festival for this <unclear>dedication</unclear> <note>likely "dedicationis"</note> was also established for eight days.<-

### CHAPTER V.

-> *Judas struck many neighboring nations: he himself, along with his brother Simon, delivered the besieged Gileadites and Galileans: and having defeated Timothy once and again, and having captured the city of Ephron—which had refused him passage—and having slain every male thereof; at last they returned to Mount Sion with their number intact and joyful to sacrifice to the Lord: meanwhile, the leaders who had been left in Jerusalem, while fighting against the Gentiles contrary to Judas' command, were slain: Judas truly overran Hebron and Azotus, after their idols were overturned.* <-

**23** And he took those who were in Galilee and in Arbatta, with their wives and children and all that they had, and brought them into Judea with great joy.

**24** And Judas Maccabeus and his brother Jonathan crossed the Jordan and traveled a three-days' journey through the desert.

**29** And they rose up from there by night and marched toward the fortress.

**30** And it happened at dawn, when they lifted their eyes, behold, a vast people without number, carrying ladders and siege engines to capture the fortress and attack them.

**31** And Judas saw that the battle had begun, and the cry of war went up to heaven like a trumpet, and there was a great shout from the city.

**32** And he said to his army: "Fight today for your brothers."

**33** And he came behind them in three companies, and they sounded the trumpets and cried out in prayer.

**35** And Judas turned aside to Maspha <note>Mizpah</note>, and attacked and captured it; and he killed every male in it, took its spoils, and burned it with fire.

**36** From there he proceeded and captured Casbon, and Maked, and Bosor, and the other cities of Gilead.

**37** But after these events, Timothy gathered another army and camped opposite Raphon, across the stream.

**38** And Judas sent men to spy on the army; and they reported back to him, saying: "All the Gentiles who are around us have converged upon him, a very great army.

**39** And they have hired Arabs to help them, and they have camped across the stream, ready to come against you in battle." And Judas went to meet them.

**40** <note>Printed as 4; context indicates verse 40</note> And Timothy said to the captains of his army: "When Judas and his army approach the stream of water, if he crosses over to us first, we will not be able to withstand him, for he will surely prevail against us.

**41** But if he is afraid to cross and camps on the other side of the river, we will cross over to them and will prevail against him."

**42** Now as Judas approached the stream of water, he stationed the officers <note>original: "scribas populi," scribes of the people who served as military marshals</note> by the stream and commanded them, saying: "Leave no man behind, but let all come to the battle."

**43** And he crossed over to them first, and all the people after him; and all the Gentiles were crushed before them, and they threw down their weapons and fled to the temple that was in Karnaim.

**44** And he captured that city and burned the temple with fire, along with everyone who was in it; and Karnaim was subdued, and could no longer stand against the face of Judas.

45 And Judas gathered together all the Israelites who were in Gilead <note>A region east of the Jordan River</note>, from the least to the greatest, along with their wives, their children, and a very great army, to come into the land of Judah.
46 And they came as far as Ephron. This was a large city situated at the entrance of the pass, and very strongly fortified. It was impossible to turn away from it to the right or to the left; the only path was directly through the middle of it.
47 But those who were in the city shut themselves in and blocked the gates with stones. Then Judas sent a message to them with peaceful words,
48 Saying: "Let us pass through your land so that we may go to our own land. No one will harm you; we will only pass through on foot." But they would not open to them.
49 So Judas commanded a proclamation to be made in the camp, that every man should take his position where he was.
50 And the men of valor took their positions. He attacked the city all that day and all that night, and the city was delivered into his hand.
51 And they killed every male with the edge of the sword, and he utterly destroyed the city and took its spoils. Then he passed through the whole city over the bodies of the slain.
52 They then crossed the Jordan into the great plain, opposite Beth-shan <note>An ancient city at the junction of the Jordan River Valley and the Jezreel Valley</note>.
53 And Judas was gathering those who fell behind and encouraging the people all along the way, until they arrived in the land of Judah.
54 They ascended Mount Zion with joy and gladness and offered burnt offerings, because not one of them had fallen until they returned in peace.

56 Joseph the son of Zechariah and Azariah, the commanders of the forces, heard of the successful deeds and the battles that had taken place.

58 So they gave orders to those who were in their army, and they marched toward Jamnia.
59 But Gorgias <note>A Seleucid general</note> and his men came out of the city to meet them in battle.
60 And Joseph and Azariah were put to flight even to the borders of Judea. About two thousand men of the people of Israel fell that day, and there was a great retreat among the people.
61 This happened because they did not listen to Judas and his brothers, thinking they would perform some great act of bravery.
62 However, they were not of the lineage of those men through whom salvation was given to Israel.
63 Meanwhile, the man Judas and his brothers were greatly honored in the sight of all Israel and of all the Gentiles wherever their name was heard.
64 And people gathered to them, shouting joyful acclamations.

67 On that day, some priests fell in battle while they sought to perform deeds of bravery, for they went out to battle without prudent counsel.
68 And Judas turned aside to Azotus <note>Ashdod</note> in the land of the foreigners; he pulled down their altars, burned the carved images of their gods with fire, took the spoils of the cities, and returned to the land of Judah.

### CHAPTER VI.

> *Antiochus is repulsed from the wealthy city of Ely-*
> *mais and comes to Babylon; there, having heard of the*
> *misfortunes his people suffered in Judea, he falls*
> *into a deathly sickness out of grief, confessing that*
> *this happened to him because of the wickedness he*
> *had practiced against the Jews. Upon his death there,*
> *while Judas was besieging the citadel of Jerusalem,*
> *his successor and son, called Antiochus Eupator,*
> *gathered a most powerful army against Judas but*

1 And King Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes</note> was traveling through the upper provinces, and he heard that there was a city called Elymais in Persia, most noble and rich in silver and gold.
2 Its temple was very wealthy, containing golden coverings, breastplates, and shields left by Alexander, son of Philip, the Macedonian king who first reigned in Greece.
3 So he came and sought to take the city and pillage it, but he was not able to, because the plan became known to those who were in the city.
4 They rose up against him in battle, and he fled from there and departed with great sadness, returning to Babylon.
5 Then someone came to him in Persia to report that the armies that went into the land of Judah had been put to flight.
6 He heard that Lysias had gone out with a strong force at first and was driven back by the Jews, and that they had grown strong in arms, resources, and much spoil which they took from the camps they destroyed.
7 He also heard that they had pulled down the abomination <note>The "Abomination of Desolation," a pagan altar or idol</note> which he had built upon the altar in Jerusalem, and had surrounded the sanctuary with high walls as it was before, as well as Beth-zur, his city.
8 And it happened that when the king heard these words, he was terrified and deeply moved. He fell upon his bed and sank into a wasting sickness because of grief, for things had not turned out for him as he had intended.
9 He remained there for many days, for great sadness was renewed within him, and he realized he was about to die.
10 He called all his friends and said to them: "Sleep has departed from my eyes, and I have collapsed and lost heart because of anxiety.
11 And I said in my heart: 'Into what great tribulation have I come, and into what floods of sadness am I now plunged—I who was once cheerful and beloved in my power!'
12 But now I remember the evils I did in Jerusalem, from which I took all the spoils of gold and silver that were in it, and I sent orders to destroy the inhabitants of Judah without cause.
13 I know, therefore, that it is because of these things that these evils have found me; and behold, I perish in great sadness in a foreign land."
14 Then he called Philip, one of his friends, and appointed him over his whole kingdom.
15 He gave him his crown, his robe, and his ring, so that he might bring up his son Antiochus and nourish him to be king.
16 And King Antiochus died there in the one hundred and forty-ninth year <note>Approximately 163 BC by the Seleucid calendar</note>.
17 When Lysias learned that the king was dead, he set up Antiochus, the king's son, to reign in his place...

# THE SECOND BOOK OF MACCABEES

<insert>
->**C H A P T E R IV.**<-

Onias, due to the slanders of Simon, went to Seleucus; his brother Jason, seeking the high priesthood, promised the king many talents of silver, and having obtained the priesthood, he subverted all the worship of God. Menelaus then saw to it that Jason was deprived of the priesthood by promising even more talents to the king. When Menelaus failed to provide what was promised, his brother Lysimachus succeeded him. When Onias rebuked Menelaus for his sacrilege, he was murdered by Andronicus at Menelaus's urging. For this reason, by order of Antiochus, Andronicus was executed in the same place. After Lysimachus was overwhelmed by the people, Menelaus was accused before the king but was acquitted through the use of bribes, while his innocent accusers were put to death.
</insert>

### C H A P T E R IV.

1 But the aforementioned **Simon**, who had been the informer against the temple funds and his own country, began to speak ill of Onias, as if Onias himself had incited Heliodorus to these actions and had been the instigator of these evils. 
2 He dared to call the provider for the city, the defender of his nation, and the zealot for the law of God, a plotter against the kingdom. 
3 But when the enmity proceeded so far that murders were committed by some of Simon’s close associates, 
4 Onias, considering the danger of this contention and noticing that Apollonius—the governor of <term>Coele-Syria</term><note>A region covering parts of modern Lebanon and Syria</note> and Phoenicia—was acting in a frenzy to increase Simon's malice, went to the king. 
5 He did this not as an accuser of his fellow citizens, but considering the common utility of the entire multitude within himself. 
6 For he saw that without the king's providence it would be impossible for peace to be restored to affairs, and that Simon would not cease from his folly. 
7 But after the death of Seleucus <note>King Seleucus IV Philopator</note>, when Antiochus, who was called "the Noble" <note>original: *Nobilis*, referring to his title "Epiphanes," or "the Manifest God"</note>, had taken over the kingdom, **Jason**, the brother of Onias, began to seek the high priesthood by foul means. 
8 He approached the king, promising him three hundred and sixty talents of silver, and eighty talents from other revenues. 
9 Beyond this, he promised another hundred and fifty if he were granted the authority to establish a <term>gymnasium</term><note>A Greek school for athletics and education</note> and an <term>ephebia</term><note>A training school for young men or 'ephebes'</note> for himself, and to enroll the people in Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch. 
10 When the king had granted this and Jason had obtained the leadership, he immediately began to move his fellow tribesmen over to the customs of the heathens. 
11 And setting aside those rights which had been established for the Jews by kings as a matter of humanity—through John the father of Eupolemus, who had conducted a legitimate embassy to the Romans regarding friendship and alliance—he abolished the laws of the citizens and established wicked institutions. 
12 For he dared to establish a gymnasium right under the citadel itself, and to place the best of the young men in <unclear>brothels</unclear> <note>The Latin *lupanaribus* here likely refers to the Greek *petasos*, or broad-brimmed hats associated with Hermes, which were seen by traditional Jews as a mark of pagan corruption, though the translator here uses a more derogatory term</note>. 
13 This was not the beginning, but a certain increase and progress of heathen and foreign behavior, because of the nefarious and unheard-of wickedness of the impious Jason, who was no true priest. 
14 So much so, that the priests were no longer devoted to the duties of the altar, but despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices, they hastened to participate in the wrestling arena and its unlawful distributions, and in exercises of the discus. 
15 Holding the honors of their fathers as nothing, they considered the Greek glories to be the best.

<column-break/>

16 Because of these things, a dangerous contention took hold of them, and they emulated the institutions of those whom they desired to be like in all things, even though they had them as enemies and destroyers. 
17 For to act impiously against the divine laws does not pass without punishment; but the time following will declare this. 
18 When the five-year games were being celebrated at Tyre and the king was present, 
19 the wicked Jason sent sinful men from Jerusalem, carrying three hundred <term>didrachmas</term><note>A Greek silver coin</note> of silver for a sacrifice to **Hercules**. But those who carried them asked that they not be spent on sacrifices, as it was not appropriate, but that they be designated for other expenses. 
20 So these were indeed offered by the sender for the sacrifice of Hercules, but because of those present, they were given toward the construction of <term>triremes</term><note>Ancient warships with three banks of oars</note>. 
21 When Apollonius, the son of Mnestheus, was sent into Egypt on account of the officials of King Ptolemy Philometor, and Antiochus learned that he had been excluded from the affairs of the kingdom, he looked out for his own interests. He departed from there, came to Joppa, and then to Jerusalem. 
22 He was magnificently received by Jason and the city, and entered with torchlights and praises; and from there he turned his army toward Phoenicia. 
23 After a period of three years, Jason sent **Menelaus**, the brother of the aforementioned Simon, to carry money to the king and to bring back answers concerning necessary matters. 
24 But Menelaus, having been commended to the king, and having magnified the appearance of his power, turned the high priesthood toward himself by outbidding Jason by three hundred talents of silver. 
25 Having received the mandates from the king, he arrived, possessing nothing worthy of the priesthood, but bearing the spirit of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a wild beast. 
26 And so Jason, who had supplanted his own brother, was himself deceived and driven out as a fugitive into the region of the Ammonites. 
27 Menelaus obtained the leadership, but as for the money promised to the king, he did nothing about it, even though Sostratus, who was in charge of the citadel, made the demand. 
28 (For the collection of the taxes belonged to him.) For this reason, both were summoned to the king. 
29 Menelaus was removed from the priesthood, succeeded by his brother **Lysimachus**; and Sostratus was put in charge of the Cyprians. 
30 While these things were happening, it occurred that the people of Tarsus and Mallus moved to sedition because they had been given as a gift to Antiochis, the king’s concubine. 
31 Therefore, the king came in haste to quiet them, leaving behind one of his companions, **Andronicus**, as his deputy. 
32 Menelaus, thinking he had found an opportune time, stole some gold vessels from the temple and gave them to Andronicus; and others he had sold in Tyre and throughout the neighboring cities. 
33 When Onias had learned of this for certain, he rebuked him, while keeping himself in a safe place at Antioch near **Daphne** <note>A famous sanctuary and grove near the city of Antioch</note>. 
34 Therefore Menelaus, approaching Andronicus, asked him to kill Onias. When Andronicus came to Onias and, giving his right hand with an oath (though he was suspected by him), persuaded him to come out of the sanctuary, he immediately murdered him, having no fear of justice.

<summary>This chapter describes the corruption of the Jewish high priesthood as Jason and then Menelaus buy the office from King Antiochus IV, leading to the forced adoption of Greek customs in Jerusalem and the murder of the rightful high priest, Onias III.</summary>
<keywords>Onias, Jason, Menelaus, Antiochus IV Epiphanes, Hellenization, gymnasium, high priesthood, Simon, Jerusalem, sacrilege, Andronicus</keywords>

35 For this reason, not only the Jews but also many other nations were indignant and deeply aggrieved by the unjust murder of such a great man.
36 When the king returned from the regions of Cilicia, the Jews in Antioch, along with the Greeks, approached him to complain about the wrongful killing of Onias.
37 Antiochus was truly saddened at heart for Onias; moved to pity, he shed tears as he remembered the deceased man’s sobriety and great modesty.
38 His anger was kindled; he ordered **Andronicus** <note>The official who carried out the murder of Onias</note> to be stripped of his purple robe and led through the entire city. Then, in the very same place where he had committed the sacrilege against Onias, the king ordered the sacrilegious man to be put to death, the Lord rendering to him the punishment he deserved.
39 Meanwhile, many acts of sacrilege had been committed in the temple by **Lysimachus** <note>The brother of the usurping high priest Menelaus</note> with the counsel of **Menelaus**. When the news spread, the multitude gathered against Lysimachus, for much gold had already been carried away.
40 As the crowds rose up and were filled with rage, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and began to use violent force, led by a certain tyrant <note>In this context, an oppressive leader</note> who was as advanced in years as he was in madness.
41 But when the people realized Lysimachus’s intent, some grabbed stones, others sturdy clubs, and some threw handfuls of ashes at Lysimachus.
42 Many of his men were wounded, some were struck down, and all were put to flight; as for the sacrilegious man himself, they killed him near the treasury.
43 Because of these events, legal proceedings began to be moved against Menelaus.
44 When the king came to **Tyre**, three men sent by the elders presented the case before him.
45 Seeing he was being defeated, Menelaus promised **Ptolemy** <note>Ptolemy son of Dorymenes, an influential official</note> a large sum of money to persuade the king in his favor.
46 So Ptolemy went to the king in a certain courtyard, where he was resting for the sake of the cool air, and led him away from his previous judgment.
47 Thus, the king acquitted Menelaus—the source of all this malice—of the charges; but these wretched men, who would have been judged innocent even if they had argued their case before the **Scythians** <note>The Scythians were considered by Greeks and Romans to be the most barbaric and uncivilized of peoples</note>, he condemned to death.
48 Those who had prosecuted the cause for the city, the people, and the sacred vessels quickly suffered this unjust punishment.
49 Even the people of Tyre were so indignant at this that they provided for their burial with great generosity.
50 Menelaus, however, stayed in power due to the greed of those in high places; he grew in malice, constantly plotting against his own fellow citizens.

### CHAPTER V.

->*Armed armies and their skirmishes are seen in the air over Jerusalem for forty days: Jason invades Jerusalem and cruelly slaughters the citizens, then dies miserably in a foreign land: Antiochus, after slaughtering, imprisoning, and selling countless people in Jerusalem, plunders the temple: upon leaving, he leaves behind cruel governors to afflict the people: and again, having sent the commander Apollonius, he kills many: but Judas Maccabeus with his followers withdrew into a desert place.*<-

At the same time, Antiochus prepared his second expedition into Egypt.
2 It happened that throughout the whole city of Jerusalem, for forty days, horsemen were seen racing through the air, wearing robes of gold and armed with spears, like organized companies of soldiers.

<column-break/>

3 There were visions of horses running in ranks, and hand-to-hand skirmishes, the clashing of shields, a multitude of helmeted men with drawn swords, the hurling of missiles, the glitter of golden armor, and every kind of breastplate.
4 Therefore, everyone prayed that these omens might turn out for good.
5 But when a false rumor spread that Antiochus had died, **Jason** <note>The former high priest who had been ousted by Menelaus</note> took no fewer than a thousand men and suddenly attacked the city. As the citizens fled to the walls and the city was finally taken, Menelaus fled into the citadel.
6 Jason, however, did not spare his own citizens in the slaughter; he did not realize that success against one’s own kinsmen is the greatest of misfortunes, imagining instead that he was capturing the trophies of enemies rather than those of his own people.
7 Yet he did not obtain the high priesthood; the end of his plotting was only disgrace, and he fled once more into the land of the **Ammonites** <note>A region in modern-day Jordan</note>.
8 In the end, he met a wretched death. Accused before **Aretas**, the king of the Arabs, he fled from city to city, hated by everyone as a fugitive from the laws and an abominable man—an enemy of his country and citizens—he was eventually driven into Egypt.
9 He who had driven many from their own country perished in a foreign land, having traveled to the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans; there was a contemporary belief, mentioned elsewhere in Maccabees, that the Jews and Spartans shared a common ancestry</note>, hoping to find refuge there because of their kinship.
10 He who had left many others unburied was himself cast out unmourned and unburied, neither granted a foreign burial nor sharing in the tomb of his ancestors.
11 When these events were reported, the king suspected that the Jews were about to abandon their alliance with him. Enraged, he set out from Egypt and took the city by force of arms.
12 He ordered the soldiers to kill and not spare anyone they met, and to slaughter those who retreated into their houses.
13 There followed a massacre of young and old, the destruction of women and children, and the killing of virgins and infants.
14 In the space of just three days, eighty thousand were slain, forty thousand were taken prisoner, and no fewer were sold into slavery.
15 But even this was not enough: he dared to enter the temple—the holiest place in all the earth—with Menelaus, who was a traitor to the laws and his country, acting as his guide.
16 Taking the holy vessels in his wicked hands, which had been placed there by other kings and cities for the adornment and glory of the place, he handled them profanely and contaminated them.
17 Antiochus, so deranged in his mind, did not consider that God was angry for a little while because of the sins of the inhabitants of the city; this was why the holy place was overlooked.
<margin>† See Chapter 3, verses 25 and 27.</margin>
18 Otherwise, had they not been involved in many sins, he would have been struck down and driven back from his boldness as soon as he arrived, † just as **Heliodorus** <note>The Syrian official who had previously tried to plunder the temple and was stopped by a divine vision</note> was when he was sent by King Seleucus to plunder the treasury.

### C H A P T E R VI.

*Through a leader sent by the king, the Jews are driven away from the law of God, and the temple is most foully profaned. The Jews, dispersed through various regions, are forced into the sacrifices of idols. The punishment of two women is described because they had circumcised their sons, and those celebrating the Sabbath are burned together. It is shown, however, that this affliction is not from God abandoning his people, but correcting them. The noble martyrdom of the elderly Eleazar is recounted, who refused to eat pork or even to pretend to do so.*

1 But not long after, the king sent a certain elderly man of Antioch to compel the Jews to turn away from the laws of their fathers and of God;
2 and also to defile the temple that was in Jerusalem, and to rename it after **Jupiter Olympius** <note>Zeus, the chief of the Greek gods</note>; and the one in Gerizim to be named after **Jupiter the Hospitable**, according to the character of those who inhabited the place.
3 The incursion of evils was most wicked and heavy for everyone.
4 For the temple was full of the luxury and revelry of the Gentiles, and of those who dallied with prostitutes; women even forced themselves into the sacred buildings, bringing in things that were not permitted.
5 The altar was also full of illicit things which were prohibited by the laws.
6 Neither were the Sabbaths kept, nor were the traditional feast days observed, nor did anyone simply confess himself to be a Jew.
7 They were led by bitter necessity on the king’s birthday to the sacrifices; and when the festivals of **Liber** <note>Another name for Bacchus or Dionysus, the god of wine</note> were celebrated, they were forced to go around in honor of Liber, crowned with ivy.
8 A decree went out to the neighboring Greek cities, at the suggestion of Ptolemy, that they should act in the same way against the Jews, forcing them to sacrifice.
9 And those who would not adopt the customs of the Gentiles were to be killed; thus, one could see the misery.
10 For two women were accused of having

<column-break/>

circumcised their children; these women, after being led publicly through the city with their infants hanging at their breasts, were cast headlong from the walls.
11 Others, who had gathered in nearby caves to celebrate the Sabbath day in secret, were betrayed to Philip and burned with fire, because they feared to help themselves with their own hands out of respect for the religion and its observance.
12 Now I beseech those who shall read this book, that they be not terrified by these adversities, but consider that these things happened not for the destruction, but for the correction of our race.
13 For it is a sign of great favor when sinners are not allowed to go on in their own way for a long time, but are immediately met with retribution.
14 For the Lord does not patiently wait, as he does with other nations, to punish them in the fullness of their sins when the day of judgment arrives;
15 but he has decided regarding us that, should our sins reach their limit, he would then take vengeance on us.
16 For this reason, he never removes his mercy from us; though he corrects us with adversity, he does not abandon his people.
17 But let these few words be said as a warning to the readers. Now we must come to the narrative.
18 Therefore, **Eleazar**, one of the leading scribes, a man advanced in age and of noble countenance, was being forced to eat pork, with his mouth being pried open.
19 But he, embracing a most glorious death rather than a hateful life, went forward voluntarily to the torture.
20 Considering how one ought to approach such a thing, and patiently enduring it, he determined not to admit illicit things for the love of life.
21 Those who stood by, moved by an unjust pity because of their long-standing friendship with the man, took him aside and asked that meat which he was permitted to eat be brought, so that he might pretend to have eaten the meat of the sacrifice, as the king had commanded.
22 They did this so that, by this act, he might be delivered from death; and because of their old friendship with the man, they showed him this kindness.
23 But he began to consider the dignity of his age and the eminence of his years, and the gray hair of his innate nobility, and his conduct from a child which had been of the best; and according to the requirements of the holy law established by God, he answered quickly, saying he wished to be sent to the underworld <note>original: "infernum" — the place of the dead</note>.
24 "For," he said, "it is not worthy of our age to pretend, lest many young people, thinking that Eleazar, at ninety years old, has gone over to the life of foreigners,
25 should themselves be deceived because of my pretense and for the sake of a short moment of corruptible life; and through this, I would bring a stain and a curse upon my old age.
26 For even if I were delivered from the punishments of men in the present time, I shall not escape the hand of the Almighty, whether living or dead.
27 Therefore, by bravely departing this life, I shall show myself worthy of my old age;
28 and I shall leave a brave example to the young, if with a ready mind and fortitude I undergo an honorable death for the most grave and holy laws." Having said this, he was immediately dragged to the torture.

# C H A P T E R VII.

*The immense and most bravely endured tortures of seven brothers and their mother because they would not eat swine’s flesh: and how consistently they told the king that damnation was prepared for him for his cruelty: and how the mother exhorted her sons.*

It happened also that seven brothers together with their mother were apprehended and compelled by the king to eat swine’s flesh against the law, being tortured with whips and thongs.
2 But one of them, who was the first, spoke thus: "What do you ask, and what do you wish to learn from us? We are ready to die rather than transgress the laws of God given by our fathers."
3 The king, being angry, ordered frying pans and brazen pots to be heated; and when they were immediately heated,
4 He ordered the tongue of the one who had spoken first to be cut out; and, after the skin of his head was pulled off, his hands and feet were also cut off, while his other brothers and mother looked on.
5 And when he was now made useless in every way, he ordered fire to be brought and for him to be fried in the pan while still breathing; and while he was being tortured for a long time in it, the others together with their mother exhorted one another to die bravely,
<margin>† Deuteronomy 32: 36, 43</margin>
6 Saying: "The Lord God will look upon the truth and will be comforted in us, † just as Moses declared in the protestation of the song: 'And he will be comforted in his servants.'"
7 So after the first one died in this manner, they led the next one to be mocked; and, after the skin of his head was pulled off with the hair, they asked if he would eat before he was punished in every single limb of his body.
8 But he, answering in his native language <note>original: "patria voce" — likely referring to Aramaic, the common language of the Judeans at the time</note>, said: "I will not do it." Because of this, he also received the same tortures as the first in his turn.
9 And being at his last breath, he said: "You, most wicked man, destroy us in this present life; but the King of the world will raise us up, who have died for his laws, unto the resurrection of eternal life."
10 After him, the third was mocked; when his tongue was demanded, he quickly put it out and bravely stretched forth his hands,
11 And said with confidence: "I possess these from heaven, but for the sake of God's laws I now despise them, because I hope to receive them back from him."
12 So much so that the king and those who were with him wondered at the young man's spirit, for he considered the tortures as nothing.
13 And after he had died, they tormented the fourth in a similar way.
14 And when he was now near death, he spoke thus: "It is better, being put to death by men, to look for hope from God, to be raised up again by him; for you, there will be no resurrection to life."

15 And when they brought the fifth, they tormented him. But he, looking at the king, said:
16 "Having power among men, though you are corruptible, you do what you will; but do not think our race is forsaken by God.
17 Only wait patiently, and you shall see his great power, and how he will torment you and your offspring."
18 After him they led the sixth, and he, as he began to die, spoke thus: "Do not err in vain; for we suffer these things for ourselves, sinning against our God, and marvelous things have happened among us.
19 But do not think it will go unpunished for you, that you have attempted to fight against God."
20 But the mother was marvelous beyond measure and worthy of good memory, who, seeing seven sons perish within the space of a single day, bore it with good courage because of the hope she had in God.
21 She exhorted each of them in her native language bravely, filled with wisdom; and, joining a man's heart to a woman's thought,
22 She said to them: "I do not know how you appeared in my womb; for I did not give you spirit and soul and life, nor was it I who joined together the limbs of each of you.
23 But indeed the Creator of the world, who formed the birth of man and who found the origin of all things, will give you back spirit and life again with mercy, just as you now despise yourselves for the sake of his laws."
24 Now Antiochus, thinking himself despised and the voice of the speaker a reproach, while the youngest was still left, not only exhorted him with words but also affirmed with an oath that he would make him rich and happy, and that if he turned from the laws of his fathers, he would have him as a friend and provide him with all necessary things.
25 But when the young man would not yield at all, the king called the mother and urged her to advise the youth for his own safety.
26 After he had exhorted her with many words, she promised she would persuade her son.
27 So, leaning toward him and mocking the cruel tyrant, she said in her native language: "My son, have pity on me, who carried you in my womb for nine months, and gave you milk for three years, and nourished you, and brought you to this age.

29 So it shall be that you do not fear this executioner; but being made a worthy partner to your brothers, accept death, so that by that mercy I may receive you again with your brothers."
30 While she was still saying these things, the young man said: "Whom do you wait for? I do not obey the command of the king, but the command of the law which was given to us through Moses.
31 But you, who have been the inventor of all malice against the Hebrews, shall not escape the hand of God.
32 For we suffer these things for our sins.
33 And if for a little while the Lord our God has been angry with us for our rebuke and correction, he will again be reconciled to his servants.
34 But you, O wicked and most shameful of all men, do not be vainly puffed up with empty hopes, inflamed against his servants;
35 For you have not yet escaped the judgment of the Almighty God, who sees all things.

## C H A P T E R VIII.

*Judas Maccabeus, having called for God’s help, after several victories, defeated Nicanor—who had promised himself a certain victory over the Jews—after first exhorting his own men to constancy. More than 20,000 of Nicanor's army were killed, along with Timotheus and Bacchides, so that Nicanor, fleeing alone, declared that the Jews have God as their protector.*

1 But Judas Maccabeus, and those who were with him, entered secretly into the villages: and calling together their kinsmen and friends, and bringing in those who remained faithful to <term>Judaism</term> <note>original: "Judaïsmo" — this is one of the earliest historical uses of the term to define the Jewish religion as a distinct way of life</note>, they led out six thousand men.
2 And they called upon the Lord to look down upon the people who were being trampled by everyone: and to have mercy on the temple, which was being defiled by the wicked:
3 To also have mercy on the destruction of the city, which was about to be leveled to the ground, and to hear the voice of the blood crying out to Him:
4 To remember also the most wicked deaths of innocent children, and the blasphemies uttered against His name, and to be indignant over these things.
5 Now when Maccabeus had gathered a multitude, he became irresistible to the Gentiles: for the wrath of the Lord was turned into mercy.
6 And coming unexpectedly upon villages and cities, he set them on fire: and occupying strategic locations, he inflicted no small slaughter on the enemy:
7 He was carried out on such excursions mostly at night, and the fame of his valor spread everywhere.
8 But when Philip saw that the man was gradually making progress and that things were turning out successfully for him more frequently, he wrote to Ptolemy, the governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, to bring help to the king's affairs.
9 And he quickly sent Nicanor, the son of Patroclus, one of his chief friends, giving him no fewer than twenty thousand armed men from various nations, to wipe out the entire race of the Jews, joining with him also Gorgias, a man of war and highly experienced in military matters.
10 And Nicanor determined to pay the tribute for the king, which was to be given to the Romans—two thousand <term>talents</term> <note>A talent was a massive unit of weight/currency; 2,000 talents was a staggering sum required by the Treaty of Apamea</note>—from the sale of captive Jews:
11 And he immediately sent to the coastal cities, calling them to the purchase of Jewish slaves, promising that he would sell ninety slaves for a talent, not considering the destruction

<column-break/>

12 But when Judas found out, he told the Jews who were with him of Nicanor's coming.
13 Some of them, being terrified and not believing in the justice of God, took to flight:
14 But others sold whatever they had left, and together they prayed to the Lord to rescue them from the wicked Nicanor, who had sold them even before he had come near them;
15 And if not for their own sake, yet for the sake of the covenant <note>original: "testamentum"</note> made with their fathers, and for the sake of His holy and magnificent name called upon them.
16 But Maccabeus, having called together seven thousand who were with him, urged them not to be reconciled to the enemy, nor to fear the multitude of the foes who came against them unjustly, but to contend bravely,
17 Keeping before their eyes the outrage that had been unjustly inflicted by them on the holy place, and also the injury to the city held up to mockery, and even the laws of their ancestors which had been uprooted.
18 For they, he said, trust in their weapons and their boldness: but we trust in the Almighty Lord, who can destroy both those who come against us and the whole world with a single nod.
<margin>4 Kings 19:35; Tobit 1:21; Ecclesiasticus 48:24; Isaiah 37:36; 1 Maccabees 7:41.</margin>
19 He also reminded them of the help God had given to their ancestors: and how, under Sennacherib, one hundred and eighty-five thousand perished:
20 And of the battle they had against the Galatians in Babylonia, where, when it came to the fight, and the Macedonian allies hesitated, they themselves—only six thousand men—slew one hundred and twenty thousand, because of the help given to them from heaven: and for these things they received many benefits.
21 By these words they were made constant, and ready to die for the laws and their country.
22 So he appointed his brothers as leaders of each division: Simon, Joseph, and Jonathan, placing fifteen hundred men under each.
23 In addition to this, after the holy book was read to them by Ezra <note>original: "ab Esdra" — likely referring to a reader of the Law or a priest; the text implies a ritual reading before battle</note>, and the watchword "Help of God" was given, he himself as leader engaged in battle with Nicanor:
24 And with the Almighty as their helper, they slew over nine thousand men: and having wounded and disabled the greater part of Nicanor’s army, they forced them to flee.
25 And taking the money of those who had come to buy them, they pursued them in every direction,
26 But they returned because they were limited by the hour: for it was the day before the Sabbath: for which reason they did not continue the pursuit.
27 And gathering their weapons and spoils, they kept the Sabbath, blessing the Lord who delivered them on that day, distilling the beginning of mercy upon them.
28 And after the Sabbath, they divided the spoils among the disabled, the orphans, and the widows: and the rest they and their own people kept.
29 When these things were done, and a general prayer was made by all, they petitioned the merciful Lord to be reconciled to His servants to the end.
30 And of those who were with Timotheus and Bacchides fighting against them, they slew over twenty thousand: and they captured high fortifications: and they divided more prey, making equal portions for the disabled, the fatherless, and the widows, and also for the elders.

### CHAPTER IX.

*Antiochus, having been put to flight from Persepolis, while he meditated on the utter destruction of the Jews, was struck by God with terrible pains in his bowels. With worms swarming from his body and an unbearable stench, he acknowledged his crimes and promised a late amendment; he died a deserved death after writing a letter to the Jews urging them to remain subject to his son.*

1 At that same time, Antiochus was returning dishonorably from the region of Persia.
2 For he had entered the city called Persepolis, and attempted to rob the temple and oppress the city; but when the multitude rushed to arms, they were put to flight. And so it happened that Antiochus, after his flight, returned in disgrace.
3 And when he had come near Ecbatana, he learned what had happened to Nicanor and Timotheus.
4 Swelling with anger, he thought he could vent the injury done by those who had put him to flight upon the Jews; therefore he commanded his chariot to be driven without stopping, hastening the journey, while heavenly judgment urged him on. For he had spoken so proudly, saying that he would come to Jerusalem and make it a common graveyard for the Jews.
<margin>2 Chronicles 16:9</margin>
5 But the Lord, the God of Israel, who sees all things, struck him with an incurable and invisible plague. For as soon as he finished speaking those words, a dire pain of the bowels seized him, and bitter internal torments.
6 And this was indeed quite just, since he had tortured the bowels of others with many and strange torments, though he in no way ceased from his own malice.
7 Moreover, filled with pride and breathing fire in his mind against the Jews, he ordered the business to be accelerated; but it happened that as he was rushing along, he fell from the chariot, and his limbs were racked by the heavy collision of his body.
8 And he, who just before seemed to himself to command even the waves of the sea—filled with pride beyond human measure—and to weigh the heights of mountains in a scale, was now humbled to the ground and carried in a <term>litter</term> <note>original: "gestatorio" — a portable chair or bed carried by servants</note>, bearing witness to the manifest power of God within himself.
9 So that worms swarmed from the body of the impious man,

<column-break/>

and while he lived in sorrow, his flesh fell away; the army was also burdened by his smell and stench.
10 And the man who shortly before thought he could reach the stars of heaven, no one could now carry because of the intolerable stench.
11 From this point, therefore, being brought down from his great pride, he began to come to a knowledge of himself, warned by the divine plague, as his pains increased every moment.
12 And when he himself could no longer bear his own stench, he spoke thus: "It is right to be subject to God, and for a mortal not to think himself equal to God."
13 This wicked man even prayed to the Lord, though he was not to obtain mercy.
14 And the city, which he was hastening to reach so he could level it to the ground and make it a graveyard of those he had piled up, he now desired to set free.
15 And the Jews—whom he had said he would not even consider worthy of burial, but would give to the birds and wild beasts to be torn apart and would exterminate them with their little ones—he now promised to make equal to the citizens of Athens.
16 The holy Temple also, which he had previously plundered, he promised to adorn with the finest gifts, to multiply the holy vessels, and to provide the expenses pertaining to the sacrifices from his own revenues.
17 Beyond this, he even promised that he would become a Jew himself, and would travel through every place on earth proclaiming the power of God.
18 But as the pains did not cease (for the just judgment of God had come upon him), in despair he wrote a letter to the Jews in the form of a petition, containing these words:
19 "To the excellent Jewish citizens, much health, and welfare, and happiness, from King and Prince Antiochus.
20 If you and your children are well, and all things are according to your mind, we give the greatest thanks.
21 And I, being established in weakness, yet mindfully and kindly remembering you, having returned from the regions of Persia and being seized with a heavy illness, deemed it necessary to have a care for the common interest.
22 Not despairing of myself, but having great hope of escaping the illness.
23 Yet considering that my father also, at what times he led an army in the upper regions, showed who should take up the leadership after him.
24 So that if anything contrary should happen, or any difficult news be reported, those in the regions, knowing to whom the sum of affairs was left, might not be troubled.
25 In addition to this, considering that the powerful men nearby and the neighbors are lying in wait for the opportunity and waiting for the outcome, I have designated my son Antiochus as king, whom I often commended to many of you when I went into the upper kingdoms; and I have written to him the things hereunto added.
26 Therefore I pray and request you, remembering the benefits received publicly and privately, that each of you preserve your faith toward me and toward my son.
27 For I trust that he will act with moderation and humanity, following my purpose, and will be well-disposed toward you."
28 Thus the murderer and blasphemer, having been struck most miserably, and just as he had treated others, died a wretched death in the mountains in a foreign land.
