29 And Philip, his foster brother <note>original: "collactaneus" — literally one fed with the same milk; a close childhood companion</note>, took the body away; but fearing the son of Antiochus, he went away to Ptolemy Philometor in Egypt.

### CHAPTER X.

*Judas Maccabeus, having purified the temple and the city, celebrates an eight-day festival and decrees it to be observed every year. Eupator succeeds his father Antiochus in the kingdom; Ptolemy, having died by poison, is replaced by Gorgias as governor of the region, who frequently harasses the Jews in battle. The Jews defeat both him and Timothy and various enemy fortifications, with many thousands slain, after five horsemen appear from heaven who had come to the aid of the Jews.*

1 Now Maccabeus, and those who were with him, by the Lord's protection, recovered the temple and the city.
2 But he destroyed the altars which the foreigners had built in the streets, and also the shrines.
3 And having purified the temple, they made another altar; and striking fire from stones <note>original: "de ignitis lapidibus" — likely referring to striking flint to produce a new, "pure" fire for the altar</note>, they offered sacrifices after two years, and set forth incense, and lamps, and the **bread of the presence** <note>original: "panes propositionis" — also known as showbread</note>.
4 When these things were done, they fell prostrate upon the ground and besought the Lord that they might fall into such evils no more; but that, if they should ever sin, they might be corrected by Him more gently, and not be delivered to barbarians and blasphemous men.
5 Now it happened that on the same day the temple had been polluted by the foreigners, on that very same day the purification was performed, on the twenty-fifth day of the month which was **Chislev** <note>original: "Casleu" — the ninth month of the Hebrew calendar, occurring in November/December</note>.
6 And they celebrated it with joy for eight days in the manner of the **Feast of Tabernacles** <note>original: "in modum tabernaculorum" — a major Jewish autumn festival</note>, remembering that a short time before they had celebrated the solemn day of Tabernacles in the mountains and in caves like wild beasts.
7 For this reason, they carried **thyrses** <note>original: "thyrfos" — ceremonial wands or branches wreathed in ivy or vine leaves</note> and green boughs and palms before Him who had successfully brought about the cleansing of His place.
8 And they ordained by a common statute and decree for the whole nation of the Jews, that they should keep those days every year.
9 Such was the end of the life of Antiochus, who was called "the Illustrious" <note>original: "Nobilis" — referring to his title Epiphanes</note>.
10 Now we shall relate the things done under Eupator, the son of that impious Antiochus, summarizing the evils that occurred in the wars.
11 For when he took up the kingdom, he appointed a certain Lysias over the affairs of the realm, the chief commander of the military in Phoenicia and Syria.
12 For Ptolemy, who was called Macer, decided to be a keeper of justice toward the Jews, and especially because of the wickedness that had been done against them, he sought to deal peacefully with them.
13 But for this he was accused by his friends before Eupator; and when he frequently heard himself called a traitor because he had abandoned Cyprus, which Philometor had entrusted to him, and having moved to Antiochus "the Illustrious" had also departed from him, he ended his life with poison.
14 But Gorgias, when he was governor of those parts, took on mercenaries and frequently made war against the Jews.
15 But the Jews who held the strategic strongholds received those who had been driven from Jerusalem, and attempted to wage war.
16 But those who were with Maccabeus, beseeching the Lord through prayers that He would be their

<column-break/>

helper, made an assault upon the fortifications of the **Idumeans** <note>original: "Idumæorum" — the Edomites, traditional rivals of Israel located to the south</note>.
17 And pressing on with great force, they took the places, killed those who stood in their way, and together slew no fewer than twenty thousand.
18 But when some had fled into two very strong towers, having all the equipment necessary for defense,
19 Maccabeus, leaving Simon and Joseph, and also Zacchaeus, and those who were with them in sufficient number, to besiege them, turned himself to those battles which were more urgent.
20 But those who were with Simon, led by greed, were persuaded by money by some who were in the towers; and having accepted seventy thousand **didrachmas** <note>original: "didrachmis" — a silver coin worth two drachmae</note>, they let some of them escape.
21 But when it was reported to Maccabeus what had been done, he gathered the leaders of the people and accused them of having sold their brothers for money, by letting their adversaries go.
22 He therefore executed those who had become traitors and immediately occupied the two towers.
23 And managing all things successfully with arms and his own hands, he slew more than twenty thousand in the two fortifications.
24 But Timothy, who had previously been defeated by the Jews, having gathered an army of foreign multitudes and assembled the **Asian cavalry** <note>original: "equitatu Asiano" — horsemen from the Seleucid eastern provinces</note>, arrived as if he would take Judea by force of arms.
25 But Maccabeus and those who were with him, as he approached, prayed to the Lord, sprinkling earth upon their heads and girding their loins with sackcloth.
26 Prostrating themselves at the base of the altar, they prayed that He would be merciful to them, but be an enemy to their enemies and an adversary to their adversaries, as the law says.
27 And so after prayer, taking up their arms, they advanced a long way from the city, and having come near the enemy, they halted.
28 At the first light of the sun, both sides joined battle: the one side having the Lord as the guarantor of victory and success along with their own valor; the other side having their own bold spirit as their leader in war.
29 But, when the battle was at its height, there appeared to the adversaries from heaven five men on horses, adorned with golden bridles, providing leadership to the Jews.
30 Two of whom, having Maccabeus between them, shielded him with their own armor and kept him safe; but they cast darts and thunderbolts at the adversaries, so that they were both confounded with blindness and, being filled with confusion, they fell.
31 There were slain twenty thousand five hundred, and six hundred horsemen.
32 But Timothy fled to Gazara <note>original: "Gazaram" — the ancient city of Gezer</note>, a strong garrison, which Chereas commanded.
33 But Maccabeus and those who were with him, rejoicing, besieged the garrison for four days.
34 But those who were within, trusting in the strength of the place, cursed beyond measure and cast out wicked words.
35 But when the fifth day dawned, twenty young men of those who were with Maccabeus, inflamed in their minds because of the blasphemy, courageously approached the wall, and with a fierce spirit, they climbed up.
36 But others also climbing up in like manner, attempted to set fire to the towers and the gates, and to burn those cursers alive.
37 And having for two days continuously...

# CHAPTER XI.

*Judas Maccabeus defeats the massive army of the fierce Lysias, relying on the help of a horseman sent from heaven; noticing this, Lysias makes peace between the Jews and the king: letters from Lysias, Antiochus, and the Romans to the Jews, and from Antiochus to Lysias on behalf of the Jews are recorded.*

1 But a short time later, Lysias, the king's governor <note>original: "procurator" — a high-ranking administrative official acting on the king's behalf</note>, kinsman, and chief of affairs, took very poorly the things that had happened.
2 Gathering eighty thousand men and all the cavalry, he came against the Jews, thinking he would make the city a dwelling place for the Gentiles,
3 and that he would hold the Temple for financial gain, like the other shrines of the nations, and put the priesthood up for sale every year.
4 He gave no thought to the power of God, but was unbridled in his mind, trusting in his multitude of infantry, thousands of horsemen, and eighty elephants.
5 Entering Judea and approaching Bethsura—a fortified place in a narrow pass about five stadia <note>A stadium was approximately 600 feet; five stadia is roughly half a mile, though other historical sources suggest Bethsura was further from Jerusalem.</note> from Jerusalem—he began to assault that stronghold.
6 When Maccabeus and his followers learned the strongholds were being attacked, they, along with all the people, begged the Lord with weeping and tears to send a good Angel for the safety of Israel.
7 Maccabeus himself was the first to take up arms, urging the others to face the danger with him and bring help to their brothers.
8 And as they went forward together with a ready spirit, there appeared before them at Jerusalem a horseman in white clothing, brandishing a golden spear.
9 Then they all together blessed the merciful Lord and were strengthened in spirit; they were ready to break through not only men, but the fiercest beasts and walls of iron.
10 They went forward eagerly, having a helper from heaven and the Lord showing mercy upon them.
11 Charging like lions <note>original: "Leonum autem more"</note> upon the enemy, they struck down eleven thousand infantry and sixteen hundred horsemen.
12 They put all the rest to flight; most of them escaped wounded and naked <note>original: "nudi" — likely meaning they had stripped off their heavy armor to flee faster</note>. Even Lysias himself escaped by a shameful flight.
13 Because he was not a senseless man, he reflected on the defeat he had suffered. Realizing the Hebrews were invincible because they relied on the help of the almighty God, he sent to them,
14 promising he would agree to all just conditions and would compel the king to become their friend.
15 Maccabeus agreed to Lysias's requests, considering the common good in all things; and whatever Maccabeus wrote to Lysias concerning the Jews, the king granted.
16 For the letters written to the Jews by Lysias were to this effect:

<column-break/>

->LYSIAS to the people of the Jews, greetings.<-
17 John and Absalom <note>original: "Abesalom"</note>, who were sent by you, delivered your writings and asked that I fulfill the requests made through them.
18 Therefore, I have explained to the king whatever could be brought before him; and whatever the situation permitted, he has granted.
19 If you maintain your loyalty in these matters, I will try to be a cause of good for you in the future.
20 As for the details, I have commanded these men and my own envoys to discuss them with you.
21 Farewell. In the year one hundred and forty-eight, on the twenty-fourth day of the month of Dioscorus <note>The month name varies in ancient calendars; it likely refers to a Macedonian month.</note>.
22 The king's letter contained this: 
->KING Antiochus to his brother Lysias, greetings.<-
23 Since our father has been translated among the gods <note>A polite reference to the death and deification of the previous king, Antiochus IV.</note>, we wish those in our kingdom to live without disturbance and attend to their own affairs.
24 We have heard that the Jews did not consent to my father’s plan to bring them over to the Greek way of life <note>original: "ritum Græcorum" — Hellenization</note>, but prefer to keep their own customs, and therefore ask us to allow them their own laws.
25 Wishing this nation also to be at peace, we have decided that the Temple should be restored to them, so they may live according to the customs of their ancestors.
26 You will do well, therefore, to send word to them and give them your right hand <note>original: "dexteram dederis" — a formal gesture of offering peace or an alliance</note>, so that knowing our will, they may be of good heart and attend to their own interests.
27 The king's letter to the Jews was as follows: 
->KING Antiochus to the Jewish Senate and the rest of the Jews, greetings.<-
28 If you are in good health, it is as we wish; we ourselves are also well.
29 Menelaus came to us, saying you wish to return to your own people who are with us.
30 Therefore, to those who return by the thirtieth day of the month of Xanthicus <note>A month in the Macedonian calendar, roughly corresponding to March/April.</note>, we give a pledge of security,
31 so that the Jews may use their own foods and laws as they did before; and let none of them suffer trouble in any way for things done through ignorance.
32 We have also sent Menelaus to speak with you.
33 Farewell. In the year one hundred and forty-eight, on the fifteenth day of the month of Xanthicus.
34 The Romans also sent a letter, which read as follows: 
->QUINTUS Memmius and Titus Manilius, envoys of the Romans, to the people of the Jews, greetings.<-
35 Whatever Lysias, the king's kinsman, has granted you, we also grant.
36 But concerning the matters he judged should be referred to the king, send someone immediately, after discussing it carefully among yourselves, so we may decide as is best for you; for we are traveling to Antioch.
37 Therefore, hurry to write back, so that we also may know your intentions.
38 Farewell. In the year one hundred and forty-eight, on the fifteenth day of the month of Xanthicus.

### CHAPTER XII.

*Judas and his commanders, relying on divine help, fight successfully against the people of Joppa, Jamnia, the Arabs, and the cities of Casphin and Ephron; likewise against Timothy, who had a massive army, against the garrison of Carnion, and against Gorgias. After certain Jews were killed who had taken offerings from idols, Judas arranges for a sacrifice to be offered for their sins.*

**W**hen these agreements had been made, Lysias went to the king, and the Jews devoted themselves to farming.
2 But those who remained—Timothy and Apollonius the son of Gennaeus, as well as Hieronymus and Demophon, and Nicanor the governor of Cyprus <note>original: "Cypriarches" — the commander or governor of Cyprus</note>—would not let them live in peace and quiet.
3 Furthermore, the people of Joppa committed a terrible crime: they asked the Jews who lived among them to board boats they had prepared, along with their wives and children, as if there were no ill-will between them.
4 This was done according to a public decree of the city, and the Jews agreed, having no suspicions for the sake of peace. But when they had gone out into the deep water, the people of Joppa drowned no fewer than two hundred of them.
5 When Judas learned of this cruelty committed against the people of his own nation, he gave orders to the men who were with him. Having called upon God, the righteous judge,
6 he went against the murderers of his brothers. He set the harbor on fire at night, burned the boats, and put to the sword those who had escaped the fire.
7 After doing this, he departed as if he intended to return and uproot all the people of Joppa.
8 But when he heard that those in Jamnia also wanted to act in the same way toward the Jews living among them,
9 he fell upon the people of Jamnia by night and set fire to the harbor and the ships, so that the light of the fire was seen in Jerusalem, two hundred and forty stadia <note>approximately 27 miles</note> away.
10 When they had gone nine stadia from there while marching against Timothy, at least five thousand Arabs and five hundred horsemen attacked him.
11 A fierce battle took place, and by the help of God it turned out well. The remaining Arabs were defeated and begged Judas for a right hand of fellowship <note>original: "dextram sibi dari" — a formal pledge of peace or a handshake</note>, promising to provide pastures and to be helpful in other ways.
12 Judas, thinking they would indeed be useful in many things, promised peace; and after they had received the "right hand," they departed to their tents.
13 He also attacked a certain fortified city, surrounded by bridges and walls, which was inhabited by a mixed multitude of Gentiles; its name was Casphin.
14 Those who were inside, trusting in the strength of their walls and their store of food, acted quite arrogantly, provoking Judas with insults, blaspheming, and saying things that are not lawful.
<margin>† Joshua 6:20</margin>
15 But Maccabeus, having called upon the great Prince of the world—who in the time of Joshua threw down the walls of Jericho without battering rams or siege engines—fiercely attacked the walls.
16 Having captured the city by the will of the Lord, he carried out such an incredible slaughter that the neighboring

<column-break/>

lake, which was two stadia <note>about 400 yards</note> wide, appeared to flow with the blood of the slain.
17 From there they traveled seven hundred and fifty stadia and came to Charax, to the Jews who are called Tubianians.
18 They did not catch Timothy in those places; he had left without accomplishing anything, though he had left a very strong garrison in one location.
19 But Dositheus and Sosipater, who were commanders under Maccabeus, went out and killed those Timothy had left in the garrison, ten thousand men.
20 Then Maccabeus, having organized six thousand men around him and distributed them into cohorts, went out against Timothy, who had with him one hundred and twenty thousand infantry and two thousand five hundred horsemen.
21 When Timothy learned of Judas’s arrival, he sent the women, children, and the rest of the baggage ahead to a fortress called Carnion; for it was impregnable and difficult to reach because of the narrow passes of the region.
22 When Judas’s first cohort appeared, fear struck the enemies because of the presence of God, who sees all things. They fled in all directions, so that they were often knocked down by their own men and wounded by the points of their own swords.
23 Judas pursued them vigorously, punishing the unholy, and he struck down thirty thousand of their men.
24 Timothy himself fell into the hands of Dositheus and Sosipater; with many pleas he begged to be released alive, because he held the parents and brothers of many of the Jews, who might be neglected <note>original: "decipi" — to be deceived or, in this context, to suffer through his death</note> if he were killed.
25 When he gave his word that he would restore them according to the agreement, they let him go unharmed for the sake of their brothers' safety.
26 Judas then marched to Carnion, where he killed twenty-five thousand people.
27 After their flight and destruction, he moved his army to Ephron, a fortified city where a multitude of diverse nations lived. Strong young men standing before the walls fought back bravely; in this place there were many siege engines and a supply of missiles.
28 But when they had called upon the Almighty, who by His power shatters the strength of the enemy, they took the city and struck down twenty-five thousand of those who were inside.
29 From there they went to the city of the Scythians <note>Scythopolis, modern-day Beth-shean</note>, which was six hundred stadia from Jerusalem.
30 But the Jews who lived among the Scythopolitans testified that they were treated kindly by them, and that they had acted modestly toward them even in times of misfortune.
31 So they gave them thanks and exhorted them to continue to be well-disposed toward their race; then they arrived in Jerusalem as the solemn Feast of Weeks <note>original: "die solenni septimanarum" — Pentecost</note> was approaching.
32 After Pentecost, they marched against Gorgias, the governor of Idumea.
33 He went out with three thousand infantry and four hundred horsemen.
34 When they engaged in battle, it happened that a few of the Jews fell.
35 But a certain Dositheus, one of Bacenor’s horsemen and a brave man, caught hold of Gorgias; and while he wanted to take him alive, a certain Thracian horseman rushed him and cut off his shoulder; and so Gorgias escaped to Mareshah <note>original: "Marefa"</note>.

The narrative highlights the liberation of Jewish captives and the observance of the Pentecost festival in Jerusalem.</summary>

36 But as those who were with Esdris <note>original: "Esdrin"</note> fought for a long time and were exhausted, Judas called upon the Lord to become their helper and leader in the war.
37 Starting a cry in his native language <note>Hebrew or Aramaic</note> and raising a shout with hymns, he struck fear into Gorgias’s soldiers and put them to flight.
38 Then Judas, having gathered his army, came into the city of Adullam <note>original: "Odollam"</note>. When the seventh day arrived, they purified themselves according to custom and kept the Sabbath in that same place.
39 On the following day, Judas came with his men to take up the bodies of those who had been struck down, to place them with their relatives in the tombs of their ancestors.
<margin>† Deuteronomy 7:25.</margin>
40 But under the tunics of the slain, they found sacred offerings of the idols that were at Jamnia, † which the law forbids the Jews to touch. It became manifest to everyone that this was the reason they had fallen.
41 Therefore, they all blessed the righteous judgment of the Lord, who had made hidden things manifest.
42 Turning then to prayer, they begged that the sin which had been committed might be completely blotted out. But the most valiant Judas exhorted the people to keep themselves without sin, seeing with their own eyes what had happened because of the sins of those who were struck down.
43 And after making a collection, he sent twelve thousand silver drachmas <note>A Greek silver coin; the total was a very large sum for a religious offering</note> to Jerusalem to be offered as a sacrifice for the sins of the dead, thinking well and religiously concerning the resurrection.
44 (For if he had not hoped that those who had fallen would rise again, it would have seemed superfluous and useless to pray for the dead.)
45 And because he considered that those who had fallen asleep with godliness had great grace laid up for them.
46 It is therefore a holy and wholesome <note>original: "salubris"</note> thought to pray for the dead, so that they may be released from their sins.

### CHAPTER XIII.

->*Menelaus, the Jewish defector, is put to the ultimate punishment by order of Antiochus. Antiochus, leading a massive army against the Jews, is defeated and repulsed more than once, with many of his soldiers killed. While Philip rebels, the king humbly confirms a peace treaty with the Jews by oath, offers a sacrifice in the Temple, and appoints Judas as governor of Ptolemais.*<-

1 **I**n the one hundred and forty-ninth year, Judas learned that Antiochus Eupator was coming with a great multitude against Judea,
2 and with him was Lysias, the protector and overseer of the kingdom's affairs. He had with him one hundred and ten thousand footmen, five thousand horsemen, twenty-two elephants, and three hundred chariots equipped with scythes.
3 Menelaus also joined them, and with great deceit he urged Antiochus on—not for the safety of his homeland, but hoping that he would be established in power.
4 But the King of kings <note>Referencing God's sovereignty over earthly rulers</note> stirred up the mind of Antiochus against the sinner. When Lysias suggested that Menelaus was the cause of all the evils, the king ordered him to be seized and put to death in that place, according to their custom.
5 Now there was in that place a tower fifty cubits high <note>About 75 feet</note>, containing a great heap of ashes; it had a ledge hanging over the precipice.
6 From there, the king ordered the sacrilegious man to be thrown down into the ashes, while everyone pushed him toward his destruction.

<column-break/>

7 And by such a law it happened that the transgressor of the law died, and Menelaus was not even given a burial in the earth.
8 This was quite just: for because he had committed many sins against the altar of God—whose fire and ash were holy—he himself was condemned to death in the ashes.
9 But the king, with a mind unrestrained, was coming to show himself even more cruel to the Jews than his father had been.
10 When Judas learned of this, he commanded the people to call upon the Lord day and night, that as He had always done, He would now help them;
11 for they feared being deprived of the Law, their homeland, and the holy Temple. He prayed that the Lord would not allow the people, who had only recently breathed a little, to be subjected again to blasphemous nations.
12 So, when they had all done this together and begged the Lord for mercy with weeping and fasting, lying prostrate for three continuous days, Judas exhorted them to prepare themselves.
13 He himself, having consulted with the elders, decided to go out and commit the outcome of the matter to the judgment of the Lord, before the king could move his army into Judea and seize the city.
14 Thus, giving power over all things to God, the Creator of the world, and exhorting his men to fight bravely and stand even unto death for the laws, the Temple, the city, the homeland, and their fellow citizens, he stationed his army near Modin.
15 Giving his men the watchword "Victory of God," he chose the bravest young men and attacked the king’s quarters at night. He killed four thousand men in the camp and the largest of the elephants, along with those who were positioned upon it.
16 Having filled the enemy's camp with extreme fear and confusion, and after successfully completing the deed, they departed.
17 This was done as the day was breaking, with the protection of the Lord helping him.
18 But the king, having had a taste of the Jews' daring, tried to take the difficult positions by strategy.
19 He moved his camp toward Beth-zur <note>original: "Bethsuræ"</note>, which was a fortified stronghold of the Jews; but he was put to flight, he was checked, and he was weakened.
20 To those who were inside, Judas sent necessary supplies.
21 But a certain Rhodocus from the Jewish army revealed the secrets to the enemy; he was sought out, captured, and imprisoned.
22 The king again held a parley with those in Beth-zur; he gave his right hand <note>a sign of a peace treaty</note>, received theirs, and departed.
23 He engaged in battle with Judas but was defeated. When he learned that Philip, who had been left in charge of affairs at Antioch, had rebelled, he was dismayed in mind. Entreating the Jews and submitting to them, he swore to all the conditions that seemed just. Having been reconciled, he offered a sacrifice, honored the Temple, and presented gifts.
24 He embraced Maccabeus and made him governor and prince from Ptolemais <note>Modern-day Acre</note> even unto the Gerrenes.
25 But when he came to Ptolemais, the people there took the treaty of friendship poorly, being indignant lest they should break the covenant.
26 Then Lysias went up to the judgment seat and explained the reasoning, calmed the people, and returned to Antioch. In this way, the king's departure and return proceeded.

### C H A P T E R XIV.

At the suggestion of Alcimus, who had been deprived of the high priesthood, Nicanor is sent against the Jews by King Demetrius. Upon hearing of Judas’s famous deeds, Nicanor makes a friendship with him. However, later forced by the king, he breaks this bond. When he is unable to capture Judas, he threatens the destruction of the temple and attempts to seize the noble Jewish elder, Razias. When Razias sees he is about to be captured by the enemy, he chooses to take his own life with a most steadfast spirit rather than suffer indignities from his foes, even throwing his own intestines at them with his own hands.

1 But after a period of three years, Judas and those with him learned that Demetrius, the son of Seleucus, had arrived through the port of Tripoli with a powerful force and ships at a favorable location,
2 And that he had taken control of the regions against Antiochus <note>Antiochus V Eupator</note> and his general Lysias.
3 Now a certain man named Alcimus, who had previously been high priest but had willfully defiled himself in the times of "commingling" <note>original: "commistionis," referring to the period when Jewish and Greek customs were forcibly mixed</note>, realized that there was no way of safety for him, nor any access to the altar.
4 He came to King Demetrius in the one hundred and fiftieth year <note>roughly 162 BCE in the Seleucid calendar</note>, offering him a golden crown and a palm branch, and also olive branches <note>original: "thallos"</note> which seemed to belong to the temple. On that particular day, he remained silent.
5 But finding an opportunity for his madness, he was called to a council by Demetrius and asked what things and plans the Jews relied upon.
6 He replied: "Those Jews called Hasideans <note>original: "Assidæi," meaning 'the pious ones'</note>, who are led by Judas Maccabeus, nourish wars and stir up seditions, and do not allow the kingdom to be quiet.
7 For I, too, having been deprived of my ancestral glory—I mean the high priesthood—have come here:
8 First, indeed, maintaining loyalty to the king's interests, and second, looking out for my fellow citizens: for our entire race is not a little harassed by their wickedness.
9 But I beg you, O King, having learned all these details, look after the region and our race according to your humanity <note>original: "humanitatem," meaning kindness or civility</note> which is well known to all.
10 For as long as Judas survives, it is impossible for there to be peace in these affairs."
11 When such things had been said by him, the other friends of the king, who were hostile toward Judas, further inflamed Demetrius.
12 He immediately sent Nicanor, the commander of the elephants, as a general into Judea:
13 Giving orders that he should capture Judas himself, scatter those who were with him, and appoint Alcimus as the high priest of the greatest temple.
14 Then the Gentiles, who had fled from Judas in Judea, joined Nicanor in crowds, thinking that the miseries and calamities of the Jews would be the prosperity of their own affairs.
15 When the Jews heard of Nicanor’s arrival and the gathering of the nations, they sprinkled themselves with earth and prayed to Him who established His people forever, and who protects His own portion with evident signs.
16 At the commander's order, they moved immediately from there and met at the fortress of Dessau.
17 Now Simon, the brother of Judas, had engaged Nicanor in battle, but he was startled by the sudden arrival of the adversaries.

<column-break/>

18 Nevertheless, Nicanor, hearing of the valor of Judas’s companions and the greatness of soul they displayed in the struggles for their country, was afraid to make a judgment by blood.
19 For this reason, he sent Posidonius, Theodotius, and Matthias to offer and receive the right hand of peace.
20 And when a long council was held concerning these things, and the leader himself reported to the multitude, the opinion of everyone was unanimous: to agree to the friendship.
21 Therefore, they appointed a day on which they might meet privately between themselves; chairs were brought out for each and placed.
22 But Judas ordered armed men to be at favorable locations, lest perhaps some evil might suddenly arise from the enemy; and they held a suitable conference.
23 Nicanor remained in Jerusalem and did nothing unjust; he even dismissed the crowds of people that had gathered.
24 He always held Judas dear from his heart and was well-disposed toward the man.
25 He even asked him to take a wife and father children. Judas held his wedding, lived quietly, and they lived a common life.
26 But Alcimus, seeing their affection for one another and their agreements, went to Demetrius and said that Nicanor was agreeing to foreign interests and had designated Judas, the plotter against the kingdom, as his successor.
27 Therefore the king, provoked and irritated by the worst of these accusations, wrote to Nicanor, saying that he was heavily burdened by the agreement of friendship, and commanded him to send Maccabeus to Antioch in chains immediately.
28 When these things were known, Nicanor was dismayed and took it hard if he were to make void those things which had been agreed upon, since he had been in no way harmed by the man.
29 But because he could not resist the king, he watched for an opportunity to carry out the command.
30 But Maccabeus, seeing that Nicanor was acting more sternly toward him and exhibiting a fiercer manner than was customary, understood that this austerity was not for the good. Having gathered a few of his men, he hid himself from Nicanor.
31 When Nicanor realized he had been strongly outwitted by the man, he came to the great and most holy temple; and while the priests were offering the customary sacrifices, he ordered the man to be handed over to him.
32 When they stated under oath that they did not know where the man was whom he sought, he stretched out his hand toward the temple,
33 and swore, saying: "Unless you hand Judas over to me in chains, I will level this shrine of God to the ground, I will dig up the altar, and I will consecrate this temple to Father Liber <note>the Roman name for Dionysus or Bacchus, the god of wine and theater</note>."
34 After saying these things, he departed. The priests, however, stretching out their hands toward heaven, called upon Him who was always the defender of their nation, saying:
35 "You, O Lord of all things, who have need of nothing, willed that the temple of Your dwelling be among us.
36 And now, O Holy Lord of all the holy, keep this house undefiled forever, which was recently cleansed."
37 Now a certain Razias, one of the elders from Jerusalem, was reported to Nicanor. He was a man who loved the city and had a good reputation, who for his affection was called "father of the Jews."
38 For a long time, he had held to his purpose of constancy in Judaism <note>the practice of the Jewish faith</note>, and both his body and his soul—

### CHAPTER XV.
*Judas strengthens his men against Nicanor, who despises the power of God, first by an exhortation and then by revealing a nightly vision concerning the sight of Jeremiah praying for the people of Israel. Having hope in God, they strike down a massive army, cutting off the head and hand of Nicanor, which are hung in Jerusalem as a memorial of divine protection; his blasphemous tongue is given piece by piece to the birds, and that day is established as an annual solemnity.*

<margin>1 Maccabees 7:26</margin>But Nicanor, when he learned that Judas was in the regions of Samaria, planned to attack with all his force on the day of the Sabbath.
2 But the Jews who were forced to follow him said: "Do not act so fiercely and barbarically, but show honor to the day of divine sanctification, and honor Him who sees all things."
3 That unhappy man <note>original: "infelix," meaning wretched or ill-fated</note> asked if there was a Mighty One in heaven who commanded the Sabbath day to be kept.
4 And when they answered, "It is the living Lord Himself, the Mighty One in heaven, who commanded the seventh day to be observed,"
5 he replied: "And I am mighty on earth, who commands you to take up arms and fulfill the king's business." However, he did not succeed in carrying out his plan.
6 And Nicanor, indeed, raised up in supreme pride, had planned to set up a common trophy of victory over Judas.
7 But Maccabeus always trusted with all hope that help would come to him from God.
8 And he exhorted his men not to fear the coming of the nations, but to keep in mind the help given to them from heaven, and now to hope for victory from the Almighty.
9 And having spoken to them from the Law and the Prophets, and reminding them also of the battles they had fought before, he made them more ready for action.
<column-break/>
10 And so, having encouraged their spirits, he also pointed out the deceitfulness of the Gentiles and their violation of oaths.
11 He armed each of them, not with the protection of shield and spear, but with excellent words and exhortations, and by telling them a dream worthy of belief, through which he made them all joyful.
12 This was the nature of the vision: Onias, who had been high priest, a good and kind man, modest in appearance, gentle in character, and graceful in speech, who had been practiced in virtues from childhood, was stretching out his hands and praying for all the people of the Jews.
13 After this, another man appeared, remarkable for his age and glory, and of great dignity in the aura surrounding him.
14 Then Onias answered, saying: "This is a lover of the brothers and of the people of Israel; this is he who prays much for the people and the entire holy city: Jeremiah, the prophet of God."
15 And Jeremiah stretched out his right hand and gave Judas a golden sword, saying:
16 "Accept this holy sword as a gift from God, with which you shall strike down the adversaries of my people Israel."
17 Encouraged therefore by the words of Judas—which were truly great and able to rouse the spirit and strengthen the hearts of the young—they decided to fight and engage manfully, so that valor might decide the business, because the holy city and the temple were in danger.
18 For there was less concern for wives and children, and likewise for brothers and relatives; their greatest and primary fear was for the holiness of the temple.
19 But even those who were in the city felt no small anxiety for those who were about to engage in battle.
20 And now, when everyone was waiting for the judgment of the matter, and the enemies were at hand, and the army was drawn up, the beasts <note>These "beasts" (bestiæ) refer to war elephants used by the Seleucid army</note> and the cavalry were placed in a favorable position.
21 Maccabeus, seeing the approach of the multitude, the diverse preparation of weapons, and the fierceness of the beasts, stretched his hands toward heaven and called upon the Lord who works wonders, who gives victory to the worthy not according to the power of arms, but as it pleases Him.
22 And he prayed in this way: "You, Lord, who sent your angel under Hezekiah, king of Judah, and slew one hundred and eighty-five thousand from the camp of Sennacherib:

23 And now, Ruler of the heavens, send your good angel before us in fear and trembling because of the greatness of your arm,
24 so that those who come with blasphemy against your holy people may be struck down." And he ended his prayer thus.
25 But Nicanor and those with him moved forward with trumpets and songs.
26 Judas, however, and those with him, encountered them with prayers, calling upon God.
27 Fighting with their hands but praying to the Lord in their hearts, they struck down no fewer than thirty-five thousand, being greatly delighted by the presence of God.
28 And when they had finished and were returning with joy, they learned that Nicanor had fallen in his armor.
29 Then, after a shout was raised and a great commotion followed, they blessed the Almighty Lord in their native language <note>original: "patria voce," likely referring to Aramaic or Hebrew</note>.

40 For just as it is harmful always to drink wine or always to drink water, but to use each in turn is delightful — so too, if the style of the writing be always perfectly precise, it will not be pleasing to the reader. Here, therefore, it shall be concluded.

The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, <note>A reference to the royal messianic lineage through King David, fulfilling the Old Testament promise that the Messiah would come from David's line.</note> the son of Abraham.
2 Abraham fathered Isaac.
And Isaac fathered Jacob.
And Jacob fathered Judah and his brothers.
3 And Judah fathered Phares and Zara of Thamar. <note>Thamar (Tamar) was the daughter-in-law of Judah; her unusual inclusion, along with other women in this genealogy, is notable — Matthew deliberately names several women of remarkable stories in the lineage of Christ.</note>
And Phares fathered Esron.
And Esron fathered Aram.
4 And Aram fathered Aminadab.
And Aminadab fathered Naasson.
And Naasson fathered Salmon.
5 And Salmon fathered Booz of Rahab. <note>Rahab was a Canaanite woman from Jericho; her inclusion in the genealogy is striking and considered significant by biblical commentators.</note>
And Booz fathered Obed of Ruth. <note>Ruth was a Moabite woman, whose story of loyalty and faithfulness is told in the Book of Ruth.</note>
And Obed fathered Jesse.
And Jesse fathered David the king.
6 And David the king fathered Solomon, of her who had been the wife of Urias. <note>A discreet reference to Bathsheba, whose union with David followed the death of her husband Uriah the Hittite — a troubled episode recounted in 2 Samuel 11–12.</note>
7 And Solomon fathered Roboam.
And Roboam fathered Abiam.
And Abias fathered Asa.
8 And Asa fathered Josaphat.
And Josaphat fathered Joram.
And Joram fathered Ozias.
9 And Ozias fathered Joatham.
And Joatham fathered Achaz.
And Achaz fathered Ezechias.
10 And Ezechias fathered Manasses.
And Manasses fathered Amon.
And Amon fathered Josias.
11 And Josias fathered Jechonias and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. <note>The "deportation to Babylon" refers to the Babylonian Exile of 597–586 BC, when the Israelites were carried off into captivity by King Nebuchadnezzar — a defining catastrophe in Jewish history. Matthew uses this event as one of the three great milestones structuring his genealogy.</note>

<column-break/>

12 And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechonias fathered Salathiel.
And Salathiel fathered Zorobabel.
13 And Zorobabel fathered Abiud.
And Abiud fathered Eliacim.
And Eliacim fathered Azor.
14 And Azor fathered Sadoc.
And Sadoc fathered Achim.
15 And Achim fathered Eliud.
And Eliud fathered Eleazar.
And Eleazar fathered Mathan.
And Mathan fathered Jacob.
16 And Jacob fathered Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ. <note>Note the deliberate shift in language here: throughout the genealogy the formula is "fathered," but at this point Matthew says Joseph was the husband of Mary, "of whom was born Jesus" — carefully avoiding any claim of biological paternity by Joseph, in keeping with the doctrine of the Virgin Birth.</note>
17 So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David to the deportation to Babylon, fourteen generations; and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ, fourteen generations. <note>The number fourteen may carry symbolic significance: in Hebrew numerology (gematria), the letters of the name "David" (דוד) add up to fourteen, suggesting a deliberate literary structuring of the genealogy to emphasize the royal Davidic identity of Jesus.</note>

->*How the Magi came with gifts to the newborn Christ; concerning Herod's cruelty toward the infants, and Christ's exile into Egypt, and his return to the land of Israel.*<-

<margin>Luke 2:7.</margin> Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, behold, there came Magi <note>Wise men or scholars from the East, often associated with the study of stars.</note> from the east to Jerusalem,
2 Saying: Where is he that is born King of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the east, and are come to adore him.
3 When Herod the king had heard these things, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.
4 And assembling all the chief priests and the Scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ should be born.
5 But they said to him: In Bethlehem of Judea: For so it is written by the Prophet:
<margin>† Micah 5:2. John 7:42.</margin> 6 And thou Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, art by no means the least among the princes of Judah: for out of thee shall come forth the captain who shall rule my people Israel.
7 Then Herod, privately calling the Magi, learned diligently from them the time of the star which appeared to them:
8 And sending them into Bethlehem, he said: Go and search diligently after the child: and when you have found him, bring me word again, that I also may come and adore him.
9 And when they had heard the king, they went their way: and behold, the star which they had seen in the east went before them, until it came and stood over where the child was.
10 And seeing the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy.
11 And entering into the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they adored him: <margin>† Psalm 71:10.</margin> and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
12 And having received an answer in their sleep that they should not return to Herod, they went back by another way into their own country.
13 And after they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in sleep to Joseph, saying: Arise, and take the child and his mother, and fly into Egypt, and be there until I shall tell thee. For it will come to pass that Herod will seek the child to destroy him.
14 Who arose, and took the child and his mother by night, and retired into Egypt:
15 And he was there until the death of Herod: that it might be fulfilled which the Lord spoke by the Prophet, saying: <margin>† Hosea 11:1.</margin> Out of Egypt have I called my son.
16 Then Herod, perceiving that he was deluded by the Magi, was exceeding angry: and sending ministers, he killed all the male children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the borders thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently inquired of the Magi.
17 Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet, saying:
<margin>Jeremiah 31:15.</margin> 18 A voice in Ramah was heard, lamentation and great mourning; Rachel bewailing her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.

19 But when Herod was dead, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in sleep to Joseph in Egypt,
20 Saying: Arise, and take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel: for they are dead that sought the life of the child.
21 Who arose, and took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel.
22 But hearing that Archelaus reigned in Judea in the room of Herod his father, he was afraid to go thither: and being warned in sleep, he retired into the quarters of Galilee.
23 And coming he dwelt in a city called Nazareth: that it might be fulfilled which was said by the Prophets: That he shall be called a Nazarene.

### C H A P T E R V.

*In this he delivers the beatitudes: he calls the Apostles the salt of the earth and the light of the world: he did not come to destroy the law or the prophets, but to fulfill them, teaching about not being angry with a brother but being reconciled to him, about not lusting after a woman, about casting away a stumbling member, about not divorcing a wife except in the case of adultery, not swearing oaths nor resisting evil, loving enemies, and doing good to those who do not deserve it.*

### C H A P T E R VI.

->*Christ teaches how almsgiving and prayer are to be performed, and delivers to the disciples a form of praying, and of forgiving offenses to others: likewise how fasting is to be done: that treasure is to be stored not on earth but in heaven, the eye must be cleansed, one cannot serve two masters: he thus forbids worry concerning food, clothing, and tomorrow.*<-

**T**ake care that you do not perform your righteousness before men, to be seen by them; otherwise you shall have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.
2 Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be honored by men. Amen I say to you, they have received their reward.
3 But when you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing:
4 So that your almsgiving may be in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will repay you.
5 And when you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites, who love to pray standing in the synagogues and at the corners of the streets, so that they may be seen by men; amen I say to you, they have received their reward.
6 But you, when you pray, enter into your room, and having shut the door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will repay you.
7 And when praying, do not speak much, as the heathens do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking.
8 Therefore, do not be like them; for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.

<margin>† Luke 11:2.</margin>
9 Thus therefore shall you pray: † Our Father, who art in heaven: hallowed be thy name.
10 Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.
11 Give us today our <term>supersubstantial<note>original: "supersubstantialem"; a literal translation of the Greek "epiousios." While common translations use "daily," this term suggests bread that is "above all substance" or spiritual/Eucharistic nourishment.</note></term> bread.
12 And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
13 And lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil. Amen.

<margin>† Ecclesiasticus 28:3, 4, 5. Below 18:35. Mark 11:25.</margin>

15 But if you do not forgive men, neither will your Father forgive you your sins.

### CHAPTER VII.

*Demetrius son of Seleucus, after Antiochus and Lysias were killed, obtains the kingdom of his fathers. Having received accusations against Judas Maccabeus, he sends the leader Bacchides and the accuser Alcimus, who was appointed priest, to afflict the children of Israel. But when they were unable to prevail against Judas, the king sent Nicanor, who, like those before him, when he could not succeed by deceit, attacked Judas with force. He was defeated by him twice, and after prayers were sent up to God, Nicanor was killed with his entire army. His head and right hand, which he had haughtily held up against the holy place while mocking the sacrifices of the Jews, were cut off. An annual day of victory was established among the Jews to celebrate this.*

1 In the hundred and fifty-first year, Demetrius son of Seleucus departed from the city of Rome and went up with a few men to a city by the sea, and there he began his reign.
2 And it happened that as he entered the palace of the kingdom of his fathers, the army seized Antiochus and Lysias to bring them before him.
3 When the matter became known to him, he said: Do not show me their faces.
4 And the army killed them. So Demetrius sat upon the throne of his kingdom.
5 Then there came to him wicked and godless men from Israel, and Alcimus was their leader, who desired to be made high priest.
6 And they accused the people before the king, saying: Judas and his brothers have destroyed all your friends, and have driven us out of our land.
7 Now therefore, send a man whom you trust, so that he may go and see all the ruin he has brought upon us and the king's regions, and let him punish all his friends and those who help them.
8 Then the king chose from among his friends Bacchides, who ruled beyond the great river <note>The Euphrates</note> in the kingdom, and was faithful to the king; and he sent him
9 To see the destruction that Judas had caused; he also appointed the godless Alcimus to the priesthood, and commanded him to take vengeance on the children of Israel.
10 So they set out and came with a great army into the land of Judah, and they sent messengers and spoke to Judas and his brothers with peaceful words in deceit.
11 But they did not heed their words, for they saw that they had come with a great army.
12 And there gathered together to Alcimus and Bacchides a group of scribes to ask for what was just.
13 The first among them were the <term>Assideans<note>original: "Assidæi"; from the Hebrew "Hasidim," meaning "the pious ones," a group of Jews devoted to the strict observance of the Law.</note></term> who were among the children of Israel, and they sought peace from them.
14 For they said: A man who is a priest of the seed of Aaron has come; he will not deceive us.
15 And he spoke peaceful words to them and swore to them, saying: We will bring no harm upon you or your friends.
16 And they believed him. Then he seized sixty men from among them and killed them in a single day, according to the word that is written:
<margin>† Psalm 78:1, 2, 3.</margin>
17 † The flesh of your saints and their blood they have poured out around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them. <note>original: "Carnes sanctorum tuorum..."; This quote is from Psalm 79 (numbered 78 in the Vulgate).</note>
18 And fear and trembling fell upon all the people, for they said: There is no truth or

<column-break/>

judgment in them, for they have broken the decree and the oath that they swore.
19 Then Bacchides moved the camp from Jerusalem and settled in Bethzecha; and he sent and seized many of those who had fled from him, and he slaughtered some of the people and threw them into a great pit.
20 He then committed the region to Alcimus and left a force with him to assist him. And Bacchides went away to the king.
21 But Alcimus struggled greatly for his high priesthood.
22 And all those who were troubling their own people gathered to him, and they gained control of the land of Judah and caused a great plague in Israel.
23 And Judas saw all the evils that Alcimus and those with him did to the children of Israel, much more than the Gentiles had done.
24 And he went out into all the borders of Judea round about and took vengeance on the men who had deserted, and they ceased to go out into the region any longer.
25 But Alcimus saw that Judas and those with him were prevailing; and realizing that he could not withstand them, he returned to the king and accused them of many crimes.
<margin>† 2 Maccabees 15:1.</margin>
26 † Then the king sent Nicanor, one of his more noble princes, who bore a grudge and was an enemy against Israel; and he commanded him to destroy the people.
27 And Nicanor came to Jerusalem with a great army, and he sent to Judas and his brothers with peaceful words in deceit,
28 Saying: Let there be no fight between me and you; I will come with a few men to see your faces in peace.
29 And he came to Judas, and they greeted one another peacefully; but the enemies were prepared to kidnap Judas.
30 And the word was made known to Judas that he had come to him with deceit; and he was terrified of him and did not wish to see his face anymore.
31 And Nicanor realized that his plan had been uncovered, and he went out to meet Judas in battle near Capharsalama.
32 And about five thousand men from Nicanor’s army fell, and the rest fled into the city.
33 After these things, Nicanor went up to Mount Sion, and some of the priests of the people went out to greet him in peace and to show him the <term>burnt offerings<note>original: "holocaumata"; sacrifices where the entire animal is consumed by fire as an act of devotion.</note></term> which were being offered for the king.
34 But mocking them, he despised them and defiled them, and spoke haughtily.
35 And he swore in anger, saying: Unless Judas and his army are delivered into my hands, immediately when I return in peace, I will burn down this house. And he went out in great anger.
36 Then the priests entered and wept before the face of the altar and the temple, and weeping they said:
37 You, O Lord, chose this house that your name might be called upon in it, that it might be a house of prayer and supplication for your people.
38 Take vengeance on this man and his army, and let them fall by the sword; remember their blasphemies, and do not allow them to remain.
39 And Nicanor went out from Jerusalem and pitched his camp at Beth-horon, and the army of Syria met him.
40 But Judas camped in Adasa with three thousand men; and Judas prayed and said:
<margin>† 4 Kings 19:35; Tobit 1:21.</margin>
41 † When those sent by King Sennacherib <note>An ancient king of Assyria who besieged Jerusalem.</note> blasphemed you, O Lord, an angel went out...

### C H A P T E R VIII.

*Judas, having heard of the very famous reputation and courage of the Romans, which are recounted here, sends messengers to strike a treaty with them, so that the Jews might be liberated from the Greek yoke by their protection. The Romans, in turn, send back a copy of the treaty to Judas, engraved on bronze tablets, which is recorded here.*

1 And Judas heard the name of the Romans, that they are powerful in strength, and they agree to all things that are requested of them: and whoever approached them, they established friendships with them, and because they are powerful in strength.

2 And they heard of their battles, and the good deeds they performed in Galatia, <note>Referring to the Roman victory in the Galatian War of 189 BC.</note> how they conquered them and brought them under tribute:

3 And how much they did in the region of Spain, and that they brought under their power the mines of silver and gold that are there, and possessed every place by their counsel and patience:

4 And places that were very far from them, and Kings who had come against them from the ends of the earth, they crushed, and struck them with a great blow; the others, however, give them tribute every year.

5 And Philip and Perseus, the king of the Ceteans, <note>The "Ceteans" or Kittim refers here to the Macedonians; Philip V and his son Perseus were the last kings of Macedon defeated by Rome.</note> and the others who had taken up arms against them, they crushed in war and conquered them.

6 And Antiochus the Great, king of Asia, who had brought war against them, having one hundred and twenty elephants, and cavalry, and chariots, and an exceedingly great army, was crushed by them. <note>Antiochus III was defeated by Rome at the Battle of Magnesia in 190 BC.</note>

7 And how they took him alive, and ordained that he, and those who reigned after him, should pay a great tribute, and give hostages, and a prescribed amount.

8 And the region of the Indians, and the Medes, and the Lydians, <note>The Vulgate text says "Indians and Medes," but historical geography suggests this was likely Ionians and Mysians in the original context.</note> from their best regions: and having taken these from them, they gave them to King Eumenes. <note>Eumenes II of Pergamum, a Roman ally.</note>

9 And how those who were in Greece <note>original: "Helladam"</note> wished to go and take them away: and the matter became known to them,

10 And they sent against them a single leader, and they fought against them and many of them fell, and they led away their wives and

<column-break/>

children as captives, and plundered them, and possessed their land, and destroyed their walls, and reduced them to slavery even unto this day:

11 And the remaining kingdoms, and the islands that had sometimes resisted them, they destroyed and brought under their power.

12 But with their friends, and those who relied upon them, they maintained friendship, and they obtained the kingdoms that were nearby and those that were far off: because whoever heard their name was afraid of them.

13 For those whom they wished to help to reign, reigned; and whom they wished, they deposed from the kingdom: and they were greatly exalted.

14 And in all these things, no one wore a crown, nor was clothed in purple, to be magnified by it. <note>The author highlights the Republican nature of Rome, contrasting it with the Hellenistic monarchs.</note>

15 And because they had built a senate house for themselves, and daily three hundred and twenty men consulted together, always taking counsel for the multitude, that they might do the things that are worthy:

16 And they commit their government to one man <note>In reality, Rome had two consuls, but the author may have perceived the executive power as unified.</note> every year to rule over all their land, and all obey one, and there is no envy or jealousy among them.

17 And Judas chose Eupolemus, the son of John, the son of Jacob, and Jason, the son of Eleazar, and sent them to Rome to establish friendship and alliance with them.

18 And so that they might take away from them the yoke of the Greeks, because they saw that the kingdom of the Israelites was being pressed into slavery.

19 And they went to Rome, a very long journey, and entered the senate house, and said:

20 Judas Maccabeus, and his brothers, and the people of the Jews have sent us to you to establish an alliance and peace with you, and to enroll us as your allies and friends.

21 And the proposal was pleasing in their sight.

22 And this is the copy of the response they wrote back on bronze tablets, and sent to Jerusalem, so that it might be a memorial of peace and alliance among them there.

-> 23 MAY IT BE WELL WITH THE ROMANS, <note>original: "BENE SIT ROMANIS"</note> and the Nation of the Jews, on sea and on land forever: and may the sword and the enemy be far from them. <-

24 But if war looms against the Romans first, or any of their allies in all their dominion:

25 The Nation of the Jews shall bring help, as the occasion shall dictate, with a whole heart:

26 And to those who are fighting, they shall not give nor supply grain, weapons, money, or ships, as it has pleased the Romans: and they shall keep their commands, receiving nothing from them.

27 In like manner, if war happens to the Nation of the Jews first, the Romans shall help from their soul, as the occasion shall permit them:

28 And to those who help, grain, weapons, money, or ships shall not be given, as it has pleased the Romans: and they shall keep their commands without deceit.

29 According to these words the Romans made a covenant with the people of the Jews.

30 But if after these words one side or the other shall wish to add or take away anything from these, they shall do so by their own purpose: and whatever they add or take away shall be ratified.

31 And also concerning the evils that King Demetrius has done against them, we have written to him, saying: Why have you made your yoke heavy upon our friends and allies, the Jews?

32 If therefore they approach us again, we will execute judgment for them against you, and we will fight you by sea and by land.

## CHAPTER IX.

*Bacchides and Alcimus are sent against Judas again by Demetrius. Judas, resisting most bravely with a very small army, is killed and mourned. Amidst the grave affliction of the pious Israelites, his brother Jonathan is chosen to take his place. To avenge the death of his brother John, Jonathan strikes the sons of Jambri during a wedding. After a thousand men of Bacchides' army are slain, Alcimus is struck with paralysis by God for his impious works against the holy place and dies. Bacchides, unable to destroy Jonathan by either trickery or force, enters into a treaty with him and departs, never to return to Judea.*

1 Meanwhile, when Demetrius heard that Nicanor and his army had fallen in battle, he set out to send Bacchides and Alcimus again into Judea, and the right wing <note>original: "dextrum cornu"; in ancient warfare, the "right wing" often designated the most elite or senior divisions of the army.</note> with them.
2 They took the road leading to Gilgal and camped in Mesaloth, which is in Arbela; they seized it and killed many people.
3 In the first month of the one hundred and fifty-second year <note>This date follows the Seleucid era, corresponding to roughly 160 BCE.</note> they brought their army to Jerusalem.
4 They arose and went to Beeroth with twenty thousand infantry and two thousand cavalry.
5 Now Judas had camped in Elasa, and three thousand chosen men were with him.
6 When they saw the great size of the enemy army, they were very afraid; many slipped away from the camp, until only eight hundred men remained.
7 When Judas saw that his army had melted away and the battle was pressing hard upon him, his heart was troubled, for he had no time to gather them, and he was discouraged.
8 He said to those who remained: "Let us arise and go against our adversaries, to see if we can fight them."
9 But they tried to dissuade him, saying: "We cannot; let us rather save our lives now and return to our brothers, and then we will fight them; for we are but few."
10 But Judas said: "Far be it from me to do such a thing as to flee from them. If our time has come, let us die bravely for our brothers, and let us not leave a stain upon our glory."
11 The army moved from the camp and stood against them. The cavalry was divided into two parts, and the slingers and archers went before the army, with the vanguard consisting of all the strongest men.
12 Bacchides was on the right wing, and the phalanx approached from two sides, and they sounded the trumpets.
13 Those on Judas's side also shouted, and the earth shook at the sound of the armies; the battle was joined from morning until evening.
14 Judas saw that the strongest part of Bacchides' army was on the right, and all the stout-hearted men joined him.
15 The right wing was crushed by them, and he pursued them as far as the mountain of Azotus.
16 But those on the left wing saw that the right wing was crushed, and they followed behind Judas and his men, attacking from the rear.
17 The battle grew fierce, and many were wounded and fell on both sides.
18 And Judas fell, and the rest fled.
19 Then Jonathan and Simon took Judas,

<column-break/>

their brother, and buried him in the tomb of his fathers in the city of Modein.
20 All the people of Israel wept for him with great mourning, and they grieved for many days,
21 saying: "How the mighty has fallen, he who saved the people of Israel!"
22 The rest of the acts of Judas’s wars, his brave deeds, and his greatness are not written down here, for they were very many.
23 And it happened that after the death of Judas, the wicked emerged in all the borders of Israel, and all who worked iniquity rose up.
24 In those days there was a very great famine, and the whole region surrendered to Bacchides along with them.
25 Bacchides chose impious men and appointed them as lords of the region.
26 They sought out and searched for the friends of Judas, and brought them to Bacchides, who took vengeance on them and mocked them.
27 There was great tribulation in Israel, such as had not been seen since the day a prophet was no longer seen in Israel. <note>This refers to the "intertestamental" period when the Jews believed the prophetic voice had gone silent after Malachi.</note>
28 Then all the friends of Judas gathered and said to Jonathan:
29 "Since your brother Judas died, there is no man like him to go out against our enemies—Bacchides and those who are enemies of our nation.
30 Therefore, we have chosen you today to be our prince and leader in his place, to fight our battles."
31 At that time Jonathan took up the leadership and rose to take the place of his brother Judas.
32 When Bacchides learned of this, he sought to kill him.
33 But Jonathan and his brother Simon and all who were with him realized this, and they fled into the desert of Tekoa and camped by the waters of the lake of Asphar.
34 Bacchides found out, and on the Sabbath day he and his entire army came across the Jordan.
35 Jonathan sent his brother <note>This refers to John, the eldest of the Maccabean brothers.</note> as leader of the people to ask his friends, the Nabataeans, to let them store their baggage, which was very large.
36 But the sons of Jambri came out from Medeba and captured John and everything he had, and went away with it.
37 After this, it was reported to Jonathan and his brother Simon that the sons of Jambri were celebrating a great wedding and were bringing the bride from Medeba, the daughter of one of the great princes of Canaan, with great pomp.
38 They remembered the blood of their brother John, and they went up and hid themselves under the cover of the mountain.
39 They looked up and saw a great commotion and much baggage; the bridegroom came out with his friends and brothers to meet them with drums and music and many weapons.
40 They rose up against them from their ambush and killed them; many fell wounded, and the rest fled into the mountains, and they took all their spoils.
41 So the wedding was turned into mourning, and the sound of their music into lamentation.
42 They had taken vengeance for the blood of their brother, and they returned to the banks of the Jordan.
43 Bacchides heard of it, and he came on the Sabbath day to the banks of the Jordan with a great force.

48 Then Jonathan and those who were with him leaped into the Jordan and swam across the Jordan to them. <note>original: "transnataverunt"; they escaped the trap by swimming the river under fire.</note>

49 And there fell on Bacchides' side that day a thousand men. And they returned to Jerusalem.

50 And they built fortified cities in Judea—the fortifications in Jericho, and in Emmaus, and in Beth-horon, and in Bethel, and Thamnata, and Pharathon, and Tephon—with high walls, gates, and bars.

51 And he placed guards in them to act with hostility toward Israel.

53 And he took the sons of the leaders of the region as hostages and put them under guard in the citadel in Jerusalem.

54 In the one hundred and fifty-third year, in the second month, Alcimus <note>The Hellenizing High Priest who opposed the Maccabees.</note> ordered the walls of the inner holy courtyard to be destroyed, even to destroy the works of the prophets; and he began the destruction.

55 At that time Alcimus was struck; his works were hindered, his mouth was stopped, and he was dissolved by paralysis, so that he could no longer speak a word or give orders concerning his house.

56 And Alcimus died at that time in great agony.

57 When Bacchides saw that Alcimus was dead, he returned to the king, and the land was quiet for two years.

58 Then all the lawless men plotted, saying: "Behold, Jonathan and those with him live in quiet and confidence. Now therefore, let us bring Bacchides here, and he will capture them all in one night."

59 So they went and gave him this counsel.

60 And he arose to come with a great army, and he secretly sent letters to his allies who were in Judea to seize Jonathan and those with him; but they could not, because their plan became known to them.

61 And Jonathan seized fifty men from the leaders of the region who were the heads of the conspiracy and killed them.

62 Then Jonathan, Simon, and those with them withdrew to Bethbasi, <note>original: "Bethbessen"; likely Khirbet Beit Bassa, a wilderness stronghold.</note> which is in the desert, and he rebuilt its ruins and they strengthened it.

63 When Bacchides learned of this, he gathered his entire multitude and sent word to those who were in Judea.

64 And he came and set up camp above Bethbasi and attacked it for many days, building siege engines.

65 But Jonathan left his brother Simon in the city and went out into the region, coming with a select number of men.

66 And he struck Odaren and his brothers, and the sons of Phaferon in their tents; and he began to cut them down and grow in strength.

67 Simon and those with him then came out of the city and set fire to the siege engines.

68 And they fought against Bacchides, and

<column-break/>

he was crushed by them, and they afflicted him greatly, because his counsel and his campaign were in vain.

69 And he was angry with the lawless men who had given him the counsel to come into their region, and he killed many of them; then he planned to depart with the rest to his own land.

70 When Jonathan learned of this, he sent envoys to him to make peace with him and to have the captives restored to him.

71 And he willingly accepted, and did according to his words, and swore that he would do him no harm all the days of his life.

72 And he restored to him the captives whom he had previously taken from the land of Judah; then he turned and departed to his own land, and did not venture to come into their borders any longer.

73 Thus the sword ceased from Israel; and Jonathan lived in Michmash, <note>original: "Machmas"; a town north of Jerusalem that became Jonathan’s administrative center before he was officially recognized in Jerusalem.</note> and there Jonathan began to judge the people, and he destroyed the ungodly out of Israel.

### ->CHAPTER X.<-

*While Alexander the Noble, son of Antiochus, occupies Ptolemais, Demetrius attempts to strike a treaty with Jonathan, promising many things again and again. But Jonathan prefers the friendship offered by Alexander. Alexander, having defeated and killed Demetrius, marries Cleopatra, the daughter of King Ptolemy of Egypt, greatly honoring Jonathan. Furthermore, Jonathan defeats Apollonius, the general of the younger Demetrius, burning Azotus and the temple of Dagon; and he is honored again by Alexander, being given Ekron and a golden buckle.*

1 In the one hundred and sixtieth year, Alexander, the son of Antiochus, who was surnamed the Noble, <note>original: "Nobilis"; historically known as Alexander Balas, he claimed to be the son of Antiochus IV Epiphanes.</note> went up and occupied Ptolemais; and they received him, and he reigned there.

2 When King Demetrius heard of it, he gathered a very large army and went out to meet him in battle.

3 And Demetrius sent a letter to Jonathan with peaceful words, so as to honor him.

4 For he said: "Let us take the lead in making peace with him before he makes it with Alexander against us."

5 "For he will remember all the evils we have done against him, and against his brother, and against his nation."

6 And he gave him authority to gather an army, to manufacture weapons, and to be his ally; and he ordered that the hostages who were in the citadel be handed over to him.

7 So Jonathan came to Jerusalem and read the letters in the hearing of all the people and those who were in the citadel.

8 And they were struck with great fear when they heard that the king had given him authority to gather an army.

9 The hostages were handed over to Jonathan, and he restored them to their parents.

10 And Jonathan lived in Jerusalem and began to rebuild and renovate the city.

11 And he told those doing the work to build the walls and Mount Zion round about with squared stones for fortification; and they did so.

12 Then the foreigners who were in the fortifications that Bacchides had built fled;

13 Each one left his place and went into his own land.

14 Only in Beth-zur did some remain,

21 And Jonathan put on the holy robe in the seventh month, in the one hundred and sixtieth year, on the solemn day of the Feast of Tabernacles: <note>original: "scenopegiæ"; the Jewish harvest festival where people lived in temporary booths.</note> and he gathered an army and manufactured many weapons.

29 And now I set you and all Jews free from tributes, and I waive the price of salt, and remit the crown taxes, and the third of the grain: <note>The "crown tax" was originally a voluntary gift of a gold crown to a king, which had become a mandatory and burdensome tax.</note>
30 And the half of the fruit of the trees, which is my portion, I leave to you from this day forward, so that it shall not be taken from the land of Judah, nor from the three cities which have been added to it from Samaria and Galilee, from this day and for all time:

33 And every soul of the Jews who was taken captive from the land of Judah in all my kingdom, I set free without cost, so that all may be released from tributes, even those of their cattle.
34 And all the festival days, and Sabbaths, and new moons, and appointed days, and the three days before a festival, and the three days after a festival, let them all be days of immunity and release for all the Jews who are in my kingdom.
35 And no one shall have the power to do anything or stir up trouble against any of them in any matter.
36 And let there be enrolled among the king's army about thirty thousand men of the Jews, and let them be given provisions as is fitting for all the king's forces, and from among them some shall be stationed in the strongholds of the Great King:

38 And the three cities that were added to Judea from the region of Samaria shall be considered part of Judea: so that they may be under one ruler and obey no other authority except that of the high priest.
39 Ptolemais and its surrounding lands I have given as a gift to the sanctuary in Jerusalem, for the necessary expenses of the holy things.

41 And all the surplus which those in charge of affairs did not pay in previous years, from now on they shall give toward the works of the Temple.
42 And besides this, the five thousand shekels of silver which they used to take from the account of the sanctuary every year: even these belong to the priests who perform the ministry.
43 And whoever flees to the temple in Jerusalem, or within any of its borders, because they owe money to the king or for any other matter, shall be released, and all that they possess in my kingdom shall be theirs freely.
44 And for the building or repairing of the works of the sanctuary, the expenses shall be given from the king's accounts:
45 And for building the walls of Jerusalem and fortifying it all around, the expenses shall be given from the king's accounts, and also for building the walls in Judea.
46 But when Jonathan and the people heard these words, <margin>† See 1 Maccabees 7:11.</margin> † they did not believe them nor accept them: because they remembered the great evil he had done in Israel, and how he had troubled them greatly.

52 "Since I have returned to my kingdom and have sat upon the throne of my fathers, and have obtained the leadership and crushed Demetrius and taken possession of our region,

54 Now therefore let us establish a friendship with one another: give me your daughter as a wife, and I will be your son-in-law, and I will give you gifts, and to her, gifts worthy of you."
55 And King Ptolemy answered, saying: "Happy is the day in which you returned to the land of your fathers and sat upon the throne of their kingdom.
56 And now I will do for you what you have written: but meet me at Ptolemais, so that we may see one another, and I will promise her to you as you have said."
57 And Ptolemy departed from Egypt, he and his daughter Cleopatra, and he came to Ptolemais in the one hundred and sixty-second year. <note>This is Cleopatra Thea, who would become a major political figure in the Hellenistic world.</note>

79 And Apollonius had left a thousand horsemen secretly behind them in the camp.

89 And he sent him a golden buckle <note>original: "fibulam auream"; a prestigious clasp for a cloak, reserved for the King's Inner Circle.</note>, as the custom is to be given to the kinsmen of kings. And he gave him Ekron and all its borders for a possession.
