### CHAPTER IX.

> *The wonderful conversion of Saul the persecutor, the Lord appearing to him, and Ananias being sent to him; by whom he was baptized and began in Damascus to most fiercely defend that Jesus is the Christ. The disciples truly let him down through a wall because of the traps of the Jews. Barnabas leads him to the Apostles in Jerusalem; from where, again because of injuries, he is sent to Tarsus. Peter heals Aeneas the paralytic at Lydda, and raises Tabitha at Joppa.*

<margin>Galatians 1:13.</margin>
But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the High Priest,
2 And asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any men or women of this Way <note>An early name for the Christian movement</note>, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.

### CHAPTER XII.

->*Herod, having killed James, throws Peter into prison, desiring to deliver him to the people to be killed after the Passover: but the Church praying for him without ceasing, he is led out by the help of an Angel, bringing great joy to the brothers: and when an inquiry was made concerning the prison guards, Herod departs for Caesarea: and since he did not reject the divine honors offered by the people, he was struck by an Angel, and being consumed by worms, he died.*<-

4 When he had apprehended him, he cast him into prison, delivering him to four squads of four soldiers to be guarded, intending to bring him forth to the people after the Passover.

### CHAPTER XIII.

*Saul and Barnabas are commanded by the Holy Spirit to be set apart for the work of preaching among the Gentiles; and when the magician Bar-Jesus (also called Elymas), who resisted their preaching, was blinded at Paul's word, Sergius Paulus believes. In Antioch of Pisidia, Paul discourses more widely about Christ in the synagogue; but as the Jews blaspheme and stir up persecution against them, they turn to the Gentiles according to the prophecy of Isaiah.*

1 Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, among whom were Barnabas, and Simon who was called Niger <note>original: "Niger" means "Black," likely indicating his origin or complexion</note>, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manahen, who was the foster-brother of Herod the Tetrarch <note>A "Tetrarch" was a ruler of one of four divisions of a region; this refers to Herod Antipas</note>, and Saul.
2 As they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said to them: "Set apart for me Saul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them."
3 Then, after fasting and praying and laying their hands upon them, they sent them away.
4 And so, being sent by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus.
5 And when they had come to Salamis, they preached the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they also had John <note>John Mark</note> in their service.
6 And when they had traveled through the whole island as far as Paphos, they found a certain magician, a false prophet, a Jew whose name was Bar-Jesus,
7 Who was with the Proconsul <term>Proconsul: a Roman governor of a senatorial province</term> Sergius Paulus, a prudent man. He, having called for Barnabas and Saul, desired to hear the word of God.

### CHAPTER XIV.

*Many Jews and Gentiles at Iconium take up faith in Christ; a riot is stirred up by the Jews against the Apostles, who flee to Lystra, where Paul heals a man lame from his mother's womb; he and Barnabas can barely restrain the people and the priests, who want to sacrifice to them as gods because of this; but after a crowd is stirred up by Jews arriving from elsewhere, Paul is stoned and left for dead; when he had risen, he and Barnabas return to Antioch, encouraging the disciples in various places*

<column-break/>

*and ordaining elders.*

Now it happened at Iconium that they entered the synagogue of the Jews together, and spoke in such a way that a great multitude of both Jews and Greeks believed.

2 But the Jews who were unbelieving stirred up and embittered the minds of the Gentiles against the brothers.

3 Therefore they stayed there for a long time, acting boldly in the Lord, who gave testimony to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands.

4 But the multitude of the city was divided: some were with the Jews, and some were with the Apostles.

5 And when an attempt was made by both the Gentiles and the Jews, along with their leaders, to treat them shamefully and stone them,

6 Becoming aware of it, they fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra, and Derbe, and the surrounding region, and there they preached the gospel.

7 And at Lystra, a certain man was sitting who was weak in his feet, lame from his mother's womb, who had never walked.

8 This man heard Paul speaking. Paul, looking at him and seeing that he had faith to be healed,

9 Said with a loud voice: Stand upright on your feet. And he leaped up and walked.

10 And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the Lycaonian language: The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men.

11 And they called Barnabas "Jupiter," and Paul "Mercury," because he was the chief speaker. <note>In Greek mythology, Jupiter is Zeus and Mercury is Hermes. Hermes was the messenger of the gods, explaining why they identified him with Paul, the primary orator.</note>

## CHAPTER XV.

### C H A P T E R XVI.

*Paul at Lystra circumcises Timothy, whom he had taken with him, and delivers the doctrines of the Apostles to be observed throughout various cities: they are forbidden by the Holy Spirit to preach in Asia and Bithynia: Paul, however, being called into Macedonia by a vision, they set out: and first preaching at Philippi, they are received with hospitality at the house of Lydia: but after Paul casts out a spirit of divination, they are beaten with rods and cast into prison: where, after an earthquake occurs and their chains are loosed, the prison guard is converted: and on the following day the magistrates beg them to leave the city.*

**P**aul arrived at Derbe and Lystra. And behold, a certain disciple was there named Timothy, the son of a faithful Jewish woman, but with a Gentile father. <note>Timothy’s mixed parentage made him a unique bridge between Jewish and Greek cultures, though it also necessitated the social compromise mentioned in verse 3.</note>
2 The brothers who were in Lystra and Iconium gave a good testimony of him.
3 Paul wanted this man to go out with him: and taking him, he circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places. For they all knew that his father was a Gentile. <note>Paul performed this not because he believed circumcision was necessary for salvation—as established in the previous chapter—but as a practical measure to avoid offending the Jewish communities they intended to evangelize.</note>
4 And as they passed through the cities, they delivered to them the doctrines to be kept, which had been decreed by the Apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem.
5 And so the Churches were strengthened in faith, and increased in number daily.
6 Passing through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word of God in Asia.
7 And when they had come into Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia: and the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them.
8 But when they had passed through Mysia, they went down to Troas.
9 And a vision was shown to Paul in the night: A certain man of Macedonia was standing, and beseeching him, and saying: Cross over into Macedonia and help us.
10 And as soon as he saw the vision, we immediately sought to set out for Macedonia, being certain that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. <note>original: "evangelizare" - to bring good news.</note>
11 Sailing from Troas, we came with a straight course to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis;
12 And from there to Philippi, which is the leading city of that part of Macedonia, a colony. <note>A "colony" in the Roman sense was a city settled by retired soldiers, enjoying special tax status and Roman legal rights.</note> And we stayed in this city for some days, conferring together.
13 And on the Sabbath day, we went outside the gate by a river, where there seemed to be a place of prayer; and sitting down, we spoke to the women who had gathered.
14 And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple from the city of Thyatira, a worshiper of God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened to attend to those things being said by Paul.
15 And when she was baptized, along with her household, she pleaded, saying: If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay. And she compelled us.
16 And it happened, as we were going to pray-

<column-break/>

-er, a certain girl having a spirit of divination <note>original: "spiritum pythonem." In Greek mythology, the Python was the serpent guarding the oracle at Delphi; the term was used for those who predicted the future.</note> met us, who brought great profit to her masters by fortune-telling.
17 This girl, following Paul and us, cried out, saying: These men are servants of the most high God, who announce to you the way of salvation.
18 And she did this for many days. Paul, being grieved and turning around, said to the spirit: I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to go out of her. And it went out that same hour.
19 But her masters, seeing that the hope of their profit had gone, seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the forum to the rulers:
20 And presenting them to the magistrates, they said: These men disturb our city, as they are Jews:
21 And they announce a custom which is not lawful for us to receive or to practice, since we are Romans. <note>The tension here is between Jewish religious practices and the legal privileges of being a Roman citizen.</note>
22 And the crowd ran together against them: and the magistrates, having torn off their tunics, ordered them to be beaten with rods.
<margin>† 2 Corinthians 11:25. Philippians 1:13. 1 Thessalonians 2:2.</margin>
23 And when they had inflicted many lashes upon them, they cast them into prison, commanding the guard to keep them diligently.
24 Having received such a command, he put them into the inner prison, and fastened their feet in the stocks. <note>original: "ligno" - literally "the wood," referring to the wooden frame used to restrain prisoners' legs.</note>
25 But at midnight, Paul and Silas were praying and praising God: and those who were in custody heard them.
26 Suddenly, however, a great earthquake occurred, so that the foundations of the prison were moved. And immediately all the doors were opened: and everyone's chains were loosed.
27 The prison guard, having been awakened and seeing the doors of the prison open, drew his sword and wanted to kill himself, thinking the prisoners had fled.
28 But Paul cried out with a loud voice, saying: Do yourself no harm: for we are all here.
29 And having asked for a light, he rushed in: and trembling, he fell down at the feet of Paul and Silas:
30 And leading them outside, he said: Masters, what must I do so that I may be saved?
31 And they said: Believe in the Lord Jesus: and you shall be saved, you and your household.
32 And they spoke the word of the Lord to him, with all who were in his house.
33 And taking them in that hour of the night, he washed their wounds: and he was baptized, he and all his household immediately.
34 And when he had led them into his house, he set a table for them, and rejoiced with all his household, believing in God.
34 <note>The original text repeats the number 34 for verse 35.</note> And when it was day, the magistrates sent the lictors, saying: Dismiss those men. <note>Lictors were officers who carried out the orders of Roman magistrates, including punishments.</note>
36 The prison guard reported these words to Paul: Because the magistrates have sent word that you are to be released: now therefore, come out and go in peace.
37 But Paul said to them: They have beaten us publicly, without condemnation, though we are Roman men, and cast us into prison, and now they cast us out secretly? Not so: but let them come,
38 And they themselves lead us out. The lictors reported these words to the magistrates. And they were afraid, having heard that they were Romans:
39 And coming, they pleaded with them, and leading them out, they asked that they depart from the city.
40 Departing from the prison, they entered the house of Lydia: and having seen the brothers, they comforted them, and set out.

### CHAPTER XVII.

->*Much fruit being produced in Thessalonica through Paul’s preaching, a riot is stirred up against him by the Jews, and likewise in Berea: Paul disputes with the Jews and philosophers in Athens: and he converts Dionysius the Areopagite to Christ along with certain others.*<-

1 When they had traveled through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews.
2 According to his custom, Paul went in to them, and for three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,
3 Explaining and pointing out that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead: and that "this Jesus, whom I announce to you, is the Christ."
4 And some of them believed, and were joined to Paul and Silas; as were a great multitude of the worshiping Gentiles, and not a few noble women.
5 But the Jews, being moved with envy and taking some wicked men from the common crowd, formed a mob and set the city in an uproar: and standing by the house of Jason, they sought to bring them out to the people.
6 And when they did not find them, they dragged Jason and certain brothers to the rulers of the city, crying out: "These men, who turn the world upside down, have come here also,
7 Whom Jason has received; and these all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus."
8 And they troubled the people and the rulers of the city who heard these things.
9 And when they had taken security from Jason and the others, they let them go.
10 But the brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea. When they arrived, they went into the synagogue of the Jews.
11 Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, for they received the word with all eagerness, daily searching the Scriptures to see if these things were so.
12 And many of them indeed believed, as did a number of honorable Gentile women and men.
13 But when the Jews of Thessalonica learned that the word of God was preached by Paul in Berea also, they came there too, stirring up and troubling the multitude.
14 And then the brothers immediately sent Paul away to go as far as the sea: but Silas and Timothy remained there.
15 And those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens; and having received a command from him for Silas and Timothy to come to him as quickly as possible, they departed.
16 Now while Paul waited for them in Athens, his spirit was stirred within him, seeing the city given over to idolatry.
17 Therefore he disputed in the synagogue with the Jews and the worshipers, and in the marketplace every day with those who were present.
18 And certain Epicurean and Stoic philosophers <note>The Epicureans sought pleasure and peace of mind, while the Stoics emphasized duty and endurance; both were influential schools of thought in ancient Greece.</note> debated with him, and some said: "What does this babbler <note>original: "seminiverbius," literally a "seed-word scatterer," implying one who picks up scraps of learning and repeats them without understanding.</note> want to say?" But others said: "He seems to be an announcer of new gods," because he preached Jesus and the resurrection to them.

<column-break/>

19 And they took him and led him to the Areopagus, <note>The Areopagus, or "Mars Hill," was the meeting place of the high council of Athens, where matters of religion and philosophy were judged.</note> saying: "May we know what this new doctrine is that you are speaking?
20 For you bring certain new things to our ears: we want to know therefore what these things mean."
21 (For all the Athenians and the strangers visiting there spent their time in nothing else but either telling or hearing something new.)
22 Paul, standing in the middle of the Areopagus, said: "Men of Athens, I perceive that in all things you are, as it were, quite religious. <note>original: "superstitiosiores," which can mean "very religious" or "somewhat superstitious." Paul uses a tactful word to engage his audience.</note>
23 For as I passed by and saw your idols, I found also an altar on which was written: TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Therefore, what you worship without knowing, this I announce to you.
<margin>† Genesis 1:1. † Above [Acts] 7:48.</margin>
24 † God, who made the world and all things in it, since He is Lord of heaven and earth, † does not dwell in temples made with hands,
25 Nor is He served by human hands as though He needed anything, since He Himself gives to all life, and breath, and all things:
26 And He has made from one all the race of men to dwell upon the whole face of the earth, determining the appointed times and the boundaries of their habitation,
27 That they should seek God, if perhaps they might feel after Him or find Him, although He is not far from each one of us.
28 For in Him we live, and move, and exist: as also certain of your own poets have said: 'For we are also His offspring.' <note>Paul is quoting the Greek poet Aratus or Cleanthes here to build a bridge with his audience.</note>
29 Being then the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Divine is like gold, or silver, or stone, carved by the art and thought of man.
30 And God, overlooking the times of this ignorance, now announces to men that all everywhere should repent,
31 Because He has appointed a day in which He will judge the world in equity, by the Man whom He has appointed, giving faith to all by raising Him from the dead."
32 And when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some indeed mocked, but others said: "We will hear you again concerning this."
33 So Paul went out from among them.
34 But certain men joined him and believed: among whom was also Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

->*Paul at Corinth practices his craft with Aquila, and although the Jews blasphemed at his preaching, he nevertheless hears in a vision that many people there are to be converted to the faith: but after a year and a half he is accused by the Jews before Gallio the proconsul, and after many days he comes to Ephesus, and strengthens the brothers in various regions: Apollos vehemently convinces the Jews, showing from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ, although he only knew the baptism of John.*<-

1 After these things, departing from Athens, he came to Corinth:

### CHAPTER XIX.

*At Ephesus, Paul commands certain disciples of John—who had only been baptized with John’s baptism—to be baptized in the name of Jesus, and he obtains the Holy Spirit for them through the laying on of hands; preaching there, he performs many signs: regarding the Jews who, without believing, tried to drive out demons in the name of Jesus as preached by Paul; many confessing their sins burn their superstitious books: Demetrius the silversmith stirs up a grave riot against Paul, which Alexander finally manages to quiet with difficulty.*

1 And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having traveled through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples:

2 And he said to them: "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?" But they said to him: "We have not even heard if there is a Holy Spirit."

3 But he said: "In what then were you baptized?" They said: "In John’s baptism."

<margin>† Matthew 3:11. Mark 1:8. Luke 3:16. John 1:26. Above 1:5 & 11:16.</margin>
4 Paul said: † "John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus."

5 Upon hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

6 And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.

7 There were about twelve men in all.

8 And entering the synagogue, he spoke boldly for three months, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God.

9 But when some were hardened and did not believe, speaking evil of the way of the Lord before the multitude, he departed from them and separated the disciples, reasoning daily in the school of a certain Tyrannus.

10 This continued for two years, so that all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Gentiles.

11 And God performed extraordinary miracles by the hand of Paul:

12 So much so that handkerchiefs and aprons <note>original: "sudaria, & semicinctia," likely meaning sweat-cloths and work aprons used by Paul in his trade</note> were carried from his body to the sick, and the diseases left them, and the evil spirits went out from them.

13 Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists attempted to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying: "I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul preaches."

14 Now there were seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, who did this.

15 But the evil spirit answering said to them: "Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?"

16 And the man in whom the wicked demon was leaped upon them, and mastering both of them <note>though seven sons are mentioned, the text here uses "amborum" (both), a common textual variant</note>, he prevailed against them, so that they fled from that house naked and wounded.

# C H A P T E R XX.

> *Paul, having traveled through various parts of Macedonia and Greece, preaches in Troas until midnight: and when the young man Eutychus, falling from the third story, was dead, Paul raised him to life: and having traveled through various places, he exhorts the elders called from Ephesus to be vigilant in ruling the Church, foretelling that they would see him no more.*

1 And after the uproar was ceased, Paul called unto him the disciples, and embraced them, and departed for to go into Macedonia.

3 And there abode three months. And when the Jews laid wait for him, as he was about to sail into Syria, he purposed to return through Macedonia.
4 And there accompanied him Sopater of Pyrrhus the Berean; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus.

6 And we sailed away from Philippi after the <term>days of unleavened bread</term> <note>the Jewish festival of Passover</note>, and came unto them to Troas in five days; where we abode seven days.
7 And upon the <term>first day of the week</term> <note>original: "Una sabbati," Sunday</note>, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them, ready to depart on the morrow; and continued his speech until midnight.
8 And there were many lamps in the upper chamber, where they were gathered together.
9 And there sat in a window a certain young man named Eutychus, being fallen into a deep sleep: and as Paul was long preaching, he sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third story, and was taken up dead.
10 And Paul went down, and fell on him, and embracing him said: "Trouble not yourselves; for his life is in him."
11 When he therefore was come up again, and had broken bread, and eaten, and talked a long while, even till break of day, so he departed.
12 And they brought the young man alive, and were not a little comforted.
13 And we went before to ship, and sailed unto Assos, there intending to take in Paul: for so had he appointed, minding himself to go afoot.
14 And when he met with us at Assos, we took him in, and came to Mitylene.

16 For Paul had determined to sail by Ephesus, because he would not spend the time in Asia: for he hasted, if it were possible for him, to be at Jerusalem the day of <term>Pentecost</term> <note>a major Jewish festival fifty days after Passover</note>.
17 And from Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called the <term>elders of the church</term> <note>original: "majores natu," the presbyters or leaders</note>.

19 Serving the Lord with all humility of mind, and with many tears, and temptations, which befell me by the lying in wait of the Jews:
20 And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have showed you, and have taught you publicly, and from house to house,
21 Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks..."

### CHAPTER XXI.

*As Paul travels toward Jerusalem after various voyages, the prophet Agabus foretells the afflictions he was to suffer in Jerusalem; yet he cannot be turned aside by the tears of his friends from going up to Jerusalem, being ready even to undergo death for Christ. When he arrived in Jerusalem, James persuaded him to purify himself with five men who had taken a vow; while he was doing this, he was seized by the Jews, but was rescued from their hands by the tribune, by whom he was led into the barracks bound in chains; nevertheless, he obtained permission to speak to the people.*

1 And it came to pass that after we were torn away from them and had set sail, we came with a straight course to Cos, and the following day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
2 And finding a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail.

<column-break/>

3 Now when we had sighted Cyprus, leaving it on the left, we sailed into Syria and came to Tyre: for there the ship was to unload its cargo.
4 And having found disciples, we stayed there seven days: who told Paul through the Spirit that he should not go up to Jerusalem.
5 And when those days were over, we departed and went our way; and they all accompanied us, with their wives and children, until we were outside the city: and we kneeled down on the shore and prayed.
6 And when we had said farewell to one another, we went on board the ship; and they returned to their own homes.
7 But we, having finished the voyage from Tyre, came down to Ptolemais: and having greeted the brethren, we stayed with them for one day.

12 And when we heard these things, both we and those of that place pleaded with him not to go up to Jerusalem.

14 And when we could not persuade him, we ceased, saying: "The will of the Lord be done."

26 When the centurion heard this, he went to the <term>tribune</term> <note>original: "tribunum," the commander of the Roman cohort</note> and reported it to him, saying: "What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen."
27 Then the tribune came and said to him: "Tell me, are you a Roman?" And he said: "Yes."
28 And the tribune answered: "I obtained this citizenship for a great sum of money." And Paul said: "But I was even born a citizen."
29 Immediately, therefore, those who were about to torture him withdrew from him. The tribune also was afraid after he realized that he was a Roman citizen, and because he had bound him.
30 The next day, however, wishing to know more diligently for what cause he was being accused by the Jews, he released him and ordered the priests to assemble, along with the whole <term>council</term> <note>the Sanhedrin, the supreme legal and religious body of the Jews</note>; and bringing Paul down, he set him before them.

# CHAPTER XXIII.

*Paul, standing before the priests and the whole council, calls the high priest—who had ordered him to be struck in the face—a whitewashed wall, but excuses himself for not knowing he was the high priest. When he declared there that he was a Pharisee and was being judged concerning the resurrection of the dead, a great dissension arose between the Pharisees and Sadducees. The Lord comforts Paul at night, foretelling that he must also testify of Him in Rome. After a conspiracy by many to kill Paul is detected, the tribune sends him to Caesarea, guarded by soldiers, to Felix the governor, with a letter to him which is recorded here.*

**P**aul, looking intently at the council, said: "Men and brothers, I have lived my life before God with a perfectly good conscience until this very day."
2 But the high priest, Ananias, commanded those standing by him to strike him on the mouth.
3 Then Paul said to him: "God shall strike you, you **whitewashed wall** <note>a metaphor for a hypocrite: something that appears clean and white on the outside but is filled with decay or common clay within</note>. Do you sit to judge me according to the law, and yet command me to be struck contrary to the law?"
4 And those who stood by said: "Do you revile God’s high priest?"
<margin>† Exod. 22:28.</margin> 5 And Paul said: "I did not know, brothers, that he is the high priest. For it is written: *You shall not speak evil of the ruler of your people.*"
<margin>† Phil. 3:5.</margin> 6 But knowing that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, Paul cried out in the council: "Men and brothers, I am a Pharisee, the son of Pharisees; it is concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead that I am being judged!"
7 And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the multitude was divided.
<margin>† Matt. 22:23.</margin> 8 † For the Sadducees say there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit; but the Pharisees acknowledge both.
9 Then a great cry arose. And some of the Pharisees stood up and argued, saying: "We find no evil in this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?"
10 And when the dissension became great, the tribune, fearing that Paul might be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and snatch him from among them by force, and bring him into the barracks.
11 But the following night, the Lord stood by him and said: "Be constant; for as you have testified of me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome."

<column-break/>

12 When it was day, some of the Jews gathered together and bound themselves by an oath, saying they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
13 There were more than forty men who had made this conspiracy.
14 They went to the chief priests and the elders and said: "We have bound ourselves under a great curse to taste nothing until we kill Paul.
15 Now, therefore, you and the council notify the tribune to bring him down to you, as if you were going to determine something more certain about him. But we, before he comes near, are ready to kill him."
16 When Paul’s sister’s son heard of the ambush, he came and entered the barracks and told Paul.
17 Then Paul, calling one of the centurions to him, said: "Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him."
18 So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said: "The prisoner Paul asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you."
19 The tribune, taking him by the hand, stepped aside with him privately and asked him: "What is it that you have to tell me?"
20 And he said: "The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as if they were going to inquire something more certain about him.
21 But do not believe them; for more than forty men from among them are lying in wait for him, having bound themselves by an oath not to eat or drink until they kill him. And now they are ready, waiting for your promise."
22 The tribune then dismissed the young man, charging him: "Tell no one that you have made these things known to me."
23 And calling two centurions, he said to them: "Prepare two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, and seventy horsemen, and two hundred <term>spearmen</term> <note>original: "lancearios," light-armed troops carrying lances</note>, from the third hour of the night;
24 and provide mounts, so that they may set Paul on them and bring him safely to Felix the <term>governor</term> <note>original: "praesidem," referring to the Roman procurator</note>."
25 (For he feared that perhaps the Jews might seize him and kill him, and he might afterwards suffer slander, as if he were going to accept money.)
26 He wrote a letter containing these words:

->CLAUDIUS Lysias, to the most excellent governor, Felix, greetings.<-

27 This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them, when I came upon them with the army and rescued him, having learned that he is a Roman.
28 Wishing to know the cause for which they accused him, I brought him down to their council.
29 I found him to be accused concerning questions of their law, but having no crime worthy of death or of bonds.
30 And when it was reported to me of the ambush they had prepared for him, I sent him to you, notifying his accusers also to state their case before you. Farewell.
31 So the soldiers, according to their orders, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris.
32 And the next day, leaving the horsemen to go with him, they returned to the barracks.
33 When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul before him.

### CHAPTER XXIV.

*Paul is accused before Governor Felix by Tertullus, the orator for the Jews; he responds by denying the crimes attributed to him, yet confesses himself a Christian, stating he is being judged concerning the resurrection of the dead. Felix and his Jewish wife Drusilla hear Paul speak on the Christian faith; however, since Felix did not receive money from Paul, he left him bound for his successor, Porcius Festus.*

1 After five days, the high priest Ananias descended with certain elders and a certain orator named Tertullus, who approached the governor against Paul.
2 And when Paul was summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: “Since we enjoy great peace through you, and many things are corrected through your foresight,
3 we acknowledge this always and everywhere, most excellent Felix, with all gratitude.
4 But so as not to detain you longer, I beg you to briefly hear us according to your clemency.
5 We have found this man to be pestilent, a stirrer of seditions among all the Jews throughout the whole world, and a ringleader of the <term>sect of the Nazarenes</term> <note>original: "sectae Nazarenorum," an early, often dismissive term used for the followers of Jesus of Nazareth</note>.
6 He even attempted to violate the temple, and when we apprehended him, we wished to judge him according to our law.
7 But the tribune Lysias came upon us and with great violence took him out of our hands,
8 ordering his accusers to come to you. By examining him yourself, you will be able to learn about all these things of which we accuse him.”
9 And the Jews also joined in, saying that these things were so.
10 Paul then answered (after the Governor gestured for him to speak): “Knowing that you have been a judge over this nation for many years, I will defend my case with good courage.
11 For you can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship.
12 And they did not find me disputing with anyone in the temple, nor gathering a crowd in the synagogues,
13 nor in the city; neither can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me.
14 But I confess this to you: that according to the <term>Way</term> <note>original: "sectam," often translated here as "the Way," the early name for the Christian movement</note>, which they call a heresy, I so serve my God and Father, believing all things written in the Law and the Prophets;
15 having hope in God, which they themselves also look for, that there will be a future resurrection of the just and the unjust.
16 In this, I also strive to always have a conscience without offense toward God and toward men.
17 After many years, I came to bring alms to my nation, and offerings, and vows.
<margin>† Above 21:26</margin>
18 In the midst of these, they found me purified in the temple, not with a crowd nor with a riot.
19 But there were certain Jews from Asia, who ought 

<column-break/>

to have been present before you to accuse me, if they had anything against me.
20 Or let these men themselves say if they found any iniquity in me while I stood before the council,
<margin>† Above 23:6</margin>
21 unless it be for this one exclamation alone, which I cried out while standing among them: ‘Concerning the resurrection of the dead, I am being judged by you today!’”
22 But Felix, having very certain knowledge of this Way, delayed them, saying: “When the tribune Lysias comes down, I will hear you.”
23 And he ordered a centurion to guard him, and that he should have some rest, and not to prohibit any of his friends from ministering to him.
24 After some days, Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and called for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus.
25 But as he spoke of justice, and chastity, and the judgment to come, Felix was terrified and answered: “For now, go; when I have a convenient time, I will call for you.”
26 At the same time, he also hoped that money would be given to him by Paul, because of which he frequently called for him and spoke with him.
27 But when two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And wishing to show favor to the Jews, Felix left Paul bound.

### CHAPTER XXV.

*Festus does not comply with the Jews who treacherously requested that Paul be brought to Jerusalem; instead, he hears his accusers and Paul's response at Caesarea. When asked by Festus if he wished to be judged on these matters in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar. Festus explains Paul’s case to King Agrippa, who desires to hear him; on the following day, by Festus's order, Paul is brought before Agrippa and Bernice.*

1 Therefore, when Festus had come into the province, after three days he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea.
2 The high priests and the leading men of the Jews approached him against Paul and petitioned him,
3 asking for a favor against him: that he would order him to be brought to Jerusalem, while they laid an ambush to kill him on the way.
4 But Festus answered that Paul was being kept in Caesarea, and that he himself would be departing shortly.
5 “Therefore,” he said, “let those among you who are powerful go down with me, and if there is any crime in the man, let them accuse him.”
6 Having stayed among them no more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea, and the next day he sat on the <term>tribunal</term> <note>original: "tribunali," the official judicial seat of a Roman magistrate</note> and ordered Paul to be brought in.
7 When he was brought in, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges which they could not prove.
8 Paul offered his defense: “I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar.”
9 But Festus, wishing to show favor to the Jews, answered Paul and said: “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be judged there before me concerning these things?”
10 But Paul said: “I stand at Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be judged. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well.

### CHAPTER XXVI.

*Paul defends his cause before Agrippa: recounting the order of his conversion to Christ, and showing that he has preached to Jews and Gentiles under divine protection: he responds to Festus, who says he is mad from too much learning, and wishes that all might be Christians: Agrippa says he could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.*

1 Then Agrippa said to Paul: "You are permitted to speak for yourself." Then Paul, stretching out his hand, began to give his defense.

3 especially since you are expert in all the customs and questions which are among the Jews; for which reason I beg you to hear me patiently.
4 Indeed, all the Jews know my life from my youth, which was from the beginning among my own people in Jerusalem;
5 they knew me from the start (if they are willing to give testimony) that according to the strictest sect of our religion, I lived as a Pharisee.
6 And now I stand subject to judgment for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers,
7 to which our twelve tribes, serving God night and day, hope to attain. Concerning this hope, O King, I am accused by the Jews.
8 Why is it judged incredible among you if God raises the dead?
9 And I indeed once thought that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
<margin>Above 8:3.</margin>

<margin>Above 9:2.</margin>
12 In which circumstances, † while I was going to Damascus with the authority and permission of the chief priests,

It is hard for you to kick against the goad.' <note>A 'goad' was a spiked stick used to drive oxen; the metaphor implies resisting a divine nudge only causes more pain to oneself.</note>

17 delivering you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I now send you,
18 to open their eyes, that they may be converted from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among the saints, through the faith that is in me.'

### CHAPTER XXVII.

*Paul is led toward Rome by the centurion Julius, sailing through various places: however, with the wind opposing them, they barely reach a certain place in Crete; although Paul predicted the voyage would be dangerous, they depart and suffer a great storm: finally, after Paul's consolation—who, recounting a revelation made to him regarding the safety of all, encouraged them to take food—having suffered shipwreck, they all escape unharmed.*

1 And when it was decided that he should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and the other prisoners to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan cohort.
<margin>† 2 Corinthians 11:25</margin>
2 † Boarding a ship of Adramyttium <note>Adramyttium was an ancient port in Mysia, modern-day Turkey.</note>, intending to sail along the coasts of Asia, we set out, with Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, remaining with us.
3 And the following day we arrived at Sidon. And Julius, treating Paul humanely, permitted him to go to his friends and care for himself.
4 And when we had set out from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary.
5 And sailing over the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Lystra <note>Most manuscripts read "Myra" here, a port in Lycia; the transcription "Lystra" is a known variant or error in some Latin editions.</note>, which is in Lycia.
6 And there the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy, and he put us on board.
7 And when we had sailed slowly for many days, and had barely reached Cnidus, the wind preventing us, we sailed under the lee of Crete, near Salmone.
8 And barely sailing past it, we came to a certain place called Fair Havens <note>original: "Boniportus"</note>, near which was the city of Thalassa.
9 Now when much time had passed, and when sailing was no longer safe because the Fast <note>This refers to the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), indicating it was late autumn when Mediterranean navigation became dangerous.</note> had already passed, Paul comforted them,
10 Saying to them: Men, I see that the voyage begins to be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our souls.
11 But the centurion believed the pilot and the captain more than those things which were spoken by Paul.
12 And since the harbor was not suitable for win-

<column-break/>

tering, the majority reached the decision to sail from there, if by any means they could reach Phoenix to winter, a harbor of Crete facing toward the southwest and the northwest.
13 And when the south wind blew gently, thinking they could hold their purpose, they set sail from Assos and skirted Crete.
14 But not long after, a tempestuous wind, which is called the Euroaquilo <term>Euroaquilo</term> <note>A violent "northeaster" storm wind common in the Mediterranean.</note>, struck against her.
15 And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, giving the ship up to the gusts, we were driven along.
16 And running under the lee of a certain island called Cauda, we were barely able to secure the lifeboat.
17 Which, when they had taken it up, they used supports to undergird the ship; and fearing lest they should fall into the Syrtis <note>The Syrtis Sands were notorious quicksands off the coast of North Africa.</note>, they lowered the gear and so were driven.
18 And we being violently tossed by the storm, the next day they threw the cargo overboard.

26 However, we must reach a certain island.
27 But after the fourteenth night had come, as we were sailing in the Adriatic Sea, about midnight, the sailors suspected that some land was appearing to them.
28 And dropping the sounding lead <term>bolidem</term> <note>original: "bolidem," a weighted line used to measure water depth.</note>, they found twenty fathoms; and separated a little further from there, they found fifteen fathoms.
29 Then fearing lest we should fall into rocky places, they cast four anchors from the stern and prayed for daybreak.

31 Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers: Unless these remain in the ship, you cannot be saved.
32 Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the lifeboat and let it fall away.
33 And when the light began to appear, Paul urged them all to take food, saying: Today is the fourteenth day that you have waited and continued fasting, taking nothing.
34 Therefore I urge you to take food for your health: for not a hair of the head of any of you shall perish.
35 And when he had said these things, taking bread, he gave thanks to God in the sight of all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat.

### C H A P T E R XXVIII.

*Paul and his companions are kindly received by the natives on the island of Malta, where Paul, bitten by a viper, suffers no harm; he restores the father of Publius, the chief of the island, to health, and heals many others. From that place, they sail and finally arrive at Rome. There, Paul calls together the leaders of the Jews and explains why he appealed to Caesar. On an appointed day, he preaches about Christ; many do not believe his words, which Paul shows was predicted by Isaiah. For two years, he preaches the faith in Christ to all who come to him.*

1 And when we had escaped, we then learned that the island was called Malta <note>original: "Melita"</note>. But the natives <note>original: "Barbari"; used here to mean non-Greek speakers, not necessarily "uncivilized"</note> showed us no small kindness.
2 For having kindled a fire, they refreshed us all because of the rain that was falling and the cold.
3 But when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened onto his hand.
4 When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another: "Surely this man is a murderer, who, though he has escaped from the sea, Vengeance <note>original: "ultio"; likely referring to the personified goddess of Justice/Retribution, Dike</note> does not allow him to live."
5 But he shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm.
6 They, however, expected that he would swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But after they had waited a long time and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god.
7 In that neighborhood were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and for three days kindly provided for us.
8 It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fevers and dysentery. Paul went in to him, and when he had prayed and laid his hands on him, he healed him.

<column-break/>

9 When this was done, all the others on the island who had diseases came and were cured.
10 They also honored us with many honors, and when we sailed, they provided us with the things we needed.
11 After three months, we set sail in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered at the island, which had the "Twin Brothers" <note>original: "Castorum"; referring to Castor and Pollux, the Gemini, patrons of sailors</note> as its figurehead.
12 And when we arrived at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days.
13 From there, sailing around, we reached Rhegium; and after one day, a south wind blowing, we came on the second day to Puteoli.
14 Where, having found brothers, we were invited to stay with them for seven days; and so we came to Rome.
15 And from there, when the brothers heard of us, they came to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he gave thanks to God and took courage.
16 And when we had come to Rome, Paul was permitted to stay by himself with a soldier to guard him.
17 After three days, he called together the leaders of the Jews. And when they had assembled, he said to them: "I, brothers, though I have done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans.
18 Who, when they had examined me, would have let me go, because there was no cause for death in me.
19 But when the Jews spoke against it, I was forced to appeal to Caesar—not that I had any accusation to bring against my nation.
20 For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you. For it is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain."
21 But they said to him: "We have received no letters about you from Judea, nor has any of the brothers who arrived reported or spoken any evil of you.
22 But we desire to hear from you what you think; for concerning this sect, it is known to us that it is spoken against everywhere."
23 And when they had appointed a day for him, many came to him at his lodging, to whom he explained, testifying to the kingdom of God, and persuading them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets, from morning until evening.
24 And some believed the things that were said, but some did not believe.
25 And since they did not agree among themselves, they departed after Paul had spoken one word: "Well did the Holy Spirit speak through the prophet Isaiah to our fathers,
<margin>† Isaiah 6:9; Matthew 13:14; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10; John 12:40; Romans 11:8.</margin>
26 Saying: † Go to this people and say to them: You shall indeed hear with your ears and not understand; and seeing you shall see and not perceive.
27 For the heart of this people has grown dull, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have closed their eyes; lest perhaps they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.
28 Therefore, let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen."
29 And when he had said these things, the Jews went out from him, having much dispute among themselves.
30 And he remained for two whole years in his own rented lodging; and he received all who came to him,
31 Preaching the kingdom of God and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all confidence, without hindrance.

<meta>This page transitions from the narrative of the Acts of the Apostles, where Paul finally reaches Rome as a prisoner, to the beginning of his theological masterpiece, the Epistle to the Romans. It marks the shift from Paul’s travels to his formal doctrinal teaching.</meta>

# THE EPISTLE
# OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL
# TO THE ROMANS.

### CHAPTER ONE.

*Paul commends his Evangelical office, and because of his great zeal for preaching the Gospel, he desired to visit the Romans; showing that the Gentiles <note>original: "Ethnicos"; referring to non-Jewish nations</note> who, though knowing God from his creations, had cast away his worship, honoring instead the images of created things, were deservedly abandoned by God: and as a punishment for this, they fell into the abominable crimes which are listed here.*

<margin>$\dagger$ Acts 13:2</margin>
1 Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an Apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God,
2 Which he had promised beforehand through his Prophets in the holy Scriptures
3 Concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh,
4 Who was predestined the Son of God in power, according to the spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead:
5 Through whom we have received grace and Apostleship for the obedience of faith among all nations for the sake of his name,
6 Among whom you also are the called of Jesus Christ:
7 To all who are at Rome, the beloved of God, called to be saints. Grace to you and peace from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ.
8 First, I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you: because your faith is spoken of in the whole world.
9 For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his son, that without ceasing I make mention of you
10 Always in my prayers: beseeching that by some means, at last, I may have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come to you.
11 For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual grace to strengthen you:
12 That is, that I may be comforted together with you, through that faith which is common to both you and me.
13 Now I would not have you ignorant, brethren: that I have often purposed to come to you (but have been hindered until now) that I might have some fruit among you also, even as among the rest of the Gentiles.
14 To the Greeks and to the Barbarians, to the wise and to the unwise, I am a debtor:
15 So (as much as is in me) I am ready to preach the Gospel also to you who are at Rome.
16 For I am not ashamed of the Gospel. For it is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes, to the Jew first, and to the Greek.
<margin>$\dagger$ Habakkuk 2:4; Galatians 3:11; Hebrews 10:38</margin>
17 For the justice <note>original: "Justitia"; often translated as "righteousness" in modern English Bibles</note> of God is revealed in it from faith to faith: as it is written: $\dagger$ *The just man lives by faith.*
18 For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of those men who hold back the truth of God in injustice:

<column-break/>

19 Because that which is known of God is manifest in them. For God has manifested it to them.
20 For his invisible attributes, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made: his eternal power also, and divinity: so that they are without excuse.
<margin>$\dagger$ Ephesians 4:17</margin>
21 $\dagger$ Because when they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, nor gave thanks: but they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened:
22 For professing themselves to be wise, they became fools.
23 And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of a corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of serpents.
24 Wherefore God gave them up to the desires of their heart, unto uncleanness: to dishonor their own bodies among themselves:
25 Who exchanged the truth of God for a lie: and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.
26 For this cause God delivered them up to shameful passions. For their women changed the natural use into that use which is against nature.
27 And likewise the men also, leaving the natural use of the women, burned in their lusts one toward another, men with men working that which is filthy, and receiving in themselves the recompense of their error which was fitting.
28 And as they did not like to have God in their knowledge: God delivered them up to a reprobate sense, to do those things which are not convenient <note>original: "non conveniunt"; things that are not proper or fitting for human conduct</note>,
29 Being filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication, avarice, wickedness, full of envy, murder, contention, deceit, malignity, whisperers,
30 Detractors, hateful to God, contumelious, proud, haughty, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents,
31 Foolish, dissolute, without affection, without covenant, without mercy.
32 Who, having known the justice of God, did not understand that they who do such things are worthy of death: and not only they that do them, but also they that consent to them that do them.

### CHAPTER II.

*He rebukes the Jews who, by the law given to them, condemned the Gentiles while they themselves committed the same things, since God will render to every man according to his works: so much so that even the Gentiles, who perform the requirements of the law by their natural light, are to be considered as circumcised, and shall judge those who glory only in the knowledge of the law and circumcision of the flesh, while acting contrary to the law.*

<margin>$\dagger$ Matthew 7:2</margin>
1 Therefore you are inexcusable, O man, whoever you are that judges. $\dagger$ For in that which you
<meta>catchword: judge</meta>

It concludes with a stern warning against hypocrisy, addressing those who judge others while committing the same offenses.</summary>

This page shifts the focus to those who consider themselves morally superior—specifically addressing the Jewish community and those who hold the Law of Moses—arguing that mere possession of the Law does not exempt one from God's judgment if one does not follow it.</meta>

...you judge another, you condemn yourself: for you do the same things that you judge.

2 For we know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things.

3 But do you think, O man, you who judge those who do such things and yet do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God?

4 Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, and patience, and long-suffering? Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?

5 But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you treasure up for yourself wrath on the day of wrath, and the revelation of the just judgment of God,

<margin>† Matthew 16:27</margin>
6 † Who will render to every man according to his works:

7 To those indeed, who by patience in good work, seek glory, and honor, and incorruption, eternal life:

8 But to those who are contentious, and who do not obey the truth, but believe iniquity, there is wrath and indignation.

9 Tribulation and anguish upon every soul of man that works evil, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek:

10 But glory, and honor, and peace to everyone who works good, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek:

<margin>
† Deuteronomy 10:17; 2 Chronicles 19:7; Job 34:19; Wisdom 6:8; Ecclesiasticus 35:15; Acts 10:34; Galatians 2:6; Colossians 3:25; † Matthew 7:21; James 1:22.
</margin>
11 † For there is no respect of persons <note>original: "acceptio personarum"; meaning God does not show favoritism based on status or nationality</note> with God.

12 For whoever have sinned without the law, will perish without the law; and whoever have sinned in the law, will be judged by the law.

13 † For it is not the hearers of the law who are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified.

14 For when the Gentiles <note>The "nations" or non-Jews who did not receive the Mosaic Law on Mount Sinai.</note>, who do not have the law, do by nature the things that are of the law, such as these, not having the law, are a law unto themselves:

15 Who show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts accusing or even defending one another,

16 On the day when God shall judge the secrets of men, according to my Gospel, through Jesus Christ.

17 But if you are called a Jew, and rest in the law, and glory in God,

18 And know his will, and approve the more useful things, being instructed by the law,

19 You are confident that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light of those who are in darkness,

20 An instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, having the form of knowledge and of truth in the law.

21 You, therefore, who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach that one should not steal, do you steal?

22 You who say one should not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who loathe idols, do you commit sacrilege?

23 You who glory in the law, do you dishonor God through the transgression of the law?

<margin>† Isaiah 52:5; Ezekiel 36:20.</margin>
24 († For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you, as it is written.)

25 Circumcision indeed profits if you observe the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision <note>original: "praeputium"; literally 'foreskin'. Paul is saying the physical sign of the covenant is voided by disobedience.</note>.

26 If, therefore, the uncircumcised keep the justices of the law, shall not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision?

27 And shall not that which is by nature uncircumcision, if it fulfills the law, judge you, who by the letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law?

28 For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly; nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh:

29 But he is a Jew who is one inwardly; and the circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; whose praise is not from men, but from God.

### CHAPTER III.

*In some way the Jews excel because of the promises made to them by God, which will be fulfilled, although some of them were unbelieving: but all, both Jews and Gentiles, are subject to sin: from which the law does not deliver, but faith in Christ the Reconciler <note>original: "propitiatorem"; one who makes amends or restores a relationship</note>, so that no one should glory in the works of the law.*

1 WHAT, then, is the advantage of the Jew? Or what is the profit of circumcision?

2 Much in every way. First indeed, because the words of God were entrusted to them.

<margin>† 2 Timothy 2:13; † John 3:33; † Psalm 115:11.</margin>
3 For what if some of them did not believe? † Shall their unbelief make the faith of God of no effect? Far from it.

<margin>† Psalm 50:6.</margin>
4 † But God is true: † and every man a liar, as it is written: † That you may be justified in your words: and may overcome when you are judged.

5 But if our iniquity commends the justice of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath?

6 (I speak according to man.) Far from it: otherwise how shall God judge this world?

7 For if the truth of God has abounded through my lie unto his glory, why am I also still judged as a sinner?

8 And not (as we are blasphemed, and as some say that we say) let us do evil that good may come: whose damnation is just.

9 What then? Do we excel them? Not at all. For we have charged that both Jews and Greeks are all under sin,

<margin>† Galatians 3:22; † Psalm 13:3.</margin>
10 As it is written: † Because there is not any man just:

11 There is none that understands, there is none that seeks after God.

12 All have turned aside, they have become useless together; there is none that does good, no, not even one.

<margin>† Psalm 5:11; † Psalm 139:4; † Psalm 9:7; † Isaiah 59:7; Proverbs 1:16; † Psalm 35:2; † Galatians 2:16.</margin>
13 † Their throat is an open sepulcher, with their tongues they acted deceitfully: † The poison of asps is under their lips:

14 † Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness:

15 † Their feet are swift to shed blood:

16 Destruction and misery are in their ways:

17 And the way of peace they have not known:

18 † There is no fear of God before their eyes.

19 † Now we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are in the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become subject to God:

20 Because by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified before him. For through the law comes the knowledge of sin.

21 But now without the law the justice of God is manifested; being witnessed by the law and the Prophets.

22 And the justice of God through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe in him: for there is no distinction:

23 For all have sinned, and do need the glory of God.

24 Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus,

25 Whom God has proposed as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to the showing of his justice...

...of his righteousness, for the remission of past sins.
26 Through the forbearance of God, for the demonstration of his justice in this time: that he himself might be just, and the justifier of him who is of the faith of Jesus Christ.
27 Where then is your boasting? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No: but by the law of faith.

# CHAPTER IV.

*Justification does not occur through the works of the law, but from faith in God, by which it was credited to Abraham as righteousness before circumcision was given to him, which he received afterward; he was to be the father of all who would imitate his faith, not by the law but by the righteousness of faith: moreover, he believed God that he would be the father of many nations through the offspring promised to him, even though both he and his wife Sarah had passed the age suitable for bearing children.*

1 What shall we say then that Abraham our father according to the flesh has found?
2 For if Abraham was justified by works, he has reason to boast, but not before God.
<margin>† Genesis 15:6; Galatians 3:6.</margin>
3 For what does the Scripture say? † Abraham believed God: and it was credited to him as righteousness.
<margin>James 2:23.</margin>
4 Now to him who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace, but according to debt.
5 But to him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness according to the purpose of the grace of God.
6 Just as David also describes the blessedness of the man to whom God credits righteousness without works:
<margin>† Psalm 31:2.</margin>
7 † Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered.
8 Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin.
9 Does this blessedness then remain only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was credited to Abraham as righteousness.
10 How then was it credited? When he was circumcised, or uncircumcised? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.
<margin>† Genesis 17:10, 11.</margin>
11 † And he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of faith which he had while uncircumcised: that he might be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, so that it might be credited to them also as righteousness:
12 And the father of circumcision, not only to those who are of the circumcision, but also to those who follow the footsteps of that faith which our father Abraham had while uncircumcised.
13 For the promise to Abraham, or to his seed, that he should be heir of the world, was not through the law: but through the righteousness of faith.
14 For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void, and the promise is abolished.
15 For the law works wrath. For where there is no law, there is no transgression.
16 Therefore it is of faith, so that according to grace the promise

<column-break/>

might be firm for all the seed, not only to those who are of the law, but also to those who are of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,
<margin>† Genesis 17:4.</margin>
17 (As it is written: † I have made you a father of many nations) before God, in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead, and calls those things which are not as though they were.
18 Who against hope believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations, according to what was said to him: † So shall your seed be. <margin>† Genesis 15:5.</margin>
19 And being not weak in faith, he did not consider his own body now dead, since he was almost a hundred years old, nor the deadness of Sarah's womb:
20 He did not waver at the promise of God through distrust, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God:
21 Being fully aware that whatever he promised, he is able also to perform.
22 And therefore it was credited to him as righteousness.
23 Now it was not written for his sake alone, that it was credited to him as righteousness:
24 But also for us, to whom it shall be credited, if we believe in him who raised up Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead;
25 Who was delivered up for our sins, and rose again for our justification.

# CHAPTER V.

*Having been justified by faith, he says, we boast not only in hope, but even in adversities: for if Christ died for us while we were still ungodly, much more will he save those already justified by his blood: and just as through the one disobedience of Adam we all sinned and died; so through the obedience of the one Christ, we are justified unto life from many offenses.*

1 Therefore, being justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
<margin>† Ephesians 2:18.</margin>
2 † By whom also we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and boast in the hope of the glory of the sons of God.
<margin>† James 1:3.</margin>
3 And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: † knowing that tribulation works patience:
4 And patience, trial <note>original: "probationem"; here meaning character proven by testing</note>; and trial, hope:
5 And hope does not disappoint: because the charity of God is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, who is given to us.
<margin>† Hebrews 9:14; 1 Peter 3:18.</margin>
6 For why did Christ, when we were yet weak, according to the time, † die for the ungodly?
7 For scarcely for a just man will one die: yet perhaps for a good man someone would dare to die.
8 But God commends his charity toward us: because while we were yet sinners, according to the time,
9 Christ died for us: much more then, being now justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him.
10 For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son: much more, being reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.
11 And not only so: but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom we have now received reconciliation.
12 Wherefore as by one man sin entered into this world, and by sin death; and so death passed upon all men, in whom all have sinned.

<summary>This passage details the Pauline doctrine of justification by faith, using Abraham's belief in God's promise as the foundational example that predates the Law. It concludes by explaining how Christ's sacrificial death reconciles humanity to God, reversing the legacy of sin and death introduced by Adam.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, specifically focusing on the theological bridge between the universal reign of death through Adam and the reign of life through Jesus Christ. It transitions into the practical implications of baptism and the believer's relationship to the Law.</meta>

-># EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL<-

13 For until the law, sin was in the world: but sin was not imputed, when the law was not.
14 But death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin after the likeness of the transgression of Adam, who is a figure of him who was to come. <note>Adam is presented here as a "type" or "pattern" of Christ—where one brought death, the other brings life.</note>
15 But the gift is not as the offense: for if by the offense of one many died: much more has the grace of God, and the gift in the grace of one man, Jesus Christ, abounded unto many.
16 And the gift is not as it was by one sin: for the judgment indeed was from one unto condemnation: but grace is from many offenses unto justification.
17 For if by one man’s offense death reigned through one: much more those who receive abundance of grace, and of the donation, and of justice, shall reign in life through one, Jesus Christ.
18 Therefore, as by the offense of one, judgment came upon all men to condemnation: so also by the justice of one, the gift comes upon all men to justification of life.
19 For as by the disobedience of one man, many were made sinners: so also by the obedience of one, many shall be made just.
20 But the law entered in that the offense might abound. But where the offense abounded, grace did superabound.
21 That as sin has reigned unto death, so also may grace reign through justice unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

### C H A P T E R VI.

*We are baptized in Christ, so that having died to sin we might henceforth walk in newness of life: just as Christ, having died and been buried once, rose again to a new life, to die no more: therefore let us no longer obey sin or its desires, but being released from the law, and freed through the grace of Christ from sin, and having been made servants of justice, let us surrender our members in service to justice, unto life, whereas before we had surrendered them to impurity unto death.*

1 What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
2 God forbid. For we who are dead to sin, how shall we still live in it?
3 Do you not know that all we who are baptized in Christ Jesus, are baptized in his death?
<margin>† Galatians 3:27. Colossians 2:12.</margin>
4 † For we are buried together with him by baptism into death; that as Christ is risen from the dead by the glory of the Father, † so we also may walk in newness of life.
<margin>† Ephesians 4:23.</margin>
5 For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection.
<margin>Hebrews 12:1. 1 Peter 2:1. & 4:2.</margin>
6 Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin may be destroyed, and that we may serve sin no longer.
7 For he who is dead is justified from sin.
8 But if we be dead with CHRIST: we believe that we shall live also together with Christ:
9 Knowing that Christ, rising again from the dead, dies now no more, death shall no more have dominion over him.
10 For in that he died to sin, he died once: but in that he lives, he lives to God.

<column-break/>

11 So you also reckon yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God, in Christ Jesus our Lord.
12 Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, so as to obey the lusts thereof.
13 Neither yield your members as instruments of iniquity unto sin: but yield yourselves to God, as those who are alive from the dead: and your members as instruments of justice to God.
14 For sin shall not have dominion over you: for you are not under the law, but under grace.
15 What then? Shall we sin, because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid.
<margin>† John 8:34. 2 Peter 2:19.</margin>
16 † Do you not know, that to whom you yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants you are whom you obey, whether it be of sin unto death, or of obedience unto justice?
17 But thanks be to God, that you were the servants of sin, but have obeyed from the heart unto that form of doctrine, into which you have been delivered.
18 Being then freed from sin, you have been made servants of justice.
19 I speak a human thing <note>original: "Humanum dico" — Paul acknowledges he is using a human analogy (slavery) to explain a spiritual reality due to the limitations of his audience.</note>, because of the infirmity of your flesh: for as you have yielded your members to serve uncleanness, and iniquity unto iniquity: so now yield your members to serve justice unto sanctification.
20 For when you were the servants of sin, you were free from justice.
21 What fruit therefore had you then in those things, of which you are now ashamed? For the end of them is death.
22 But now being freed from sin, and become servants to God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end eternal life.
23 For the wages of sin is death. But the grace of God is eternal life, in Christ Jesus our Lord.

### C H A P T E R VII.

*In the likeness of a woman whose husband is deceased, we are released through Christ from the law by which the impulses of sins were made more vehement, so that we may serve Christ in newness of spirit: but by the occasion of the law judging sin, sin exerted itself more and grew, although the law was holy and spiritual: indeed, even now, with the kindling of the flesh opposing us, we are enticed—however much we resist—to those things which according to reason we detest, and which are contrary to the law.*

1 Do you not know, brethren (for I speak to those who know the law) that the law has dominion over a man as long as he lives?
<margin>† 1 Corinthians 7:39.</margin>
2 † For the woman who is under a husband, while her husband lives, is bound to the law: but if her husband be dead, she is loosed from the law of her husband.
3 Therefore, while her husband lives, she shall be called an adulteress, if she be with another man: but if her husband be dead, she is delivered from the law of her husband: so that she is not an adulteress, if she be with another man.
4 Therefore, my brethren, you also are become dead to the law by the body of Christ; that you may belong to another, who is risen again from the dead, that we may bring forth fruit to God.
5 For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which were by the law, did work in our members, to bring forth fruit unto death.
6 But now we are loosed from the law of death, in which we were held, so that we should serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter.
7 What shall we say then? Is the law sin?
